It's like a Michael Mann movie without any sauce. I think the main issue is while Mann's movies show such reverence and interest in its characters, Nolan could care less about fleshing his characters out beyond the first dimension so he can fit in more explosions and car chases. But don't worry, characters say Reddit philosophy quotes every other sentence so this movie is actually really deep and thought-provoking. Back to the characters, I find this to be the movie's biggest shortcoming. While Heath Ledger gives a fantastic performance as the Joker, the script he's working with offers him little help. Nolan's depiction of the Joker is so bland - he's an agent of chaos who does crime because he finds it fun. That's it. We never learn a thing about the Joker outside of his relationship to Batman. And that type of character can work. Anton Chigurh is a fantastic villain who fits a similar archetype to the Joker. But Chigurh works because we see the impact he has on the other characters in No Country for Old Men - how his nihilistic lack of motivation chills Ed to his core and makes him question everything he's been led to believe. But Batman/Bruce Wayne has no real character arc in this movie. In the first act his a bland superhero who beats up the bad guys, and in the third act he's still a bland superhero who beats up the bad guys. He learns nothing. He never grows. He never reflects on what the Joker represents, just chases him over and over until he finally catches him with the help of his cool gadgets. So what's the moral here? Batman just needed more gadgets to beat the Joker? The other characters in this film are of little interest either. Harvey Dent is a white knight ruthless prosecutor who chases down the bad guys and beats them up. Then he gets blown up and his world gets turned upside down because he chases down the people who wronged him and shoots them. I feel like this could be an interesting commentary on the criminal justice system being the other side of the coin of criminality itself, but the film is so afraid of depicting law enforcement with a shred of scrutiny that it plays it all completely straight. Harvey Dent is not a depiction of the corruption inherent in law enforcement, he's an awesome, flawless hero to all who is tragically brought down by the Joker. Because corruption isn't inherent in the system, rather it's propagated by a few bad apples like the Joker and his goons. How can I say this all so definitively? Because the movie tells us it definitively. It leaves nothing up to interpretation and tells us exactly what we should take away from each scene. "You either die a hero or live long enough to become the villain," "Some men just want to watch the world burn," etc. When characters aren't directly talking about what's happening in the scene or beating each other up, they're telling the audience what they should take away from the scene. Nolan's writing is so unsubtle I'm surprised he doesn't have Joker hold up a sign that says "I'm the bad guy." I genuinely have no idea why this film is so beloved. Maybe because it was such a shock in 2008 to see a superhero movie that's actually dark. But if you ignore the superhero dressing and analyze this film for what it is - a crime film - it just doesn't do anything to stand out among the plethora of far better crime films that have come before and since.

Looking back on this almost 20 years later and my biggest takeaway is how insecure this movie is. Dark Knight is CONSTANTLY SCREAMING its themes at you in the most dramatic, self indulgent way possible. You’ll have the Joker literally look at the screen and state “I’m an agent of chaos” while Gordon and Batman wax poetically on whether people are naturally good or evil. Worst of all, the movie will go out of its way to tell the viewer that some people are simply irredeemable and need to be put down. Contrast that to how the Spider-Man movies will try to tackle the heavy subject of villain redemption. Sure the execution is childish but at least it tries!   I came away with the theory that Nolan thought that superhero movies were not good enough to stand on their own so he had to water this down into the most grounded, serious, “adult” version of the Batman possible. The problem isn’t that The Dark Knight has nothing to say. It’s that it has so much confidence in how profound those things are that it rarely bothers to dramatize them. The movie is a long, slow, plodding mess that does not get the buy in necessary to take it self so seriously. Two hours and thirty minutes and no one gets developed. Gordon is always right and never pushed to grow, Harvey’s turn felt superficial and rudimentary, Rachel was literally in the movie to die. Worst of all, the Joker. We get so much time to develop and build on them relationship between him and Batman; how they’re mirrors of each other, how their philosophies are contradictory, how they mess with each other’s head. Instead we get Joker stating funny quips and theorize on le society. And I’m sorry but this movie and this performance is no where near good enough to justify the worship the Joker and this movie at large gets.

Para mí, The Dark Knight es la mejor película de la trilogía. Lo que más me gustó fue la forma en que se desarrolla el personaje de The Joker y cómo se opone ante Batman para intentar destruir Gotham. La historia es más compleja y madura que la de la primera película, y se nota que Nolan elevó el nivel en todos los aspectos. La actuación de Heath Ledger como Joker me pareció excelente. Consigue transmitir perfectamente la locura y el caos del personaje, convirtiéndolo en uno de los villanos más memorables del cine. Aunque hay momentos en los que la película puede sentirse un poco lenta o pesada, especialmente por su duración, sigue siendo una experiencia que vale la pena. Al terminarla me dejó una muy buena sensación y entendí por qué tanta gente la considera una de las mejores películas de superhéroes de todos los tiempos. Algo que hace especial a esta película es la forma en que Christopher Nolan utilizó cámaras IMAX para muchas de las escenas más importantes. Esto permitió mostrar Gotham, las persecuciones y las secuencias de acción con una escala impresionante que todavía hoy se siente espectacular. Además, Nolan intentó evitar el uso excesivo de CGI, prefiriendo efectos prácticos siempre que fuera posible. Gracias a esto, muchas escenas conservan una sensación de realismo que las hace envejecer mejor que otras películas de superhéroes de la misma época. Esa combinación entre IMAX, efectos prácticos y una dirección muy cuidada es una de las razones por las que la trilogía sigue siendo tan recordada.

This is everyone’s favorite adaptation of Batman? Are we watching the same movie? In celebration of the Lego Batman’s dlc release tomorrow I decided that this movie needed a rewatch. First, Heath Ledger is phenomenal. Outside of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash , Heath Ledger is probably my favorite performance ever. Bale has never completely convinced me as either Bruce Wayne or Batman. And the voice sucks!!!! Pattinson’s Bruce feels like someone consumed by being Batman while Bale’s Bruce often feels like he is simply operating within Nolan’s crime story. I heavily prefer Reeves’ dark and gothic Gotham to Nolan’s much brighter Chicago setting city. There are times when TDK feels less like a Batman movie and more like an extremely well-made crime thriller that happens to have Batman in it. How can I even call this a Batman movie when Joker commands most of the screen time? Batman feels strangely disconnected from being the “world’s greatest detective”. The fingerprint reconstruction scene is supposed to demonstrate his detective abilities, but it mostly amounts to technology doing the detective work for him rather than Batman being this great detective with supreme intelligence. The same goes for his equipment. Reeves makes Bruce’s obsessive commitment to building and modifying his own gear part of his characterization whereas Nolan’s Batman has Lucius Fox seemingly hand him whatever the plot requires. And what exactly is this sorry ass excuse for this brightly lit Batcave? Some of the movie’s logic also loses me. The entire Hong Kong sequence feels excessive and out of place. Batman supposedly doesn’t kill despite blowing things up everywhere he goes. Rachel falls off a skyscraper and walks away seemingly unharmed. More importantly, the Joker’s plans work with almost supernatural precision. Every person seems to react exactly as he anticipates, every piece falls into place, and almost nothing meaningfully disrupts his schemes. Ledger is so magnetic that he makes you want to overlook it but it’s hard. I also understand the thematic purpose of the Joker having no conventional motive. He represents chaos and wants to prove that civilized people can be pushed into abandoning their morals. But committing chaos for the sake of it has never been as interesting to me as it apparently is to everyone else. The character motivation feels deliberately vague in a way that doesn’t completely work for me. Still, I don’t want my complaints to make it sound like I think this is a bad movie. Far from it. Nolan knows how to construct a great movie, and there are some incredible sequences here. The truck flip and the hospital blowing up remain ridiculously cool. I also wonder how much of the Batman debate is generational. A lot of millennials grew up with Bale as the Batman, while Gen Z got Pattinson at a formative age. Maybe I’m simply more drawn to what Reeves thinks Batman should be: this lonely gothic loser detective boy that’s inseparable from Gotham itself. I just think Reeves’ The Batman runs laps around this iteration of Batman. The Dark Knight is a good movie but I’m just not convinced it’s my version of a great Batman movie. B+ish

This time was different. First of all, the Joker. What a f*cking villain!!! How he manipulates everyone in the movie, even Harvey, the Gotham's "White Knight", who was the hope to stop organized crime and became Batman existence needless. The Joker always was two or three steps ahead. And Heath Ledger ... I know Joaquín Phoenix was deeply inspired by Jared Leto when he played Joker in the "Joker" movie, from 2019. Batman was fine, Fox was the best, and Harvey more of the same. I liked how Harvey's character was always the only hope to make Gotham a city criminal free. And how Joker  knew that, and started to miscontrue and manipulate all the tale to screw it up. Also, the Batman rule of "no kill" bringing it to the limit, and in the finale, with the Ferris, to demostrate that people is bad and how they will kill others for their own survival. But, like Batman said, people was still good hearted and empathic, and didn't blow everyones up. On the other hand, back in the days I didn't like much the fights, and today I kinda think the same, but this time I was able to better appreciate what was happening in each scene. The scene when Alfred burns Rachel's letter.... Nolan, what a fucker you are... In real life I think it's a bad choice, because Rachel's final wish to Bruce, was let him know that other man has reached her heart. And surely that would have helped Bruce get over his loss faster. But that resonates with the ending of Nolan's film, as it mirrors the moment when Gordon and Batman decide to cover up Harvey's final crimes as "Two-Faces" in order to keep hope alive in people's hearts and portray him as a hero who didn't live to see a new day. It all sounds very poetic, but it echoes what Harvey himself said at the beginning—and Batman at the end: "You either die a hero, or you live long enough to become a villain." This sentece, apart of being so realistic, is incredible and one of the best senteces in cinema. But, as a final message, I didn't like that sometimes you have to lie to keep people happy. I think telling the truth is always better, and more than nothing: Is true. Although, thinking about it now, maybe the director was trying to tell us that that was going to happen to him from then on. I don't know, but it was weird. To sum up finally, this shit was good . 9/10. "Porque no es un héroe. Es un Caballero Oscuro" 🦇🚬🍿

It’s really interesting how for a movie all marketed and focusing around the Joker and the pandaemonium he causes, how the central ideas all revolve around duality. At it’s core it’s all about honing in on characters wants vs their needs. Selfish desires vs responsibilities. Batman desperately wants Rachel, to settle down and have a happy life. But is obviously responsible to keeping up his mantle as Batman. By letting Harvey be Gothams white night Batman in his hopes and dreams is no longer needed. But unlike Bruce, Harvey can be Gotham’s savior and Rachel. Or so he thinks. Harvey thinks he can have his cake and eat it too. Using the law to put all the cities criminals behind bars, but attempting to do so under an inherently corrupt and decaying system makes him vulnerable to the same dangers that Batman himself is. You can do this with every character and it just keeps looping around like a snake eating its own tail. While understanding want vs need is such a basic attribute to solid screenplays and character work, this film has that idea built into its thematic DNA. As a result it’s rock solid and still as absolutely perfect as it’s hyped up to be.

Looks pretty but a narrative mess. You can clearly see the seams where different narratives get welded together, too bad all lead to nowhere. Too many villains, and only Kingpin gets a motive that is PeterB's counterpart, neither of which get explored, we only see the resolution. Instead we get a coming-of-age story with Miles Morales, a teen that has it all, but having contempt for it; it just don't sit right with him. His new private school is too elitist, but we only see him having trouble socially as well as being overwhelmed with schoolwork, good thing  he's an A+ student. Why does he want to become Spiderman? No idea, sure he saw his masked weirdo get killed in front of him, but others came, other that were far more capable that were not keen on having dead weight to lug around. The idea of not doing schoolwork was part of his plan, but bailing on being Spiderman wasn't. Is that his motivation, looking cool? Why was he so eager to get the Spider-people's approval? Miles' story is that of an uncomplicated character: he gets everything, does the right thing and the only blemish is his character is the fact that he idolised a crook. Funny thing is it gets resolved immediately. Don't you worry, your favourite Miles Sue is super dooper simple to understand: he is perfect, yuppie!

I will never enjoy any installment in this franchise because the original Art Director, who is responsible for everything people loved about the animation, was fired after 2 years of working on the movie, and credited solely as a “Visual Consultant” despite so many of his initial storyboards and animation tests being copied clip for clip included in the final cut. Alberto Mielgo, the guy who made The Witness and Jibaro on Love, Death, and Robots, wanted to revolutionize animation and change the industry. He did that, but was robbed of all the credit. I wondered if I would like this more on rewatch. When I watched this the first time, I probably had a lot of Marvel fatigue, and I liked Across the Spider-Verse a lot since. But I think this is a tough rewatch as well as a tough thing to watch after having watched... even more Marvel stuff, including Deadpool & Wolverine. I want to get the most technical problem I have out of the way, though: for as innovative and psychedelic as this animation is, I think it's hard to look at sometimes. Visually, there are just too many ideas and not all of them work. The "halftone shader"? Love it. The chromatic aberration effects? They get a little distracting sometimes. The way they render depth of field? Hate it. When they are running out of the lab through the cafeteria, there is a shot that begins only with scientists sitting at a table out of focus (because our heroes aren't in frame yet). It looks horrible. When anything is very out of focus, it looks horrible. (I don't recall having these quibbles with Across; I assume without reading my review that they ironed out the kinks of this aesthetic.) Now, not unlike the look, the story and its comedy both have moments while also having problems. My problems with the story are enormous in 2026, and it's a testament to what I do like about this movie that it gets a positive score from me. Because... if I really had to say, I would say I do not like this movie. It's just so... I'm sorry, it's just so Marvel. Self-congratulatory IP-waving? Check. Bad science fiction? Check. Unwelcome self-reflexive glibness? Check. Unrelatably high stakes? Check. I have gone from having a distaste for these qualities in Marvel stories to simply not tolerating them. I remember being bummed on my first viewing of this movie that it felt like it ended on a hamfisted "and you could be Spider-Man too, so care about him and his many revenue-generating incarnations, please" note. I completely forgot that it's way more crass up front. The early character development in this movie is not Miles Morales as Spider-Man or Peter Parker as Spider-Man or a different Peter Parker as Spider-Man. It's Spider-Man as intellectual property. And it's not like other superhero fiction hasn't done this. I know specifically of Superman and Wonder Woman fiction that acknowledges their celebrity in-world, even going so far as to include comic books of these characters (like this movie does). But the ends justify the means so much better in those stories. This just feels like Marvel reminding you of how big Spider-Man is in our world, not his own. Because the Spider-Man of this movie's (main) world is one of two people. It's Peter Parker, who died early and isn't established all that well in any real detail. Again, he and every other Spider-Man are overshadowed by Spider-Man (tm). Or, it's Miles Morales, who gets Spider-Mogged in his own movie. I just find his arc to be really unsatisfying: he's bad at Spider-Stuff until he's pretty suddenly not and... Guys, this plot is all and only about fixing and inserting a USB drive (which Sweatpants Peter himself mocks in typical Marvel movie fashion... guys, if you want to talk me into the idea that your movie is bad, don't be upset when I agree with you). Bad. Science. Fiction. And we run away from all of Miles's worldly relationships immediately in order to remedy multiversal concerns of little tangibility (though they do try to humanize Kingpin and it's more convincing than it has much right to be). Furthermore, when you blast past reality with that much impatience, I begin to have my own impatience about your inability to tell stories about heroism that have any real-life connections. We do not need superheroes to model how to act in the face of a supercollider when we've fallen on the magical thumb drive that saves the world. We need models of actual interpersonal bravery and compassion (but then again I would say that as a Wonder Woman fan), for when we're challenged with much more likely problems. Look. It has moments and a groundbreaking (if flawed) look. But, again... it's just SO Marvel. And I'm really, really tired of that tone and those problems that are so common to these stories. Next time you consume a Marvel story, I want you to try something. Ask "what if I didn't care about the most extremely made-up parts of this?" I think it makes these stories fall apart really often and reveals how much Marvel expects us to just buy in as a matter of course. I think you see this attitude in the way they flex Spider-Man as IP here and do an MCU victory lap around the X-Men movies (which have rich stories apart from the mutations) in Deadpool & Wolverine. This movie is about Spider-Man (tm), not Miles Morales. I wish I'd learned more about him, what he cares about, and the people who live on the same Earth as him. And I don't think these are unreasonable demands to make on a story.

Je ne suis généralement plus trop fan des films de super-héros (merci marvel), mais il faut dire que cette nouvelle saga a su attirer mon attention au vu des critiques qu'elle a suscité y compris au niveau de ceux qui ne sont pas fan de super-héros. J'ai d'abord trouvé le film très drôle, les gags sont vraiment bien amenés et pas trop lourd, que ce soit le père qui demande à son fils de lui dire "je t'aime", ou simplement les situations inconfortables dans lesquelles Miles se trouve. Le rythme assez rapide du film permet de ne pas s'ennuyer, et cela est d'autant plus appuyé vers la fin avec les différents styles d'animation proposé en fonction d'où proviennent les différents personnages. Au niveau de l'intrigue par contre c'est moins bien de manière générale, bien que je trouve le début avec la mort de Peter Parker assez réussie, la suite va vraiment être un peu trop basique à mon gout. Il y a d'abord l'antagoniste qui a mon sens n'a qu'un proto-développement un peu bâclé, des facilités un peu grossières comme la meuf spiderman qui est dans le labo et qui arrive à la rescousse, c'est assez curieux. J'ai aussi trouvé qu'il y a eu un certain manque de progressivité dans le power up de Miles, genre il passe vraiment du tout au tout sans transition, sans vraiment se découvrir. Bref, l'histoire bien que trop basique se regarde bien grâce aux touches d'humour et l'animation originale. Un bon moment.

Rivisto dopo un paio d'anni, è esaltante! Uno dei prodotti più freschi e contemporanei che si sia visto in due decenni. Graficamente sbalorditivo, un perpetuo dinamismo che però non confonde, dettagli, scritte, invenzioni, strizzate d'occhio al linguaggio fumettistico...e una storia che regge! Regge benissimo: personaggi semplici ma non banali, sviluppi semplici ma non noiosi...la riprova che un film (anche) per bambini/ragazzi non deve essere stupido. Commovente quando serve, buffo per sdrammatizzare, e aggiornato rispetto al vecchio, ormai consunto e ripetitivo Peter Parker: qui siamo più vicini al ghetto, alla cultura hip-hop, a una Brooklin sporca e povera che richiede eroismo per essere salvata - moralmente, si intende.

Вторая часть (хотя это скорее продолжение) Убить Билла меня немного разочаровала. В начале я бы, правда, хотел отметить несколько моментов, которые мне понравились. Прежде всего это эпизод обучения у мастера Пэй Мэя. Фактически это собирательный образ всех кунг-фу-фильмов, особенно той их части, где главный герой проходит обучение у мастера и постепенно познаёт мастерство определённого боевого искусства. Отдельно хочется отметить работу со звуком: звуки ударов, диалоги и даже шумы окружающей среды очень точно передают атмосферу старых гонконгских боевиков. Здесь же хорошо заметно главное отличие двух частей. Если в первой преобладает эстетика японского кино — самурайских фильмов и классических фильмов о мечах, — то во второй Тарантино гораздо сильнее обращается к традициям гонконгского кунг-фу. Понравился и финальный разговор Беатрикс с Биллом, в котором наконец проясняются некоторые моменты, оставшиеся непонятными раньше. При этом Тарантино снова использует свой любимый приём — рассказывает историю нелинейно, перемещаясь между разными моментами времени и постепенно складывая события в единую картину. Однако разочаровавших меня моментов оказалось больше. Во-первых, остальные участники банды Билла кажутся какими-то невзрачными и недостаточно проработанными. Единственной действительно запоминающейся для меня остаётся О-Рен Исии: мы понимаем, откуда она пришла, что сформировало её характер и почему она стала такой, какой мы её видим. Да даже про её телохранительницу Гого нам рассказывают больше, чем про Верниту Грин — первую жертву Беатрикс, которая погибает практически сразу после появления в фильме. Во-вторых, мне показалась странной логика поведения самих убийц. Все они позиционируются как профессиональные и крайне опасные бойцы, но при этом совершают поступки, которые выглядят совершенно нелогично. Зачем Бадд скрывает, что меч остался у него? Зачем Элли Драйвер вообще нужен меч Хаттори Хандзо? И зачем Бадд даёт Беатрикс фонарик в гробу, фактически помогая ей выбраться? В какой-то момент возникает ощущение, что персонажи действуют не как профессиональные убийцы, а так, как нужно сюжету для следующей сцены. И, наконец, я так и не понял, зачем вообще было разделять эту историю на два фильма. Для меня это не две самостоятельные части и даже не две логические главы одной истории это один фильм, искусственно разделённый пополам. Если бы в первой части мы увидели начало и конец истории, а вторая раскрывала бы события между ними, объясняя то, что осталось за кадром, такое решение имело бы для меня гораздо больше смысла. Здесь же я не почувствовал, что у каждой части есть собственная драматургическая функция. В итоге Убить Билла 2 это фильм, который, безусловно, стоит посмотреть, особенно если понравилась первая часть. Но лично для меня он работает скорее как необходимое продолжение, позволяющее закончить начатую историю, чем как фильм, который хочется пересматривать сам по себе.

The difference in energy between Vol.1 and Vol.2 is pretty huge. This is really a movie that should be watched back-to-back, Vol.1 followed immediately by Vol.2. The two films are designed to create an overall rise and fall in energy, so watching them separately makes that difference in tone work against your expectations. In that sense, I almost wish they had released the whole thing as one sprawling, deeply idiosyncratic epic rather than splitting it into two volumes. Vol.2 is almost an epilogue, with a lot more explanation and exposition, and it has very little of the roller-coaster, jukebox-like exhilaration of Vol.1. Still, the parts that parody the techniques and conventions of kung fu movies made me grin. I loved the feeling of, “Yes! That’s exactly the bit you should be picking up on.”

O ritmo desacelerado deste segundo volume funciona como uma faca de dois gumes, especialmente diante da energia intensa e do visual marcante herdados da Parte 01. Essa quebra drástica de expectativa faz com que as batalhas percam aquela tensão prolongada do primeiro filme, adotando resoluções tão rápidas que dão a impressão de um roteiro apressado para fechar as pontas, como se a pressa estivesse em terminar a briga, e não em saborear o conflito. Ainda assim, o impacto dos vilões continua intacta, mantendo o ar de ameaça constante ao redor da protagonista. ── ⟡ ˙⚔ ̟ Apesar desse tropeço no ritmo dos confrontos, o grande trunfo desta continuação é como ela expande a personagem de Beatrix. Se o primeiro filme já havia desenhado sua força através do luto, o Volume 02 mergulha de vez na sua história e nos seus traumas, trazendo uma carga emocional que lembra o verdadeiro coração da obra: o espetáculo das lutas é secundário diante do peso humano e da jornada íntima de Beatrix. É a história dela, de sua sobrevivência e de sua reconstrução que move tudo. ── ⟡ ˙⚔ ̟ Contudo, toda essa carga dramática acumulada acaba cobrando o preço justamente no encontro mais esperado. O confronto final com Bill, embora traga camadas simbólicas fascinantes sobre o peso do passado e a genialidade do golpe final, deixa um amargo de oportunidade perdida. Considerando que Bill representava o eixo central e o motor de toda a busca da Beatrix, a resolução acaba fazendo o personagem parecer subutilizado diante do mito construído ao longo dos dois filmes. ── ⟡ ˙⚔ ̟ Portanto, o filme frustra em seu desfecho ao deixar o confronto final com Bill com um gosto de oportunidade perdida, fazendo o grande motor da história parecer menor diante do mito construído. No entanto, a simbologia do golpe final e a sensação agridoce que fica no final reforçam que, embora o encerramento pudesse ter ido mais longe, a verdadeira vitória está na alma de Beatrix: ela finalmente silencia os fantasmas, abandona os escombros e encontra a paz para seguir em frente.

Hacer una reseña de esta película es algo innecesario cuando ya tienes una reseña de la primera porque literalmente parecen la misma película, todos los elemento, ritmo, estética e identidad se transmite de una a otra, y aunque sé que Tarantino dice que son la misma película tampoco exageramos, es obvio que son películas distintas porque puedes notar como algunas aspectos se intensifican en esta segunda entrega, pero es todo en temas de edición y post producción porque más allá de eso si está madre estuviera pegada una con la otra sería una sola película. Lo que trato de decir es que es muy notorio que la intención original era tener un mega corte y no está división en dos partes, y el único motivo por el que estas dos película se sienten distintas es porque estos weyes vieron la recepción de la primera parte e intensificaron ciertos elementos en la edición del segundo volume, y bien por ellos porque todo salió nice. Algo que si puedo mencionar es que esta película es mucho más caricaturesca que la primera parte, lleva ciertos segmentos a puntos que has de cuenta estás viendo Naruto, pero también sucede algo similar con las escenas “serias” que se ven más fuertes y seriesonas, lo cual me lleva a pensar que todo esto es una consecuencia de que estamos en el clímax o final de la historia por lo que todas las escenas en general exageran con más intensidad todo. ¿Lo considero algo malo? No, pero es un cambio en el tono que no puedo ignorar y que quería mencionar porque podría ser cuestión de gusto o disgusto. Tipo el personaje de Pai Mei está en un borde muy peligroso para mí, aunque no lo logre atravesar. Siempre que se trata de una historia de venganza solemos tener este momento de “la venganza es mala” y la afrontación del dilema de obtener lo que quieres y sus consecuencias, y no es porque todos los escritores estén universalmente de acuerdo con ello, es porque narrativamente enfrentarte a un final que es exactamente lo que buscaba el personaje suele ser aburrido y anticlimqtico. Es claro desde la primera película que Tarantino no tiene intención alguna de meterse en esos dilemas y profundizar en sus personajes de esta forma, y no lo digo como algo malo, de hecho de cierta forma es valiente simplificar las cosas aquí, pero debo admitir que tras la muerte de Bill me habría gustado ver algo más, lo que sea, es para mi el único pero real que tengo con la película y es uno a medias porque siempre supe que iba ser así, hasta estoy contento que todo esa sección previa a la pelea con la hija estuviera ahí porque pudo haber sido peor. Lo que trato de decir es que haber conseguido exactamente lo que esperaba es similar a cuando consigue exactamente lo que quiere, ¿y después que? Me habría gustado ver algo más que un simple “ahora tiene a su hija y Bill está muerto”. Parece que estoy diciendo muchas quejas, pero la realidad no podría estar más lejos de ello. Kill Bill Vol. 2 me mamó y si hablo de dos cosas en específico que no me terminaron de convencer es solo gracias a que todo lo demás está súper bien. Tarantino puede ser un pendejo, pero el wey tiene salsa en los dedos y prepara pura obra culinaria.

Without completely discarding the relentless frenzy of violence from Vol. 1 , Kill Bill: Vol. 2 presents a radically different approach to the narrative. And personally—I'll just say this up front—I enjoyed this second part even more than the first. The continuation of arguably the most famous revenge plot in cinema history dials it down a notch to embrace a darker, slower, and dialogue-heavy tone. Tarantino shifts away from a nod to martial arts cinema toward a full homage to the Spaghetti Western, something he achieves through high-tension close-ups, wide shots of desert landscapes, and a soundtrack featuring the legendary Ennio Morricone and Riz Ortolani. This is probably the reason I liked Vol. 2 more; Western tropes are a weakness of mine, and Tarantino executes them flawlessly. The final scenes between Bill and The Bride are simply masterful. David Carradine makes the Superman monologue truly hypnotic, and the anti-climatic resolution of Bill’s death—an oasis of peace lasting just five steps—is the perfect closure for a story that has barely let you breathe.

Barry Egan will, without question, be physically and verbally abusive to Lena over the course of their relationship, even if he really does love her. Everything we learn about Barry, from how he treats his sisters to his pathological lying to his general inability to control his emotions, points toward this. He is violent, unstable and untrustworthy—and love, for all its beauty, is a turbulent force, not a calming one. Self-control is exactly what it sounds like: it comes from the self , not from a lover. Barry's "quirky" traits would be entirely forgivably from a character standpoint if he recognized his own flaws and made any attempt to improve or mature in ways that really matter. Telling someone you want to stop crying all the time and telling someone you want to stop lying all the time are two different things, and Barry is only interested in the former. The credits rolled and all I felt was scared for Lena, a character whose sole narrative purpose is to inexplicably love Barry. Really not trying to be annoyingly contrarian here, but this was just a tough first watch in 2026. I can see why it was important to so many oddballs, introverts, quiet creative types and whatnot back in the day. Seeing a version of your own weirdness depicted, victorious, and loved is, I imagine, very affirming. But I am baffled by how many people I know identify with Barry. He simply does not deserve the good things happening to him. I want to believe that if you made this movie today, it would be broadly rejected. Undeniably beautiful filmmaking, though. Shitty L.A. never looked better. But no.

I turned this film on to fill up time whilst pining for my boyfriend, he recommended it to me this afternoon on his work break and I'm sorry Fin but this film was a slog. I tried, really did, in theory it should be a perfect film for me; autistic 'literally me' character finds his true love (literally me) with a kooky side plot, good visuals, a great score and Philip Seymour Hoffman. Unfortunately it failed to grip me immediately and then proceeded to continue to struggle and try to grasp onto my brain like a toddler holding a wet fish. It was overly complex with absolutely nothing deep which led to a raging headache an hour in. I paused 30 minutes in to brush my teeth, brushing my teeth was preferable and more important to me than this film!! I really want to like it because the acting is great, the visuals are beautiful, the score is brilliant. I specifically enjoyed a few shots, the first appearance of the blonde guys stepping out of a car, the phone booth lighting up when Barry connects with Lena, the first kiss scene and the second when they meet at the hotel. This film does have merits and yet I had no connection to it, its just left me frustrated because I want to connect with Barry but I couldn't. Maybe it was his violent outbursts to his annoying but ultimately harmless sisters, maybe it's just Adam Sandler (it's not because he's great here and I loved Uncut Gems), maybe it's that his romance is unearned, I'm not sure. Maybe it's a movie for boy autists and I'm too Frances Ha coded fuck knows!! Unlike When Harry Met Sally or Submarine or a litany of other life affirming, love affirming films I've watched that make me cry over my beautiful boyfriend and up the ante on the yearning, this film just left me blank. It all felt so unearned and unbaked and usually I can accept that but it also touts itself as grandiose beyond its means. Maybe I believed the hype too much, maybe I'm not a PTA fan, maybe I'm a faux cinephile, maybe it's just not that great. Watchlist

Adam Sandler wears soothes? Yes, and he plays in a PTA movie. It’s a strong reflection on anxiety and the constant pressure to be accepted by others. PTA made a brilliant and unorthodox choice casting Sandler in this role. In my opinion, it’s his best performance and the one that represents him most truthfully. He’s known as a comedy actor and something of a clown, but he also has a real soul and genuine emotion. Those emotions come through powerfully in the scenes where color floods the screen. He cannot express his emotions and keeps everything inside, so he destroys things because he cannot control himself. That said, the story isn’t really my type. It’s a bit too dreamy, and the sudden shift from his lack of confidence to having the guts to confront the people who hurt him felt exaggerated. And somehow he knows how to fight four blond guys? I’m still not sure what that was all about. Even though there were some aspects I found incoherent, I have to give real appreciation to the cinematography, it’s still flashing in my head. The long tracking shots that move around the character, and the moments where Sandler awkwardly walks toward Lena Leonard (Emily Watson), are simply stunning. The compositions are striking.

Definitivamente está es una de mis películas de romance favoritas. No es perfecta en lo absoluto, pero tiene un alma y un corazón que te contagia durante toda la película. El personaje de Barry es (por el momento) mi protagonista favorito de la filmografía de PTA. La inocencia de Barry se ve contrastada con sus problemas de irá principalmente impulsadas por su pasado más violento. Su búsqueda de amor está obstaculizado por su inhabilidad de aceptar quien es y mentir de su pasado. Esto se ve por el como sus hermanas se comportan con el, burlandose y tratándolo como un idiota solamente por ser diferente. Inclusive si Barry les dice que no quiere hablar de esas situaciones, sus hermanas lo tratan peor por ser diferente. La carencia de comprender a Barry es lo que lo lleva a querer alejarse y volverse su propia persona. Pese a los traumas y el dolor de Barry, cuando el encuentra el amor hace todo lo posible para mantenerlo. Se da cuenta de sus errores al mentir y empieza a reconocer quién es el y que quiere hacer para mantener su amor. Hace todo dentro de su poder para proteger a quien más ama y busca el resolver sus problemas sin involucrar a nadie más. Esto hace el amor en Barry, lo convierte en una persona más genuina y capaz de hacer hasta lo imposible para buscar compañía y amor en otros. Y a través de este viaje uno puede ver las aventuras en las que Barry se encuentra y su convicción inocente para buscar ese amor verdadero. En términos de negativos, yo diría que solo Barry resplandece como personaje. Los demás personajes son muy planos y básicos, con Ledra siendo nada más que el interés romántico de Barry. Casi no se le da caracterización y, considerando que es de romance la película, uno tiene que sentir porque ese romance es importante. Aquí no se siente debido a que uno no conoce casi nada de Ledra y se ve como un personaje plano contrastando lo increíblemente escrito de Barry. A lo mejor pudieron darle más tiempo a ala película a enfocarse en Ledra y el como ella se enamora de Barry, no solo Barry de ella. Y los demás personajes son carismáticos pero no tiene mucha urgencia, y el antagonista es gracioso cuando aparece pero poco más. En general que la historia solo se enfoque en Barry crea una película bella, pero uno no puede evitar pensar que pudieron darle más tiempo para brillar a otros personajes. Para terminar, la música es tan etérea  y hermosa, apoyando al viaje de Barry. Toda la banda sonora es un deleite auditivo y hace que el amor de Barry y Ledra se convierta en real. Esto se complementa con la excelente cinematografía de PTA donde se ve lo confiado que está después de sus anteriores trabajos y como el sabe lo que quiere hacer y demostrar. Esta película me hace creer en el amor.

We rarely suffer any physical harm from “betrayal.” Betrayal is something that is born in the heart, something that wounds the heart. And it’s incredibly difficult to grasp what betrayal actually is. Perhaps betrayal only comes into existence when either you or the other person feels that something is “betrayal.” That’s how I think it works. Betrayal can exist even without any action behind it, and in essence, it is just as much a betrayal as one that involves an actual act. If both are guilty, then perhaps neither is. Surely, everyone lives with countless betrayals inside themselves that they never actually act upon. And perhaps that is why, when we ourselves are betrayed, we suffer from the fact that we have no choice but to forgive the other person as someone who is guilty of the very same thing we are. And because it hurts, we close our eyes to it. Both of us. The movie does feel somewhat drawn-out overall, but I found it interesting how it makes you feel that everything that happens between people ultimately happens inside their hearts. Perhaps I felt that even more strongly because the two leads, who are both beautiful yet somehow strangely devoid of sex appeal, seemed almost like empty “vessels.”

RATING: Below Average (4/10) My initial takeaway is that I’m heavily concerned this is one of my brother’s favorite movies. For context, whether it makes me prude or conservative, I’m not a massive fan of extensive nudity in films. I prefer to keep my box office and boobs separate. I also couldn’t appreciate the messaging from Kubrick due to the constant sexual undertones and overall “cuck energy”. The film also lacks a cohesive plot and rather aimlessly follows Cruise’s character, really only displaying his prowess and range as an actor. His performance makes me wish a top tier director would cast him for a film outside his current action blockbusters. Sydney Pollack felt flat and lackluster while Nicole Kidman was exploited and one dimensional in an unremarkable supporting cast. On a high note, the cult mansion scene was executed perfectly, finding myself heavily invested in the intoxicating atmosphere. This act highlighted the simple, jarring score, setting a precedent for building suspense. I did feel satisfied with the ending as in a convoluted way, it tied the lack of plot together. While I’d never watch it again, I could see the appeal to a certain audience as it emulates a Walmart-version Midsommar.

“I’m not gonna tell you their names… no, I’m not going to tell you their names… but if I did, I don’t think you’d sleep so well at night.” If I could describe this film in one word it would be TOPICAL. If it came out today I feel like it would either be the only thing people talked about or it would be so heavily censored that it wouldn’t even be released. The fact that Kubrick suddenly died from a heart attack just 4 days after a private screening is heartbreaking and also a bit strange? All respect to him, he’s a legend, but it definitely makes you wonder. I really enjoyed this film and was completely invested throughout. My only complaints are the pacing and how graphic it was. At times it genuinely felt like a miniseries the way it was paced. The amount of naked people was also just so uncomfortable 😭. I get that some of it is vital to the story and the nature of the secret society but it just felt sooo excessive at times. The score was so simple yet so haunting and the piano was so unsettling even just by alternating between two notes. This was definitely one of the most suspenseful films I’ve seen and it does a great job of putting you in every mysterious moment. The scene where he’s walking through the streets after he leaves Domino’s is absolutely brilliant, I was on the edge of my seat. Overall this was a great film and I can see why many would say that it’s Kubrick’s best. I loved the premise and think it’s such an interesting concept but there were just some minor things I didn’t like. If Letterboxd had a 3.75 stars option then I’d pick that.

Nessuno sa catturare l'anima e l'abisso umano attraverso gli occhi come Stanley Kubrick. È un viaggio tesissimo dentro le crepe di una coppia apparentemente indistruttibile, scossa dal dubbio e dalla tentazione di essere altro, per poi comprendere che essere "normali" non è una condanna ma una salvezza. Le scene della villa in maschera sono tra le più disturbanti e magnetiche mai girate; la nudità è abbondante ma di un'eleganza assoluta, priva di qualsiasi volgarità. L'ultimo atto costruisce una tensione paranoica soffocante, alimentata dalla lucida consapevolezza dell'impotenza individuale di fronte a poteri invisibili e inaccessibili. Prova maiuscola di Nicole Kidman e Tom Cruise — al netto di un doppiaggio italiano imbarazzante —, impreziosita da una recitazione complessa che risente positivamente delle reali tensioni dei due protagonisti. Da guardare, non da vedere.

I can only imagine what was within the 40 cut minutes of this film, which were destroyed after Kubrick’s death. It almost feels like a warning to how the uppermost people of the world exist. It’s scary because it could be true. Key word “could”. Some films are scary because we know they are real somewhere, but this one is purely unknown. Alas, how unknown is it really, how far-fetched do the events in this film actually seem? This is what Kubrick seemed to want to show us with his final film. To tell us to keep our Eyes Wide Open in a corrupt world that thrives on us keeping them Shut. However, this what I feel could be an underlying theme. Obviously this film is based on an older novella as I discovered, which shares a different message. Just as interesting though. Tom Cruise did wonders in this film, can’t wait to see him in Digger. The ambiance was unbelievably tense, that piano was dreadful, in a good way. The dialogue and scenes were so encapsulating. Truly a work of art. Finally as promised, a lighter paragraph. If Die Hard and Gremlins are Christmas movies (for the record I think they both are), is Eyes Wide Shut as well? Food for thought.

Still such an amazing film, with incredible performances from Kidman and Cruise! I hate when people say sex shouldn’t be in films, because this movie makes a pretty strong argument for why it can be an important part of storytelling. It isn’t there just for the sake of being provocative; it actually plays an important role in the story, the characters, and the themes the film is exploring.I especially love watching Bill change throughout the film. Every time I rewatch it, I notice more about his journey and how the events of the night slowly challenge the way he sees himself, his marriage, and the world around him. Cruise does such a fantastic job showing that change. Kubrick’s direction is incredible, and there’s something so hypnotic about the way this entire movie is filmed. The atmosphere, the cinematography, the music, and the pacing all come together to create an experience that feels completely unique. Kidman and Cruise are both fantastic, and watching them share the screen makes the film even more fascinating. Their performances feel incredibly committed, and there’s so much going on beneath the surface of their characters. I also can’t help but think about how much of a financial risk a film like this would be today. A major studio probably wouldn’t take the same kind of chances on a movie this strange, slow, ambitious, and adult-oriented.

You could say I’ve found myself in a Double Bind. I’m incredibly torn on this. The film is both undoubtedly ahead of its time and deeply of its time. It has a complete and total understanding of fandom and stan culture most contemporary films should be jealous of, before either had even been born let alone matured to what they are now. The psychological examination of Mima is fascinating and the film abandons all tradition when it comes to structure to force its audience into her perspective and feel as though you’re losing your mind along with her. However, in the twisty third act that level of intense scrutiny when it comes to Mima’s psychology is left by the wayside. I’m not a fan of the Rumi twist. When a film is entirely about the inner workings of someone’s mind and then suddenly decides to be about someone else’s sudden mental break I’m just left a little annoyed. It’s not even that it feels like it comes out of nowhere but that it’s so much less interesting. Suddenly the film is about a bitter, older, fatter woman desperately deluding herself as she cloys for the attention a younger, prettier, thinner girl is getting. A played out trope that’s usage here borders on misogynistic? Mima’s struggle isn’t about perfection (which is why the claim Black Swan ripped this movie off beat for best makes no sense to me, clearly took inspiration but the cores are so different) it’s about identity. So the personification of her struggle with identity no longer being a part of her but someone else seems to undermine that journey. Especially, because once Rumi is revealed, the film ends and Mima is perfectly fine and self assured again. I just feel underwhelmed. Something so interesting becomes so dull. It feels like the film is dedicated to trying to tell an earnest story about being a woman in the spotlight and in some places it succeeds but in others it feels like it falls directly in line with what it’s trying to critique. I’m not someone that thinks rape or sexual assault should never be depicted. Artists have a right to create art about anything they want to. These things are real so of course there should be stories about them. And while the sexual assault and rape scenes (whether real ir acted) are intentionally disturbing in an affective way, they also seem to be drawn and directed in such a way to titillate the viewer. Now, I understand that this is a film about voyeurism and it’s absolutely drenched in metaphor. I don’t think this is just some misogynistic torture porn it’s not that simple. I think it tries to be a story exposing the horrific reality many women face, whether that be the threat of sexual violence or being pressured and pushed into uncomfortable situations or society’s crazymaking obsession with youth and fame and attention being forced upon them. I think in some places it succeeds and in some places it fails. Part of me thinks a big reason why this has the reputation it does is because it’s an anime and if this same film were made in live action there would be less fondness for it. And I mean it is a very well animated film although not much differentiates it from most anime I’ve seen on a technical level. On a thematic level I think everything here is pushing towards a cohesive whole. Every element has something to do with fame and audience and compromise and voyeurism and obsession. There is a thematic throughline here that is definite. But that seems to come at the expense of a throughline for our narrative and characters. Which I’m often more than happy to look past but here so much of this film is built around character. It’s almost a character study of Mima for most of its runtime. So to have that element become so muddled is a real shame. I did really enjoy my time with this. It’s so disorienting and thrilling but I struggle to look past how disappointed I was with the ending, and it’s half baked condemnation of misogyny and rape culture.

quite a trippy and confusing film but it was good and different from a lot of films I've seen. it's a film that discusses explicitly how much control the patriarchy has over women, and esp how women in the entertainment industry barely have any control over themselves and what they want to do, that doesn't matter to the industry, everything mira "agrees" to hurts her, mentally and physically, she is used and sexualised and only agrees to it bc she feels she has to, "this is just a part of the business" and she doesn't really realise that she can say no, not that it would matter if she did. this lack of care ntrol she has spirals throughout the film as she has no idea whats going on anymore, what she's done and can't distinguish dreams from reality, emphasising how little control she has over her own life, so much that it's barely even hers anymore and she just tunes in at random moments. and the ending shows how men's "ownership" of women in the industry has always been happening, rumi represents what mira could have become, and rumis persona being pop idol mira clearly shows how much being a pop idol herself with all the expectations affected rumi, while she was not successful like mira was she still clung onto her past bc it is likely when she felt the most desired in an industry and world where approval (esp from men) is key to success, (and who doesn't want to be loved/adored?) so she separated herself as she is from who she used to be/wanted to be as a way of coping (and I think that she also experienced sexual assault like mira did, which definitely impacted her, I think esp bc of her reaction to mira doing the tape scene). however, since it did have a few scenes of sexual assault (one in an acting setting but still) and personally I don't like seeing those in media I don't think I will be watching this film again but it does a very deep dive into the horror of the exploitation of women in the entertainment industry.

There's not much profit in it, but frankly, I already have enough money (for myself to live off, so don't get any bright ideas that I'm Richie Rich). The whole point of making money is to ultimately be able to do what you want with your life. Some men want to race cars, others to raise large families, others to hunt and fish. I want to direct adult films and be a stud. (I also have higher-minded, more conventional artistic goals as relates to my own people, the Hindus, but those might be more of a later-life thing. I have time.) I tell you this to make it clear that I'm not approaching Perfect Blue from a feminist angle. My view is that all of life, from the smallest bacterium to the blue whale, is an abattoir where the strong feast upon the weak. While fossil fuels allowed us a brief reprieve from Malthusian brutality for a short few centuries, our population has increased, our technology has stagnated, and our climate is changing to the point that the "law of the jungle" is once again taking hold. I view Perfect Blue as a chronicle of the return of Japanese civilization (and all civilization more broadly) to something more primal as humanity leaves our peak years behind us. My expectation is that humans in 2200 will envy the lifestyles of peasants in 1200. Mima is a pop idol trying to transition into becoming an actress. As an idol, she mostly performed for horny middle-aged men and local louts, and she hopes for a more dignified career as she ages. Ironically, her background and the changing times get her cast in "degrading" roles, and her breakout role is playing a stripper who gets raped by the crowd. (Don't mind that scribbling you hear in the background, I'm just taking notes for my own work.) She also strips for various photoshoots (to my pleasure, said shots show her vulva - director Satoshi Kon doesn't pussy out in the way Western directors would). Throughout the film, we're treated to various shots showing murders and such, only to then hear a director yelling "Cut!" and realize that it was just shots from her acting career. So when actors and directors associated with Mima start turning up dead and an ugly stalker obsessed with Mima arrives without any cameras around, we start to realize that Mima is in actual danger. Figuring out what's real and what isn't is most of the fun of the film's incredible plotting, and while I personally didn't like the happy ending and twist culprit (I think it would have been more interesting to see Mima raped and killed by a deranged stalker, frankly), I understand that normal audiences would not be okay with that, and poor Mr. Kon probably wouldn't be invited to direct more high-budget films. My personal ending is that the film fades to black as the stalker assaults Mima. I watched Perfect Blue in the theater on a lark when I happened to come across its listing on Fandango (I watched Paprika by Kon years ago and was not impressed, so it's unlikely I would have watched this on my own without the prod from the theater). I'm utterly thrilled with Cinemark for airing all these re-releases and remasters (there's a remaster of classic anime Angel's Egg later this year that I also can't wait to catch). Most new films are frankly trash (they're all remakes or sequels because our present reality is so shitty that there's no source material to make movies about). But there's happily enough great movies from civilization's peak that we could just air them all in a loop and have more than enough to satisfy a human lifetime.

Mind warping, gross, stressful. I say all of this as a compliment. It's insane and depressing how this movie's handling of the subject matter has only gotten more and more accurate through the years. The boundaries between celebrities and fans have only gotten blurrier, with the internet playing a major role, but in a much larger scale. The entertainment industry's relentless exploitation of young women has only gotten worse too, with Katseye being a recent example of this constant and needles sexualization of people who're still trying to find their feet. Rumi's character is so interesting to me. I wholeheartedly believe that her idol persona came from a place of concern, but the deep seated resentment for how her own career turned out to be seeped into those concerns, twisting it into a complete breakdown of her sense of self. Victims of a system who should do nothing but beg for forgiveness and disappear completely.

I knew Rumi was up to something this whole time, and can I just point out how behind every beautiful talented women in the industry, there’s always going to be a sick perverted stalker unfortunately. Overall, this film confused me but I think in the end, Mima is basically coming in terms with her true identity. Which is just Mima, not idol Mima or actress Mima. I would also like to point how I instantly thought of the artwork Agnus by Konstantin Korobov while watching this film.

Diría que la comedia debe de ser el género más complicado dentro de la subjetividad cinematográfica. Una película cómica necesita provocar risas, al igual que una dramática necesita despertar la empatía oculta. ¿Qué pasa cuando una comedia no genera gracia al espectador? Bien, este ha sido mi caso con *El gran Lebowski*. La historia nos pone en los zapatos de Jeff Lebowski/Dude, un idiota perroflauta que se mete en una misión de millonarios. El contraste entre la solemnidad del Gran Lebowski y la de Dude es gracioso. El viejo es alguien elegante y bien hablado; en cambio, Dude es un porrero que va en bata o con ropa de estar por casa todo el día. La tarea que le dan a Jeff es sencilla: dar un millón de dólares a los secuestradores de Bunny. La esposa de Lebowski es una jovencita que está buena y que está con el anciano por dinero. Es decir, estamos ante una sugar baby que está con un carcamal. Que Lebowski esté con una niñata así demuestra su vanidad y su necesidad de mostrarle a la gente su poder económico mediante la compra de una joven actriz porno. Seguramente lo necesite porque no tiene nada realmente a su nombre y anhela ser poderoso. Todos esos discursos que le da a Jeff sobre el trabajo son pura mierda viniendo de él. «Con los ricos y poderosos siempre un poco de paciencia». Jeff hará su misión con Walter... Oh, Walter, ¡qué pesado me has parecido! Walter debe de ser uno de los personajes más insoportables que he visto en una película, en general. Pierde los nervios y, en vez de hablar, grita todo el rato gilipolleces. Hasta Jeff lo sabe, pero no dice nada por cariño. Entre que relaciona todo con Vietnam, se cree el Rambo de los bolos, apunta con armas al hispano pedófilo... Yo creo que Walter es un personaje que no despierta indiferencia: o te hace mucha gracia, o se te hace pesado. El otro gran compañero de bolos es Donny, quien no tiene un rol en la película. Solo se dedica a «interrumpir» debido a que no se entera de lo que hablan y quiere ser incluido. En general, su función es que Walter grite, nada más. Su muerte tiene un chiste que debería hacer gracia sobre dónde le han disparado, pero, como no le han disparado, simplemente sufre un infarto. Hablando de la protagonista femenina, Maude Lebowski, no me ha parecido súper graciosa. Juliane Moore me pareció muy graciosa en *Boogie Nights* o en *Kingsman*, por decir algo más moderno, pero en esta película me ha sabido a poco. Es la hija cínica del Gran Lebowski y su «relación» con Jeff es follar para quedarse embarazada. Ella odia a su padre por ser un inútil, como Jeff, pero que se las da de importante por haber heredado lo que su esposa tenía. No está mal para despertar risas, pero a mí no me ha llegado ese personaje. Si tú me das cinismo, tienes que hacerlo con un argumento que lo justifique. La misión se desarrolla con momentos cómicos y algunos momentos insoportables de Walter, como la escena de la cafetería. Luego descubrimos que no había millón de dólares y todo era una farsa para librarse de esa actriz porno de poca monta. Los «villanos» alemanes son bastante idiotas. Me hace gracia que su característica sea el nihilismo y estén desmotivados durante todas sus acciones. No está mal, pero cuando veo ese duelo final con la bola de bolos y a Walter arrancando una oreja... apagué el cerebro. Cuando al final sale el narrador, pensé que esto era una broma. Es un cowboy cualquiera que es la voz narrativa y dice: «Al final, Dude está tranquilo por todos nosotros». Gracias, Dios de los vaqueros, no pensé que el porreta iba a estar tranquilo después de esto. Hablando de la fotografía y la cinematografía, he de decir que me han gustado. Aunque sea de película de serie B, he de decir que me gusta que sea intencional. La historia es cómica y no necesitas una fotografía IMAX 70 mm. La banda sonora es una delicia. Los Coen tienen un gusto muy bueno para las canciones. Ya sea cuando Dude escucha su mixtape o cuando está alucinando, sabes que hay un temazo de fondo. Las escenas alucinativas están bien, pero tampoco me han pillado con las ganas de encontrármelas. Son escenas que vemos mientras Jeff está inconsciente y sirven para ver cómo su mente interpreta los acontecimientos que vive. La actuación de Jeff Bridges es la mejor, la verdad. Me sorprende que la película haya reunido a Bridges, Philip Seymour Hoffman y Juliane Moore. Las actuaciones, muy bien. A modo de conclusión, quiero decir que la película tiene la base y todo lo necesario para ser graciosa y que a una vasta mayoría le encante, pero a mí precisamente no me ha pillado gracioso. Creo haber destacado todos los demás aspectos de forma positiva (actuaciones, fotografía, banda sonora y, en cierto modo, la historia), pero su comedia no me ha encandilado. Entonces volvemos a la premisa: ¿una película cómica puede ser buena si no puede hacerte reír? Mi respuesta es sí, pero si el resto de cosas consiguen compensar esa carencia. Si la película depende íntegramente de la comedia y a alguien, por alguna razón, no le ha hecho gracia, no pasa nada; tal vez le haga gracia otro día o nunca se la genere.

So this is the movie everyone fucking loves? Was The Big Lebowski funny? Yes. Was it the funniest movie I've ever seen? Yeah... NO. I went into this with pretty high expectations because I've heard so many people call this one of the funniest movies ever made. I also really like the Coen brothers, so I was expecting to laugh my ass off. I didn't. Not once. And that's probably the biggest problem I had with it. I understood the jokes, I thought the characters were funny, and I could see why people love it, but I just never found myself actually laughing out loud. It was more like sitting there thinking, “Okay, that's pretty funny.” The story itself worked really well though. It's such a stupid fucking situation that somehow keeps getting more complicated. The Dude gets mistaken for someone else, gets dragged into this whole kidnapping situation and suddenly he's involved in all kinds of bullshit he clearly doesn't want to be involved in. And then there's Walter. Walter is probably my favorite part of the movie. This man is fucking insane. Every single situation somehow turns into a war because Walter refuses to just chill for five seconds. And the gag with Donny constantly trying to talk while Walter tells him to shut up every time was pretty funny. Poor Donny just wanted to participate. I also have to talk about Peter Stormare because I fucking love that dude. He barely has anything to do in this movie compared to some of the other characters, but he was still great. Every time he showed up I was like, “YOOOO IT'S PETER STORMARE.” His character is basically just this weird, silent, intimidating Swedish guy who looks like he's about to commit a crime at any second. I don't even know what it is about him, but I just love watching this man in movies. The characters were definitely the strongest part of the movie. The Dude is obviously iconic. He's basically a man who has completely given up on life and somehow still gets dragged into every possible problem. He doesn't even seem surprised anymore when something ridiculous happens. Walter is the complete opposite. He treats every tiny problem like it's a military operation. And Donny is just... there. I also really liked how bowling was basically connected to everything. I didn't expect the movie to lean this hard into bowling, but somehow it worked. You have this ridiculous crime story happening, but everyone is still somehow finding time to go bowling. That was probably the most unique thing about the movie for me. Because honestly, I didn't find much else that stood out. The cinematography was fine, but nothing really blew me away. It looked like a normal movie to me. There weren't many shots where I thought, “Holy shit, that looks amazing.” And that's usually something I really appreciate in movies. I also think I expected the whole thing to feel more unique. Everyone talks about The Big Lebowski like it's this completely insane experience that you've never seen anything like before. And while the characters definitely have their own personalities, the actual movie didn't feel THAT special to me. Maybe that's why I didn't connect with it as much as I wanted to. I know this is one of those movies that has a massive fanbase and I can absolutely understand why. It's well written, the characters are memorable, the dialogue works, and the whole story is pretty damn entertaining. I just wasn't laughing. And when your entire reputation is being one of the funniest movies ever, that's kind of a problem for me. I still had a good time watching it though. It was never boring and I definitely don't regret watching it. I just expected something way more memorable, especially after hearing people hype this movie up for years. Maybe I'll appreciate it more on a rewatch. Maybe I was just in the wrong mood. Maybe I need to become a professional bowler first. For now though, it's just a good movie to me. 6/10 bowling balls TIM OUT Good watch, but bro... where was the fucking laughter?

The Big Lebowski is one of those films that is unapologetically different; quirky and absurd, meandering and carefree, hilarious and ‘slap in the face’ crude at times. It is a film that seems to be ridiculous for the sake of it, but looking a bit deeper, it is almost a conceptual adaptation of the film The Big Sleep and many other old noirs, and it hides an ingenious commentary on a century old film law that will change the way you see it forever. The film is very entertaining throughout the entire two hour showing, and features the classic unique humor of films common before the marvel era. The editing often adds to the hilarity of many moments, –particularly when ‘the Dude’ as Lebowski likes to call himself is drugged or unconscious–but it is low-key for most of the film to match the mood. The film also feels very real, as the Mise-en-sćene is on point, capturing the Dude’s lazy lifestyle in the grubbiness of his house and the favorite bathrobe which he always wears. The music is similarly on point, and the needledrops somehow set the correct mood just about every time. The dialogue is quirky and a little weird sometimes, which admittedly matches the overall vibe of the film, as do the abundant F-bombs permeating the entirety of the show. The story however is the biggest ‘strength’ of the movie if I may be so bold as to call it that. Borrowing from many common tropes of classic noir and mystery films, The Big Lebowski takes them and twists them ingeniously with the anti-hero archetype, to write a story about a deadbeat loser who likes bowling being thrown into a mystery with his life at stake. It is presented well for the most part, and though I'm not a fan of how some of the storytelling is omniscient, the laidback and unhurried feel of the story make up for it. At the very start of the movie, the narrator, when talking about the Dude says “I won’t call him a Hero–Because what is a hero?–but sometimes there’s a man…the man for his time and place” and the rest of the movie struggles with this question, and Dude’s identity as an unlikely hero, ultimately exploring the themes of impermanence, how to abide in an indifferent world, and the virtue of enjoying a simple life. (Bonus: The Hays Code/Adaptation Theory) There is another way to look at The Big Lebowski, which re-contextualizes everything about the way we see it. In adaptation theory, there are three main types of adaptations, Literal, Traditional, and Radical/Analogical. This new way to look at The Big Lebowski sees the film as a radical adaptation of The Big Sleep, a noir film we previously watched. We can see parallels between the two films left and right, but there’s one major difference, the Hays code. The Hays code was a rule in filmmaking implemented in the 1930’s that prohibited the inclusion of any immoral or violent content into the films. The Big Lebowski seems to be a commentary on the Hays code; a loose adaptation of The Big Sleep but without skirting around all the questionable content. For some people this is a massive revelation and changes their entire perspective of the film, and while I love the creative and innovative idea, my perspective on the movie wasn’t drastically altered because of this particular, seemingly random reference. Overall, The Big Lebowski is a good Noir-Parody/Comedy film that loves a good laugh and an F-bomb, with a likable antihero and an interesting story behind its adaptation.

I’ve probably seen this a few times too many, and the lore of Lebowski — books, festivals, etc — got a bit much for a while there. But it remains one of my favourites by the Coens, really, when it comes down to it, this and Fargo are the films that stand up the best from the immediate era after they made their name. For me, anyway. I mean, a couple others sure. Of course. But this and Fargo back to back was a top run, really. Watched it again, and my favourite bit in it is the circular passing of language. Characters that are connected by a scene, but not really connected by context, or sometimes not even connected by a scene will pass language between one another. Maude Lebowski introduces The Dude to the word ‘Johnson’ as slang for penis. Then the Nihilists bust into his bathtub and threaten to cut off his Johnson. It’s a great way of positioning The Dude as the conduit this madcap world of screwball comedy is passing through. Superb cast, cameos, and performances. Great soundtrack. I like to think Sam Elliott’s “Stranger” narrator meeting The Dude and interacting, while the Tumbling Tumbleweed song plays, is an oblique reference to the bar in the Overlook in the Shining, when Jack Nicholson’s character says to the barkeep, “I like you Lloyd, I always have”. But then, enough of my yappin

The Dude abides. He doesn’t align with an ideology, he doesn’t classify himself as anything but The Dude. He isn’t deeply opinionated or bound by his roots and his past. He simply does what makes him happy and content. He goes bowling, he smokes weed and most importantly he has his rug which really ties the room together. Throughout the film he is constantly dragged away from his simple life by people of all types of ideologies. The nihilists, the fascists, war veterans, corrupt pornographers and of course the big Lebowski. What connects all these different factions is LA; early 90s LA. The specific time and location where all of these people of strong beliefs congest and complicate life for the dude. He’s simply a tumbleweed in the wind, dragged literally and figuratively into the web of crime and corruption often by Walter. Walter who is constantly exploding into violence yet claims he once dabbled in pacifism. The Coens create such an amusing critique of ideologies using the contrast to the dude. Every other character is driven by money, sex or violence despite what they say. Even Maude and Donny aren’t as pure as the dude as they both seek out sex/money by the end, despite generally being very good characters. The Coens show how nobody truly follows their beliefs and every character contradicts themselves. The Nihilists don’t care about anything yet constantly pursue the ransom money. The big lebowski acts like a successful man yet it’s all a facade to get money in the first place. Then the film takes a turn towards the end as it carries through the character development and commentary from the first half and starts to become an outlook on the human condition. “I guess that's the way the whole durned human comedy keeps perpetuatin' itself down through the generations. Westward the wagons, across the sands of time” . That’s what this film is at its core, a human comedy. Balancing nihilism and cynicism whilst being the funniest and most quotable film of all time.

En fin de compte, je crois que c'est un film qu'on a beaucoup trop mis sur un piédestal alors qu'il faut être honnête et se l'avouer...c'est pas si ouf. Alors oui, c'est divertissant. Les 1h30 passe à une vitesse folle, tout est fait pour que tu passes un bon moment devant. L'esthétique est efficace, le montage s'arrête jamais de bout en bout. Et puis, vu que c'est des dragons....................je pense qu'on y est tous très sensibles, c'est sûrement la créature fantastique la plus fantasmé et ce pour une raison : les dragons, c'est cool. L'oeuvre réussit à nous investir émotionnellement, clairement. On est prit par les personnages, on se prend d'affection pour certains, on se met à en détester d'autres,...donc je dirais que ça marche bien. Enfin, les designs dans leur ensemble sont bien foutus, que ce soit au niveau des dragons comme des personnages, tout fonctionne. Donc, ça parait être vraiment bien ce que je raconte, alors pourquoi je l'adore pas ? Parce que c'est un film basique. Et je suis désolé hein, mais tout fonctionne, sans que rien ne soit nouveau. Dans tout les points forts que j'ai émis, tout est ok, tout marche, sans vraiment réussir non plus. Et c'est là que pour moi le film a été un échec, c'est qu'il n'a jamais réussit à me surprendre, à m'étonner. Il est simple, straightforward et ne cherche jamais à nous donner plus que ce qu'on à déjà reçu. Ça répond simplement à nos attentes, sans aller plus loin. Que ce soit visuellement ou narrativement, ça reste très plat. Les couleurs sont sympas sans sortir de l'ordinaire, le travail sur les lumières, pareil et l'histoire va droit au but, avec un dynamisme presqu'un peu trop prononcé. Alors oui, c'est un bon script, oui l'animation est très bien, mais moi ça ne me suffit pas pour y voir un grand film d'animation américain. Selon moi, ça reste une oeuvre qui fait pale figure à côté d'un Chat Potté 2 par exemple. Ça c'est un grand film d'animation américain qui pousse son concept, qui impressionne en mêlant 3D et 2D, utilisant des petits moments de musique hyper intense mais qui sait aussi utiliser son drame avec un message beau et puissant. Y'a des moments plus lent, stressant, bref c'est un vrai roller coaster qui ne se laisse pas emporter par son scénario mais qui comprend les enjeux de l'oeuvre. Ça, c'est fort, ça c'est beau. Bref, c'était mignon, sympa, j'ai passé un bon moment, mais j'y vois pas un grand film.

I love this movie because it reminds you that taking the unconventional path might be slightly harder, but it is far more rewarding in the end. It also reminds you that you never have to be alone and that there will always be people to support you. No matter how crazy your idea is, you have to find the right people. The unique relationship between Hiccup and Toothless pulls you in, making you wish that you had your own pet dragon. Overall, the movie is sweet and a must-watch for anyone looking to spend a cosy Sunday afternoon reminiscing your childhood.

I will forever love this movie; it's just so good and easily one of the best animated movies I've seen. The animation, the story, the characters, everything about this movie is beautiful. It’s such an enjoyable film, and getting to watch dragons will always be fascinating to me. I adore Hiccup and Toothless's bond; it is so pure and one of the most beautiful, unique friendships in cinema. It serves as a perfect example of the movie's most important theme: tearing down prejudice. I found it so brilliant how the story uses humans and dragons to teach us that we shouldn't let prejudice or fear dictate our perspective of others who seem different from us. Getting to watch Hiccup and Toothless's friendship slowly grow and get stronger is absolutely fantastic. We see Hiccup genuinely getting curious about Toothless, beginning to study him and get to know him from a more empathetic and understanding perspective, instead of just seeing him as something to kill like the other Vikings do. I love that it's a very universal message that we can all learn from, kids and adults alike. The soundtrack is a must-mention when talking about this movie because it is just so good. It's one of my favorites, and the track "Test Drive" always gives me chills when I listen to it. Of course, the sequence itself is also amazing to watch, but the soundtrack definitely elevates it to being truly epic and iconic.
