“Here I was born, and there I died. It was only a moment for you; you took no notice.” As someone who has previously enjoyed each Hitchcock film I’ve been exposed too, I genuinely cannot bring myself to understand why this is so hyped. All the praise I see for this has to do with the symbolism and metaphors but can we talk about the actual narrative for a second? The plot here is one of the most contrived stories I’ve ever seen in a film, attempting to do way too much yet never taking the time to fully commit. Madeline is compelling for the first half but once the second half starts she doesn’t matter because the “character” isn’t real; Judy however is, but you don’t care to root for her because she’s an accomplice to murder and in love with the most mediocre man ever. Speaking of which: Scottie is such a boring main character. He’s a terrible PI who doesn’t get caught only because the person he’s following knows he’s there, he’s incredibly abusive to Judy prior him figuring out who she really is (No, grief is not an excuse), and ultimately he also just has an affair with whom he believes to be a married woman. My point is: none of the character are compelling or root-able by the end except for Midge, but the movie forgets about her even being a character following the second act. I get this is a very internal film from Hitchcock, but that doesn’t mean it’s a good movie. Yes the color, editing, and sound are great; but what I value most is narrative and this narrative is awfully paced with an abysmal payoff. I know this is going to go become one of my certified hot takes but I’ve gotta stand on business. Hitchcock is still on my Mount Rushmore of horror directors. But if you want to be an honest critic (even just for fun on Letterboxd), you gotta not just glaze everything a great director puts out. This wasn’t received well when it came out and I can see why. Is Hitchcock still a certified master? Yes. Do I still think this movie is kind of a narrative shitfest? Also yes.

I understand why this film is considered a classic and why it's popular but it's not for me. I found Alfred Hitchcock’s use of dolly zooms, slow and quiet scenes and color was a really unique and cool way of conveying confusion and the “vertigo effect”. Some scenes were put in a first person perspective of Scottie when he's experiencing acrophobia and there's a dolly zoom going downward. I thought this was really interesting because it lets the viewer experience this with him instead of just watching, I thought this fit really well with the whole disorienting and spiraling themes of the movie. Another thing Hitchcock did in Vertigo that was impressive to me was his use of color. When Scottie first spots Madeleine in the restaurant, she's wearing bright green and the background is a really bright red/pink, It's all so vibrant and surreal so I thought again this really fits that whole confusing vibe of everything But, nevermind how pretty the shots were, the coloring and cinematography just wasn't enough to keep me fully engaged with this film. The pacing got kind of unbearable after a while, the whole sequence of Scottie following Madeleine while she wandered around, and following her as she drove I thought went on for a little too long. So, overall I get why Vertigo is so well liked but personally I wouldn't watch this again.

Vertigo has been considered one of the best movies that you can view in your life. From the different camera movements and scenes, this movie establishes the difference between obsession and what is true to life. The film starts out with a vibrant array of colors, ranging on the full color spectrum. This reveals a brighter mood at the beginning of the film and creates the illusion that everything is alright. The colors in the film later will introduce red and green tints that respectivly represent danger and mystery. One example of this is the hotel scene where the hotel sign shines into the room while you wonder if it actually is madaline. With the hair being the origional color and her wearing the same suit you can see that it actualy is madaline. We can also see the danger happen while detective is having the dream and can see what madaline has seen in the past when she was going "crazy". Theere is also the theme of obsession and creating an image of someone that they cannot live up to. We can see when Madaline supposidly dies that the detective is completley broken down and cannot function as he always has since he was in love. This then over time creates the image of Madaline as she once was and when he meets her again as a different person, he cannot be content of who she is now and needs to change her to what he has envisioned. I feel that this film really challenged me to sit through it and really focus on whwat is actually happening. I feel that movies need a concrete plot and I feel that the story has to be known to the watcher. In conclusion I feel that this film deserves the rating that I gave it because of the story it had and not the cinematography or the score.

I jumped at the opportunity to see a Hitchcock that I'd never seen before at one of my local cinemas. I love 'Rope' and 'Rear Window', so hearing that 'Vertigo' is one of Hitchcock's masterpieces seemed like a no-brainer. To discover that it's actually one of most overrated films ever made was a bit upsetting to say the least. We all left the cinema with a sour taste in our mouths, wishing we could get out $16 back and that someone had told us the truth: 'Vertigo' actually kind of sucks. Hitchcock: the master of suspense. Little to no suspense in the whole film. What makes many of his other films great is that we as the audience know things that the characters don't. Never the case here. The pacing? Painfully slow and borderline unengaging. The twist was apparent from halfway through the film, so the second half was just enduring one sad and tiresome display of misogyny after another. How Jimmy Stewart became such a popular heart-throb in the 40s-60s is beyond me. He just mostly plays unlikable assholes that somehow women still like. Plenty of people seem to say how gorgeous this film looks as well. The depiction of San Francisco, the bright colours, and the one major dream sequence stand out of bold and expressive. Yet, so much of the film is also filmed in bland locations, with uninspired set-pieces and straight-forward blocking. I wasn't nearly as impressed as I expected to be. Then, to wrap everything up. The ending is terrible, with no sense of mystery or closure to hold onto, just a sad dead-end with no real enjoyment or satisfaction. The entire second half is a painful ordeal. It's hard to believe I watched the same film that hundreds of thousands of men and women over the last 58 years have given 8/10, 9/10, or 10/10 reviews to, or called Hitchcock's masterpiece. A predictable, slow, stale, offensive and mostly just off-putting drag. Sad. 4/10

La entrega no solo representa el vértigo sino que intenta crear una sensación de caer al abismo a través de la psique fracturada. Es asi que Scottie se obsesiona y entra en una espiral hacia su parte más retorcida que distorciona su concepto de amor por la obsesión del fantasma de una mujer casada que esta tratando de resucitar debido a su propia culpa. Y no es que la este reviviendo, mas bien manipula a la novia que conoce después para que sea igual a la otra mujer. La historia es interesante pero no me enganchó lo suficiente para permanecer atenta a todo, pienso que pudo durar menos; con respecto a las actuaciones y planos de cámara son buenas, pero no se esforzaron en el soundrack, lamentable.

Estadounidenses Não Sabem Beijar Nem mesmo a direção de Alfred Hitchcock foi suficiente para fazer o roteiro de Alec Coppel e Samuel A. Taylor resultar em um bom filme. A Midge (Bárbara Abel Geddes) é o maior exemplo da baixa qualidade do roteiro, porque ela é inútil na trama e desenvolvimento das demais personagens. A fotografia de Robert Burks é incrível, porque ele criou cenas lindas que complementaram a trama com mais camadas, um trabalho ímpar. Que mel é esse que o Scottie (James Stewart) tem? Um velho feio e desprezível desses. Dito isso, gosto muito como o filme muda nossa percepção sobre ele aos poucos. Hitchcock é um excelente diretor, porém a obra ser teatral, e depender muito disso para funcionar fez com que a imersão nunca fosse completa, principalmente porque tal teatralidade fazia os personagens se manterem nos mesmos ambientes quando não fazia sentido. Eu esperava muito mais desse que é um dos, se não o maior clássico do cinema. Esse é um dos poucos casos em que eu acho que uma nova adaptação de um filme seria bem-vinda.

Le vertige de Scottie, qui semblait être un élément central au début, m’a finalement paru assez peu exploité. L’idée autour de Madeleine/Judy et l’obsession de Scottie sont intéressantes, surtout quand on comprend toute la manipulation, mais ça n’a pas suffi à me faire apprécier le film. Même la révélation finale m’a laissé assez froid. Je reconnais son importance et ses qualités cinématographiques, mais personnellement, je n’ai pas pris le plaisir que j’espérais devant ce film. Peut-être que je l’apprécierai davantage avec le temps, mais pour l’instant, grosse déception.

Is this the greatest film of all time? Spare me. The plot is idiotic. Why does Judy go along with Scottie's creepy nonsense? Does she really think she can bail? Why doesn't she move from the hotel? Didn't Gavin give her a massive amount of money so she can fuck off from San Francisco forever? Is she trying to get caught? Is she fishing for a guy who can denounce her to the police? Why is she wearing the jewel from the crime scene? If so, why is she squirming when Scottie subjects her to his makeover? And what about the plan? How could he know that Scottie wouldn't make it up those stairs? Or what if Scottie waited until someone went upstairs, like a nun? Wouldn't that just invalidate the whole charade? How are they gonna get off the tower without being seen??? And Judy's still dressed as Madeleine, hair painted and everything! How could Scottie bring Madeleine's corpse up there, and if Scottie killed her there, why didn't the nuns, who came upstairs immediately when Scottie and Judy went there, hear Madeleine struggle? And, more than anything? Are we just gonna continue pretending the very visible threads Hitchcock pulls his characters through are psychologically real or in any way convincing? Or are we finally ready to admit they're just character contrivances some French critics in the 60s glazed over because they were 25-year-old dudes trying to prop up an unwieldy pseudo thesis who didn't give much of a fuck if women were written convincingly? Or if plots were written convincingly? Judy/Madeleine's character is utter nonsense from a psychological standpoint. Gavin's plot is unbelievable. Vertigo may look good, but for everyone still moping around the fact that Jeanne Dielman was pushed into being #1 on Sight & Sound should just go back and really look at the sham that is saying Vertigo is anything more than OK.

The first thing I liked that Hitchcock did was add a point of view to the film. When watching and seeing from Scottie's point of view, it helps you have a better understanding of the movie. We see this constantly when Scottie is driving and is following Madeline through San Francisco. From this, you can see Scottie, but you also get to see where he is going and how he is constantly following her. The point-of-view shot was used multiple times in the film, and another time is when he is running up the stairs at the church trying to save Madeline. In this scene, the point-of-view shot shows Scottie's acrophobia and how it is preventing him from saving the love of his life. To add on, in this scene, the dolly zoom was used to emphasize his fear and add suspense to the film to see if he will be able to save her. The dolly zoom was used twice, and both times it was to show his fear. In my opinion, the first dolly zoom was foreshadowing because his fear led to someone dying, and then later in the film that happened again when he was running up the church; even though fake Madeline didn’t die, Scottie thought she did. I also think that color in this film was very important and adds to Scottie's obsession because when we see Scottie, there is usually something red around him; for example, we once saw Scottie wearing a red suit, and red reflects danger and evil, and at the end of the movie Scotties obssesion caused him to become evil towards judy especaillywhen he made her wear the certian clothes. In my opinion, the “Cardinal Sins of Cinema” I struggled with the most in this movie was it being too slow. It's weird because there were times when I felt that some scenes were too long and some were too short. Times when I thought it was too long were when Scottie was driving and following Madeline, for example when they were driving into the woods and the bay; I felt that they could have been just a little shorter. I also wish that the ending scene was longer because I feel that the ending was abrupt. She fell through the window, then it just ended. In my opinion, I prefer when movie endings wrap up the story more and not leave it up for interpretation. Some people may think this movie is too old, but I honestly don't think so because I know if I had watched this in 1958, I would have been gagged by the plot twist. The coloring of this film also adds another element to it that makes it a classic. I feel like I didn’t enjoy it as much because I am used to watching movies now with better action and more complex plot twists. Overall, though, I feel this still can be considered a movie classic even though I would never rewatch it again.

I was very shocked by the way the film ended because I was not expecting the story to take the direction that it did. After Madeleine supposedly committed suicide, John became obsessed with her and was unable to move on. When Judy came into his life, he wanted to change everything about her so that she would resemble Madeleine. Eventually, John took Judy back to the bell tower where Madeleine had “died” , the reason why he took Judy there was because he wanted to relive what had happened and become the hero he was not able to be the first time. Judy was scared and upset about being there, but John was determined to make it to the top. Once they reached the top of the bell tower, Judy became startled when she saw a shadowy figure and backed away and ended up falling to her death. I think the way that this movie was created was beautiful. There were a lot of colors, lighting, and sound effects that really stood out to me. For instance, when Judy is done with her makeover to look like Madeleine, there is a part where she steps out of the powder room and the lighting changes. Judy looks sad at first, but then she starts to smile, while John looks at her almost like he is seeing the ghost of Madeleine. This scene stuck with me because the expressions of the characters, lighting, and the sound effects, make everything seem eerie and unsettling. I think that this film is important to film studies because of the cinematography, along with the psychological effects that it produces. For instance, the obsession that John has with trying to make Judy more like Madeleine is quite alarming and can make for an interesting topic in studies.

Coming out of Rear Window , my expectations for Hitchcock were that this would be a small, yet creatively-shot movie. Instead, it was massive, intricate, and impressive from all filmmaking standpoints—until its throwaway of an ending. Vertigo was a dark and complex story which keeps its audience on edge and guessing as there is never a moment where at least one of its characters isn’t going insane. It’s not a simple story with simple characters like Rear Window , and it definitely doesn’t leave anyone with a good feeling. The tricks that Hitchcock used to make some of the sequences magnificent are incredible to learn about, and the visuals—whether they be the stunning, colorfully-charged cinematography or the masterworks of 1950s editing that makes us feel uncomfortable yet fill us with wonder at the same time, this is a journey. The pure intention behind the focuses and the frames and even the shapes leave the viewer with a lot to dissect, until the ending discourages everything. This film was written incredibly well and its plot twist was a genuine shock. It felt like, through all its twists and turns, it was building up to a magnificent crescendo, but instead, its ending seemed to forget everything about the movie. Sure, it may seem like poetic justice, but that doesn’t change the fact that it didn’t make sense. Hitchcock impressed me with Vertigo, but I left frustrated as all the bells and whistles and hooks didn’t pay off in the end. For a journey of all sorts that never finds its destination, watch Vertigo. For a simple yet satisfying story, watch Rear Window .

Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo reminds us that a movie, no matter the age, with a compelling story, engaging characters, and a genius use of visual techniques can create an entertaining cinematic experience. This movie shines in all these categories and, personally, has made this film a personal favorite of mine.  The first aspect of the film I really enjoyed was the emphasis on color as meaning. Hitchcock was a master at showing and not telling with a film, and this movie really proves that. The film’s Technicolor made Hitchcock’s storytelling through color really shine. You can tell when the film intends to invoke a certain idea or emotion, such as Madeleine’s silhouette shots with the green neon lights from the hotel sign illuminating the space. It seemed as though green invoked a sense of mystery to Madeleine’s character as Scottie slowly began to unravel the truth behind her aura. The color red also comes into play as it helps emphasize Scottie’s slow turn to obsession and lust for Madeleine’s image. The ultra-vibrant Red restaurant, a strong example of this technique, started to appear more frequently as Scottie began to spiral into psychological obsession. Another technique I really appreciated was the film’s pacing. Vertigo highlighted the importance of setting the plot with a slow start, and using that slow pace to parallel a sense of mystery and suspense. This film didn’t feed action in every scene; it kept the audience intrigued by creating a compelling case. The compelling Madeline case made me pay attention to the film even more, and as I realized, it surely rewarded me in the end with the movie’s signature twist. Pacing is really important because the more you pay attention, the more the film rewards you. To be honest, Vertigo did not challenge me in any of its aspects. Honestly, it was really refreshing watching a film that was slow and long because it helped me feel more connected to the story. This film did not feel forced or rushed; the unique story felt authentic to human experience. The psychological aspect of the film felt real because obsession, no matter what it can be about, could be experienced by anyone. With the success of the movie Obsession in 2026, I can see some similarities between both. Now, this doesn’t mean Vertigo Is the 1950s version of Obsession, but I can see some parallels between Bear’s character and Scottie's character. Both characters form a perfect image of their women, and with this obsession, slowly evolve from innocent loveable characters, to serious toxic individuals. After watching Obsession, I do have a better understanding of Vertigo. Watching Obsession helped me understand Scottie’s character on a much deeper level, especially because of the parallels with Bear. I could somehow know what Scottie was feeling and how his obsession would cause harm to his life after recalling what Bear went through in Obsession. In conclusion, Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo deserves to be recognized as a true classic. Its compelling, suspenseful, and rewarding story stands out among many modern films.

My Vertigo watching experience was magical but also intense at the same time. During the confrontation between Scottie and Judy at the church, the camera was zoomed super close to both Judy's and Scottie's faces heightening the tension between the two. Today was my 30th birthday! I took my parents out to lunch and then brought them back to my place. We were going to head out to an IMAX re-release of The Shining, but my mother didn't like the trailer, which is just the scene where a river of blood sloshes out of the elevator. My father was also unenthusiastic about my pitch for the film - "It's about the white man's murder of the Native Americans!". I also had some mild reservations about rewatching a movie I'd just watched 6 months prior. The whole point of this hobby is to broaden my horizons after all. So we decided to stay in and watch a film on my new 65" TV. I presented two alternatives - Vertigo and Goldfinger. The moment I mentioned Alfred Hitchcock and the San Francisco setting (we're in the Bay Area), my mother was sold on Vertigo. I was also excited to watch what I've regularly seen ranked as the best film ever made (alongside Citizen Kane). By coincidence, I'd just seen Vertigo star James Stewart in a holiday screening of It's a Wonderful Life, and here I got to see him go from the charismatic leader he was there to a broken, twisted man driven mad by a combination of his vertigo (phobia of heights) and trauma over his apparent love interest (the wife of a man who hired him as a private eye) committing suicide in front of him. When he finds a woman a year later who looks exactly like his lover, the mystery around his lover's suicide starts to unravel and the viewer gets disoriented so badly from the revelation that we truly understand the sensation of "vertigo" ourselves. My mother was excitedly pointing out various landmarks she recognized ("That's the presidio! That's Sausalito!") as the film progressed, and we resolved to visit more of the Bay Area together. To my and my father's amazement, she also predicted various plot points before they transpired ("She's not dead! It's a dummy!", "The necklace! He'll know it's her from the necklace!"). Philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer observed that a man inherits his intellect from his mother, and I see the truth of that. After we finished watching the movie and my parents left, I re-read Roger Ebert's essay describing the film in his Great Movies and finally had the context to appreciate it. I close with a quote from it. "As Scottie embraces “Madeleine,” even the background changes to reflect his subjective memories instead of the real room he’s in. Bernard Herrmann’s score creates a haunting, unsettled yearning. And the camera circles them hopelessly, like the pinwheel images in Scottie’s nightmares, until the shot is about the dizzying futility of our human desires, the impossibility of forcing life to make us happy. This shot, in its psychological, artistic, and technical complexity, may be the one time in his entire career that Alfred Hitchcock completely revealed himself, in all of his passion and sadness. (Is it a coincidence that the woman is named Madeleine—the word for the French biscuit which, in Proust, brings childhood memories of loss and longing flooding back?) Alfred Hitchcock took universal emotions, like fear, guilt, and lust, placed them in ordinary characters, and developed them in images more than in words. His most frequent character, an innocent man wrongly accused, inspired much deeper identification than the superficial superman in today’s action movies."

Une histoire riche, pleine de rebondissement ou le spectateur est manipulé de A à Z par le génie de Hitchcock. Il nous immerge dans la tête et les sensations de Scottie, on croit tout ce que l'on voit comme lui, mais... avant lui, on fini par comprendre, et on voit ce héros perdre la tête et céder à son obsession. Une position glaciale ou cette homme détruit une personne réel pour retrouver une illusion, pour finir sur une fin avec une "chute" horrible autant psychologiquement que physiquement... A voir absolument ! Je dirai même que si il y avait un seul film à voir, ce serait celui-ci !

AFI Silver. Hitchcock/Hermann. 70mm. Everyone loves a Hitchcock film, but a Hitchcock/Hermann film? Amazing. AFI did a series of all eight films that featured the historic collaboration between director Alfred Hitchcock and musician Bernard Herrmann. Per AFI: "Hitchcock and Hermann collaborated on eight films over an 11-year period. Despite their differing backgrounds and opposite temperaments, "Benny and Hitch" formed a close working relationship, resulting in some of their most beloved and enduring works." I was able to see seven out of the eight films at AFI Silver! This was the third film I saw at AFI. This is one of my favorite films of all time, full stop. It's hard to describe just how brilliant this film is in every way, and that includes the score. As AFI states, this is "Alfred Hitchcock's supreme achievement, the fullest expression of his cinematic obsessions and the one that goes the furthest in pursuit of them." It's hard to overstate how good this film is. And seeing it on 70mm was of course a real treat.

После смерти Папы Римского кардиналы собираются для выбора нового главы католической церкви. Процесс превращается в настоящую борьбу, ведь у каждого кандидата оказывается свой скелет в шкафу. Зрителя погружают в атмосферу мрачных коридоров Ватикана. Звукорежиссёр позволяет услышать шаги, шёпот и даже дыхание героев, что одновременно создаёт напряжение и интимную обстановку для обсуждения вопросов веры. Сохранение традиции или реформа религиозных институтов? Глава церкви - менеджер или пастырь? Может ли он сомневаться? Какие человеческие слабости нельзя в нём принять? Все эти вопросы практически не поднимаются в "Конклаве". Триллер здесь тоже сложно найти. Главный герой узнает тайну одного из кандидатов, делает её публичной, баланс сил на голосовании меняется - и так несколько раз. Тогда зачем это всё нужно? Ответ разочаровывающе банален: фильм является реакцией на выборы в странах Запада. Да, это очередное обсуждение "правых популистов", "левых либералов" и прочих словосочетаний, не вызывающих уже ничего, кроме скуки. Хорошо, фильм хочет говорить про политику, а не про религию. Будет ли здесь показан интересный конфликт идей? Нет. В самом начале зрителю чётко говорят: "Вот правые, они очень плохие. Вот левые, они хорошие, но им чего-то не хватает для победы". Ни аргументов, ни дискуссии здесь не будет. То есть, чтобы сопереживать местной драме, нужно заранее находиться в определённой части политического спектра. Финал фильма, когда зритель узнает, кто и в какой обстановке победил Главного Буржуина, может вызвать только нервный смешок.

conclave isn’t bad at all, but this is genuinely one of the more disappointing movies i’ve watched. i went into it with pretty high expectations because the whole setup sounded SO interesting, and the movie definitely has the ingredients for something incredible. the Vatican setting, the secretive atmosphere, the politics, everyone hiding something… i was ready to be completely hooked. Ralph Fiennes was really good though, and i liked watching Cardinal Lawrence try to keep everything under control while slowly realizing that basically everyone around him has their own agenda. the whole process of the conclave was probably my favourite part because there’s this constant feeling that one little reveal could completely change everything. but the actual mystery just didn’t hit me as hard as i wanted it to. there were some twists that were interesting, but by the end i was more like “oh… okay” than completely shocked. i think that’s what disappointed me most because the movie spends so much time building up this huge sense of intrigue that i expected the payoff to absolutely destroy me. it’s still really well-made, the performances are strong and the atmosphere is great, but i just wanted MORE from it. maybe if i hadn’t gone in with such high expectations i’d feel differently.

Le Pape est mort. Au Vatican, un conclave se forme pour désigner qui succédera au Saint-Père. Structurellement composé de suspense, Conclave, nous plonge dans les coulisses de « l’Entreprise » la plus vieille au monde. La mise en scène d’Edward Berger installe une ambiance feutrée aux airs de Polar huit clos, porté par un casting international cohérent avec le propos, Ici ce n’est pas tant l’élection qui importe mais ce besoin de justesse que cherche sans fin le Cardinal Lawrence, joué par Ralph Fiennes. Sujet objectivement sensible, le film ne manquera pas d’évoquer les dernières casseroles que tirent l’Eglise, sans en faire le sous thème de son film. J’en retiens 20 minutes de trop, ralentissant un rythme déjà peu dynamique compte tenu de l’Arene (le Vatican) et de ses composants (les Cardinaux). Pas la plus grande révélation mais un sujet intéressant avec un vrai plus sur la mise en scène et la musique

Very interesting look at the intersection of faith and morality, and how human nature plays with what is right and wrong in a religious sense. Nobody is perfect, and our mistakes are what makes us human The cinematography here is so good. The votes were given such a big part, and I don't think there was enough drama and explanation as to who was voting for who and why. We didnt see any courtship, or deliberation, or anything. A vote happened, a skeleton came out for a front runner, and the votes all changed. To me it could have been explored further There were some really beautiful scenes with powerful monolaugues. I specifically think of the scene in the theater, the scene with them all walking with the umbrellas, and the opening scene with the dead pope The messaging was good in the literal aspect, but I felt the way it was done was pretty performative. There was no real buildup for the big twist at the end, and while I love the idea it just felt so poorly done to me I also feel like there was not enough explored religiously. Some surface level themes were there, but I feel there was an opportunity to make some real statements and they shyed away, especially with questioning faith, what makes us faithful, who deserves to be treated how, etc.

Oh, I’m honestly in shock. This film is absolutely fascinating, and I’d recommend it regardless of what you believe. The acting is simply phenomenal, and the score works in such perfect synergy with the visuals. It knows exactly when to emphasize a moment, create tension, or leave you with a sense of mystery. The story itself feels like a small detective mystery intertwined with political intrigue, tangled destinies, and genuine character development. I was particularly impressed by how the characters evolve throughout the film, how their perspectives and perceptions change, and how we’re gradually presented with new details that reshape our understanding of the people we thought we knew. I also loved getting a glimpse into the inner workings of a Vatican conclave: how a pope is elected, the traditions, and all the behind-the-scenes politics. It’s fascinating in its own right. Throughout the film, I found myself repeatedly admiring what I was watching. At one point, I genuinely thought, This is a 9/10. And then... the final twist happened. I won’t spoil it, but my jaw was on the floor. I was completely blindsided. I genuinely have no words. I don’t even know how to feel about this film anymore. It doesn’t erase everything the movie accomplished before that, but the ending clashes deeply with my personal beliefs. My personal take: if you cut the last 15 minutes, this would have been perfect.

Conclave feels like a story about the difference between faith and certainty. It takes place inside one of the most powerful religious institutions in the world, but the film is less interested in religion itself than in what happens when human beings convince themselves they understand something greater than them. What makes the film resonate is how every cardinal carries his own idea of truth. They speak about God, tradition, and morality, but underneath those beliefs are ambition, fear, ego, and insecurity. The conclave becomes a reminder that even the most sacred institutions are still operated by imperfect people. Lawrence is what gives the story its emotional weight. His crisis of faith isn't portrayed as weakness. If anything, his doubt makes him one of the few people capable of genuine reflection. The film quietly suggests that certainty can be more dangerous than disbelief because certainty leaves no room for humility. What lingers is the idea that faith might require doubt. To believe while acknowledging you could be wrong is completely different from using belief as proof of your own righteousness. The characters most convinced of their moral purity often seem the least capable of questioning themselves. The final revelation reinforces everything the film has been asking. Humanity constantly tries to create categories, rules, and structures to make existence easier to understand. But life has never been obligated to fit neatly inside them. Conclave stays with me because it suggests that maybe the opposite of faith isn't doubt. Maybe it's certainty. The moment you believe you have all the answers is often the moment you stop searching for truth.

Holy smokes: you just can't beat cardinals ripping clouds and chatting shit in the smoking area. Conclave is beautiful in every way; a mystery of many locked boxes and a ritual of politics & grief that flows between ecclesiastical drama, internal struggle and the quiet mundane. The framing and design of the architecture show a hostile opulence across time, that which secludes and outlives all, just as each marble hotel room bears witness to just a few nights of its occupant's life. An ancient ritual persists with electronic locks and x-ray security, espresso machines and hotel toiletries. Just as much attention is given to the bus ride and meals times as rounds of voting - each process is just as important in how it determines who will be the spiritual leader of m/billions. Through the mundanities, the conclave is demystified; however, we are still kept at arms reach, barred not only from participation, but knowledge of every other iteration, left to wonder about the thousands of cardinals (and sisters) of the Curia throughout history, the decisions made and the influence they have had on world events. The very brief extract of choral music we get is just divine, it's no wonder pre-modern folks heard the beauty of the heavens in it as it echoed through those high ceilings. The homily that follows is such a beautiful (hopeful) distillation of faith in the modern age, faith as something that breathes and changes, something human that should be in conversation with doubt and interpretation, a united church of mutual respect and integration and openness. In order to believe, one must accept that they cannot fully understand. Interspersed with grand affairs of scandal, there's a real tenderness to the scenes in between: the stillness of a dead man's room, left lived-in and undisturbed; letting yourself feel the grief of a dear friend lost when you has to keep it together for so long; asking someone to quietly pray with you while you're whole world is falling down. Bit of a tacked-on twist ending, but that's the book's fault, and apparently the author has been locked into a twisty Shyamalan brand that harms his ability to tell a good story. Nevertheless, through this and his other interactions with Cardinal Benitez, Cardinal Lawrence, a Church 'Liberal', is able to truly heed his own words. I know it would be hard to track, but I really feel like you shouldn't be able to vote for yourself in the conclave...

À la poursuite d'un gros magot, on ne sait jamais vraiment pourquoi ils veulent tout cette argent (puisque tout ce qu'ils peuvent acheter, ils le volent). Je trouve que, les scènes d'action ont très mal vielli. À la fin, on ressent bien qu'ils ont vécu une longue aventure mais je n'ai rien ressenti de très grandiose ou jolie (contrairerement à "Lawrence d'arabie"). Malgré quelques coup d'éclat et qualités inhérentes aux western (tension, punchline, décor, musique), je n'ai éprouvé qu'ennui, à attendre la scène suivante jusqu'à l'interminable fin.

I'm beginning to feel that I'm more a fan of the revisionist and neo-westerns, that take the genre and stretch and shake out what it is and what it can be. This was a great disappointment after the brisk and entertaining Fistful of Dollars and absolutely did not need to be three hours long. Every moment when Tuco is on-screen is a crime against me. It feels like Leone engaged in his own self-parody, with a now much dumber Blondie and Tuco falling from shenanigan to shenanigan, they learn nothing and proceed to the next. I've read enough articles to see people analysing this film through the lens of the futility of war or the violence and cruelty of the Old West, but frankly, it offers such a simplistic and mean-spirited point of view that I just didn't enjoy its wanton brutality. There are some fantastic segments and cinematography in this (the climax, the bridge fight, the introduction of Angel Eyes, the walk through the desert and the church) but its interspersed by plodding, frustrating sections. It could've been great with a good edit, alas, it's clear Clint did this one for the money.

Хороший, плохой, злой и неважно, кто какой, потому что все уроды Очередное дельце, которое теперь проходит на фоне Гражданской войны в США. Фильм, очевидно, смотрится намного масштабнее предыдущих из "Долларовой трилогии". Локаций больше, яркие главные герои, интересная завязка, повышенные ставки в стиле классического вестерна — круто. И тем не менее, у меня больше неприятных впечатлений, чем приятных. Во время просмотра меня не покидало ощущение, что на экране я вижу незнакомых героев. Что главный герой трилогии, что полковник Дуглас нравились мне из-за своей человечности. Да, это дикий запад с дикими законами и разумеется, понятие морали тут очень растяжимо. Но это не мешает в главному герою в "За пригоршню долларов" по-доброму общаться с барменом и помогать семье, попавшей в беду. Это не мешает ему признать мастерство полковника Дугласа в "На несколько долларов больше", более того, подружиться с ним и вести дело вместе. В этом же фильме, герой Клинта Иствуда стал ухмыляющиймся отморозком, что меня очень расстроило. Да, сцена с исполнением мечты Капитана армии севера вроде как показывает его эмпатию, но вряд ли он бы стал взрывать тот мост, если бы сам в этом не нуждался. Так что им просто было по пути и он между делом угодил желаниям Капитана. В остальном главный герой хладнокровная пафосная и молчаливая картонка, и мне жаль это говорить. У него была своя, в каком-то смысле добрая харизма мальчишки-проныры, это подкупало. Ну да ладно, теперь о Дугласе. Во втором фильме он предстаёт перед зрителем как прагматичный, расчётливый профессионал с моральным кодексом или как минимум чувством чести. Опять же, он признал способности героя Иствуда и пошёл с ним на дело. Делился с ним переживаниями и опытом. Про его основную мотивацию я вообще молчу, желание отомстить за сестру это достаточно благородно (оставляем за скобками моральную сторону вопроса, опять же, это вестерн в котором важно зрелище). Здесь же, Дуглас тоже стал отморозком и это грустно. Получив власть в лагере армии севера он пользовался своим положением ради наживы, избивал людей и т.д. Но если оставить эмоции и попытаться трезво взглянуть на картину, то она выглядит вполне логично. В условиях отсутствия закона и морали люди меняются не в лучшую сторону, особенно ,когда на кону большие деньги. Особенно, когда на фоне идёт война. И вполне логично, что человечность героев стирается и остаются только атрибуты, по которым можно отличить друг от друга ожесточивчихся, расчеловеченых героев. Просто, это не совсем та атмосфера, которую я ожидала от фильма. А если это и была главная мысль, то она здесь не раскрыта. Что до Туко, за ним мне было наблюдать интереснее всего. Его не было в предыдущих фильмах, поэтому я изначально воспринимала его, как такого, жалкого жадного прохвоста. Отличный и яркий персонаж. Дополнительное наблюдение: не скажу, что фильм скучный, просто в некоторых моментах затянут. Вполне возможно, что он так состарился. Этот фильм вызвал во мне противоречивые эмоции, и это, на самом деле, здорово. Потому что я не написала ни слова о первых двух, хотя они мне понравились. Рада, что ознакомилась, просто немного озадачена послевкусием.

I honestly don’t know how to review this movie. I hated the first hour of the movie as it took forever to get going. But when the main plot finally developed, it was good. Slow start, but by the end of hour three I was sold. One of the weirdest movies I’ve ever watched. Another thing about the first hour was that I was like “this is a western that takes itself so seriously and I this classic doesn’t hold up today at all” but I realized I was the serious one… The beats this movie was going for wasn’t to be cool and wasn’t cheesy, it was being done ironically as this western is actually an offbeat comedy in many ways and you can even go as far as saying a “buddy comedy” (even though they earnestly try to kill each other more than once lol)! When I finally realized that, I was able to enjoy the movie so much more. In this three hour movie there is probably only about 30-40 minutes of dialogue…again, super weird. But the musical score is absolutely incredible and more than makes up for the lack of dialogue. There are several very recognizable pieces and the score lends to several undeniably classic music montages and scenes that are just so cool to have finally seen. I’d sum the movie up like this: The Ugly beginning, The Good second act, And the BAD-ASS ending

عملت ري واتش للفلم ودا ريفيو محدش مهتم يقرأه عن **The Good, the Bad and the Ugly** فيلم ويسترن ممتع جدًا، وأكتر حاجة شدتني فيه هي الشخصيات نفسها، خصوصًا **The Ugly**. الشخصية دي حرفيًا بتسرق أي مشهد تظهر فيه. طماع، كذاب، أناني وانتهازي، ومع ذلك عنده كاريزما تخليك مستمتع بيه رغم إنك عارف إنه شخص مش كويس. والفيلم عمومًا مش قائم على فكرة إن فيه «خير وشر» بشكل بسيط، كل شخصية عندها دوافعها وطريقتها في النجاة، وده اللي مخلي الصراع بينهم ممتع. كمان العلاقة بين الثلاثة من أحسن الحاجات في الفيلم، لأن كل واحد فيهم عايز يوصل لنفس الهدف، لكن مستحيل يثق في التاني. الفيلم طويل شوية، لكن بصراحة مقدرتش أزهق منه، خصوصًا مع الموسيقى والإخراج والجو العام. **The Ugly من أكتر الشخصيات اللي علقت معايا، والفيلم نفسه واحد من أفضل أفلام الويسترن اللي شوفتها.**

Tengo que reconocer que el western no es un género que me atraiga especialmente y que, en ocasiones, puede llegar a hacérseme algo repetitivo, pero tenía una deuda con esta película y muchas ganas de verla, y he de decir que me ha dejado una sensación completamente distinta. A pesar de sus casi tres horas, no he sentido que se me hiciera realmente pesada, y eso me parece uno de sus mayores méritos, si bien es cierto que hay algún momento en el que el ritmo se resiente y algunas partes se podrían haber acortado. Leone se toma su tiempo, pero sabe perfectamente cómo utilizarlo. Cada plano, cada silencio, cada mirada y cada duelo están construidos con una clara intencionalidad. La película tiene una personalidad enorme, unos paisajes espectaculares (joder, qué bonita es España), una fotografía increíble y una puesta en escena que hace que hasta los momentos más pausados tengan algo que decir. Los tres protagonistas funcionan y se complementan ciertamente bien, y me ha dejado especialmente buen sabor de boca que ninguno sea el típico héroe o villano perfectamente definido, sino que todos se muevan por sus propios intereses y tengan su propia moral. Además, la banda sonora es absolutamente brutal y consigue elevar muchas escenas que ya de por sí funcionan, especialmente en el tramo final, donde se respira pura tensión hasta el último segundo. Una película que entiendo perfectamente que sea considerada un clásico.

枪的战斗迅雷不及掩耳，而莱昂内成功利用电影语言延宕了枪与枪的对决。不发一言的角色，脸部特写的切换，时间酝酿了空间的紧张感，关注瞄准与被瞄准的辩证关系，耐心等待时机后才是期待已久的一枪毙命。莱昂内的音乐是不断重复的旋律动机，尴尬时刻所导致的窘迫感，抑或是成功突围陷阱的崛起，是全片反反复复的主题。幽默感的存在，又是对严肃西部电影的革新，这也是现代牛仔精神覆灭的体现，类似黑泽明眼中的日本武士精神，在现代性的浪潮下土崩瓦解。布遍粗粝的真实感，人物脸部的残痕类同砖瓦的破败，蚊子甚至还肆无忌惮地在演员脸上爬动，被摄影机一并捕获。三个家伙皆为利来，行动线因利益关系不断调整变化。财宝之路碰上国家士兵，两种战斗动机的比对。结尾三人大战是影史经典，不是演员的动作，而是摄影的动作，是剪辑的动作，是音乐的动作。

I couldn’t predict a single thing that happened in this movie. This movie was so filled with energy and life to the point where I couldn’t even fathom somebody writing the story, the  entirety of the story just felt so unscripted, so natural, so sudden that every scene I was wondering, what are the writers gonna do here? Where can they take it from here? And I never ever had a clear answer. With modern movies it feels like I always know what the writer is planning to do next, but throughout this entire movie, I was just constantly flabbergasted at the concept that somebody sat down and thought of the story and wrote it down. Something else I’d like to mention that I noticed in this movie that when comparing it to modern media struck me as so fresh and new with the amount of quiet waiting, there was in this movie. This movie is full of moments where the characters wait and listen and think, where the actors truly get to shine and let their expressions speak for themselves. Which not only added to the realism of it all, but also opened up opportunities for so much more storytelling storytelling that felt much more deep and grounded and real. It feels like in modern movies the directors expect the audience to be stupid, they say everything so unbelievably clear. There is nothing expected of you, everything is just laid out clearly, but in this movie, a lot of the movie is just facial expressions, eye movements, little subtle hints of story that you have to pick up on on your own and I love it.

Un western spaghetti ? C'est peu dire. Sergio Leone prend un malin plaisir à dynamiter le genre américain par excellence en créant une nouvelle mythologie autour de trois personnages inoubliables et aussitôt classiques. Blondin, le bon, l'est surtout pour sa gueule. Sentenza, la brute, l'est avec tous ceux qui se mettent sur son chemin. Tuco, le truand, n'est qu'une petite frappe sans envergure, mais plutôt attachante. Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef et Eli Wallach au sommet de leur art, lancés dans une incroyable chasse au trésor. Et en prime : la musique d'Ennio Morricone...

Laden with thematic depth and reflections on violence, relationships, money, and obviously the intersections of those three, The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly may be a little too long but it’s also far more emotionally engaging than the other films in the Dollars trilogy. Eli Wallach’s scenes around the halfway mark, convincing himself and Blondie both that he truly cares for him are an incredible showcase of talent and bring the film’s ideas into focus. When Clint Eastwood shows up in the town to help Tuco shoot his way through Angel Eyes’s crew of bandits, asking him “Were you gonna die alone?” the bizarro brotherhood between these characters is crystal clear. They love each other, they have each other’s backs, but Tuco in particular can’t stop himself from stabbing Blondie in the back. Blondie knows this, and just accepts that that’s the way it is - he treats Tuco accordingly. From there we move to the bridge sequence, as pointed a war satire as there ever was, and finally, what is probably, for my money, the greatest sequence in movie history, the cemetery. With a bit more research and a couple of ancillary texts, I could probably write a few thousand words on the overwhelming scale of the setting and the goal of the characters in being there. My final (and initial) thoughts on this movie are that this is not Sergio Leone, Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef, or even Eli Wallach’s movie (although he has quite a claim to it). It’s Ennio Morricone’s. Every single scene is not just elevated by the music, it’s made by it. This score is so perfect, so tonally dialed-in, that it carries the movie even more than John Williams’s work on The Empire Strikes Back does. Of course, in the case of Star Wars , the music doesn’t need to support every scene in the same way. In a movie like this one, with sparse dialogue and beautiful yet largely unexciting visuals, the music is able to be the main character. It fits each scene like off-the-rack pants fit a 5’10”, 160lb white man - that is to say, nothing has ever fit better. It’s considered one of the best of all time for a reason, but it really does stand out as exceptional in an already incredible movie.

The film begins by introducing its three main characters. And it does it so brilliantly that it might just have one of the greatest character introductions in cinema history. Clint Eastwood plays the Good — Blondie, as he is called in the film. Lee Van Cleef plays the Bad — Angel Eyes. And Eli Wallach plays the Ugly — Tuco. Although all three performances are excellent, Eli Wallach's performance as Tuco is easily my favorite. He gets more screen time than the other two, but more importantly, somehow manages to become incredibly likable despite being, well… Tuco. Coming from extreme poverty, Tuco has embraced banditry and has absolutely no idea what morality even means. He's selfish, greedy, opportunistic, and constantly looking for the easiest way to make money. Blondie, on the other hand, is a lone wolf who lives by his own rules. And then there's Angel Eyes — compared to the other two, he's more refined and knows exactly how to position himself alongside whoever holds the power. During the Civil War, for example, he rises to the rank of colonel and uses the army to further his own interests. In that sense, the three characters can almost be seen as three different social types: The Bad is disciplined, military, and part of the system. The Good is a scruffy outsider who refuses to belong to any system. The Ugly is essentially a poor man from the countryside who has chosen banditry and is desperately looking for a shortcut to wealth. And that's what makes the three characters so interesting: these aren't just Western archetypes. They're three types of people we can still recognize around us today.

Detachment, directed by Tony Kaye of American History X fame, follows Adrien Brody's Henry, a drifting substitute teacher who struggles to inspire the students to take an interest in their education, as the educational system around him and his colleagues crumbles. A traditional setup in a lot of ways, but Detachment separates itself through its script and its editing, a mismatch of filmmaking styles, and a multitude of different character perspectives. The result is a relentless whirlwind of misery that, despite its best efforts, I failed to connect with. Detachment was written by Carl Lund, an interesting figure in the film industry, with only one writing credit to this day. What we do know, however, is that he used to be a public-school teacher, which quickly becomes apparent through this script — a raw and direct story that clearly comes from a place of personal rage and frustration. The movie is heavily critical of the state of the educational system, with each character serving as a vessel that represents a different struggle. Whether it be pressures from budget cuts, parents' unrealistic expectations of the school, or children with a struggling home life, it's all in here in one big — depressing — package. The result is a very nihilistic movie that offers little to no hope in its story. I'm not opposed to bleakness in film — Mike Leigh's Naked (1993), a British classic, also happens to be drenched in bleakness, with characters that embody the darkest outlooks on life, with little to no hope to be found. Detachment presents itself in a similar vein but lacks the narrative focus found in Leigh's classic. The movie clocks in at around one hour and thirty minutes but features multiple perspectives from a wide array of characters, which it struggles to juggle. There is a talented ensemble cast curated here, but most of the runtime is dedicated to Brody's character. Brody is competent in the role, but it was never clear why this character was the focal point — he's not a particularly likeable character, and even in moments where he does a good deed, he does so with a dejected and defeated energy, making him feel predictable and unengaging. Marcia Gay Harden's character felt like the more interesting focal point, with her pressures kicking off the story. Not only was her character more intriguing, but with the movie covering multiple teachers, students, and parents, her character being the headteacher would have made for a much better narrative framework to connect all these characters and bring a more natural focus. The juggling nature of Detachment also carries through into its filmmaking. Tonally, as we cut between Brody's shift in the classroom and his extracurricular miseries, the film switches from dreamlike, surreal composition — like that of a Terrence Malick film — to a more grounded, documentarian shooting style. Both styles feel at odds with each other and never come together in a satisfying way. Chaotic energy is part of the film's DNA, and the editing does a lot to feed that through: fast-paced cutting, continuity errors, intercutting between perspectives. Some may argue that this is an intentional choice given the themes, but after a while it becomes overbearing. Heat's (1995) famous bank-robbery shootout scene hits as hard as it does not just because the action is so exhilarating, but also because the editing kicks into a different gear. The moment works because the edit contrasts with the rest of the film — Detachment never allows itself that same contrast. With so many different characters and perspectives, all rendered in that same frantic style, there's nothing to alleviate the gloom. What can't be argued is that Detachment comes from a place of real conviction. Carl's script is full of despair and rage, and the themes of his writing have been successfully translated to the screen. However, I just wish the film had a little more restraint.

ho pensieri contrastanti su questo film. Alla fine è indubbiamente molto carino, brody come sempre è il gotto ma purtroppo è il film stesso ad avere dei palesi problemi. Questo film cerca di trasmettere messaggi giusti come la critica alle istituzioni, alla società odierna, alla scuola, ai rapporti umani e chi più ne ha più ne metta. Tutti questi messaggi (anche se giusti per carità) hanno creato un minestrone confusionario di scene a tratti toccanti, a tratti quasi banali e non necessarie. Molti dei problemi trattati in questo film si sono praticamente ridotti a semplici clichè che non riescono effettivamente a far breccia completamente in chi guarda, infatti penso che per apprezzare questo film tu debba già aver condotto riflessioni e conclusioni in merito a questi argomenti per conto tuo, altrimenti purtroppo non riuscirà a passarti molto. In se comunque è un film carino, ma come detto prima, si è voluto fare troppo. Sebbene questo, almeno dalle descrizioni, fosse un film incentrato sulla scuola e le sue criticitá odierne, la parte più forte e toccante del film è stato il rapporto tra il protagonista ed erica, che sebbene l’inizio mi abbia dato l’impressione di una sindrome da crocerossina, si è evoluto bene e avrei gradito molto più un focus su quest’ultimo. Naw, I'd just work at Petco or something... One helluva gritty film... Adrien Brody plays a substitute teacher working at one of the roughest schools in the district. Though he's able to handle everything well, he has own personal problems and struggles under the weight of them. It's the bleak antithesis to those hopeful films where a teacher comes in and transforms the lives of the worst behaved students... Not even one second in this classroom and they're already threatening to beat his ass. Meanwhile, he remains stoic and handles his business without missing a beat. Brody is easily the greatest part of the film. The genius of this title is that you find its meaning through his persona where he's just so focused on doing what he needs to do, not letting a single thing get to him. Though he's primarily the focus, you also see just how many teachers are dealing with it. Some of them are struggling to keep it together and some have long sense just given in to the sheer insanity of it. Even in this, surprisingly lily white, school there are some kids in particular that are so deranged that they're destined to go and become the next Charles Manson. Some even threaten to do terrible things to the teachers. Each of their subplots shows that it's an endless cycle of abuse. Hell, after calmly enduring some petty shit on his first day, you see our protagonist go off on a healthcare worker. ( And yet...who shall weep for the nurses... ) On the messaging... I would absolutely be lying if I said that it didn't feel preachy in a way that feels more over-the-top, especially when they really hammer in the point that the parents are to blame for all of this. Some of the melodramatic piano music kinda lays it on way too thick rather than just letting the scenes speak for themselves. It never truly earns the emotion that it desperately wants you to have. Oftentimes, it's borderline darkly humorous simply because of how fucking insane this community is. It's like a damn hate sink where everyone is ready to attack any teacher that walks into that building. The speed at which he is falsely accused of being inappropriate, even when he got to know this teacher more closely than any of them, before they drop it seems like it was being evil just for the hell of it. While I understand that the students aren't meant to be the focus, since doing so would undermine the point of the film, they still feel like caricatures that don't seem realistic. They never show you small glimpses on how he's able to actually to transform this class. Still... As melodramatic as the entire subplot where he takes in a young runaway, you still have to admire just how heartfelt it is. In fact, I would argue and say they could've made a better film if it had focused solely on this. ( Which again, works to a fault because it shows just how much they try to cram things in... ) This cast was surprisingly stacked. James Caan reminded me how much I missed him. I shouldn't have lost it when I saw Isaiah Whitlock Jr. thinking he was going to say his immortal line. You can't deny that it's just a surface level dramatized view of just how terrible the education system within this country is. Nihilistic, but there is truth to it. I'd argue and say it's even worse than that. No matter what, there is absolutely no way in hell that I would work for any group beyond middle school. I always thought it took a special kinda person to want to teach those grades. Another one of those depressing films that don't offer you any true solutions by the end of it. Still makes me happy I was raised in the suburbs. "The worst part about this job is that nobody says thank you"...yeah, I can't even make a stupid joke about that...I felt that one...

o substituto é um filme que me interessa muito mais pela ferida que existe por trás de sua própria forma do que pela maneira como ele tenta falar sobre educação. porque tony kaye faz um filme sobre um professor substituto que entra numa escola pública em crise, mas filma esse ambiente como se estivesse entrando num lugar onde todas as pessoas já chegaram emocionalmente depois do fim do mundo. não existe propriamente a promessa de transformação pedagógica. existe exaustão. adrian brody é perfeito pra isso porque o personagem praticamente já chega interpretado pela própria postura corporal. henry não entra naquela escola com a energia do professor idealista que vai descobrir sua vocação. ele entra como alguém que aprendeu a não criar raízes. o título, é menos uma característica profissional do que uma estratégia de sobrevivência. ele observa alunos, colegas, familiares e desconhecidos, mas tenta não se deixar possuir por nenhum deles. a ironia é que o próprio ato de observar acaba produzindo vínculos que ele gostaria de evitar. e kaye filma essa distância de maneira muito particular. o filme parece estar constantemente oscilando entre documentário, drama televisivo, videoclipe, ensaio visual e diário subjetivo. tem câmera na mão, animação, desenhos sobre a imagem, fotografias, textos, imagens em baixa definição, cortes abruptos, planos que parecem ter sido arrancados de um arquivo pessoal. às vezes isso é poderoso porque dá a sensação de que estamos dentro de uma consciência fragmentada. outras vezes é excessivo, porque kaye parece tão ansioso pra comunicar o estado emocional do personagem que a própria forma começa a gritar aquilo que a atuação já estava dizendo. esse é, pra mim, o grande problema e também a grande virtude do filme. tony kaye é um diretor que não parece confiar na neutralidade da câmera. ele quer que cada sequência carregue uma posição emocional. em a outra história americana , isso aparecia através da manipulação formal e do contraste entre preto e branco e cor. aqui ele leva essa tendência pra um território ainda mais subjetivo. a escola não é simplesmente uma instituição filmada. ela é quase uma paisagem mental da alienação contemporânea. o problema é que o roteiro às vezes reduz essa complexidade a uma série de afirmações bastante explícitas. o filme quer falar sobre professores desvalorizados, adolescentes abandonados, famílias ausentes, burocracia educacional, sexualização precoce, depressão, pobreza e a transformação da escola em uma instituição que precisa administrar problemas sociais muito maiores do que ela consegue resolver. tudo isso é legítimo. mas frequentemente o filme parece ter medo de que o espectador não tenha entendido, então coloca outra camada de sofrimento por cima. isso fica especialmente evidente na maneira como alguns estudantes são construídos. há momentos em que eles parecem menos personagens do que manifestações de determinados problemas sociais. a garota prostituída, a adolescente que procura afeto, o aluno agressivo, a professora esgotada. o filme possui uma indignação genuína, mas às vezes sua indignação transforma pessoas em símbolos. é uma diferença importante: quando o filme observa uma pessoa sofrendo, ele pode ser devastador; quando precisa explicar o significado daquele sofrimento, torna-se muito mais convencional. e tem algo bastante curioso na relação entre henry e os alunos justamente porque ele tenta não ser o “salvador”. isso diferencia de boa parte do subgênero do professor inspirador. não existe uma grande sequência em que o professor encontra a técnica pedagógica perfeita e muda uma turma inteira. henry sabe que uma pessoa sozinha não consegue consertar uma estrutura social quebrada. ele pode escutar alguém, oferecer algum cuidado, impedir uma pequena tragédia, mas não pode transformar a escola em outra coisa. isso dá ao filme uma dimensão política interessante, mesmo quando ele se torna sentimental demais. a escola aparece como o lugar onde todas as falhas da sociedade chegam ao mesmo tempo. professores precisam lidar com alunos cuja vida doméstica está destruída, adolescentes procuram nos outros aquilo que não recebem em casa, administradores respondem a estatísticas e avaliações, famílias transferem responsabilidades. a escola não criou necessariamente essas condições. ela simplesmente é o lugar onde elas se tornam impossíveis de ignorar. por isso eu gosto particularmente das cenas em que o filme deixa de discursar e simplesmente acompanha henry trabalhando. existe uma tensão entre cuidar dos outros e não conseguir cuidar de si mesmo que brody sustenta muito bem. a voz baixa, o olhar cansado, a maneira como ele ocupa os espaços. ele não interpreta um homem vazio. interpreta alguém que construiu o vazio deliberadamente pra não precisar encarar aquilo que existe por baixo. e aí mercedes, a jovem prostituída torna essa contradição ainda mais dolorosa. a relação entre os dois funciona porque henry não consegue simplesmente permanecer um observador. ele reconhece nela uma vulnerabilidade que desperta algo que sua filosofia de distanciamento não consegue controlar. ao mesmo tempo, o filme precisa tomar cuidado pra não transformar essa relação em uma fantasia de redenção masculina, e felizmente tem momentos em que ele consegue preservar a assimetria e o desconforto da situação. o avô de henry também é essencial pra compreender o personagem. o passado não aparece apenas como informação biográfica, mas como aquilo que torna impossível pra ele permanecer completamente desprendido. o filme vai revelando que o “ substituto ” não nasceu de uma filosofia sofisticada. nasceu de trauma, culpa e perda. e isso é muito mais interessante do que a superfície de “professor desencantado”. por outro lado, existe uma espécie de romantização da depressão e do sofrimento que considero problemática. às vezes parece acreditar que quanto mais devastada estiver uma pessoa, mais profundamente humana ela é. a fotografia, a trilha, a montagem e as performances trabalham constantemente pra elevar a dor ao estatuto de experiência quase poética. em seus melhores momentos isso produz uma melancolia genuína. nos piores, parece que o filme está transformando sofrimento em estética. essa ambivalência é muito tony kaye. ele é um cineasta profundamente emocional, mas sua emoção frequentemente vem acompanhada de uma necessidade quase compulsiva de tornar visível a emoção. ele não quer apenas que você perceba que alguém está triste. quer que a textura da imagem fique triste, que a montagem fique triste, que o desenho fique triste, que a música fique triste. às vezes é lindo. às vezes é como alguém sublinhando três vezes uma frase que já estava sublinhada. no fim, acho que o título acaba sendo mais importante do que toda a retórica sobre educação. henry passa o filme tentando se manter separado do mundo, como se observar fosse uma maneira de não sofrer. mas a própria experiência de ensinar demonstra o contrário: olhar verdadeiramente pra outra pessoa já é uma forma de envolvimento. você pode se recusar a salvar o mundo, e provavelmente deve, porque ninguém consegue, mas não consegue observar uma pessoa em sofrimento indefinidamente sem que alguma coisa dentro de você responda. e talvez o filme seja mais forte justamente nessa contradição. henry quer ser espectador de uma sociedade em colapso, mas descobre que não existe posição neutra diante da dor. tony kaye pode exagerar, sentimentalizar e transformar sua indignação em espetáculo, mas é difícil dizer que ele não acredita profundamente naquilo que está filmando.
Bom filme, bem construído, boas cenas, abre muito à interpretação pessoal, bons atores. Senti um apelo à estética gótica, porém, nada que atrapalhe de verdade o enredo do filme.

In the beginning, I thought it was going to be an ultimate 5-star movie, but it just didn’t click for me. Neither did it make me feel anything, which is strange. The plot had everything, trauma, coping mechanisms, escapism, refusal to attach to people, isolation, incest, suicide, all the heaviest topics, yet it still made me feel nothing. I watched it throughout the day, 15 minutes at a time and finally finished it at midnight. We all go through difficult things, but self-isolation and detachment are simply not the solution. I think Henry ended up losing himself and even though he tried to make the world a bit better, he still hurt everyone around him. Also what Henry said about life being extremely hard and us simply needing to survive it, is one of the most demotivating things that leads to self-destruction and a pessimistic point of view. It won’t let you take pleasure in the small details of daily life. I don’t agree with this mindset and I generally don’t like people who live in grief and forget they only have one life to live, so wasting it on “detachment” and running away from yourself is kinda wrong. One more thing I really hated about this movie was when Henry said we are all the same. No, we are not. I definitely cannot relate to that kind of person. I appreciated a lot of things about him, but I disagree with him on a lot of topics. (Actually, maybe that was the point, to make us see where you end up by detaching yourself from your true nature and the rest of the world)

“A child’s intelligent heart can fathom the depth of many dark places. But can it fathom the delicate moment of its own detachment?” An “of its time” movie if I’ve ever seen one, early 2010s to its core. A predictable script sometimes lacking nuance, yet pristinely workable with stunning monologues littered throughout. The editing was surprisingly experimental, too; its use of mixed media and varied speed and colour added that extra bit of depth, and the wide angles were so jarring. I went in expecting a moving tale of the distressing complexities of being a teacher (think ‘Half Nelson’, ‘Steve’) but boy did Tony Kaye take this up a few notches. ‘Detachment’ covers so many bases you really don’t know which way it will turn next. Ultimately it is a simple encapsulation of how trauma is felt so profoundly, so vastly. It is generational and deeply cyclical, the ripple effect hard to avoid. Devastating on all accounts, but cynically hopeful (oh how I love a paradox). I, too, feel like a non-person.

Bien, sans être un très grand film. Henry Barthes est professeur remplaçant. Il est assigné trois semaines dans un lycée difficile de la banlieue new-yorkaise, et il s'efforce de toujours garder ses distances. Adrien Brody est excellent, et le personnage est bien plus complexe qu'il n'y paraît. Il n'est pas un saint : il a choisi le détachement pour se protéger des émotions négatives, sauf que ça le coupe aussi des positives. C'est ce qui rend le film juste il ne peut pas être là pour les deux filles qui auraient besoin de lui. Ce que Tony Kaye réussit, c'est le portrait du corps enseignant. Les espoirs, le doute, le ras-le-bol, la fatigue, parfois la haine du métier et des élèves. Chaque prof incarne une façon différente de tenir, et tous sont touchants. Kaye appelle ça un paysage d'émotions. Le film évite aussi le récit attendu. On croit qu'il va conquérir les gamins et leur redonner une voix, et Kaye refuse complètement ce jeu. Ma réserve : c'est parfois hyperbolique et didactique. Kaye assène ses points à coups de masse, et certaines scènes sont là uniquement pour choquer. On sent la volonté de nous mettre le nez dedans plus que la confiance dans le récit. Beau, dur, et un peu trop démonstratif pour moi.

"I'm not here,you may see me but I'm hollow" حين يصبح الابتعاد وسيلة للبقاء هناك أفلام تحاول أن تشرح لنا العالم، وهناك أفلام تجعلنا نشعر بثقله دون أن تمنحنا فرصة للهروب منه. وفيلم Detachment ينتمي إلى النوع الثاني؛ فهو ليس مجرد فيلم عن التعليم أو عن معاناة المعلمين والطلاب، بل تأمل مؤلم في الإنسان حين يصبح محاصرًا بين ما يشعر به وما يستطيع التعبير عنه، وبين حاجته إلى الآخرين وخوفه من الاقتراب منهم. منذ عنوانه، يضع الفيلم أمامنا فكرة أساسية: الانفصال العاطفي. ذلك الابتعاد الذي قد يبدو في البداية نوعًا من القوة أو السيطرة على الذات، لكنه قد يكون في الحقيقة وسيلة دفاع يلجأ إليها الإنسان بعدما يصبح الألم أكبر من قدرته على احتماله. فأحيانًا لا يبتعد الإنسان لأنه لا يحتاج إلى أحد، بل لأنه يحتاج إلى الآخرين أكثر مما يستطيع الاعتراف به. وأحيانًا لا يكون الصمت دليلًا على البرود، بل محاولة أخيرة لحماية ما تبقى من روح أنهكتها التجارب. ### الفكرة — عالم مليء بالناس، لكنه عاجز عن التواصل يتناول الفيلم عالم التعليم من زاوية تتجاوز المناهج والدرجات والنجاح الأكاديمي. فالمدرسة هنا ليست مجرد مكان لنقل المعرفة، بل مساحة تتقاطع فيها معاناة الطلاب، وعجز المعلمين، وضغوط المجتمع، وتلك المسافة المتزايدة بين الإنسان والإنسان. هنري بارثس، الذي يؤدي دوره أدريان برودي، معلم بديل ينتقل بين المدارس دون أن يسمح لنفسه بالانتماء الكامل إلى أي مكان. يبدو هادئًا ومتماسكًا، لكنه يحمل داخله ماضيًا مؤلمًا يجعله مترددًا في بناء علاقات عميقة مع الآخرين. إنه يعرف كيف يستمع، وكيف يفهم ألم الناس، لكنه يجد صعوبة في السماح لأحد بأن يقترب من ألمه الخاص. وهنا تكمن المفارقة التي يمنحها الفيلم عمقًا إنسانيًا كبيرًا: قد يكون الإنسان قادرًا على فهم الآخرين، لكنه عاجز عن إنقاذ نفسه. وقد يمنح الآخرين الكلمات التي يحتاجون إليها للاستمرار، بينما لا يجد الكلمات المناسبة ليواجه بها حياته. الفيلم لا يصور هنري باعتباره بطلًا مثاليًا أو شخصًا يمتلك إجابات عن كل شيء؛ بل يقدمه إنسانًا يحاول أن يؤدي دوره في عالم لا يعرف كيف يتعامل مع جراحه. وهذا ما يجعل شخصيته مؤثرة؛ لأنها لا تنتمي إلى عالم الأبطال الخارقين، بل إلى عالم الأشخاص الذين يواصلون حياتهم رغم أنهم لا يعرفون تمامًا كيف يفعلون ذلك. ### الإبداع في الطرح — الألم الذي لا يحتاج إلى صراخ من أكثر الجوانب إبداعًا في Detachment طريقته في تصوير المعاناة النفسية. فهو لا يعتمد دائمًا على الأحداث الكبيرة أو المواجهات المباشرة، بل يمنح التفاصيل الصغيرة مساحة واسعة كي تكشف ما تعجز الشخصيات عن قوله. تتداخل الصور والذكريات والحوارات والمونولوجات لتخلق إحساسًا بأننا لا نشاهد العالم من الخارج فقط، بل نقترب من الطريقة التي يراه بها إنسان مثقل بتجاربه. والمدرسة، بما تحمله من فوضى وضغوط وعلاقات متوترة، تصبح صورة مصغرة لمجتمع يعاني من أزمة أعمق: أزمة في القدرة على الإصغاء، وفي فهم احتياجات الآخرين، وفي الاعتراف بأن وراء كل سلوك إنسانًا له قصة لا نعرفها. إن الإبداع هنا ليس في تقديم فكرة جديدة تمامًا، بل في الطريقة التي تتشابك بها الأفكار الإنسانية مع الأسلوب السينمائي. فالفيلم يستخدم صورًا وتكوينات بصرية غير تقليدية ليجعلنا نشعر بالاضطراب الداخلي للشخصيات، وكأن الشكل نفسه أصبح امتدادًا لحالتها النفسية. ### التمثيل — أداء يحمل ما لا تقوله الكلمات يقدم أدريان برودي أداءً هادئًا ومشحونًا بالمشاعر المكبوتة. فهو لا يعتمد على الانفعالات الصاخبة بقدر ما يعتمد على النظرات، والتردد، ونبرة الصوت، والمسافة التي يتركها بين شخصيته وبين العالم المحيط بها. إن هنري شخصية يصعب فهمها بالكامل، وهذا جزء من قوتها. فكلما حاولنا الاقتراب منها، اكتشفنا أن هناك شيئًا لا تستطيع قوله، أو ربما لا تعرف كيف تقوله. وتقدم بيتي كاي، في دور إيريكا، حضورًا إنسانيًا مؤلمًا يضيف إلى الفيلم بعدًا آخر من أبعاد الإهمال والوحدة والحاجة إلى الحنان. ومن خلال الشخصيات المحيطة بهما، لا تبدو المعاناة حكرًا على فرد واحد، بل حالة تتخذ أشكالًا مختلفة، وتترك آثارًا متفاوتة في كل إنسان. قوة التمثيل في الفيلم تكمن في أنه لا يجعل الشخصيات مجرد أدوات لإيصال رسالة اجتماعية؛ بل يمنحها تناقضاتها وضعفها واحتياجاتها، حتى نشعر أن لكل منها حياة كاملة تتجاوز حدود الشاشة. ### الأثر النفسي — حين نكتشف أن الصمت ليس دائمًا سلامًا ربما أكثر ما يجعل الفيلم مؤثرًا هو أنه يضعنا أمام أشكال مختلفة من الوحدة. هناك من يختار الابتعاد عن الآخرين، وهناك من يُترك وحيدًا رغم محاولاته المستمرة للتواصل، وهناك من يعيش وسط الناس لكنه يشعر بأنه غير مرئي. والفيلم يجعلنا نتساءل: كم مرة مررنا بجانب إنسان ولم ننتبه إلى ما يحمله داخله؟ وكم مرة فسرنا صمت شخص بأنه عدم اهتمام، بينما كان في الحقيقة عاجزًا عن التعبير؟ وكم مرة أخفينا نحن أنفسنا خلف الهدوء، لأننا لم نعرف كيف نطلب المساعدة؟ إنه لا يطلب منا أن نبرر كل تصرف مؤلم، ولا أن نعتبر كل شخص ضحية بلا مسؤولية؛ بل يدعونا إلى أن نكون أكثر انتباهًا إلى التعقيد الإنساني الذي لا يظهر دائمًا على السطح. ومع ذلك، لا يقدم الفيلم الانفصال العاطفي باعتباره حلًا ناجحًا. فهو يكشف ثمنه أيضًا: أن تحمي نفسك من الألم قد يعني أحيانًا أن تحرمها من القرب والدفء والانتماء. وأن تتجنب التعلق بالآخرين قد يجنبك بعض الخسارات، لكنه قد يجعلك تخسر أشياء لا يمكن تعويضها. ### الخاتمة — أن تبقى إنسانًا رغم كل شيء Detachment ليس فيلمًا يمنحك شعورًا مريحًا بأن كل شيء سينتهي على ما يرام. إنه فيلم يتركك أمام أسئلة ثقيلة عن التعليم، والمجتمع، والطفولة، والوحدة، وعن قدرة الإنسان على الاستمرار حين لا يجد من يفهمه. لكنه، وسط كل هذا الألم، لا يخلو من لحظات إنسانية تذكّرنا بأن التواصل، مهما بدا صعبًا، يظل ممكنًا. وأن مجرد رؤية شخص آخر، والإصغاء إليه، والاعتراف بمعاناته، قد يكون أمرًا أكثر أهمية مما نتخيل. إن Detachment هو حكاية الإنسان الذي يبتعد عن العالم كي لا ينكسر، ثم يكتشف أن الابتعاد نفسه قد يكون شكلًا آخر من أشكال الانكسار. إنه فيلم عن أولئك الذين يواصلون أداء أدوارهم في الحياة، بينما يحملون في داخلهم أشياء لم يستطيعوا مواجهتها بعد. وعن أولئك الذين يمنحون الآخرين ما كانوا يتمنون أن يحصلوا عليه هم أنفسهم. وربما أكثر ما يبقى منه بعد المشاهدة هو هذا السؤال: هل نبتعد عن الآخرين لأننا لم نعد نحتاج إليهم، أم لأننا نخشى أن نحتاج إليهم ثم نفقدهم؟ قد لا يقدم الفيلم إجابة نهائية، لكنه يجعلنا ندرك أن الإنسان، مهما حاول أن يبدو مكتفيًا بنفسه، يظل بحاجة إلى أن يُرى، وأن يُفهم، وأن يشعر بأنه ليس وحده في هذا العالم.

Narra a trajetória de um professor substituto que tenta ao máximo salvar os adolescentes de se entregarem à decisões erradas ou simplesmente desistirem de tentar. Além de ser um homem solitário cheio de traumas e problemas para resolver, ele não deixa de se preocupar com o próximo. Pra mim fica evidente quando ele traz Erica pra casa, uma adolescente que vendia seu corpo nas ruas por dinheiro, ele tenta ajuda-lá porque sabe que ela não tá ali por prazer ou porque acha certo, ela tá ali por abandono, falta de instrução. E por ter visto a mãe dele se matar de overdose, ele talvez se enxergasse um pouco nela (erica) na perspectiva de ser uma pessoa lidando com problemas e enxerga também a própria mãe nela porque sabe que para ela se matar assim como fez a mãe dele é muito provável. O filme inteiro ele tenta ser forte ajudando pessoas com os problemas delas, sendo que ele mesmo não suporta os dele.

Detachment felt less like watching a movie and more like sitting in a room where nobody knows how to ask for help Every character looked like they were carrying something heavy without ever saying it out loud The film is quiet but not empty and every scene has this strange feeling that something is already broken before it even starts Adrien Brody was honestly the reason I stayed completely invested because he never tries to force emotions yet you can feel every single one of them just by the way he looks at people The movie is not subtle all the time and sometimes it pushes its message a little harder than it needs to but somehow it still works because the emotions feel real instead of manipulated There were moments that genuinely hurt not because they were dramatic but because they felt familiar in a way that is difficult to explain It is one of those films that makes you think about the people around you after it ends and reminds you that everyone is fighting something you probably will never see The ending did not leave me shocked or amazed It left me quiet and I think that was exactly the point Not every story is supposed to fix the pain sometimes it just wants you to acknowledge that it exists I would not call this a masterpiece because it has a few moments where it loses its balance but it definitely stayed in my head much longer than I expected

I expected this to be primarily about the school system and while it of course is, on a broader scale it feels like it tackles generational divide more than anything. The youth are expected to learn and be guided by those who came before, but what of the problems plaguing that generation? How can you teach and guide when you feel aimless and lost yourself? Being older does not inherently mean being wiser, and so often these people are thrust into a position of responsibility when they were never given the guidance they’re now expected to pass on. These issues chain all the way back through the generations that came before and they will continue to all those that will follow. At one point do you change from the person who is guided to the one who guides, and what do you do if you’re wholly unprepared for that? Until we can solve that question, the kids really don’t stand a chance.
