Poor Things: Slut-Shaming Happening Both Onscreen and Off When a film receives such high praise while simultaneously stirring up so much controversy, where exactly does the problem lie? Is it the film itself, the audience, or even society at large? The movie is saturated with explicit sex scenes—some have gone so far as to call it pornography, saying "male audiences are having the best time." Others have gone further, questioning whether the film is a faux-feminist work riddled with the male gaze (their reasoning being that both the screenwriter and director are men). Yes, the male gaze is indeed pervasive—but it comes from a portion of the audience's own male gaze, as well as from a strain of feminism so pedantic it engages in self-imposed moral policing. A feminism that stigmatizes sex and refuses to engage with it is, in truth, still thinking through a patriarchal lens. (1) Only "Sluts" Exist, Never "Man-Whores"? "The sexuality of a woman as private property is moral; the sexuality of a woman as a subject is immoral." This notion almost fundamentally encapsulates the logic behind most of the moral criticism surrounding this film. From a modern societal perspective, attaching moral constraints to sex is perfectly reasonable—the problem is that rather than applying such standards equally to everyone, patriarchy's stigmatization of sex is aimed specifically at women. So when audiences watch Bella on the big screen masturbating without an ounce of shame, having sex with various men, and actively choosing to become a prostitute, plenty of viewers conclude that Bella is a "slut." They see her becoming a sex worker as a form of self-objectification—even though Bella is far from ordinary, possessing none of society's ingrained moral constructs. She masturbates simply for pleasure; her sexual encounters with various men are entirely consensual—she is, as a subject, freely unleashing her desires. (Setting aside the question of whether unrestrained indulgence is justifiable, the key point here is subject versus object.) Yet audiences still insist on seeing her as an object, convinced that she has been reduced to a product whose purpose is to please men with sex. They believe that female sexual liberation is a form of self-deception, that in the end women are still being "taken advantage of" by men. So the film's abundant display of the female lead's sexual scenes actually carries no inherent sense of the gaze—it is simply presentation. Yet many female viewers feel uncomfortable with the sex scenes in the film, developing a sense that these scenes come from a male-gaze perspective. In reality, it's because they have preemptively placed themselves in the position of the object, the passive party—a mindset that presupposes oneself as the victim. So when they see the female lead's sex scenes, and it happens that the director is male, they begin to conspiracy-theorize that patriarchal forces are trying to reap benefits by encouraging female sexual liberation. They think the film is patriarchy's sugar-coated trap—but in truth, patriarchy's trap was already planted in their own minds long ago. It's worth noting that the rakish lawyer Duncan in the film proudly boasts about having slept with many women. No one morally condemns him for it. Offscreen, men are likewise never shamed for having extensive sexual experience—on the contrary, they're seen as "impressive." And yet this same Duncan still believes he has the right to criticize Bella as a slut. So it turns out only "sluts" exist—never "man-whores." (2) Enlightenment Through Prostitution? One of the film's most controversial plot points is Bella actively choosing to become a prostitute—and clearly maturing and growing through that experience. This has led many to crudely interpret it as the director suggesting that prostitution can foster a woman's intellectual growth. Admittedly, the film's chosen mode of expression is provocative, but this prostitution episode is more symbolic of what the world perceives as "depravity." "We must experience everything—not just the good, but depravity, fear, and sorrow too." This doesn't mean we all need to become sex workers; rather, it means that experiencing hardship does indeed open the door to a person's inner world of thought and spirit. Someone who has only ever experienced pleasant things is destined never to become a mature person capable of deep reflection. (3) Is the Film Advocating Sexual Liberation? What About Social Systems? So the film does explore desire, but its purpose is not to advocate unbridled indulgence. And desire comes in many forms—sex is merely one dimension of it. But undeniably, sex delivers the greatest visual impact, and shattering ingrained perceptions requires a certain degree of shock. Therefore, the film's abundance of sexual imagery is not trying to say that sexual liberation is the most important pillar of feminism, nor is it attempting to obscure other issues. It isn't even really a feminist film—one might sooner call it a libertarian film that takes a passing jab at patriarchy. Don't forget that Bella is an infant in a fully grown body, devoid of society's ingrained moral constructs, utterly loyal to her own instincts and desires. We can never become Bella. Rather, through the shock that Bella's behavior delivers to us, we become aware of how much society's concepts restrict our thinking—how they keep us trapped in perpetual cycles of self-moralizing and judging others. As a surreal film with absurdist themes, it is destined to be considered immoral by society's moral standards. Fixating on that point yields little of value. We don't need to—and cannot—become Bella, nor do we need to impose moral constraints on Bella or the film. But that doesn't stop me from intuitively finding something beautiful in Bella's purity. Ultimately, a film can never change society. When it tries to point out the absurdity of certain social rules, the public turns around and accuses it of being heretical. Perhaps it is destined to be something the masses cannot understand—poor things, pointing straight at you and me.

Watch something else.

Jean-Marc Vailée’s “Dallas Buyers Club” is an utterly adequate film. A competently made film that lacks artistic merit and solely exists to imitate other, much better, films.

نقد فیلم Dallas Buyers Club Dallas Buyers Club فیلمی درباره ایدز و داستان واقعی Ron Woodroof است؛ مردی مبتلا به HIV که پس از تشخیص بیماری، برای پیدا کردن درمان به سراغ داروهای مختلف می‌رود و در ادامه کسب‌وکاری برای رساندن دارو به بیماران راه می‌اندازد. اما مشکل اصلی من با فیلم این است که به جای پرداختن عمیق به تجربه انسانی بیماری، رنج و ترس از مرگ، خیلی زود به یک درام هالیوودی درباره تحول یک قهرمان و نجات دیگران تبدیل می‌شود. فیلمنامه برای من بسیار کلیشه‌ای و قابل‌پیش‌بینی است. Ron در ابتدا مردی متعصب و مخالف همجنسگرایان و افراد ترنس است و سپس با Rayon، یک زن ترنس، آشنا می‌شود. این رابطه قرار است یکی از مهم‌ترین بخش‌های تحول Ron باشد، اما به نظرم اصلاً رابطه‌ای عمیق و انسانی شکل نمی‌گیرد. بیشتر شاهد یک تضاد آشنای «مرد دگرجنسگرا و متعصب در برابر فرد ترنس» هستیم که بارها در سینما دیده‌ایم. شخصیت Rayon نیز به اندازه کافی ساخته نمی‌شود؛ او بیشتر وسیله‌ای برای ایجاد تحول در Ron است تا یک انسان مستقل با گذشته، پیچیدگی و زندگی خودش. تحول Ron هم برای من باورپذیر نیست. او در ابتدا از بیماری خودش وحشت‌زده و ناراحت است، اما خیلی سریع از یک فرد خودمحور به شخصیتی تبدیل می‌شود که می‌خواهد دیگران را نجات دهد. فیلم تقریباً او را به یک قهرمان نجات‌بخش تبدیل می‌کند؛ چیزی شبیه همان الگوی آشنای هالیوودی که در آن شخصیت اصلی پس از یک بحران، معنای زندگی‌اش را در نجات دیگران پیدا می‌کند. من این تحول را به اندازه کافی در رفتار و شخصیت او نمی‌بینم؛ بیشتر نتیجه آن را می‌بینم. از طرف دیگر، فیلم برای من واقعاً درباره ایدز نیست. ایدز بیشتر تبدیل به موتور داستان تحول Ron شده است. فیلم می‌توانست درباره ترس از مرگ، درد جسمی، تنهایی، از دست دادن آینده و تأثیر بیماری بر روابط انسانی باشد، اما خیلی زود به داستان مبارزه Ron با سیستم دارویی و تلاش او برای رساندن دارو به دیگران تبدیل می‌شود. به همین دلیل، تجربه انسانی بیماری برای من عمق کافی پیدا نمی‌کند. تقابل فیلم با شرکت داروسازی و سیستم پزشکی نیز بیش از حد سیاه و سفید است. Ron بیش از اندازه سفید می‌شود و طرف مقابل بیش از اندازه سیاه. به جای یک تضاد پیچیده میان منافع اقتصادی، پزشکی، قانون و نیاز بیماران، فیلم بیشتر یک طرف را قهرمان و طرف دیگر را مانع نشان می‌دهد. این ساده‌سازی، به نظرم از پیچیدگی داستان کم می‌کند. حتی شخصیت‌های فرعی نیز فرصت کافی برای تبدیل شدن به انسان‌های واقعی پیدا نمی‌کنند. فیلم بیشتر از آنها برای پیشبرد داستان Ron استفاده می‌کند. بنابراین وقتی اتفاقات تلخ برای بعضی شخصیت‌ها رخ می‌دهد، تأثیر احساسی آن برای من چندان زیاد نیست؛ چون پیش از آن رابطه انسانی عمیقی با آنها ساخته نشده است. با این حال، بازی متیو مک‌کانهی را نمی‌توان نادیده گرفت. به‌خصوص در دقایق ابتدایی، زمانی که Ron برای نخستین بار متوجه می‌شود HIV دارد، بازی او واقعاً باورپذیر است. در همان چند دقیقه، ترس و شوک شخصیت را می‌توان احساس کرد. تغییرات فیزیکی او نیز قابل توجه است. اما برای من حتی بازی خوب مک‌کانهی هم نمی‌تواند ضعف شخصیت‌پردازی و فیلمنامه را جبران کند. بازی جرد لتو نیز به نظرم بیش از آنکه از عمق شخصیت ناشی شود، روی یک شخصیت کلیشه‌ای بنا شده است. از نظر کارگردانی و فرم نیز فیلم برای من چیز ویژه‌ای ندارد. دوربین عمدتاً نامرئی است و از خودنمایی پرهیز می‌کند. بیشتر با نماهای مدیوم و تصاویر نسبتاً معمولی روبه‌رو هستیم. این رویکرد لزوماً ضعف نیست، اما برای من ویژگی بصری خاصی هم ایجاد نمی‌کند. پایان فیلم نیز کاملاً در همان مسیر کلیشه‌ای قرار می‌گیرد: قهرمانی که مبارزه می‌کند، به دیگران کمک می‌کند و در نهایت اطلاعاتی درباره سرنوشت واقعی شخصیت‌ها روی تصویر می‌آید. این پایان به جای اینکه نتیجه طبیعی و انسانی روایت باشد، برای من بیشتر شبیه جمع‌بندی آشنای یک درام هالیوودی است. در نهایت، Dallas Buyers Club برای من فیلمی است که ایده و موضوع بسیار مهمی دارد، اما ظرافت انسانی لازم برای پرداختن به آن را ندارد. فیلم می‌توانست درباره ایدز، مرگ، تنهایی، تعصب، دوستی و تغییر انسان باشد، اما بیشتر به یک داستان کلیشه‌ای درباره تحول یک مرد و نجات دیگران تبدیل شده است. نقطه قوت اصلی آن برای من چند دقیقه ابتدایی و بازی باورپذیر متیو مک‌کانهی است؛ اما این نقاط قوت برای جبران ضعف‌های فیلمنامه و شخصیت‌پردازی کافی نیستند. نمره: ۱.۵ از ۵

Biggest piece of dogshit I’ve seen this year. One of the most glaring issues with this film is how they turned Ron Woodruff into a raging homophobe, when in reality he was an openly bisexual man and an ally to the LGBT community — in deeply conservative 1980s Texas, no less. Instead, the filmmakers reshaped his story to make it more palatable: a homophobic man who spews slurs throughout the film, and as if that weren’t enough, contracts HIV and then supposedly becomes an “ally” — not because he actually joins or supports the LGBT community, but because he’s profiting off selling drugs to the HIV/AIDS community. He was never really part of the LGBT community; he was just making money off it. And no amount of praise for Jared Leto’s performance changes the fact that his portrayal was ultimately anti-trans. For one, this character doesn’t even exist. Worse, he plays into the tired trope of depicting a trans woman as “a man in a dress” — reinforcing the homophobic idea that trans women are just men in disguise. The film is shot decently well and the pacing is fine, but all of this leaves a genuinely bad taste in my mouth.

Clube de Compras Dallas definitivamente não funcionou para mim. Apesar de ser um filme muito elogiado, senti que ele se apoia mais no na ideia da sua trama e na relevância do tema do que na construção de uma narrativa realmente envolvente. O maior problema foi a redundância. A trama parece operar em um raciocínio circular, repetindo conflitos, falas e situações sem que haja uma evolução orgânica capaz de manter o interesse do espectador. Em vários momentos tive a impressão de que o filme estava muito mais fascinado pela própria proposta do que realmente disposto a desenvolvê-la de maneira rica e complexa. Também não consegui me conectar com os personagens. Não gostei do protagonista e tampouco do restante do elenco principal. Consequentemente, o drama vivido por eles não me afetou. A luta contra a AIDS, o preconceito e o sistema de saúde é um tema extremamente relevante e com enorme potencial dramático, mas, aqui, a abordagem me pareceu distante e pouco interessante. Em nenhum momento me emocionei, me comovi ou sequer me diverti acompanhando a história. Com efeito, a trama oferece poucos atrativos além de sua proposta inicial. O filme parece apostar quase exclusivamente na transformação de Ron Woodroof e em sua batalha contra a burocracia, mas o desenvolvimento acaba sendo repetitivo, sem grandes surpresas ou momentos de impacto. Até o próprio “ clube de compras ”, que dá nome ao filme e deveria ser o centro da narrativa, acaba parecendo secundário, o que me fez passar boa parte do filme pensando: cadê o clube de compras? Reconheço o comprometimento do elenco, mas, para mim, boas interpretações não foram suficientes para compensar uma história que considerei pouco (ou nada) instigante. No fim das contas, achei Clube de Compras Dallas um filme pretensioso, autossuficiente, preso à própria importância temática porém incapaz de transformar um tema tão pertinente em uma experiência verdadeiramente impactante ou divertida.

The Dallas Buyers Club that is not about the Dallas Buyers Club at all. This isn't an entirely bad movie, but to me it wasn't all that great either. I'm very conflicted when it comes to this film. It does have some high notes: the acting performances and the chemistry displayed from Matthew McConaughey and Jared Leto was great, it is a heartbreaking narrative, and contained solid cinematography. However, there are some very low points for me about this film I experienced both throughout and after the film. For example, while a true story, the script seems so artificial to me. It had no real flow, and just felt like a compilation of randomness piled onto each other for two hours. I know what the movie is about, yet I was asking myself multiple times while watching: what is this movie really even about? 2 hours felt like 4 for this movie. I'd wish we spend more time on Ron Woodroff's character before the diagnosis as well, instead of straight....BOOM....AIDS. The exposition seemed so rushed for the film. After finishing the film as well, I did research and realized that Jared Leto's character didn't even exist in real life, so it makes me question the meaning of the character in the first place... To push a narrative? To exaggerate what the lesson of the movie is supposed to be? It doesn't make sense to me. Also, according to Ron Woodroof’s primary care physician, Dr. Steven Pounders, Woodroof's ex-wife Brenda stated that he was bisexual. This is a massive contradiction than what we saw on the screen. Overall, this movie didn't do it for me. 4/10

"[Woodroof] and other characters denounce [AZT] as 'toxic,' and Woodroof recommends that customers of the buyers club dispose of what AZT they have and never take it again.... One could be forgiven for coming away [from the movie] with the sense that the medical community was poisoning HIV/AIDS patients with the drug, and keeping them from other, safer, therapies. The trouble is that AZT is actually a very effective therapy against HIV/AIDS. 'People who were consistently using AZT prolonged life for one year,' says Jonathan Engel, a medical historian at Baruch College and author of 'The Epidemic: A History of AIDS.' That may not sound like a lot, but at a time when the disease had a mortality rate of 100 percent, anything that delayed death was valuable.'" 'The stuff he was importing from Mexico was almost all useless,' Engel says. A case in point is the experimental drug Peptide T. '[Woodruff] did become a proponent of Peptide T, and he used it himself, and believed it himself,' [cofounder of the Treatment Action Group Peter] Staley says. 'It never panned out. It's a useless therapy, and it never got approved, and nobody uses it today, but the film implies that it helped him.'" Another drug that Woodroof sold, "Compound Q," was actively dangerous: "Compound Q...backfired, with at least two deaths linked to it over the course of two trials (one FDA-approved, one run "guerrilla-style" by the activist Martin Delaney). 'When it became apparent that it could kill people, the FDA tried to get buyers clubs to pull it, and everyone did pull it, except Ron Woodroof,' Staley recalls." - The Washington Post, 2013 Great movie, great acting, a terrible historical biopic that spreads dangerous lies about the AIDS crisis.

The only attempt at an actual openly lgbt character (as in, one who is given a personality) is Rayon, the trans woman played by Jared Leto and I believe the movie shows some implicit judgement towards her. McConaughey's character gets clean almost immediatly and becomes very proactive in trying to maintain his health. Rayon keeps engaging in harmful habits which make her appear more at fault for her own tragic death. Practically from the moment you see her she seems doomed, you know her choices and lifestyle are leading to her demise. And given this is a film about AIDS with a straight protagonist, that juxtaposition feels weirdly like victim blaming. "They had it coming but here's a film about the disease affecting normal everyday heterosexual people you can actually empathisize with and who try to do something about it instead of laying around being tragic" I know this has some basis on real people and I don't mean to say we can't focus on atypical protagonists for these types of stories, but the very sparse (or straight up absent) portrayal of the queer community's coordinated actions to handle the crisis and the focus instead on a straight man's individual efforts felt off and distracted me throughout the movie.
Men have it easy, they just need a generic script to secure acting wins while women have been delivering experimental and exciting performances for decades and still get snubbed

for a film which mathew mccoughney seemed to have fully locked in, DBC offers very less for a biopic of an actual man. it’s the raging homophobia - that’s slowly turned into sympathy since the community is suddenly profitable - to the enlightenment that only comes post a sacrifice of a close one (on whom the onus laid unsaid yet heavily to somehow transform a pretty aggressive character’s arc) i am not sure if this trajectory is something that woodrof deserved. or for that matter, even mccoughney who very clearly gave it his all deserved either. i also could understand why would misgendering of a transwoman probably exist in the 80s, but for a film that was made in 2013, rayon could have been played by anyone but a cis-het and rather offensive jared leto. in totality of it, i kept wanting to see the queer characters also trying to live their lives, instead of them just being miserable folks who just gather some money in order to score some drugs so they can live another day while a proudly straight protagonist makes an empire out of it. in fact, i kept waiting to see homosexuality roaring unashamed unafraid in the face of woodrof, like sure, think whatever you hold against us that’s totally your personal problem, gurl. but no, that power was never given into the hands of the characters opressed. all you get to feel towards them is sadness. as if the film never cared much for them, it’s as if they remained largely invisible, and suddenly AIDS is huge because a straight guy got it. and that’s just, sad .

Gonna get the obvious pitfalls out the way. This film is too young to be casting a cisgender man in a trans woman’s role. Boooooo!! The directors comments on this matter prove his ignorance to the community which his film is about whether he makes it about a straight guy or not. Second of all, given that it is likely that Woodroof was actually a bisexual man himself makes it a little weird that his movie version is so homophobic during this film and it is even more lgbtq erasure when added to rayons casting. I guess it’s because it’s about a journey of acceptance so definitely adds the drama but if that was the case they should’ve made the adaptation looser, not used their real names etc. other than that, this film is emotional, narratively gripping and brilliantly performed. Mcconaughey gives one of my favourite performances ever. He incredibly skilfully gives Ron so much charisma that his downfalls can be overlooked as he makes an incredibly long journey of his homophobia and he sells his desperation and heartache so well. He also is really good at making Ron the obvious dumbass that he is but also seem incredibly intelligent and dedicated when it comes to his work where you are pleasantly surprised for the character. The supporting performances are all also very nice. I found the constant hospital vibe, through the lighting or bustle or kind of minimal and slightly dingy set design really poignant in this, you can really feel everything weighing down on the dbc at all times. The fda are satisfyingly evil. The speed at which Ron moves through his character arc varies, starting with all the slurs and such and just as you think it’s gone he shows some small signs, a little comment about sissy San Francisco judges or being clearly interested in the money a lot of the time through his gold jewellery of even keeping hold of his cash whilst giving rayon his last hug.  The bond with rayon is clear and there. I think a lot of criticisms come from rayon as a character which I don’t prescribe to. There is that Ron gives her the complete bare minimum in not treating him with absolute vitriol which she feels so happy with, and the other is that she serves no purpose other than to teach Ron a lesson. I think that her happiness with Ron’s change makes sense, as they clearly formed a bond whether Ron liked it or not and he also was clearly helping the queer community. He was very interested in the profits but he did also clearly care about his clients health. I also don’t think rayons only purpose was in teaching Ron a lesson. I think that if the film is about the determination to live, she represents the colour in that, which you can really feel when she goes to the bank in a black suit for her own funeral, looking sickly with her natural hair. I do think this film shows sensitivity to the queer community, just not nearly enough for the topic it handles which is why I stunted the stars in my rating. But if you manage to ignore that it is a gorgeous story and a wonderful arc, completely by one character and failed by another, which mcconaughey absolutely carries, not to say I didn’t think this had some really great cinematography with some wondershots as well as cool sound design. I think the constant tinnitus at one point made me say ‘wow why do they keep using this it’s getting repetitive’ but eventually I realised that it acts as a reminder whenever things are going well that health wise Ron is just as doomed as he was at the beginning, he just managed to borrow some time. A very sad film. The look on mcconaugheys face when he gets clapped by his team is heartbreaking

The way it sustained tension for a long time to show inner changes, along with its realistic and documentary-like style, felt slow and dull to me. It’s a film that captures the life of a resilient person who truly lived such a remarkable life.

Much like the party that Costa throws for Tommy, Project X seems determined to be the big, explosive, definitive conclusion to the “one crazy party” sub-genre of comedy. It has everything that could possibly excite a heterosexual teenage boy in the early 2010s – alcohol, drugs, boobs, stunts, implied sex, and everything in between. And for the most part, its mission is successful; later movies that delve into this sandbox, like Office Christmas Party , don’t quite have their hearts in the same place, and it comes off feeling more tired than energetic. My feelings on Project X are actually pretty similar to Office Christmas Party – the debauchery is hardly engaging, and since that’s what the whole film is supposedly barreling towards, it has to be pretty compelling to break through. At least Project X has the excuse of solely focusing on the party. I am not exaggerating when I say there is nothing more to this film than the insanity and excess that comes from an out-of-control hormonal rager. Most of the characters are irredeemably annoying, but that’s nothing new for a film of this caliber. Their values (which, as far as I can tell, bear little difference from the movie as a whole) feel antiquated, even for 2012. It may have intentionally provided an apex (which, in turn, may have killed the sub-genre), but that doesn’t quite dovetail with the quality of the movie itself, as hard as it tries to make itself stand out. It doesn’t matter how cool you were or weren’t in high school; the shenanigans in Project X are more exhausting than anything else.

Project X si rivela una discreta commedia adolescenziale costruita con l'efficace espediente del falso documentario. Al di là della componente comica, il film propone una critica agli eccessi della gioventù e al bisogno quasi ossessivo di ottenere accettazione e popolarità. La gigantesca festa, dominata da alcol, droga e sesso, diventa così il simbolo di una ribellione adolescenziale destinata a sfuggire completamente di mano. La scelta di alternare riprese con telecamera a mano, cellulari e dashcam rende il racconto dinamico e immersivo, trasmettendo allo spettatore il progressivo deterioramento della situazione e la perdita di controllo dei protagonisti. È proprio attraverso questo caos crescente che il film racconta le conseguenze della ricerca esasperata di approvazione sociale. Il finale, volutamente sopra le righe, risulta forse fin troppo esagerato e poco credibile, ma si inserisce perfettamente nel tono folle e irriverente dell'opera. Nel complesso, Project X è una commedia divertente e coinvolgente che, dietro la sua leggerezza, riesce anche a offrire qualche spunto di riflessione sugli eccessi e sulle fragilità dell'adolescenza.

While this movie is nowhere near as good as those, I would argue that it captures its moment with far more specifity as those all have some relevance or takeaways that can still resonate. This is a cultural artifact that offers nothing more than a time capsule into the worst aspects of 2012 culture. That’s sounds harsh but considering I was the exact age/grade of the characters in this movie in 2012, I think I have a modest level of authority to speak on this topic. I think it’s really entertaining for the most part despite how unbelievable it was. But I’m not going to say it’s a good movie that holds up to time. It was never meant to be that anyway. That’s what makes it special. I should’ve poured a beer on my rug to fully immerse myself in the experience.

It’s certainly not a particularly brilliant film, but in its simplicity and sheer stupidity, it still manages to get more than a few laughs. More importantly, though, it captures the carefree nature of adolescence remarkably well, and more specifically, the culture of seeking fun through getting wasted that was so typical of Millennials. More than anything for its comedy, it works as a snapshot of a generation and a particular way of experiencing adolescence. A film that will probably resonate more with, and be more appreciated by, those who actually lived through that generation firsthand.

To be fair, American Sniper is a pretty well made film (apart from the fake baby), I found the action sequences entertaining, and Bradley Cooper’s performance was impressive given he’d mostly only been in comedies before it. The cinematography isn’t groundbreaking but there’s definitely attention to detail in the shot choices. My issues are with the screenplay. I found the strong theme of good vs evil with an unwaveringly heroic portrayal of America’s role in the Iraq war uncomfortable to watch. While bias isn’t inherently an issue, given the film is based on true events and the controversies surrounding such a significant war, I’d be concerned about someone watching the film who wasn’t aware of the context and details. His eagerness to kill (regardless of the validity of his motives) made it difficult for me to sympathise with Kyle. Furthermore, he comes across as even more unapologetically patriotic in his autobiography claiming that everyone he killed “deserved to die”. I personally find this troubling as a sentiment and wouldn’t choose to hail the person who said it to the extent Eastwood does in the film. I appreciate that since it’s based on a book, Eastwood is somewhat limited in shaping the narrative, however, I found the sequencing slightly messy and was disappointed by the dropping and ambiguity of various plot lines. I may not be the target audience for American Sniper and perhaps I’d rate it higher if I was from the US. But then I do think The Hurt Locker is an incredible film and that’s pretty American.

Once again Clint Eastwood doesn’t simply create a conservative-wet-dream here, even if sometimes in the discourse about this film, the idea might come up; I definitely disagree with the claim, that this is a glorification of the Iraq-war or any US-military operation in the western Asian area of the past 30 years. I think Eastwood simply tells the story of war from the perspective of a “brain-washed” American soldier and thus wants to us see, what someone sees, who was brought up with a rifle in their hands already and frightened by the media, who created the picture of the “dangerous Muslim terrorist” in the minds of Americans after 9/11. The central question to ask is: does Eastwood side with Bradley Cooper’s character or does he just observe his actions. When you think, that he sides with “Chris Kyle”, then this film is on the same territory as something like Michael Bay’s “Pearl Harbour”, where the US-Army is glorified. I don’t think that we are on such territory here. Through the direction and also through Cooper’s performance there is always a distinct rift between the viewer and “Kyle” as a character. Eastwood doesn’t allow us to fully identify with him. He is definitely depicted as a slightly weird guy, who is drawn into the entire topic of war and the horrors, that come with it and who also doesn’t really understand, what his actions really mean; he is someone, who cannot see clear about the horrors, that he commits, which is also why he doesn’t feel sorry. But that doesn’t mean that Eastwood himself wants us to be the same. For me this is — much like other Clint Eastwood movies, whose style of conservative filmmaking is (as I have pointed out recently in my review for “J. Edgar”) much more nuanced — an observers view on a system, where technically we should feel pity for those people, who are unable to see behind the curtain and fall right into the traps. Thus it’s also a bit dull to call this movie out for being too focussed on the American perspective and seemingly uninterested about the casualties that this man creates in Iraq. Eastwood simply doesn’t want to show this here; his focus is the story of a soldier’s life, that is destroyed by a war-machinery, that makes him believe to be heroic part of something, while eventually he’s just ammunition for the interest of someone else — kind of the idea that the first two acts of “Born of the Fourth of July” follows. This is also hauntingly shown, when “Kyle” is back home for a short time and shows his son to use a rifle, just like his father did. The cycle of violence won’t stop here, because these people are trapped in the world of serving someone else’s interests — something that’s incredibly far away from the ideology that I’d associate with Clint Eastwood. So all in all it’s a film about the lost lives of soldiers and as such it succeeds mostly. I decided to still give a rather mid rating, because for me the runtime is too long, especially since the story gets a little repetitive the longer “Kyle” stays in the war-zone. A higher focus on “Kyle’s” family life and the destruction of it would have made a better movie in my opinion, even if Eastwood is able to create some intense fighting scenes. But this should have been more like “The Best Years of our Lives” or “Apocalypse Now” and less like “Warfare”, because there’s no way that I won’t get bored at 130 minutes of people shooting around in the desert.

American Sniper works because it makes the story feel personal. The film is tense, well staged, and easy to become emotionally invested in. You are not just watching military operations from a distance. You are watching what those experiences do to the person living through them. That is what makes the film compelling. The action sequences are intense, but the quieter moments matter just as much because they show the psychological weight that comes with everything happening on screen. There is a constant feeling that the character is caught between two worlds. The battlefield. And home. And the transition between them never feels simple. That makes the story easy to connect with on an emotional level, even if the actual experiences are obviously far removed from everyday life. The direction does a good job of making the tension immediate. You understand the pressure of making decisions in seconds. You feel how quickly situations can change. And you understand why those experiences do not simply disappear when someone returns home. That emotional side is what stayed with me most. The film is not perfect, but it is gripping, well performed, and strong enough to make you care about the person at the center of it. A tense and emotionally engaging war drama that works best when it focuses on the psychological weight carried home from the battlefield.

American Sniper is a very good film, even if Chris Kyle himself is a more complicated figure than the film really gets into. Bradley Cooper is excellent, and the combat scenes are tense without feeling like they are there just to look cool. The film does a good job showing the pressure of constantly going back into that environment and then trying to act normal at home afterwards. I also think it brings up issues that do not get talked about enough, especially what repeated deployments, combat stress and that kind of responsibility can do to someone mentally. That said, knowing Kyle exaggerated or made questionable claims in interviews does affect how I view the film a bit, especially when it presents him in such a straightforward heroic way. Still, as a film it is gripping, well acted and genuinely intense. The person behind the story is more complicated than the movie makes him seem, but the movie itself is very effective.

​"Aim small, miss small." ​It is incredibly easy to see why this gets written off as the ultimate "dude-bro American propaganda" movie. It is intensely, unapologetically American, and it absolutely flattens a complex geopolitical conflict into a straightforward "America is the hero" narrative. You could go on for hours about this, and honestly, most of those critiques would be entirely well-placed. It’s also not a technically brilliant film—the pacing can feel incredibly choppy, the visual style is pretty flat, and yes, that notorious fake plastic baby completely pulls you out of the moment ​But if you dismiss it solely based on that surface-level wrapping, you're missing the forest for the trees. Despite those filmmaking flaws and the questionable depiction of America's role in the Iraq War, the movie still works because it succeeds entirely at what it actually set out to do: deliver a narrow, personal character study. ​At its core, this is about the psychological toll of deployment ​American Sniper isn't trying to be a sprawling macro-commentary on the ethics of the Iraq War. It’s about what happens to a human being when their entire reality shrinks down to the crosshairs of a sniper's scope. Clint Eastwood does a good job showing how the cumulative effect of these tours slowly erodes a person's ability to exist in normal civilian life with the time constraints that come with creating a Hollywood blockbuster ​The combat sequences are tense, aided by some incredibly sharp audio design, but the real hitter is the silence once Chris Kyle gets back to Texas. Bradley Cooper sells that weight, showing us a man who is physically sitting on his couch with his family, but mentally still scanning rooftops thousands of miles away. ​It’s wrapped in patriotic bravado and hindered by some clunky filmmaking, but underneath it all is a genuinely interesting look at the personal cost of trauma and duty. ​If you judge it by its true intent, rather than its politics or its technical polish, it does hits the target. ​All that said, it would be incredibly biased to completely dismiss the aforementioned flaws. They absolutely impact the viewing experience, and the film does require you to actively overlook some of its shortcomings in order to see the forest through what are, admittedly, some rather large trees. But if you can manage that, its true intent still shines. 3.5/5

Why yes, I CAN believe this had 11 freaking writers, because this feels like 11 different people’s view as to what the Simpsons are, and none of them mesh in a way that makes more than four moments of this any good. Like, it’s weird how much this feels like Simpsons fanfic, despite being done by 11 separate showrunners; these are all people who know Springfield pretty intimately, and so it’s extra heartbreaking that they managed to make something that feels more like A Very Special Episode of the show than anything the show has ever done. And yes, I get that they had to shoehorn a decades-long show into 90 minutes, but making this weirdly serious — separation! parental drama! Unresolved mystery! — feels like a colossal miscalculation and a betrayal of everything the Simpsons are so that they can make this feel justified as a movie. Worse, it feels like they don’t even get the characters. For example, Homer is just the dumbest, most random, most insufferable version of himself that’s ever existed, and there’s almost no line here that feels organic; it’s all [INSERT HOMER SAYING SOMETHING AGGRESSIVELY RANDOM AND UNKNOWINGLY HARMFUL] over and over, and there’s no effort to tie it into explanations as to why he’s suddenly just like this evil random gas leak version of himself. Again, I found maybe three or four of the gags to be kinda funny, and they all feel like Monorail-era level of quality. The rest feel like “ha ha we showed Bart’s dong” or “ha ha Homer flips the bird” or just oddly disconnected beats too lazy to be any good. This was a huge bummer even if it did give us the meme-era gold of “this was the worst day of your life SO FAR.” The rest? Oof.

I was selected to lead, not to read Last Watch: September 2020 Age: 51 (at time of release) Source: Disney+ 2026 Challenge: Hanks at 70 Film: #38 Director/Cast/Premise The Simpsons Movie is the 2007 animated comedy directed by David Silverman. Starring Dan Castellaneta, Nancy Cartwright and Tom Hanks the plot sees the residents of Springfield imprisoned under a glass dome. Original Thoughts 2020 Things have a habit of following trends. When your career starts to develop as an actor you get more involved in the production of films, maybe set up your own company. If you have a tv show that becomes popular you end up making a film version. South Park did it in 1999, The Simpsons did it in 2007, is it necessary? No. Was the Simpsons movie worth it? Not really. The reality is that the film was a huge financial success but suffers from a number of expected problems; there are clear pacing issues that is most likely due to the inexperience of putting out anything beyond a normal episode run time, plenty of padding which is often dull and the material/character arcs that offer nothing new from its hundreds of available episodes with far too few jokes. There is a clear over reliance of the audiences fondness for the characters. Its these viewers who paid to watch an extended version of an episode and who the studio banked on making this a success. What you get is familiarity of the Springfield setting and Simpsons regulars with the odd cameo (Tom Hanks included) and sharper animation. For good measure they throw in some themes of religion and the environment whilst ripping off Stephen Kings Under the Dome. Oh and throw in a pig...it just isn't worth it.

Just like The Simpsons, this review series has been running too long. I LOVE The Simpsons. The show has really shaped humor and culture for hundreds and hundreds of people. The show’s peak was from seasons 2-8, from 1991 to 1997. So, dear reader, you might be asking along with me: why the hell did they wait until 2007, far past when people had been saying the show had been running too long, to make The Simpsons Movie? Who the hell knows, but it really is a detriment. While the think the film definitely has its very funny moments, it lacks a lot of the intelligence, both in the humor and emotion, that the show had. The film feels like a long version of a Simpsons episode, which really doesn’t work. I think that even if you’ve never written anything in your life, the structure of a 22 minute episode is far different from the structure of a 90 minute movie. I think a lot of movies based off shows have that issue, such as The South Park Movie, but that film worked much better for a few reasons. 1. The humor in The South Park Movie was consistently gutbustingly hilarious, whereas in The Simpsons Movies, while there aren’t any stinker jokes, the majority of them are just ok. There aren’t a lot of jokes I’ll be quoting over and over all watching it. 2. The South Park movie actually plays out like a film, the story is coherent, emotional beats pay off, running jokes resolve, and you feel like you actually watched something of cinematic scale. The Simpsons movie feels a lot looser, like a TV episode, but that means that plot lines don’t make sense, or don’t resolve, the emotional bits don’t really work out, and it overall feels less cinematic. 3. The South Park Movie did something above and beyond the show. The film had a massive scale, a lot of the animation was upped, and there were a bunch of over the top Broadway style musical numbers, stuff you wouldn’t see on a typical South Park episode. The Simpsons Movie feels like an episode of The Simpsons, even down to the animation. There is very little to distinguish the film from an episode. Homer’s opening joke of “why do we pay to watch something we get on TV for free” really feels indicative of the film’s quality. Overall, not really a bad film, but not really a must watch. Definitely only recommend it for hardcore fans.

Uma experiência cinematográfica muito inteligente e autoconsciente. Os Simpsons definitivamente já tiveram dias melhores, e isso não é nenhuma novidade, mas é impossível não sorrir ao ver esses personagens de volta às telonas. O roteiro começa muito bem, com uma premissa inteligente e várias ideias genuinamente engraçadas. O problema é que, em algum ponto perto da metade, parece que eles se esqueceram completamente da própria premissa e o filme começa a se perder. Mesmo assim, é difícil não se divertir. E talvez a falta de ambição seja justamente uma das coisas mais admiráveis sobre a série. Os Simpsons não precisam reinventar a roda. Continua sendo grosseira, ácida, estúpida e estranhamente cativante na medida certa. Realmente não precisamos de muito mais. Uma das melhores piadas acontece quando os religiosos percebem que o fim do mundo chegou e que não foram salvos. Em completo desespero, eles correm para o bar em busca de uma bebida, enquanto as pessoas que já estavam no bar correm para a igreja em busca de salvação. É uma inversão tão simples, absurda e brilhantemente cínica, o tipo de piada que eles fazem parecer fácil. Eu ri muito disso. Desde o primeiro fotograma, este é Os Simpsons em sua essência. Não há nenhuma tentativa de tornar a série maior, mais profunda ou mais importante do que realmente é. É simplesmente uma boa e velha visita a Springfield, agora em uma tela muito maior. Talvez não seja um retorno à era de ouro, nem de longe, mas depois de todos esses anos, passar algumas horas com esses velhos amigos ainda é melhor do que assistir a mais uma reprise.

Llevar una de las comedias más influyentes de la historia de la televisión a la gran pantalla era una maniobra inevitable, pero cargada de riesgos. Estrenada tras años de especulaciones y en un punto donde la serie de televisión ya mostraba signos claros de desgaste creativo, Los Simpson: La película asumió el reto de transformar una dinámica televisiva de 22 minutos en un evento cinematográfico de escala global. El resultado es un largometraje sumamente entretenido, vistoso y con picos cómicos altísimos, aunque empañado por decisiones narrativas que se alejan de la esencia más pura de Springfield. El apartado visual es, sin lugar a dudas, uno de sus puntos más sólidos. La transición hacia un dibujo más estilizado, apoyado por sombreados digitales y una paleta de colores vibrante, le otorgó al largometraje la escala de evento que exigía el cine. La dirección aprovecha las dimensiones de la pantalla grande para desplegar secuencias mucho más dinámicas —como la construcción de la cúpula sobre Springfield o el escape de la familia—, respaldadas por una banda sonora de John Powell que eleva la tensión sin perder la ironía característica de la franquicia. Sin embargo, el núcleo de la historia tropieza en la definición de sus prioridades. El conflicto central opta por apoyarse de forma casi exclusiva en una crisis matrimonial entre Homero y Marge, una fórmula narrativa ampliamente explotada en la serie que aquí se percibe cargada de clichés románticos. La decisión de volcar la carga emotiva en el reencuentro de la pareja le resta espacio al desarrollo de otras dinámicas de la ciudad y fuerza un todo sentimental que por momentos se siente ajeno a la acidez satírica que convirtió a la serie en un fenómeno cultural. A esto se suma una caracterización de Homero que no termina de asentarse. Si bien cuenta con momentos memorables dentro del metraje, se extrañan aquellos rasgos de su personalidad que construyeron sus mejores épocas en televisión: esa mezcla única entre tontería entrañable, momentos de astucia involuntaria y una relación más auténtica con sus vecinos y su entorno. En la película, gran parte de sus acciones quedan subordinadas a empujar el conflicto romántico, dejando en segundo plano su faceta como catalizador del caos social de Springfield. Los Simpson: La película funciona muy bien como pieza de entretenimiento rápido y cumple con el cometido de reunir a generaciones frente a la pantalla. Posee un ritmo ágil y chistes que han quedado grabados en la cultura popular, pero al balancear los elementos, queda la sensación de que prefirió ir a lo seguro antes que arriesgarse a construir un relato verdaderamente memorable. Un hito visual y nostálgico que aprueba con solvencia, pero que se queda lejos del brillo de los mejores años de la familia amarilla. Una entrega entretenida y técnicamente impecable que cumple con el espectáculo visual que exige la gran pantalla. Sin embargo, su dependencia de un conflicto romántico trillado y la pérdida de matices clave en Homero le impiden alcanzar el nivel de los mejores capítulos de la serie.

Having premiered nearly forty years ago, The Simpsons is one of the longest last series airing on television.  However you may feel about its quality as it progresses, it is a testament to how popular it is that it has lasted as long as it has.  Of course, given said popularity, it was inevitable that movie starring the residents of Springfield would come to fruition.  When it comes to series being adapted to film, The Simpsons Movie is not among the worst of its kind and is entertaining.  However, it does come with a few of its own drawbacks. The Simpsons Movie goes for a grander plotline that is more fitting for a ninety minute feature than a half hour special.  This time, it is a series of careless accidents brought upon by Homer Simpson that brings great danger to Springfield.  Homer has been known for getting into trouble because of his stupidity or outright selfishness but it's a whole town that's at stake because of his flaws as opposed to matters with family or close friends.  It is a plot that does fit in with what the series was about, even having some clever political jokes here and there. Where the film does suffer a little is that, even with the more epic storyline, it also feels like an extended episode of the show.  This might hit a little differently for people who watch the show religiously while newcomers may be confused.  There are a few laughs to be found from fourth wall jokes and innuendos (some of which would have been censored on the actual show) but it also feels like it's fan service.  It's especially evident when random recurring characters pop up to do what the audience expects without really contributing too much to the actual plot.  Furthermore, the moments that are meant to feel emotional feel a little too quick to make way for some more jokes and action set pieces. The animation of the film keeps true to that of the show along with Matt Groening's own style.  It has been clearly been upgraded for a cinematic outing as it adds more shading and color, reflecting the higher budget.  At times it is even more fluid, partially a result of some former Disney animators having a hand in the making of it (There are a couple of humorous jokes at their expense as well).  It's a style that may not appeal to everyone, but fans of the show should be pleased that it doesn't go for something completely different on a technical level. All the original cast members return to voice their respective characters.  Dan Castellaneta does manage to capture Homer's dimwitted nature.  It is a little hard to get behind the character at times due to how emotionally distant he is for much of the film but Castellaneta is still having fun.  Julie Kavner gets more of a chance to show some range as Marge Simpson.  Bart feels a bit more short changed as he does have a potentially compelling plot but it's not given enough development though Nancy Cartwright still brings her A-game.  Albert Brooks is entertaining as a newcomer, the villainous Russ Cargill, who takes advantage of Homer's accidents in order to destroy Springfield. The Simpsons Movie is a mostly humorous, if slight adaptation of the series.  Much of the time it does feel like it is pandering to fans or stretching out a story way too thin.  Still, its entertainment value lies on its production, the voice acting and some clever writing and jokes.  It is one of the more decent theatrical adaptations of an animated TV show.

It's fine, as the potential finale to the show it's pretty good so the fact it went on for 20 more years(!) isn't a deduction in retrospect. It has the TV-to-movie problem of it being a comedy but requiring high stakes to justify its existence and the runtime. It is obviously a funny concept, and some jokes are a bit darker than the show (I'd forgotten they wanted to lynch Maggie - crazy they all moved past it) but the marriage crisis doesn't work for me in a Simpsons comedy. I think maybe because the soul-searching part never clicked with me, but also, it factually kills the vibe. It's a great character dynamic and is a high stake, but is that what we want from a comedy? Maybe it's just not a comedy style that works outside of a runtime crunch as they did in the golden age. Checking out the deleted scenes for the first time, there is a recency bias, but I wish they were left in. They feel like good writing and paid off some visual setups that didn't in the theatrical cut. You can see the sports stadium is cut in half by the dome, but only upon seeing the deleted scene we get the pay-off. First act is the highlight, the writing holds up and is still easily quotable. I find the Green Day stuff very boring, self-starring celebrity cameos are never interesting, and then it's a fairly gradual decline until the credits. It's barely a credit to an animated movie but it was nice to scan the crowd scenes and see some deep-cut Simpsons characters. We'll see how the new movie is. Hopefully it is truly the finale and Julie Kavner can finally rest her poor voice.

The movie manages to preserve the spirit of the series, with its irreverent humor, social and political satire, and that wonderfully absurd quality that has made the Simpson family a pop-culture icon. Homer is, naturally, at the heart of it all, and his perfect combination of stupidity, selfishness, and genuine love for his family still works brilliantly. It may not offer anything particularly groundbreaking compared to the series, and because it stays so faithful to its original style, at times it feels like watching a very long episode. But that's also its greatest strength: it never tries to become something The Simpsons isn't. Funny, irreverent, and packed with memorable moments. It may not be the deepest or most innovative animated movie out there, but for a Simpsons fan, it's almost impossible not to have a great time watching it.

While on the surface, this film feels like a continuation of the extremely long running beloved animated series, it really is a deeply complex insight into the world of a (almost) nuclear family on the brink of destruction due to an emotionally absent father. When considering that this movie came out in 2007 at the height of the 5th Harry Potter film, Spider-Man 3, and the newest Pirates of the Caribbean, this movie, often flies under the radar for being one of the most insightful movies of the year. However, this doesn’t mean that its impact is any less important. While, it didn’t break any records in the box office it’s still manages to give an extremely nuanced view at the detriment behind what will occur when somebody chooses themselves over their loved ones. Homer in this showcases his duality by stepping into the antagonist role by being a character that just can’t seems to stop screwing up. As a result of this, he ends up, turning his entire family and friends against him and as audience members we get to watch him deal with the isolation involved with destroying the structured comfortability associated with familial ties. This is an extremely refreshing take on the series since often cheap jokes are written off to excuse Homer for his genuinely awful behavior. This movie does something smart by allowing the audience to see how Homer’s actions towards his family create turmoil to the point of Marge literally stealing the kids to take them away from the situation Homer has caused. This film is not only a masterclass in the human condition, but it also showcases how regardless of how terrible of a person homer is he still like every human deserves forgiveness. It’s sort of a beautiful story wrapped up in a 90 minute runtime that had me laughing as hard as I did the first time I watched it. Also, it has spider pig and he’s awesome.

I think one of the reasons this works so well for me is the timelessness of the comedy, you could put this movie in theaters today and change nothing and it'd still be a hit, something that can't be said for many many comedies. Besides aging wonderfully comedically, the story here is exactly what I personally love for theatrical TV movies. There's a plot that warrants a longer runtime yet still space for small bits and antics that make it feel like I'm still watching an episode. This might sound insane but I really cannot stand it when a TV show gets a theatrical release and it feels like I'm watching TV characters in a movie not  a longer higher budget episode. Examples of ones I like are this obviously, the Bob's Burgers movie, Mask of the Phantasm, Cowboy Bebop and ofc like the Demon Slayer, JJK, AOT movies, versus things like the Fullmetal Alchemist movies that feel like transplanted characters in a plot and lowkey detracts from the overall narrative. Anyways off that tangent I really really wish they stuck with emotional beat of Marge leaving Homer a little bit longer, because as thousands of people have said that's by far the strongest moment of the whole film. The animation was something I appreciated as well, swinging the camera around and using perspective in ways you don't see in episodes. All around I had a great time, I'm sad I got banned from watching the Simpsons and didn't get to watch this growing up

I just watched Transformers for the first time, and I genuinely thought it was terrible. I know this movie has a massive fanbase and was hugely successful, but I honestly struggle to understand the appeal. For most of the runtime, it just felt like a constant barrage of explosions, screaming, fighting, cars, robots and things flying across the screen. Something is always happening, but somehow I still found it incredibly unengaging. The biggest problem for me was the plot. I know you’re supposed to just accept the concept of alien robots coming to Earth and disguising themselves as cars, but even within that setup, the story felt unnecessarily convoluted and ridiculous. Everyone is chasing the same objects, different groups keep appearing, robots are fighting robots, the military gets involved, and eventually it all just becomes noise. The dialogue also really didn’t work for me. So many lines felt unbelievably cheesy, to the point where I was genuinely uncomfortable at times. The humor, the dramatic speeches, the romantic scenes, the military dialogue – almost everything has this extremely specific mid-2000s blockbuster cheesiness to it. And I like Shia LaBeouf in plenty of other movies, but even he couldn’t really save this for me. There wasn’t a character, relationship or storyline that I felt particularly invested in. The one thing I can absolutely give the movie credit for is the visual effects. Especially considering this came out in 2007, the Transformers themselves still look impressive. The transformations are incredibly detailed, the CGI interacts convincingly with the real environments, and I can imagine that seeing this on a huge cinema screen at the time probably felt pretty revolutionary. But great effects aren’t enough for me when I don’t care about anything that’s happening around them. It also feels incredibly representative of a certain kind of American blockbuster from that era: huge cars, military hardware, attractive people, explosions, loud music and everything constantly turned up to eleven. I can see how that spectacle appealed to a massive audience, especially in 2007, but it really isn’t for me. By the end I genuinely felt exhausted rather than entertained. There’s very little here that made me think about the movie afterwards beyond wondering how something this loud could somehow still bore me. I’m definitely not a Transformers fan, and this movie certainly didn’t turn me into one. The effects are impressive, but almost everything else – the dialogue, the characters, the plot and the nonstop action – did absolutely nothing for me. I will not be watching this again.

2.5/10 "The first Transformers is actually kinda good." That's a sentence I've heard loads of times. I have no idea what's going on in the minds of the people who say that. The first Transformers is one of the most embarrassing AAA productions I know of. And it only goes downhill from here. The entire movie's attitude is just loathsome. It tries to mash a few dark and serious elements together with dialogue and comic relief straight out of a frat house. Every character is unbelievably obnoxious. I don't understand why anyone would ever want to follow these people, or why anyone would ever care about anything that's happening. The entire world this film takes place in is insufferable, and the whole thing feels like it was made by a bunch of college jocks. Everything about it is just annoying. It's also weird how often the movie seems to be attempting some kind of parody of the American government. The directing is actually okay for a production like this. The blend of on-set footage and CGI works great, and Bay directs the actors competently. What I do find hilarious, however, is just how clearly his background in music video directing shines through in quite a few shots. That - and especially how aggressively everything is geared towards being cool and badass - comes off as incredibly cringe and try-hard. Ninety per cent of the story is made up of some lame McGuffin fetch quest with stakes I couldn't care less about, because the world and the characters suck. And it all eventually culminates in one of the least exciting third acts I've ever seen. There's battle scene after battle scene, but not only do I barely know what's going on because half the Transformers look the same, I also don't really care. It's just more and more fighting, and I realised that watching Transformers transform into and out of cars had already gotten boring the third time around. This film is filled to the brim with stupid shit and is, in general, one of the most unenjoyable ways to spend two hours and fifteen minutes that I can think of.

Some say that he makes good first entries and that he always finds a place for spectacle. All I know is that this movie sucks. While the story between Sam (Shia LaBeouf) and Bumblebee (Mark Ryan) can be a grounding moment, it isn’t enough force to get it on land. Neither is Peter Cullen’s performance as Optimus Prime, the score, or the fights. Optimus owing his life to Sam does make sense though and Optimus says his iconic lines and good new lines. But that’s just about where the fun ends. First, Michael Bay doesn’t seem to respect the lore for Cybertron is supposed to be habitable, at least for the Decepticons. There’s too many subplots, the wrong tone with the military and disaster film aspects, too detailed CGI with the Decepticons being all gray, too much human stuff, bad jokes, especially Bumblebee and the lubricant and Ratchet (Robert Foxworth) saying Sam’s pheromone levels suggests he wants to have a kid with Mikaela (Megan Fox). Also the whole Sam selling his great-grandfather’s glasses on eBay is meaningless. Shia LaBeouf is just alright as Sam, he tries, but Bay, Roberto Orci, and Alex Kurtzman don’t give him much to work with. So little that Sam doesn’t feel like a hero as he’s given no space to grow into one. Megan Fox is also not impressive as she is subjected to Bay sexualizing her, even when doing something as simple as looking into what’s wrong with a car. Although that’s more so how she is dressed. Bay and Fox have history, as she was portrayed at 15 quite suggestively in Bad Boys II (2003), and Fox did not forget that. This movie doesn’t feel like a step in the right direction with Fox in Bay’s movies. Especially since she doesn’t have much of a character and is mostly here so Bay can feature the male gaze. Dwelling on humans unfortunately means Optimus and Megatron (Hugo Weaving) don’t appear until an hour in, and Megatron is not an active threat until the movie is nearly over. Speaking of Megatron, Weaving is nothing impressive. If they brought back Frank Welker, who voiced Megatron in G1 to pair with Cullen’s Optimus, it may have been more believable that these two had history. Weaving can act, he was good as Red Skull, but he can’t really in this movie. Speaking of the actual Transformers, Bumblebee having no lines gives him no character and we also don’t see him take the form of the 2007 Camaro. Jazz dying without any investment in his character is straight up shrewd. So now I’ve gotten past the problems with the characters. Does that mean the story’s good? I wish the answer was “Yes”. First, revisionist history opens a flood of confusion. The Hoover Dam was built due to the Cube (and the AllSpark) being there? And the two worlds have met before? So why then do the humans pretend they don’t know what’s happening? If none of the revisionist history was here and the events of the movie were the first time Cybertron’s inhabitants met humans on Earth, it would be a much cleaner story. Second, it takes too long to get to what really matters. It takes like 45 minutes to an hour to get to what matters, the Decepticons want the Cube and the Autobots can’t let that happen. Because of the human stuff, it prevents us from just cutting to the chase. Overall, a first entry that could have been worse, but does not provide encouragement for what’s next. 3/10 or 1½ stars.

Every character in this film is a dickhead. Racist soldiers on the chopper? Dickheads. Spike Witwicky hawking his family airlooms for a car? Dickhead.  Spike Witwicky abandoning his friend at the lake? Double dickhead. Dad Witwicky taking his son to the Porsche garage? Dickhead. Mum Witwicky obsessed about her son gooning? Dickhead. Optimus Prime? Dickhead. Ironhide? Dickhead. John Turturro? Dickhead. Meghan Fox? Actually, not a dickhead, so Michael Bay got rid of her. There is something profoundly off in the writing of this movie. I feel it's like colourblind people trying to describe a colour they've never seen; in this case, it's facsimiles of human beings trying to write American teenagers and their relationships having only devoured other films about the topic. But there's something more than that - after all, Tarantino has made a career from refashioning the obsessions of his youth (and Bumblebee does a similar thing with more love and panache) - there's something profoundly off about all of the human characters in this film. It's vexing - if it had been slightly more surreal it might have ended up an almost Lynchian take on the psychosexual underbelly of teenage popular discourse, but we've arrived  here in this weird place by  accident, as jock writers do their best to embody pop cultural tropes that grow more distorted the more they are photocopied. But look, against my better judgement, once the movie stops pretending to be a John Hughes' dog in heat, it gets better. ILM absolutely smash the ball out the park and the back half is tight. I can just imagine Bay and the head of ILM doing that Arnold hand clasp from Predator before hitting the open air gym at Venice Beach once they'd locked the movie. Even though there are better live action versions of this that are roughly the same story (Bumblebee), movies that are just leagues better (TF:One, the original 86 film) and TV shows that have more pathos in their little cybertronian finger than this entire film (Animated, Prime, Seasons two and three of Cyberverse) I will admit that this is a singular vision, and you could not mistake it for the work of anyone else. A made-by-committee Marvel movie this is not. Only Michael Bay could have made this film, and he's probably a dickhead. It's definitely Michael Bay's world: your choice if you want to spend two hours in it.

Bon... Bah c'est d'la merde. Non, soyons sérieux : les effets visuels sont très réussis. Après, est-ce que ça suffit à en faire un bon film ? Spoiler : non. Le scénario est un pétard mouillé. Bon, ça c'est pas trop grave : je suis un des plus grands défenseurs de Pacific Rim, qui lui non plus ne brille pas par son scénario (quoique il maîtrise bien plus la caractérisation et le développement de ses personnages). Mais si en plus d'un scénario pourri digne des pires Emmerich, la mise en scène est pas ouf, bah ça devient vachement insipide. Et Michael Bay a beau faire plein de transformations de robots et une tonne d'explosion, ça ne fait ni chaud ni froid. Les personnages sont mal construits, la photo est laide, les couleurs sont délavées et m'ont rappelés Snyder (et ce n'est clairement pas un compliment), et en plus dans tout ça, Bay masque la médiocrité de sa mise en scène par des boum boum et des grosses voitures. Alors il y a quelques idées par-ci par-là, et certaines scènes d'action assez rigolotes, mais c'est jamais très impressionnant, jamais d'effet whaou, et dans un film qui pourtant n'a que ça pour briller, bah c'est très con. Ceci dit, et je conclurai là-dessus, c'est divertissant. Et ça je ne peux pas le reprocher à Michael Bay : c'est moche, c'est con, mais c'est rigolo.

I wish I had a polarizing take on Transformers (2007), but as a product of the 2000s, this had little impact on my life at a time that it very well could have. Some Michael Bay enthusiasts I know are unapologetically in love with the Transformers franchise, and I'll admit that I see the appeal. This is a bombastic, explosive, ten-toes-down blockbuster with commentary about military, police, and humanity, and it looks pretty great while doing it... but similarly to some of the Americanized Godzilla films, while I had a good time with this one, it failed to leave much of a lasting impression on me. I will give the film credit for its action sequences; it's over-the-top and impressive in its blockbuster filmmaking, especially for 2007. The CGI holds up refreshingly well, and the cliches aren't executed haphazardly. I think part of the disconnect comes from a lack of literacy in Bay's filmography, which I plan to rectify sooner rather than later, but I also struggle to reconcile that with the lack of humanity in the human characters. I found the Transformers themselves infinitely more interesting than Sam, Mikaela, or any of the other human characters. Sure, that's somewhat to be expected in the Transformers movie, but this 144-minute action extravaganza spent enough time on the humans to give me more meaningful time with them or more depth to the Transformers. I suppose I can find more of that in the next three films. Ultimately, I think there's room for me to appreciate this more on rewatch, but this is good, not great to my tastes as of today.

Tldr this would go so hard if I was 6 years old When Rachel told me tonight's movie was going to be Michael Bay's Transformers , I was a bit trepidatious. It's a bit of a cultural blind spot for me - I knew a lot about the film, I'd seen a lot of clips of Shia LaBeouf from the films, but never actually watched or engaged with anything from the Transformers franchise. Suffice to say it, the cultural footprint is familiar, even if the film itself was not. Over a pre-film game of catch, as if to underline the upcoming vibes, we heard the distant roar of a Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet, some miles away. That's not a regular occurrence in northwest London but today is apparent RAF day. Rachel was hyped, and she was hyping it up. We begin in a place that is absolutely Qatar. Why? Don't ask questions, enjoy the film. Things get messy real quick and I'll say this; this film looks fantastic. It is true what they say about CGI taking a step back since 2007. Maybe it's that there's just a lot going on or that the camera is always shaking: it doesn't matter, the decepticons, the autobots, and everything in between look probably exactly how you'd want them to look in a live-action film. Where were we? Ah yeah, havoc being wreaked on the US military industrial complex, getting steadily closer to home. Why is the little decepticon dude having an orgasm while he hacks? Freaky lil guy. Shia LaBeouf is easily the best part of this film, along with John Turturro. Genuinely funny, not necessarily served with the best writing, but gets an itchy energy that works really well for the film. I vaguely remember most of my school peers thirsting over Megan Fox in early secondary school. I get that, but her near-flawless conventional beauty doesn't make up for a total absence of acting talent. It becomes apparent that choices made by Michael Bay and the production team are designed to hide this with suggestive shots, and talk about engines that is never really truly about engines. This continues to a lesser extent as the film goes on. I worry these days that I'm too close to the action. I work semi-adjacently to defence, I play a lot of Arma, and I take an interest in geopolitics and defence policy. It's this knowledge that curses me, and forces me to sigh - yes, I know, it's a film about talking cars and vehicles from space - but if you're going to embrace the military industrial complex and essentially show off its power, you can't have A-10s go from dispatch to munitions delivery in 35 seconds (it's at least 35 minutes. At least ). The characterisation of some of these people is utterly diabolical, and almost certainly a product of the time. For example, there is 1 (one) black character who doesn't spend most lines of dialogue screaming/overreacting. Sam's parents must have been the inspiration for the Payday 3 security guards ("must have been the wind" ahhhh parents). But it's ok, the plot is shaky too. It's fine to begin with, but the plot holes come thick and fast, for example: - Sector 7 captures Sam and Mikaela and it's a big sad scene and everyone's angry at each other - it's the low point to end Act 2: but the next time we see them they're all chummy and gold and on a helicopter with the Secretary of Defence? Felt unearned. - We should keep Megatron under critical infrastructure, like the Hoover dam - President Hoover founded Sector 7, after all! - Wait, why has Secretary Voight gone with the hackers™ and John Turturro and hasn't got a platoon of security detail with him? He's the mf secretary of defence!!? - We need to get the allspice - sorry - the allspark away from here: let's go to a major population centre. Nothing bad has ever happened in a major population centre. - Every time Sam or Mikaela gets caught by one of the autobots after falling a height, that's gotta hurt so damn much - Wait, that's it? what did Sam actually do there? If Megatron wanted the allspice and all it took was that, why didn't he do that first?? - Ending scene: cuck car park None of this is to say I had a bad time though 🙂 It was great fun to watch a bit of a cornerstone of 2000s cinema and a part of many of my friends' personal canon. I wasn't there early enough, so I probably missed out - that's alright by me though.

I grew up watching Transformers as a kid, and I was completely into it. I had all the little robot toys, and I can still remember having fun transforming them and playing with them while watching the cartoon. So when this movie came out, there was definitely a part of me that was excited to see these characters brought to the big screen. And honestly, Transformers delivers pretty well on that childhood nostalgia. Seeing Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, Megatron, Starscream and the rest of the Transformers brought to life with modern special effects was pretty damn cool. The designs and transformations felt like a natural evolution of what I remembered from the cartoon, and the movie actually captures a lot of the spirit of what made the original series fun. Watching these giant robots transform, fight and tear up the screen is exactly the kind of thing younger me would have loved. As an adult, though, I can also see the movie’s flaws. The story isn’t anything groundbreaking, some of the human characters and comedy don’t always work for me, and at times it feels more like a showcase for the special effects than a great story. But I never really expected Transformers to be some deep cinematic experience. I wanted to have fun with it, and that’s exactly what I got. The action is entertaining, the effects still hold up pretty well, and there’s something satisfying about seeing characters I grew up with finally getting the big-budget treatment. Is it the best movie I’ve ever seen? Definitely not. Is it a bad movie? Not at all. For me, Transformers is simply a fun, nostalgic ride that brought a piece of my childhood back to the big screen.

Desde su creación Optimus Prime en toda adaptación, su liderazgo se basa en la responsabilidad, la empatía y la protección de aquellos que no pueden defenderse por sí mismos, Optimus ni siquiera busca el gobernar, sino preservar la libertad incluso en medio de una guerra. An engaging blockbuster overall, but definitely one that loses itself its the final act. Starting off with its thrilling political intrigue, espionage, and military action, Transformers hooks you from the start with its brisk pace. LaBeouf is brilliant as Sam, flawlessly conveying his nerdy and comedic traits. The CGI’s thoroughly impressive, though they lack the holistic perspective of later films (not exactly a flaw). The character designs are brilliant (save perhaps Megatron), with the original lineup of Autobots and Decepticons being highly distinct from their respective groups. The action is fun for the most part, but certainly not as innovative or prominent as in later instalments. While Bumblebee received a major focus, I certainly wish Optimus had more screen time. Unfortunately, flaws are prevalent in the film’s middle and final acts. The Autobots hiding outside Sam’s home is cute at first, but quickly becomes obnoxious. The initial sequences with Sector 7 are largely uninteresting, hindering the previously thrilling pace. As for the final act, action sequences with the actual Transformers are brief. The overall resolution is abrupt, with Megatron feeling dumbed down for the sake of it. Still iconic, but lacks the action the Bayverse is known for. I don’t know how, but the military propaganda in Bay’s initial trilogy just works. And that ending scene is just legendary
