I honestly fell asleep the first watch through, so I had to watch it again. This is my first time watching either Aladdin, so I don't feel disturbed as others might feel about all the additions, replacements, and whatever. I felt like this version did a better—but not good—job of respecting the culture in the Middle East. The women aren't as hypersexualized in this version as it was in the original animation, straying away from Orientalism just a bit. In fact, everyone is a lot more clothed than shown in the animation. However, I'm no expert, but I've noticed that rather than representing the Middle East, there were many Indian elements like the clothes in the movie. I'm glad they didn't make Jasmine look like the typical belly dancer stereotype, but they still failed to depict what Arabian women would actually wear. Moreover, Jasmine was able to jump with the pole in the original as she was running away with Aladdin, which showed some of her fearlessness (that ultimately never got fleshed out), but in this one, she chickens out. That pissed me off because if they're trying to empower Jasmine, there was no reason to make her back out in this scene. Also, there was no need to leave her frozen in place at such a critical moment, where she could've proven herself. Sadly, the men have to save this damsel in distress once more. What surprised me the most was The Sultan having more aura in this movie. In the original, this guy was just an idiot with almost no thought of his own, but in this one, he tried to stand his ground. I guess they donated some of Jasmine's fearlessness to a man who doesn't even have a name. I really don't care if they bring some random handmaiden into the movie, but if they can make changes like that, I would've loved if they removed more of the harmful stereotypes and made Jasmine independent. It honestly feels like they watered down the original to make it seem less problematic when, really, the true meaning and intent are still there. There are several Israel sympathizers in the cast as well that have also played violent roles in other media. Yes, there's a more diverse cast that come from the Middle East but at what cost? The soundtrack did have bangers, but it sounded more Western than Middle Eastern. For example, when Jasmine played that one instrument, it just sounded like a regular guitar you'd hear in the US. When you look at the composers behind these songs, you'll quickly notice that none of them are Arab; it all adds up. As I talked about earlier with things being watered down, the lyrics to "Arabian Nights" were tweaked to make the people seem less barbaric in Arabia, but they still call them barbaric. Overall, the movie definitely made some nice changes from the original, but they weren't done right. This could've been so much better.

“He’s a little dim, but you’re just getting married. It’s not like you have to talk to him.” Guy Ritchie’s remake of the 1992 animated classic follows Aladdin as he discovers a magic lamp that contains a genie who helps him impress Princess Jasmine of Agrabah by disguising him as a prince, only to raise the suspicion of the evil vizier Jafar. Another unnecessary remake thats only success lies in the portrayal of the Genie that toed a line between a fresh take and homage, with Jasmine’s handmaiden Dalia - Genie’s future wife - a decent new character who didn’t detract from the story. Their chemistry surpassed Aladdin and Jasmine’s with much less time spent together throughout. At its worst when it’s copying the original as the flaws become glaring, especially in the portrayal of Jafar who was neither menacing nor effective as a conjurer even with the full power of the lamp. The songs were uninspiring and lacked any magic from “A Whole New World” to “Friend Like Me” to Jasmine’s new song “Speechless” that succeeds in showing off her voice while still being lacking. Cast includes Mena Massoud, Naomi Scott, Will Smith, Marwan Kenzari, Navid Negahban, Nasim Pedrad, Billy Magnussen, and Alan Tudyk as Iago, with Frank Welker the lone returnee voicing Abu.

Aladdin  is one of those movies that just sticks with you because it’s wild, loud, and honestly pretty funny. The Genie is all over the place, He’s easily one of the funniest parts of the movie. But when you actually pay attention to the story, there’s something kind of weird going on with Princess Jasmine. She’s supposed to be this rebellious princess who wants to make her own choices, but she barely gets to control what happens in her own story. Jasmine talks a lot about wanting freedom and not wanting someone else to choose her future, but the movie doesn’t really give her much room to do anything about it. Her dad is trying to decide who she should marry, Jafar is constantly trying to control everything, and even Aladdin spends most of the movie lying to her. Jasmine tries to stand up for herself, but the story keeps moving around her. It’s like she’s talking, but nobody is really listening. Another thing I noticed is how much everyone in Agrabah is constantly talking, singing, arguing, or making deals. There’s always something happening. Meanwhile, Jasmine feels like she gets pushed into the background. She has important things to say, but the movie seems more interested in Aladdin, Genie, Jafar, and all the chaos happening around them. It almost feels like Jasmine is there, but her voice gets lost in all the noise. That’s also what makes the movie kind of absurd. The whole world is crazy with magic carpets, a talking parrot, a magical lamp, and a Genie who can basically do anything. The rules don’t always make much sense, but that’s part of what makes it fun. Everyone is chasing something, whether it’s power, freedom, love, or just getting what they want. Jasmine wants freedom, but she doesn’t really get to figure out what that means for herself. Overall, I still think Aladdin is a really fun movie. The animation is colorful, the music is memorable, and Genie brings so much energy to the movie. I just wish Jasmine had more control over her own story because she actually has the potential to be one of the strongest characters. Instead, she sometimes feels like she’s just reacting to whatever Aladdin, Jafar, or her dad does next.

A young man thieves to survive in the small city he lives in. One day, he runs into a woman on the streets, who is actually the princess. Meanwhile, the kings guard is plotting his takeover and wants to build an empire. When the thief is caught sneaking into the palace, he is assigned by the kings guard to visit a magic genie and make his wishes come true. He makes a wish to have the title and appearance as a prince so he can win over the princess. When he gets invited to the kingdom, at first he makes himself out to be an idiot. Afterwards, he is able to charm her when he sneaks into her palace and take her out to see the city. The next day, the king guard discovers what he did and sends him away. However, the princess is able to bring him back by making a wish. The genie gets freed and the thief and the princess live happily.

“Naciste como un mendigo, y así te has de morir, y solo tus pulgas te han de llorar.” ¡Me gusta! Es un filme que me permito decir es muy bello, cambio absolutamente mi percepción sobre la historia de Aladdín, de pequeña me disgustaba y aburría la animada de Disney, pero la versión de Bollywood, me hace amar este filme. El personaje de Aladdín me fascina y siento que su desarrollo está realizado de forma bastante interesante. Entendemos algo desde el primer momento, Aladdín detesta ser tratado como un rezagado, odia que las personas lo juzguen como el ladrón que es sin ningún tipo de empatía. Aunque, comprendemos que es justamente ello su inseguridad, por eso el deseo que le pide al genio para cambiar quien es. “Princesa, usted merece ser admirada y no escuchada.” Pasando a Jazmín, me encanta lo que hicieron con ella, siento que el mensaje que su personaje transmite, está perfecto para el público al que apunta. A Jazmín en el reino se la rebaja por el simple hecho de ser mujer y ser una princesa, se hacen oídos sordos a su opinión y sus decisiones son completamente ignoradas. Es por lo mismo que su evolución me parece muy bella y dulce. Jazmín está harta de la exclusión que sufre y alza la voz para detener el trato injusto que se le da, enseñarles a las niñas pequeñas, que merecen ser escuchadas y tomadas en cuenta es sumamente importante, y el filme lo hace de una manera perfecta. “Debemos ser tan felices como nuestro súbdito más infeliz.” De forma técnica, me fascina, es bastante encantadora, su escenografía y sobretodo SU SOUNDTRACK, son preciosos, son canciones que podría escuchar en mi día a día sin problema alguno. Cada una de las canciones sonadas acompañan la narrativa de forma perfecta y completa. Algo a reconocer del filme es su dramatismo, dependiendo de cada opinión, puede gustar o no aquello, en lo personal, no me resulta del todo molesto, pues hasta cierto punto lo siento necesario. Un musical bastante entretenido, divertido y 100% recomendable.

Et là on pourrait se dire que ça va être.une critique de ce mode de fonctionnement et bah pas du tout c’est une validation. Le perso principal se démène, écourte ses appels pour les enchaîner et être plus performant, travaille plus que les autres, ÉVITE DE BOIRE DE L’EAU POUR PAS ALLER AUX TOILETTES et le film récompense ça ? I have a lot of mixed feelings on this one. It has some moments that were sweet. The acting was great. I've actually seen this before and remembered liking it quite a bit. But this time, I struggled a bit. Largely because I never actually really liked Chris Gardner. Everything he was doing felt really selfish. He demanded his kid stay with him even though he knows he has no way to support his kid. And as a result him and his kid have to really struggle. And it's kind of all his fault. He has another option by allowing the kid to go with his mom to New York. So the movie just made me feel frustrated and kind of pissed off at Chris that he couldn't put his own ego aside to just do what's best for his kid. Now it didn't really make sense to me that the mom didn't fight harder. I just felt like I was missing part of the story. Turns out I was and quite a bit. In the true story, Chris cheated on his wife and got his mistress pregnant. She tried to take their son but he kind of assaulted her and was arrested for that. She does end to taking their kid to New York deciding not to press charges and then eventually ends to taking the kid back after a few months to live with his dad. Then after he becomes a broker he arranged for the kid to stay with her due to his long work hours. This feels like important info to leave out. Finding this out, it just feels like the movie wasn't honest with me. And I find that to be kind of gross to be honest. If I were to treat this as a fictional story, I might feel a bit different. Still didn't like Chris Gardner, but I at least would respect that he was at least able to eventually future things out. And that itself can be a inspirational story. So the story isn't a bad one. But I am mixed on the message. In the ending, while Will Smith is narrating, he says this moment of my life is called happiness. And I don't know how I feel about that. Because having a successful career is not equivalent to happiness. Happiness can be found without success in your career. I do get that if you have no money or resources at all, and your basic human needs aren't being met, it is going to be hard to actually be happy. But having a lot of money isn't really what makes one happy. And it just feels like this movie unintentionally sends the message that to be happy you need to find success in your career, and I don't really think that's true. Anyway, the movie isn't bad exactly. It has it's good elements. But I certainly do have many issues with the movie. Enough where I don't think I would call the movie good. 5/10

The Pursuit of Happyness ist der American Dream Film schlechthin. Man muss nur alles geben, hart arbeiten und daran glauben, dann wird der Erfolg schon kommen. Nun, natürlich ist da etwas dran, egal, wie man ansonsten zu diesem Denken steht. Das Problem dieses Films liegt für mich nicht in der Geschichte, die er erzählt, denn die ist nett gemeint und zusätzlich mit toller Musik unterlegt. Doch es wird vorausgesetzt, dass wir diesen Erfolg selbst miterleben. Dass wir am Ende mindestens so aufgeregt sind wie Chris, ob er den Job nun bekommt oder nicht. Es muss das Publikum emotional mitreißen. Und hier komme ich zu meinem Hauptproblem des Films: Das schafft er einfach nicht. Jedenfalls nicht bei mir. Aber man möge mir die Möglichkeit geben, mich zu erklären. Uns werden mehrere Situationen geschildert, die Chris immer wieder den Boden unter den Füßen wegziehen. Die Ehefrau verlässt ihren Mann und ihr Kind. Die Gläubiger stehen förmlich vor der Tür. Man verliert die Wohnung. Alles Situationen, in die man nicht gelangen möchte, da sie potenziell die eigene Existenz, beziehungsweise die der Familie bedrohen. Und während uns all das geschildert und gezeigt wird, geht The Pursuit of Happyness auf die wichtigsten Fragen, die sich aus dieser Konsequenz ergeben, nicht ein. Denn, was macht all das mit den Menschen? Was macht es mit einem, ständig unsicher zu sein, was als Nächstes passiert? Und wie reagiert man darauf? Diese Fragen ergeben sich gezwungenermaßen aus der Handlung. Doch darüber erfährt man kaum etwas. Dafür sind die Dialoge/ das Drehbuch insgesamt zu oberflächlich. Es werden hier und da schöne Worte gefunden, um die Botschaft des Films zu formulieren(was in den Szenen auch sinnvoll ist, nicht nur Exposition, was der Film aussagen möchte). Aber das Innere der Charaktere wird so gut wie gar nicht beleuchtet. Dadurch verliert der Film enorm viel an Gewicht, weil die emotionalen Szenen dann natürlich nicht so stark wirken können, wie sie sollten. Hinzu kommt, dass The Pursuit of Happyness quasi durchgängig optimistisch ist. Was ich auch per se nicht schlecht finde, allerdings war es dem Film in diesem Fall meiner Ansicht nach nicht zuträglich. Das passiert hauptsächlich durch die Musik und Kamera, die beide wirklich gut sind, aber ich hätte mir gewünscht, manchmal auch etwas kälter in der Inszenierung zu sein, da man dadurch eher Mitgefühl erzeugt hätte. Somit ist tolle Kameraarbeit, tolle Musik, gutes Schauspiel und eine eigentlich motivierende Botschaft in einem zu oberflächlichen Film gefangen und kann seine Wirkung nicht so wirklich entfalten.

Shockingly, this film came out before the late-00s financial crisis. It would have felt even more relevant a year or two later, when a LOT of people were feeling a money crunch. But its concerns are sadly evergreen. Times are really tough right now, and I feel that as a parent of three kids. When the film focuses on that, it’s very effective. I want to see a struggling father succeed for the sake of his son, of course. I am quite privileged, but I think about what I would do to provide for my family if the worst happened. The film loses me in the details, though. It feels like Chris is in this mess because of many boneheaded decisions made before and during the film that strain my sympathies. His wife leaves and he insists that she’s incapable of caring for their son. Why? I’ve seen no indication that she’s a poor mother. Am I supposed to read that as Chris’ pride or his understanding that his wife is a poor provider? And his big win is becoming a stockbroker, the kind of person who creates financial crises that will put more people in these conditions. A lot of these thoughts are front-loaded in the film for me. The ending pulls at the heartstrings just right and makes me feel the joy. But I found it a slog to get there. All that aside, the big takeaway here is Will Smith. It’s a great acting performance, it’s a better box office performance. Smith was the biggest movie star of the 00s. Whether it was action, sci-fi, a rom-com, an original superhero film, his films were successful. He could take this schmaltzy, manipulative pap and make it one of the top ten films of the year. His star power was off the charts, and that’s rewlly interesting to me. Watched as part of a 20th anniversary 2006 retrospective.

Pull Yourself Up by Your Bootstraps: The Movie I get why people like, or even love this movie. It’s well made for the most part, and it boasts career best performances from both Will and Jaden Smith (not that that’s saying much in Jaden’s case, but I digress). But man, this is just straight up capitalist propaganda wrapped up in a feel good package. The movie unironically depicts Thomas Jefferson and Ronald fucking Reagan as inspirational figures! The message of this movie is essentially that you can work yourself out of poverty by working hard enough and being treated poorly by rich white guys. I understand that this is based on a true story, and that Chris Gardner actually did manage to work hard enough to get out of the dumps, but this movie isn’t interested in engaging with the class system that it relies on to get dramatic moments out of. On the contrary, it has the opposite of class consciousness in a way that hasn’t aged well in the slightest post-2008 financial crisis. I don’t hate this movie, but I hate its message and thematic content. It’s almost offensive to me, and it certainly insults my intelligence.

A melancholic watch, focusing on a beautiful father-son relationship, The Pursuit of Happyness goes onto show just how much money controls the quality of our lives. While Christopher’s character can be admired for his perseverance, grit, determination and for being a lovely father, the film glorifies the idea of “pulling yourself up from your bootstraps..” The film understands and in turn, portrays the phenomenology of poverty, struggle and sorrow without holding back. But what it fails to do is critique a system that is radically capitalistic, feeds upon ‘productivity culture’ and normalises kissing the ass of rich men just so you can ‘climb up the ladder.’ Success stories, like Christopher’s, will always be loved; they are inspiring. But one person’s success does not serve to acquit a system that constantly and deliberately keeps people on the brink of collapse and poverty.

Film del 2006, diretto da Gabriele Muccino. Chris Gardner viene lasciato dalla moglie e si ritrova ad affrontare enormi problemi economici, dovendo al tempo stesso prendersi cura del figlio piccolo Christopher. Questo film drammatico mi colpisce sempre molto personalmente. Nonostante presenti qualche limite dal punto di vista tecnico, la sceneggiatura, ispirata a eventi realmente accaduti, riesce sempre a coinvolgermi emotivamente. Narra la storia di un uomo che ha scommesso sull’investimento sbagliato e che si ritrova a dover far fronte a una serie di disavventure che si intrecciano con gravi problemi economici. Dallo sfratto all’abbandono da parte della moglie, passando per lo scarso profitto dei macchinari che cerca invano di vendere, Chris arriva a decidere di cambiare vita, trovando il coraggio e l’ambizione di intraprendere una nuova strada: uno stage non retribuito come broker. È commovente la dedizione, la passione e la resilienza di Chris, il quale, nonostante i numerosi problemi, continua imperterrito sulla propria strada, cercando di barcamenarsi tra il lavoro come venditore, la gestione del figlio e l’impegno dello stage, che prevede ore di studio ma anche l’acquisizione di nuovi clienti. Questo film ci ricorda quanto, anche nei momenti più bui, spesso ci si possa aggrappare a qualcosa, cercando di cambiare l’ordine degli addendi e, di conseguenza, il risultato della propria vita. Il coraggio di Chris, la sua abnegazione conciliata all’ambizione, hanno come propulsore principale la sofferenza, la povertà e l’incapacità di dare al proprio figlio ciò che desidera. E forse questo film, ripeto, nonostante presenti qualche pecca tecnica, mi colpisce sempre nel profondo, probabilmente proprio per le tematiche affrontate, che coincidono con un particolare periodo della mia vita. Questo lungometraggio, per quanto mi riguarda, è terapeutico: un film che, a ogni visione mi migliora l’umore e mi fa credere un po’ di più in me stesso. Per quanto concerne il comparto tecnico, la regia di Muccino prevede un utilizzo della macchina a mano che reputo disordinato e poco pulito. L’angolazione con cui viene posta la macchina da presa in alcune scene non mi convince, così come non mi convince appieno il blocking degli attori, in particolar modo nelle scene domestiche o in quelle racchiuse entro quattro mura. Risultano invece più azzeccate le scene all’aperto, ambientate in una New York movimentata, con Chris che inizialmente sembra andare quasi sempre nel verso opposto rispetto alla folla. Apprezzo l’intenzione di Muccino di mostrare anche questo volto della città, lontano dall’immagine patinata e idealizzata di New York. Will Smith è ottimo e riesce a essere estremamente coinvolgente dal punto di vista emotivo. Ottima anche la performance del giovane Jaden Smith. Voto: 8

A Classic American Dream Movie, But A Tone Deaf Film First I want to say I actually don’t dislike this film. I thought it was a good fun watch that was obviously made with lots of care and good intentions. The low lows we experience with Chris are trully devastating making it feel like your really there struggling alongside him. The amount of time and care the producers put into Chris’s personality and life make you really feel for him and see that he doesn’t deserve to be in this terrible situation. It has everything you would want in an American Dream™️ Movie. The zero to hero story, idealizing capitalism, and the ultimate message of work hard and you can achieve anything. But that’s not true. And this brings me to my main problem with this film. The Ideal (Fake) America Chris, the rest of his family and all the other characters, live in an ideal America free of racial or class bias that does not exist and has Never existed. This film focuses on the struggle of the working class black man in 1980s America but forgets about the fact he is working class and more importantly black. You really expect the audience to believe that in 1981 a rich millionaire CEO is inviting a black middle class intern with him to a football game in his private box because he just knocked on his door. Chris faces no sort of pressure or discrimination in this regard. Changing his race would have zero impact on the story. It seems Chris himself doesn’t even know he’s black. He is constantly quoting Thomas Jefferson a known racist and proud slave owner, and watching Ronald Reagan on the tv (No idea what that scene added). The film also glamorizes Chris bringing his son with him into homeless because he’s “In the pursuit of happiness” and it’s all gonna work out. While simultaneously shaming his wife for wanting to take her son away to a better place Final Notes It’s still a good movie overall aside from all these complaints. Will smith did a great job as Chris and Jayden was phenomenal. To think he was only around 7 years old when this was filmed is insane.

This feels like an Adult Swim short (derogatory). Rango has an instantly compelling premise, but too bad its execution is everything I do not want from a premise as delightfully absurd as a hero's journey from cowardly Lizard to Clint Eastwood. It's so painfully self aware and satirical of everything that it just loses the magic that it could have had. Rango is much more of a comedy than an adventure, a Western or a drama, and it sucks that this is the approach they went for. You are absolutely not supposed to watch Once Upon A Time In The West before this, because most of the elements in this film that make you go "oh shit, that's actually really cool" is just stripped from that one. I don't even like Leone or that movie that much for the matter, but I genuinely checked out once the literal main theme song is just a lackluster spoof of Man With A Harmonica. So many shots are just ripped from Leone without even any interesting remixing of ideas like what Tarantino usually does, just homage for the sake of homage. The movie itself also does not hold up on its own. Rango is supposed to be flawed, but he's so fucking irritatingly incompetent and genuinely idiotic that it makes me completely unable to root for his character. He's not a likeable loser or a charming asshole, he's just that one annoying kid in school that you lowkey understand why they're bullied. And all the characters are just whatever, Beans is the only character that I actually find kinda sweet, too bad she's just the damsel in distress. The movie also feels really really long. Could have ended like 15 minutes before if we got rid of all the shitty Leone homages and trimmed one unnecessary set piece. The animation is pretty gorgeous though, that I can't lie. It's too bad so much of it has to be a homage of Leone that it lacks originality. That (SPOILER) character appearing to Rango before the final act is a little tacky, but it's pretty cute. Puts a smile on my face.

I remember really wanting to see this when it released (though in my memory it released way earlier than it did in reality). I remember so many people singing its praises. I saved Rango for a long time, as I have with a lot of these more mainstream-but-beloved movies. As is often the case, it really has nothing going for it without nostalgia backing it up. Often looking really good, Rango opens pretty strong with a string of whacky cartoon slapstick setpieces, then it completely runs out of steam when it drops into the most generic American family, action/comedy movie template story and just plods through it with nothing memorable, no real characters, no real personality. The character designs are fun. I ended up having to pause it and return 24 hours later because it was boring me to death. I don't think a family comedy should be capable of being boring, but it's so completely lacking in an identity of it's own that there's nothing to connect to. The acid-western epiphany sequence towards the end shakes some energy into the film, by presenting the act of walking into traffic as the solution to all of your problems in a film primarily for children... And of course the epiphany is that capitalism and greed are wasting resources and destroying the earth, which is never really engaged with at all and then Rango wastes loads of water and causes massive amounts of damage and is basically bailed out by everyone else, as he is for the entire story, leaving there with pretty much nothing of value by the end. I guess the Johnny Depp mania of the era was hard carrying this thing.

Hmm muistin että tää olis ollu parempi... ei siis täysin huono mutta paljon asioita joista en pitänyt. Sekava, poukkoileva ja mitäänsanomaton tarina, unohdettavat hahmot ja todella, TODELLA pakotettua huumoria etenkin ensimmäisellä puoliskolla. Siis oikeasti, tuntui että yhden yhtä asiaa ei oteta leffan ekalla puolikkaalla tosissaan ja joka ikinen lause tuplataan jollain vitsillä, gagilla tai hassuttelulla. Ihan saatanan raivostuttavaa. Lisäksi tuo Rango hahmona on niin perseestä todella pitkään, että kun loppupuolella vihdoin jotain kauan odotettua hahmokehitystä tapahtuu, ei se ilmene mitenkään uskottavana. Onneksi jälkipuoli leffasta on ylipäätään parempi ja vakavampi sävyltään. Olisi ollut sitä alusta asti ja huumoria siroteltuna sinne tänne, niin tässä olisi ollut potentiaalia. Tuntui nyt siltä, että ne vaan tyhjensi jonkun kuratoimattoman vitsivihkosensa vaan sarjatulella, ja sitten muisti että ainiin tässä pitää joku juonikin tehdä ja ohoh meillähän olis tässä ihan hyviäkin aineksia joita vois käyttää. Sinänsä harmi, koska animaatiotyyli on hyvin ainutlaatuinen ja mieleenpainuva, ja moni visuaalinen ja esteettinen ratkaisu on todella osuvia. Ja OSA huumorista on oikein hauskaakin, tai olisi hauskaa jos sille antaisi tilaa vaikuttaa. Sinänsä idea tämmöisestä "aikuisten" animaatiosta, jossa on paljon kaksimielisiä vitsejä ja sivistyssanoja, ja melkoisen rujo animaatiotyyli, on todela hyvä ja toimisi, jos siihen uskallettaisiin nojata sellaisenaan. Nyt tämä tuntuu pokkuroinnilta lasten hömppäelokuvan ja vakavasti otettavan aikuisten leffan välillä, eikä tee kumpaakaan hääppöisesti.

Animated films are something I’d like to spend more time diving into as I go deeper into cinema. I’ve watched a good portion of the acclaimed and popular animated films over the years, and this is one that I’ve seen a long time ago. Johnny Depp’s performance as Rango is a good one for sure. He does a good job of portraying a character that almost ironically treats his life as a performance in itself. Rattlesnake Jake is one of the best animated villains in any Disney or Pixar style film I’ve ever seen, and even though he’s not in the film until the last half hour or so, it is worth the wait. I enjoy the camaraderie that the various residents of Dirt manage to develop over the troubling events that the story focuses on. Nicely timed comedic relief is a focal point here, as with most films of this genre, and doesn’t take away from the progression or characters. Overall, if you have the right expectations, it’s a fun watch if nothing else. I enjoy the western style influence and setting, and wish more animated films shared this time period.

Un film Western de mon enfance. Y'en a, ils avaient du Clint Eastwood, moi j'avais du Rango (et Woody). Donc, un film sur un Caméléon avide d'aventure qui va se retrouver dans tout un esprit Far-West, bonne idée ? J'aime beaucoup la DA qui représente bien le côté crade des habitants, façon animaux du désert sèche bien Americain. Bien détaillés, tous avec du vécu de par leurs séquelles physiques ou même psychologiques. Le rendu Western est franchement bien retranscrit, bien animé et détaillé, ce côté vide du désert qui donne franchement soif à regarder. Avec tous les codes du Western : des habitants hostiles, des pilleurs, Shérif et autres bandits au sein du village. C'est clairement le gros point que je lui donne. Ensuite, personnage assez sympathique, clairement en proie à une belle aventure, et cela le montre bien avec ce côté rêveur de quand il était encore domestiqué. Son côté maladroit, peut-être égoïste de par certains de ses choix, s'inventant un nom et une histoire pour mieux s'intégrer. Tout un passage où il paraît crédible aux yeux des autres, le rendant moins héroïque qu'il en a l'air. Mais sans compter son évolution qui résume parfaitement son caractère qui met en défaut ce qu'il devrait être : s'assumer et se construire de lui-même au lieu de mentir constamment. D'ailleurs, représentation assez rigolote pour ceux qui l'auront reconnue à ce passage, vous verrez. J'aime beaucoup tout l'enjeu concernant leur ressource de survie qu'est l'eau. Comment cela devient rare, ce qui peut créer des conflits, d'autres leaders peuvent jouer là-dessus pour asseoir leur pouvoir, et cela nous aura valu un antagoniste assez bien trouvé dans la créativité, d'animal reconnaissable et aux allures bien Western avec son arme au bout de la queue. Un bel aura, une vraie présence qui vole limite la vedette à l'autre premier antagoniste qui est plus affaires et leader. Bon, j'ai quand même eu un vrai enjeu pour suivre le film au vu d'une fatigue qui commençait à monter, ce qui fait que j'ai eu quelques passages qui donnent l'impression d'être longs et ennuyants, mais c'était peut-être moi. Cela va évidemment influencer ma note finale concernant mon expérience personnel, mais pas grave, j'assume mes responsabilités en termes de visionnage où je dois me stopper si je sens une once d'assoupissement. Mais bon, au moins le film a de bons gags, le message final est correct, et les enjeux de sécheresse parfaitement expliqués. Film sympa, sans être exceptionnel. Juste dommage que je trouve la BO assez mémorable.

Also, there are a LOT of references to testicles (like, specifically testicles) for a movie presumably intended for a child audience. I do enjoy Rango, and I think it's an oddly beautiful film with excellent character designs and a willingness to push its premise to the most entertaining limit. But it's also, and I do mean this entirely seriously and in the most literal, art-movement sense, very surrealist. For some reason I couldn't get behind this movie. Rango felt like a chameleon of a character, with the movie's theme hinging on everyone asking Rango "Who are you". Rango adopts a macho Western cowboy persona to befriend the citizens of the town, with a charisma that shoots him up to the sheriff position. It's a facade that didn't sit well for me for the majority of the movie. I felt bored of Rango's ego throughout the movie because it felt so fake. I wanted to root for him because he felt like a relatable lost soul. Yet, his switch up into playing a persona really lost me. It felt like watching a friend change their entire personality on you. Although, that is a point of the movie, but I didn't find myself enjoying it. BUT the movie was fun. It was fun watching Rango reign down back onto the town and show who's boss. The film had beautiful textures, but the colours looked drab. It felt like I was looking at dirt.

If you've never seen "Oshi no Ko", it's a very well animated, very badly written anime that tricks viewers into thinking it's good because it's so pretty. Being pretty does not make up for the bad writing. Being pretty is easy. "Rango" is ultimately a very simple and harmless children's film. Narratively it's nothing impressive. Some parts even are arguably just bad. Depp's improv is much less charming these days than it was 15 years ago, and it's got probably the worst example of the dreaded "liar revealed" trope in recent memory. But it is also one of the most artistically creative and visually impressive pieces of animation ever put to screen. It's more than just "pretty". In fact most of the film is ugly as all hell, but intentionally. Animation just being pretty doesn't excuse flawed writing, but the level of artistic talent and creativity put into this film is different from "pretty"

Rango is a really fun and unique film. It has a great protagonist, a distinct Wild West theme and presentation, and it’s hilarious. Rango is an awesome character with very strong character development. He starts as a chameleon in a tank, gets thrown in the middle of no where, fakes it til he makes it, becomes sheriff and starts proving it through moments such as standing up to Rattlesnake Jake and protecting Dirt. He ends up becoming a symbol of hope and a true hero for Dirt. The Wild West theme and the presentation of this film are amazing. The pretty sunsets and night skies, the desert setting, a great score, the sounds such as the clock hitting high noon on a Wednesday or guns reloading, and the town of Dirt give it a distinct feel. The Mariachi owls as narrators and occasionally breaking the fourth wall also added on to its feel. Rango is a really fun film with a great protagonist who goes from zero to hero. Combine that with comedy and a beautiful yet distinct Wild West presentation makes this a great watch. 8/10

“No man can walk out on his own story.” Rango is a love letter to the classic westerns of the 20th century while simultaneously being one of the greatest westerns of the 21st century. It somehow manages to follow the classic western blueprint step by step while checking off every single trope along the way, and yet there is nothing else like it. I adore Rango. The team behind this project were very clearly firing on all cylinders. The script is sharp, the plot is tight, the visuals are incredible and the voice cast is perfect. It’s just a start to finish treat of a film. There are some truly inspiring scenes in this movie. There are plenty of gags and fun throughout, but there are also several moments where it gets incredibly thoughtful, philosophical and emotional. It has to be one of my favorite animated movies at this point. Every time I revisit it I walk away with a stronger love and appreciation for it. The design for Rattlesnake Jake is S tier. The designs for every creature are incredible but the scene when Rattlesnake Jake shows up is genuinely intense.

Ha fingido ser más fuerte o seguro de lo que realmente es; pero aun así, acepta su destino. Un hombre (lagartija, creo) que está dispuesto a entregarse al espectáculo de la vida y ser el personaje principal de su propio destino. Rango empieza actuando en un terrario y termina actuando en el mundo real, hasta que la actuación se vuelve su realidad. Para mí, creo que de eso se trata un poco la vida: fingir lo que queremos ser para reconfortarnos un poco y darnos esos pequeños empujones que necesitamos en el camino. No puede evitar verme reflejado; es cine absoluto.

A natural contrarian though I may be, I have to be a genuine hater here, I did not enjoy Snatch . I'm not intimately acquainted with the genre - or the culture these films aim to 'replicate' - but this feels like parody, and not in a particularly entertaining way. While there is some semblance of stylism in the editing, the majority of these instances range from boring to tacky. The burning caravan scene is cool, and I like the POV shots of characters lying on the ground with others literally looming over them, but it’s too overused to be effective. They try to mix it up with Dutch angles to the same end, but it doesn't work for me. Powerpoint transitions, GTA split screens and rotating jpegs, I know we're living it up in the year 2000, but this looks so cheap in modern viewing. The colours are washed out to emulate a sort of grittiness but the grimmer moments just fall flat for me in the direction. The music is weirdly jaunty at moments where it doesn't quite gel with what's happening (put a pin in that) and Errol & Tony are the only marginally intimidating performances, everyone else feels a bland. Much like a lot of the dialogue, a lot of these performances feel like they’re read directly off the page. Oh man the dialogue draaaaaags. Every time Sol, Vincent and Tyrone are on screen I'm begging for them to just get on with it, every conversation feels like: The car crashes, "you just crashed the car," "why did you do that?" "yeah, why did you do that?" "well, I didn't do it on purpose," "yeah, you shouldn't have done that," "yeah" ...Like, if this is parody, I'm sure it's brilliant, but fuck me, maybe I'm too brain-rotted by instagram reels and better action films, I'm so bored, I do not care. There are some moments that tap into the inherent poetry of the cockney dialect, my favourite being 'as bent as the Soviet sickle, and as hard as the hammer that crosses it' but the majority borders on cringe. The pacing is so slow, yet whenever something interesting happens, it's over before it's even started. Anticlimactic first boxing match, anticlimactic bookie heist, anticlimactic gun shots to the head, I have no idea what we're working towards here. It feels like the same scene over and over again in pursuit of a 86-carat Macguffin. Jason Statham narrates intermittently but it's unclear why he is the POV character for the majority of this film. When the diamond conveniently happens to him at the very end, there is slight satisfaction of things coming together, but it doesn't feel particularly clever or meaningful. I wouldn't mind if there was some other sort of interesting spectacle happening at any point, but there's nothing here. The final boxing match is slightly better than any of the action pieces before it, but it's not a scratch on the Sherlock Holmes (2009) boxing match, also directed by Guy Ritchie, which is disappointing. An... interesting role for Brad Pitt...everyone saying Pitt is incomprehensible is crazy, I easily understand it, or maybe I'm just someone who is northern and actually interacts with people outside of my dialect. It always bothers me when they get A-Listers to play poor people with their perfect Hollywood teeth, though of course Pitt's performance isn't the only elephant-sized/shaped issue with the framing of the traveller community in this film. Take a shot for every racial slur - if you thought The Gentleman was bad, Snatch will give you a stroke. The Jewish stereotyping is also pretty egregious. Musically, there's this grotesquely hokey Yiddish scoring whenever a Jewish person in on screen, though arguably it specifically appears only when 'fake Jews' are on screen, i.e., The Head and the costumed thieves in the opening. If we're being charitable, this sonic stereotyping could be an exercise in satirical hyperrealism to draw attention to the false semitic surface, but I think it's unlikely. From what I understand in his other work that I've heard, John Murphy ranges from competent but boring in James Gunn's Superman (2025), to the brilliance of 28 days later , so this could swing either way. Messy, directionless, dull, and confusing in tone - this one just wasn't for me.

Scavenger Hunt #138 Film 4 of 30 Category: Watch a film with an ensemble cast The Film *Snatch* is the kind of crime film that seems completely out of control while secretly knowing exactly where every character and storyline is going. What begins with a stolen diamond quickly expands into illegal boxing, fixed fights, gambling debts, violent gangsters, incompetent criminals, and a dog that somehow becomes essential to the entire plot. There are so many characters moving toward different goals that the story could have easily become confusing. Instead, the chaos becomes the main source of entertainment. Everyone thinks they understand the situation, yet almost nobody has any real control over it. Every plan creates another problem, every criminal underestimates somebody, and the diamond keeps moving through the film as though it is mocking everyone chasing it. The comedy works because the characters take their ridiculous world completely seriously. People are threatened, kidnapped, robbed, and killed, but the movie finds humor in their terrible planning, strange personalities, and inability to communicate. It never pauses to announce a joke. The humor comes from watching confidence collapse into panic. The Direction Guy Ritchie directs *Snatch* with an incredible amount of style and energy. The rapid editing, freeze frames, exaggerated sound effects, slow motion, and sudden changes in speed make the film feel like it is constantly moving. Even scenes built entirely around conversation have momentum because of how quickly the dialogue and reactions bounce between characters. The nonlinear structure also makes the film more satisfying. Sequences that initially appear random eventually connect, and small details return with much greater importance. Ritchie repeatedly shows the same event from different perspectives, allowing one character’s victory to become another character’s disaster. The final stretch is especially strong because every storyline begins colliding at once without losing the film’s rhythm. The style occasionally comes close to overwhelming the story, but it fits this particular world. Everything is loud, grimy, fast, and slightly exaggerated. London feels like an enormous criminal maze where everyone knows somebody dangerous, but nobody knows enough to stay out of trouble. The Ensemble The ensemble is the heart of the film. Jason Statham gives Turkish the exhausted energy of someone who knows every situation is getting worse but has no choice except to keep moving. Stephen Graham is hilarious as Tommy, whose nervous reactions make him the perfect partner for Turkish. Brad Pitt nearly steals the entire movie as Mickey. His accent is almost impossible to understand, yet that becomes part of the character’s power. Everyone treats Mickey like an unintelligent outsider because they cannot understand him, but he is constantly more aware than the people attempting to manipulate him. Pitt makes him funny, unpredictable, and genuinely dangerous without ever changing the character’s relaxed attitude. Alan Ford is terrifying as Brick Top because he never needs to become overly emotional. His calmness makes every threat feel more believable. Dennis Farina brings a completely different energy as Cousin Avi, reacting to England and its criminals with constant irritation. Vinnie Jones is also perfectly cast as Bullet Tooth Tony, whose reputation alone is enough to control most rooms. What makes the ensemble especially effective is that no character feels disconnected from the film’s personality. Even people with limited screen time leave an impression. Each performance adds another form of stupidity, confidence, fear, or violence to the story. Conclusion *Snatch* is a ridiculously entertaining mixture of crime, comedy, and controlled chaos. Its story is complicated, but the film never feels weighed down by explanation. It trusts the audience to keep up and rewards that attention by bringing every strange character and seemingly unrelated detail together. The ensemble cast is what makes the entire machine work. No single character has to carry the movie because everyone contributes something memorable to it. Brad Pitt may be the standout, but the real pleasure comes from watching all these personalities collide and ruin one another’s plans. It is stylish without becoming empty, violent without losing its humor, and complicated without becoming impossible to follow. *Snatch* turns criminal incompetence into an art form and somehow makes complete disorder feel perfectly organized.

asked camille to put this on at 10pm knowing i’d fall asleep and because i wanted to be put to sleep after a weird night emotionally (and there’s no writer who lulls me into somnambulatory hazes more than sorkin, see my myriad attempts to watch the social network that see me snoozing before garfield even gets to say the line about his prada being at the cleaners) and it worked, though i strangely was able to stay awake until damn near an hour twenty with this one and between that and the tens of clips of this i’ve seen during some time-wasting endeavor or another on short-form video applications in the last five+ years i think i’ve metabolized a percentage of the meaningful content of this film that’d be tantamount to a high-A letter-grade. in dearborn, michigan there’s a horrific acres-sprawling henry ford vanity project/oversized and undercontexted memorial, where ford himself picked up and moved edison’s actual lab/residence among other architectural objects important to the late-19th–early-20th centuries’ histories (which despite its obvious odiousness is at least appreciable in the way it’s essentially a super-sized and un-concealed in its greed version of the pillaging drive of all first-world museums, the bareness of it heightening these innate contradictions in a way that’s at least interesting to think about) assumedly as a way of creating a huge synecdoche of america that southeast michigan soon-to-be factory worker children could free roam around and think about the majesty of american ingenuity and invention. during the baseball season there were weekly games where crashed-out/aging minor league players would play baseball as close as possible to how it was played in the 1800s (for the record there were some black players who participated in this but don’t think it’s lost on me or likely the players that this was the specific time period they were tasked to replicate). my dad has a distant but oft-professed love of baseball, and would take our family to sit on the grass on the hill near third-base and eat cold sandwiches and cape cod potato chips and drink izzes sometimes in the summers, an activity that none of us enjoyed or got much out of except him. and while we were sitting there he’d get romantic about baseball as this monument to american cynicism and rugged-if-not-horrific individualism/single-mindedness, how it’s great because most of the gamesmanship happens off the field (either through direct cheating a la the world series fix gatsby is implicated in or the indirect underhanded tactics on display in this movie) but that ultimately it is a game played in real time with so many uncontrolled variables so as to make the thing always feel very alive despite its conceits. i think these descriptions are a lot of the reason i came to love racing so much in my adulthood, the vast team-wide conspiracies required to pull-off certain tech violations (see jeremy clarkson’s tale of lancia tricking fia officials into thinking they’d homologated twice as many 037s as they did , a story that always struck me as a real john hanley classic) or the way that back in the 80s team principles would run any fuel with any additive so long as it made the car faster even if it made the flames invisible as pit-crew-members burned to death. as vulgar and horrific as that level of avarice can be to witness, there’s something i love and find difficult to look away from in all of it. but it should be noted from the eras of sport my dad and now i show interest in that neither of the aforementioned activities really function like that anymore, or at least the stakes are lower and more controlled, and this stakeslessness is why i think my dad found it difficult to care about the period of baseball described in moneyball and why i find it hard to care about hamilton joining ferrari (next season guys i promise). sorkin does an okay job at filling this movie with chewy people-in-rooms dialogue and the director coaxes some decent performances from pitt, hoffman and hill, and sorkin at least has similar thoughts about the game as my dad in a way that made me feel tenderly enough to write this very long review about a movie i was asleep for part of, but he seldom-if-ever works to illustrate why baseball is still a game worthy of keeping his or my father’s rapt attention and in that failure this movie ends up pretty dead on arrival, dead especially because if anyone could be convinced the conniving magic is still there in sport it’s me. but hey, fun "Sabermetrics" is the application of statistical analysis to baseball records, esp. in order to evaluate and compare the performance of individual players. The definition alone puts most people to sleep, and yet they made a movie about it. So if you haven't watch any of the trailers and don't know anything about it, Moneyball is the true story of Billy Beane (Brad Pitt), the manager of the Oakland A's who used the sabermetrics concept to stay within his ghetto Oakland budget in order to get a decent team. All the good players like Jason Giambi and Johnny Damon, after 2001, went on to play respectively for the Yankees and the Red Sox, the two most annoying and also wealthiest teams in the American league. In order to replace the star players, Billy Beane, with the help of Jonah Hill (who's character I don't know is fictional or not), crunched a bunch of numbers together to scout out the players that looked bad on paper, but because they statistically got on base a lot more, would be worth buying. This wasn't exactly a feel-good movie about how Beane used a revolutionary new method of scouting and brought a team to victory. Because, let's face it, does anyone remember Oakland winning a World Series any time since 1989? Hell no! Beane is still the GM of the A's and still, they suck big clanking moneyballs. But, the movie isn't about that. Aaron Sorkin, who co-wrote the screenplay, is a genius at getting a different message across. The Social Network wasn't about the invention of Facebook, it was about a nerdy guy who made a lot of complicated choices to become who he was. Moneyball is really about a guy who just tries a different philosophy. When Beane was in high school, the scouts all said he'd be a star player and convinced him to give up a Stanford scholarship to play for the Mets, but he bottomed out. As it's pointed out in Moneyball, this happens all the time. Not even just in baseball, but in most sports. Scouts really don't know jack shit about how a player is going to develop, so why not try this way? It seemed a perfect fit for Beane, who's portrayed by Pitt as a guy who wants badly to not have anything human to do with the players. He didn't want to have to get to know them, less he has to fire or trade them. He'd rather base everything on numbers, let the cold facts make the decisions for him. He struggles with it until he understand that you can't take romance about of baseball. These are human beings, not predictable machines, and Baseball is so ingrained in the American psyche as an escapist pastime that most people aren't going to easily accept something like sabermetrics. I liked Moneyball more than I thought I would. I didn't think there would be any point to basing a movie on something that didn't work. Hey, let's next do a movie on the development of New Coke! But, the theme sold me, and then so did Pitt's performance. Even Jonah Hill was good, not playing the sarcastic fat guy he's known for. I was hoping to see more of Oakland, but I mostly got scenes of that ghetto Coliseum, and all those shipyard structures, but that's just me. I shouldn't have expected Lake Merritt or something. The movie did last a long time so if you're not at all into baseball or the story, you might be looking at your watch.

— the kind that makes spreadsheets and sabermetrics feel as tense as a ninth-inning at-bat. Bennett Miller frames it less like a sports movie and more like a heist film where the score being cased is a full season, and it plays almost like the spiritual predecessor to Ted Lasso: an outsider's unconventional method quietly dismantling an entrenched system. The scene of Jonah Hill walking Brad Pitt through his numbers is the film's clearest thesis statement, and the camera knows it — pushing in tight enough that you can see the pixels on the screen, the data itself becoming the emotional core of the scene. That's the trick of the whole movie: turning cold math into something that comes alive. Pitt and Hill's chemistry does a lot of the heavy lifting too, Billy's practiced confidence playing off Peter's shy, introverted uncertainty in a way that never feels like odd-couple shtick. And Billy Beane's backstory isn't just texture — it's the engine underneath everything, the reason his refusal to accept mediocrity reads as compulsion rather than strategy: a guy who was once the sure thing that didn't pan out, demanding the best from everyone else because he never got to demand it from himself, and never extending that kindness back to the players under him. Even the smaller touches land — the American flag catching the light on the diamond, the surprise of seeing Liverpool's John Henry pop up as a cameo when you already bleed red for that club. There isn't a ton left to say about it at this point except that it's fully earned its status as a cult classic of the genre.

On the surface, this is an underdog story about a baseball team trying to compete with teams that have far more money and resources than they do. But underneath that, it’s such an interesting insight into a side of sport we rarely get to see. The finances, recruitment, statistics and decisions being made behind the scenes are just as important as what eventually happens on the field. What makes it even more interesting watching it now is knowing how much sport has changed since. The kind of data-driven thinking Billy is fighting to introduce has become such a huge part of modern sport, not just baseball. Analytics, finding value in players and trying to gain an advantage through information are now completely normal. You’re basically watching an approach that people thought was ridiculous become part of how modern sport operates. Then there’s Billy himself and the resistance he faces trying to change something that has been done the same way for decades. Everyone around him has their own idea of what a baseball player should look like and how a team should be built, because experience has taught them that’s simply how it works. Billy doesn’t have the money to play by those same rules, so he has to question whether the rules actually make sense in the first place. I really liked that idea. Just because something has always been done a certain way doesn’t mean it’s the best way of doing it. There’s something quite inspiring about watching someone believe in an idea while almost everyone around them is telling them it won’t work. Change means being willing to adapt, evolve and sometimes go against what everyone else accepts as normal. You might not even be the person who ultimately benefits the most from that change, but you can still be the person who proves that another way is possible.

I don't know anything about baseball, but how can you not be romantic about it? Like, genuinely. If you asked me to explain the rules right now, I'd probably embarrass myself. However, Moneyball was actually pretty fucking good. A big part of why I enjoyed it is obviously Brad Pitt. I think he's officially one of my favourite actors at this point, so putting him in basically anything is already giving the movie a head start. He genuinely carries this really well. Billy Beane is such an interesting character because he's constantly trying to prove something to himself. He keeps raising the bar even when the bar is already fucking low, and no matter what he achieves, he's never completely satisfied. That ambition is both his biggest strength and probably his biggest weakness. He's so obsessed with finding the next way to improve that he doesn't really know when to stop. He's always chasing the next goal, trying to prove that his ideas can work and refusing to accept that things have to be done the way they've always been done. Then you've got Jonah Hill playing a serious role, which is bloody weird to see at first. I'm so used to him being the comedic relief that seeing him actually play someone more reserved and serious took me a minute, but he genuinely does a great job here, and the fact that he's not constantly trying to make you laugh actually makes his character work. The craziest part is that this is based on a true story. I know absolutely fuck all about baseball, but even I could appreciate how insane it is that these people were basically trying to change the way the sport was approached by looking at things differently. Sports, but online, using only statistics? I don't think I suddenly understand baseball now, but if someone asks me about it from this point onwards, Moneyball is basically going to be my entire knowledge of the sport.

Moneyball is a baseball drama starring Brad Pitt as Billy Beane, the general manager of the Oakland A’s back in the early 2000s. The story signifies how Billy tried to build a competitive team despite having one of the smallest budgets in baseball. I feel like I saw this in bits and pieces a while ago, but I’m so glad to have watched it for a second time. If you are a sports or baseball fan I really think you would enjoy this film. On the other hand, if you don’t really care about baseball, some of the statistical/roster discussions are gonna feel dry. To be honest, most of the movie would feel dry to you because the main priority isn’t triumphant wins or thrilling scenes. The focus is more of a character/strategy drama than a conventional sports plot. Lots of dialogue and conversations surrounding the ball house. To me that doesn’t matter because the dialogue is sharp and the movie has a really good sense of momentum regardless of the stats.  I think it was really cool to witness the process of how the A’s were like a bottom of the barrel team to going on an insane win streak. You can’t give up on this film and have to stay till the end too. It’s an underdog story, but not the typical “team comes together and wins” story. If you’ve ever seen Major League, this is almost a serious version of that movie.The acting was top tier too. Brad Pitt is excellent as Beane with his smooth, charming demeanor and never giving up. Jonah Hill is great too in a more restrained dramatic role. I think the casting was awesome with how they put Pitt and Hill as the one two. Even if you don’t love baseball I think you should still give this a try. You can understand the basic concept of trying to accomplish more with less money. Although this is a safe hit of a movie, it’s always go Redsox baby.

What this movie does is highlight the true magic of film. It takes something that is generally boring and turns it into the most important thing in the world. It is transformed into something so utterly captivating and human that I can’t look away. “How can you not be romantic about baseball?” That line, delivered by Brad Pitt’s Billy Beane after watching Jeremy Brown trip and stumble back to first base after him hitting a home run, is the moment I keep coming back to every time I watch Moneyball. I gave it five out five stars. I grew up with this story because baseball has been such a huge part of my life, and still is because I’m still playing. I also believe this is Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill’s most underrated and underappreciated work. Both performances carry the film without ever feeling like they’re reaching for attention. It feels very authentic. What I find just as compelling is Billy's relationship with his own scouting team. He gets annoyed at them for judging players purely on the eye test, even though that’s the exact same way he was scouted and brought into the league himself. It’s a strange contradiction, but it’s part of what makes his character work so well for me. Beyond the performances, I think the moneyball movement itself was the most impactful moment in the history of sports. It wasn’t just about analytics changing how teams evaluate players, it was about teaching big organizations across every sport that thinking unconventionally could actually win. That idea is bigger than baseball, and it’s a big part of why this movie has stuck with me for as long as it has.n

James Edwards, a New York City police officer, encounters a suspect with unusual abilities and garners the attention of a secret government agency. He trades in his life to become Agent J and learns all about the undergroup extraterrestrial market. There is a particularly dangerous bug that causes intergalactic turmoil and war. Agents K and J try to get rid of the bug and maintain intergalactic diplomacy. Somehow, there is both a lot and a little to unpack here; the whole world of aliens hiding in plain sight is a clever setup, and the film does a good job sticking to its own rules. However, there is nothing speculative here, nor is there any allegory. I know it’s supposed to be fun, but there seems to be little to no tone or atmosphere. Everything in this film is built for a quick popcore experience, flashy effects, and little depth. Nothing was offensive, and I can't pinpoint anything that actively detracted from my enjoyment. I guess I just didn’t love it. Will Smith and Tommy Lee Jones bounce off each other, and their chemistry is fine, but it’s not my favorite buddy-cop pairing. The action sequences are fine, but the agents feel more like superheroes than law enforcement. How am I supposed to believe that these “bugs” are so tough and such a threat when Will Smith effectively wins a one-on-one fist fight? There’s spectacle and wit, but I guess MiB just didn’t hit home this time.

I finally watched Men in Black for the first time. Obviously I knew how culturally significant and iconic it became, but unfortunately I never watched it as a kid, and I think that probably would’ve changed my experience with it quite a bit. I can definitely see the appeal, especially as a kids’ movie. The whole concept of aliens secretly living among humans disguised as normal people is really creative, and combining that with two agents hunting down aliens, weird gadgets and goofy humor makes for a fun ’90s premise. The concept was probably more interesting to me than the actual story, though. The plot just never really caught me. It basically comes down to them chasing a big alien who’s looking for a galaxy hidden on a cat’s collar, and the whole thing felt pretty random and messy to me. There are some funny moments, and Will Smith does his usual charismatic Will Smith thing, but nothing about the characters or story really stood out to me. It’s been many years since I last watched Men in Black, and revisiting it reminded me just how fun it is. It’s a non‑serious sci‑fi comedy in which Will Smith plays a cop recruited into the Men in Black, a secret agency tasked with monitoring alien activity and managing what the public sees and remembers. The film thrives on deadpan humour and absurd alien encounters, and its comedic tone is one of its strongest features. It never pretends to be serious sci‑fi: instead, it leans into its own silliness with confidence. The dynamic between Agent J (James) and Agent K is the film’s emotional centre. K’s stoic professionalism, interspersed with dry sarcasm, contrasts perfectly with J’s energetic, reactive presence. J feels like a genuine apprentice, inexperienced but clearly capable, and their chemistry gives the film a likeable set of protagonists. I enjoyed the world: aliens living disguised among humans, an entire hidden ecosystem ticking away beneath everyday life, and the Men in Black quietly keeping it all in order. The MIB headquarters, the gadgets, and the neuralyzer are iconic touches, and the creature effects hold up visually — especially Edgar the Bug once he reveals his true form. The film isn’t driven by heavy themes, but there are hints worth noting: the personal cost of secrecy, shown through Agent K’s distant relationship with his former love, and the playful reminder of cosmic insignificance — that humanity is just one small part of a much larger universe. It’s a brisk watch, but never feels rushed. Plenty happens, and the pacing keeps the film light and engaging. For me, it remains a defining Will Smith comedy and a cornerstone of 90s sci‑fi cinema. A solid, enjoyable 7/10.

Time / distance and a shit-crusted legacy have tainted this a little but it shouldn't be forgotten that separated from its monumentally awful 2002 sequel , its vastly improved heavily belated 2012 quasi-reboot-sequel and its dead-eyed and embarrassing 2019 ' legacy sequel ' this thing was absolutely huge - culturally, cinematically and of course financially (pulling in over $589.3 million worldwide on a $90 million budget). Ce n’est clairement pas la première fois que je regarde Men in Black, et même après plusieurs visionnages, je trouve que le film fonctionne toujours aussi bien. Je lui mets 4/5, parce que c’est un film qui a beau avoir pris quelques années, il garde un charme et une efficacité que j’apprécie énormément. Déjà, le duo Will Smith et Tommy Lee Jones est clairement l’un des gros points forts du film. J apporte toute l’énergie, l’humour et la curiosité du personnage qui découvre complètement cet univers, tandis que K est l’exact opposé : il est blasé, sérieux et donne l’impression d’avoir absolument tout vu dans sa vie. Leur dynamique est vraiment excellente et permet au film d’enchaîner les moments sérieux avec des scènes beaucoup plus absurdes sans que ça paraisse forcé. Et puis il faut quand même parler du concept : une organisation secrète qui surveille les extraterrestres vivant parmi nous, efface la mémoire des témoins et règle les problèmes avant même que le grand public ne comprenne ce qui s’est passé. Franchement, leur méthode de travail est particulière. « Vous venez de voir un extraterrestre ? » FLASH. « Quel extraterrestre ? » Pratique, mais niveau respect de la vie privée, on repassera. J’aime énormément la façon dont le film nous fait découvrir cet univers à travers J. Au départ, il ne croit évidemment pas à tout ça et pense simplement avoir affaire à quelque chose d’inexplicable. Puis il découvre progressivement que les extraterrestres existent réellement, qu’ils sont partout et que certains ressemblent suffisamment aux humains pour vivre totalement normalement parmi nous. C’est probablement ce qui rend l’univers aussi amusant : tout peut être extraterrestre et personne ne le sait. Le film mélange également très bien science-fiction, action et comédie. Il y a de vraies scènes d’action, des enjeux et même quelques passages assez impressionnants, mais l’ensemble ne se prend jamais totalement au sérieux. C’est justement ce qui fait son charme. Les créatures sont d’ailleurs toujours aussi amusantes à regarder. Les effets spéciaux ont évidemment vieilli depuis 1997, mais personnellement ça ne me dérange pas énormément. Au contraire, je trouve que certains effets pratiques donnent encore aujourd’hui un charme particulier au film. On sent davantage le travail effectué sur les créatures et les costumes, là où certains films modernes peuvent parfois devenir tellement dépendants du numérique qu’on perd un peu cette sensation de « réel ». J’aime également beaucoup l’esthétique du film. Les costumes noirs, les lunettes de soleil, les voitures, les gadgets et cette ambiance très années 90 donnent immédiatement une identité aux Men in Black. Même sans voir le titre, quelques secondes suffisent pour reconnaître l’univers. Et évidemment, il y a toutes ces petites scènes absurdes qui font que le film reste aussi divertissant. Parce qu’on parle quand même de types en costard qui peuvent passer leur journée à gérer des extraterrestres, des armes capables de faire exploser absolument n’importe quoi et des créatures géantes… tout en gardant un calme professionnel. Moi, après avoir vu une bestiole sortir d’un endroit où elle n’avait absolument rien à faire, je pense que j’aurais demandé une mutation. Le scénario reste malgré tout assez simple et certains éléments sont aujourd’hui beaucoup plus prévisibles. On sent également que le film appartient à son époque, notamment dans son rythme et certains effets. Mais honnêtement, je ne regarde pas Men in Black pour avoir un scénario extrêmement complexe. Je le regarde parce que c’est fun, drôle, efficace et extrêmement reconnaissable. Et puis Will Smith apporte énormément au film. Il possède cette capacité à rendre son personnage drôle sans avoir besoin d’en faire constamment des tonnes. C’est naturellement amusant parce qu’il réagit exactement comme nous réagirions probablement dans certaines situations : avec beaucoup trop de questions et probablement un peu de panique intérieure. Au final, Men in Black reste pour moi un très bon divertissement et surtout un film qui a une vraie personnalité. Il n’est peut-être plus aussi impressionnant techniquement qu’à sa sortie, mais son humour, son duo principal, son univers et son ambiance fonctionnent encore très bien. Un film que je peux clairement revoir avec plaisir. Et si jamais les extraterrestres existent vraiment… j’espère simplement que les Men in Black font bien leur travail, parce que personnellement, je n’ai aucune envie de découvrir ce qui vit réellement dans les égouts de New York.

This movie is genuinely so bad. Like insane to think that the thesis to a period piece about racism is a steven universe-esque "Everyone Can Be Kind, You Just Have To Look For It". The director clearly thinks this is subversive, implying that he assumes the opposite to be the default. Obviously this adds a new undertone that what actually makes someone gross and violent is being poor. A couple notable scenes in the movie : - Don is forced by Tony to eat fried chicken. He says "no" at first, repulsed by the idea of adhering to a stereotype, but ends up caving in and enjoying it. This scene is meant to be comedic and heartwarming, mostly at Don's expense, for even daring to refuse fried chicken. - Don and Tony get stopped by a white police officer while getting home, making the former very anxious, due to his past misadventures with racist cops. However, this one is just plain nice, as Not All Cops Are Bastards, wishes them a Merry Christmas and lets them go. In summary, this movie is insanely racist, and makes blatantly false assumptions about racism in the 60s. It treats racism as an individual rather than systemic problem : you are expected to accept racism as an unchangeable truth of the world in order to engage with this piece. I'd give zero stars if I could.

On the one hand, yes, the acting is great, you’ve got Viggo Mortensen, who very rarely turns in a bad performance and is very selective when it comes to picking the right script to work on and knowing if he can make something good come out of it which he does here, and Mahershala Ali, what more do I even need to say about him that he hasn’t done already, he’s a fantastic actor and in the years since he gained a bigger spotlight he’s got Curious Case Of Benjamin Button, Predators, Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Moonlight, Hidden Figures, True Detecitve season 3, Spider-Man: Into The Spiderverse, even his channeled Wesley Snipes performance in Alita: Battle Angel was great, this guy is a fantastic actor and rightfully deserved to win Best Supporting Actor this year. If anything these two guys are the reason why the film is salvageable. But other than that, everything else about this movie is just bland and forgettable. For one thing, it’s a bad sign in the family of the person you’re making the movie off of had no idea they were even making the film without them knowing. Yeah, no joke, Shirley’s relatives condemned the film, stating that they were not contacted by studio representatives until after development, and that it misrepresented Shirley’s relationship with his family. Don’s brother Maurice Shirley said, “My brother never considered Tony to be his ‘friend’; he was an employee, his chauffeur (who resented wearing a uniform and cap). This is why context and nuance are so important. The fact that a successful, well-to-do black artist would employ domestics that did NOT look like him, should not be lost in translation.” Mahershala Ali responded with an apology to Shirley’s nephew Edwin Shirley III, saying that “I did the best I could with the material I had” and that he was not aware that there were “close relatives with whom I could have consulted to add some nuance to the character”. Writer-director Peter Farrelly said that he was under the impression that there “weren’t a lot of family members” still alive, that they did not take major liberties with the story, and that relatives of whom he was aware had been invited to a private screening for friends and family. Nick Vallelonga, Vallelonga’s son, acknowledged that members of the Shirley family were hurt that he did not speak to them, and that he was sorry that they were offended. He told Variety that “Don Shirley himself told me not to speak to anyone” and that Shirley “approved what I put in and didn’t put in.” That’s already a bad sign right out of the gate. Another problem the movie has is that follows the white savior stereotype/cliché. Peter Farrelly told Entertainment Weekly that he was aware of the white savior trope before filming and sought to avoid it. He said he had long discussions with the actors and producers on the point, and believes that it was not advanced by the film, saying it is “about two guys who were complete opposites and found a common ground, and it’s not one guy saving the other. It’s both saving each other and pulling each other into some place where they could bond and form a lifetime friendship.” New York Times writer Wesley Morris characterized Green Book as being a “racial reconciliation fantasy”. Morris argues that the film represents a specific style of racial storytelling “in which the wheels of interracial friendship are greased by employment, in which prolonged exposure to the black half of the duo enhances the humanity of his white, frequently racist counterpart”. Writing in The Hollywood Reporter, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar noted that “filmmakers are history’s interpreters, not its chroniclers.” Because when I think of somebody trying to avoid falling into clichés, it’s Peter Farrelly, whose last big directing contribution to the world was the shitpile that was Movie 43….oops. But let’s get down to the real reason why this movie does not work at all, it’s fucking Driving Miss Daisy all over again, just reverse the races, make Jessica Lange Mahershala Ali and make Morgan Freeman Viggo Mortensen and bang, it’s pretty much the same movie, there is nothing clever or unique about this movie. It’s just an Oscar bait film, the same typical Oscar bait film that we’ve been trying to get rid of for years now, and the worst part about all of this is that there was a far superior Oscar bait film that got completely snubbed this year and that was A Star Is Born, that was an example of an Oscar bait movie done 100% right avoiding a lot of the tropes and clichés and creating new twists and turns with it to create not only a great movie but one of the best movies of last year….and it got completely snubbed at the Oscars only winning 1 of its’ 8 nominations while Green Book got 3. While Green Book doesn’t level my complete anger at winning Best Picture for a lackluster movie like The King’s Speech did in 2010, the fact that Green Book won the Best Picture proves that no matter how much the Oscars thinks it’s changing its’ course and getting its’ shit together, they’re still stuck in the past by letting generic shit like this winning the top prize and trying to make people think that this was the definitive movie of the year. Green Book is just an bore of a film, I really tried to give it a fair shot but I’m sorry, this is one of the dullest and blandest Best Picture winners ever, other than Mortensen and Ali, the rest of the movie is just a forgettable lump, it’s just a bore, a bore of a film that doesn’t work at all.

I want to make very clear: this is in no way a defense of an extremely mediocre movie that under no fucking circumstances should have been in the oscar conversation let along won best fucking picture. Some rank, evil shit in this of course, but occasional moments of beauty, as is inevitable in something so relentlessly sentimental. My favorite is when Tony Lip—who has been learning how to be more romantic from Doc Shirley—writes his wife a letter that reads, “You remind me of a house. A beautiful house where all the lights are on and everyone is happy inside.” And goddamnit that is what it’s like to feel in love. Some nice tensions too. Doc Shirley is allowed to be a complicated figure—a drunk, a promiscuous gay man, and at war with the balance between “respectable” white culture and what white people would perceive as the baseness of black culture. Tony Lip is a harder pill to swallow. It is true that there is a type of guy who is so ignorant and vulgar that he feels more harmless than his more ideologically-considered peers, but the movie elides much of the nastiness that still lives in these types. Not quite as bad as I was expecting, but—again—the academy should be drawn and quartered for this one. Boneheads, the lot of them.
