I don't know yes it was heartwarming but this film annoyed me, starting with the fact that it isn't historically accurate; for instance, Shirley’s run-in with the police didn't end in an arrest and actually took place in West Virginia. Shirley wasn't cut off from his family either he stayed in touch with them yet the film portrays him as an isolated man. It also suggests that Shirley was almost completely cut off from Black culture, which wasn't true. It’s a fable about the transformation of a white protagonist. The story’s focus shifts from the issue of racial segregation itself to Tony’s personal growth. *Green Book* simplifies racism by suggesting that the friendship between Shirley and Tony can solve the problem. In reality, however, the issue lies in structural and systemic forms of prejudice. The film also tasks Shirley with rediscovering his "Black identity" in a very stereotypical way - eating KFC, listening to specific music. You can detect a hint of paternalism here; Tony acts as a mentor guiding Shirley toward this stereotypical Black identity. I see a depiction of events that reflects a liberal perspective... It’s a romanticized fantasy of reconciliation that masks structural racial inequality. Two scenes involving police officers stuck with me: one in the South, where Shirley was supposedly arrested, and one in the North, where an officer let them go. The North represented by the polite officer becomes a symbol of "progressive America," ignoring the fact that such problems were very much present in the North as well. It’s a typical liberal narrative. The *Green Book* itself was necessary even in the North. Schools there were still segregated, workplace discrimination existed, and Black people couldn't rent apartments in certain neighborhoods. So, *Green Book* is essentially a liberal fairy tale about reconciliation that reduces the problem of racism to individual transformation. Shirley is reduced to a figure whom Tony must understand and WTF -teach how to discover his Black identity. It also allows the viewer to believe that the problem lies only with the South, rather than with America and the entire system itself. Racism-historically rooted in slavery, class, labor, and capitalism-is flattened, and the film delivers a "white savior" narrative.

It’s a clichéd, boring story—despite its theme and surface, it’s a colorful, lively comedy that seems to be downright afraid to delve deeper into a social problem that is indeed important and still very much present today, and for that very reason, it’s an experience you can safely skip. If you’re interested in the topic of racism, I can wholeheartedly recommend the film *The Hate U Give*, which, - although it doesn't delve nearly as deeply into the subject as it should - conveys a much richer and more thought-provoking message.

This movie’s commentary on blackness is thinner than a piece of paper, and its understanding of racism in America is incredibly cartoonish. That said, Mahershala Ali takes this surface-level material about racial and sexual identity and attempts to translate it with some nuance. Viggo Mortensen is also quite funny. It’s occasionally wholesome, but its charming nature is more or less stamped by its excessive sentimentality. As a whole, whatever.

sean porter’s crisp, polished cinematography paints a rich, nostalgic portrait of 1960s america, wrapping the journey in warm tones and elegant period framing that instantly signals prestige filmmaking. every frame is calculated for maximum audience accessibility, capturing the shifting American landscape from sleek urban nightscapes to vintage southern estates with smooth camera movements and flawless lighting. you can see exactly why this swept the academy awards, as the glossy visual finish combines effortlessly with a crowd-pleasing, classic narrative structure that hits every emotional beat with reliable precision. the plot functions as a classic study in defensive compartmentalisation and boundary breakdown between two completely contrasting personalities. don shirley guards his emotional vulnerability behind rigid posture, refined speech, and intellectual superiority to cope with the extreme isolation of being accepted by neither white elite circles nor his own community. conversely, tony lip relies on hyper-masculine bravado and unrefined pragmatism to mask his narrow worldview. as their physical journey south progresses, the forced proximity chips away at their respective psychological armour, forcing tony to confront his latent prejudices while don is pushed to strip away his loneliness and allow genuine human connection to break through his isolated facade.

Se me han acumulado bastante las películas a las que no les he hecho reseña pero esta lo vale. Me pareció una buena película. Hay veces que no simpatizamos con ciertas personas por costumbre, por ideas o constructos de la sociedad, pero en realidad no siempre son pensamientos propios. Me hizo pensar en eso durante toda la película. Tony Lip claramente tenía actitudes influenciadas por su entorno, pero nunca se había detenido a cuestionarlas. Estaba en una posición cómoda donde simplemente aceptaba las cosas como eran, hasta que la convivencia con el Dr. Shirley lo obliga a ver más allá y entender la realidad de una forma más directa. Me gustó mucho cómo la película muestra ese cambio a través de la relación entre ambos. No es algo que pase de un día a otro, pero sí te deja claro cómo el contacto humano puede romper prejuicios. También me dejó pensando en todo lo que vivían las personas de color en esa época, y que en muchos sentidos sigue pasando. Nadie elige el color de su piel y no debería existir ninguna diferencia en el trato, oportunidades o en la vida diaria. Algo que me hubiera gustado ver más es justamente esa realidad desde una perspectiva más amplia, porque incluso el Dr. Shirley estaba en una posición privilegiada dentro de todo. Aun así, hay escenas muy bien logradas, como cuando están en la carretera y los trabajadores se sorprenden al verlos, porque rompe completamente con lo que era “normal” en ese contexto. En general es una película que, sin ser perfecta, logra hacerte reflexionar.

This is a very straightforward Hollywood movie, but it’s one that actually tries. There’s still tells - plot points will be repeated four times so that anyone watching while staring at their phone can keep up, the plot is predictable, the acting bounces between “sufficient” and “actually good” depending on the scene, and the antagonists are a one-note caricature of capitalism. But there’s some good stuff to fight against that! The film is excellently shot, with some really stellar camera work that caught my attention. And it’s a movie about racing that absolutely nails the tension and pacing needed to make something like that work. So it’s at least worth the watch.

Ford v Ferrari. 2 gigantische Unternehmen, bei denen das eine even bisschen Underdog ist, weil es noch nicht so die Erfahrung hat im Rennsport. Das würde eigentlich für ne Story schon reichen, aber genau da wird aus einer guten Geschichte eine sehr gute Geschichte. Der bessere Titel wäre nämlich Ford v Ferrari v Miles. Gerade die Konflikte innerhalb von Ford sind nämlich so spannend und mitreißend. Du fieberst eben mit Miles mit, der einfach nur sein Ding machen möchte, während diese geldgeile Company ihm immer wieder das Leben zur Hölle macht. Das ist eben noch wirksamer, weil es eine reale Geschichte ist. Der Konflikt wird tiefer, umfangreicher und vor allem greifbarer. Minispoiler: Und dann setzt der Film eben noch einen drauf. Er stellt die Frage: Wieso das alles? Und darauf, meine Freunde, weiß ich auch keine Antwort. Der Film sagt es dir auch nicht. Er lässt dich zurück mit dieser Frage. Alles, was ich weiß: Miles sieht so glücklich aus, wenn er hinter dem Steuer sitzt. Abseits davon ist der Film natürlich handwerklich großartig. Das Schauspiel ist top und die Sequenzen auf der Rennstrecke sind unglaublich immersiv. Die Charaktere bocken sich auch. Der Film macht das, was er möchte, ziemlich perfekt. Ich schwanke zwischen 3,5 & 4 Sternen. Was es wird, wird die Zeit und spätestens ein Rewatch zeigen.

Le Mans '66 ist ein sehr runder Film. Er macht zwar kaum etwas überragend, aber fast alles richtig. Während der 2,5 Stunden hat man durchgehend Spaß, weil der Film einen guten Wechsel zwischen actionreichen Rennszenen und ruhigeren Momenten findet. Die beiden Hauptcharaktere, gespielt von Matt Damon und Christian Bale, sind sofort sympathisch. Man fiebert direkt mit ihnen mit, was auch an ihren unfassbar guten Performances liegt. Die Rennszenen sind zwar nicht ganz so stark wie im *F1*-Film, weil ihnen der letzte Kick und die ganz großen Bilder fehlen. Trotzdem sind sie immer noch hervorragend inszeniert. Dafür sind sie spannender, weil man viel stärker mit den Figuren mitfiebert. Das liegt vor allem daran, dass der Film die äußeren Umstände und den Druck rund um das Rennen sehr interessant gestaltet. Leider verfällt der Film dabei etwas zu sehr in das klassische Gut gegen Böse Prinzip. Der Vorstand wikrt eindimensiol böse während die beiden Hauptfiguren eindeutig die Guten sind. Auch die Nebencharaktere bleiben insgesamt etwas zu einfach geschrieben. Trotzdem ist Le Mans '66 ein Film, mit dem man zu 100 Prozent seinen Spaß hat.

EN If you loved Cars as a child, this is the perfect adult alternative to experience that exact same vibe. The title is actually misleading: the battle with Ferrari is mostly about Ford's ego after a failed partnership attempt. The real, secondary conflict in the film is the one fought by individual talents against the bureaucratic Ford corporation, where image matters more than passion. Just like the iconic GT40, the film runs exceptionally smooth when it comes to pacing. It offers an accessible style of storytelling combined with a very strong cinematographic vision. Even though I know nothing about cars and have zero interest in them, the story kept me engaged from start to finish thanks to the human relationships. The chemistry between Damon and Bale is fantastic, their friendship feels so authentic that they almost seem like brothers at times. You can tell it's a very American story, in which Ferrari and the Italians are portrayed as fairly headstrong and arrogant to create a sharp contrast, to get that typical American underdog feeling. Furthermore, the racing sequence at the end drags on quite a bit and you occasionally see a lot of repetitive footage, but thanks to the rock-solid editing, the tension remains palpable throughout. NL Als je vroeger als kind van Cars hield, is dit het perfecte alternatief voor volwassenen om diezelfde vibe te ervaren. De titel is eigenlijk misleidend: de strijd met Ferrari draait vooral om een ego van Ford nadat een poging tot partnerschap mislukte. De échte, tweede strijd in de film is die van de individuele talenten tegen het bureaucratische Ford-concern, waar imago belangrijker is dan passie. Net zoals de iconische GT40 loopt de film qua pacing ontzettend soepel. Het is een toegankelijke manier van storytelling, gecombineerd met een hele sterke cinematografische visie. Hoewel ik zelf niets van auto's ken en het me niet interesseert, bleef het verhaal me van begin tot eind boeien door de menselijke relaties. De chemie tussen Damon en Bale is fantastisch, hun vriendschap voelt oprecht dat het soms net broers lijken. Je merkt wel dat het een heel Amerikaans verhaal is waarin Ferrari en de Italianen vrij eigenzinnig en arrogant worden neergezet om een dik contrast te creëren, zo ontstaat er ook een typische Amerikaanse underdog gevoel. Daarnaast duurt het racegedeelte op het einde vrij lang en zie je soms veel van dezelfde beelden, maar door de ijzersterke montage blijft de spanning er toch steeds inzitten.

The film is driven by a brilliant acting duo, but it’s Christian Bale who steals the show - he’s simply incredible. Bale perfectly captures the essence of a brilliant, yet difficult and uncompromising driver. Matt Damon complements him well, creating a relationship filled with rough-and-tumble, genuine friendship.

Wonderful portrayals by both lead actors. Seeing Shelby stick up for Miles, and Miles sticking to his guns despite being alone on most of his ideas really sells the bond between the two. The portrayal of sports car racing is a bit inaccurate where they have a photo finish that didn’t happen. They also talk about “the perfect lap” but in a 24 hour race you aren’t really concerned with that. Minimal nitpick that won’t detract from the movie for most people. Great power of friendship story.

The racing sequences were fantastic: thrilling, exhilarating, intense and the sound design is inescapable. They are also perfectly choreographed so you never get lost following the action. Man, those final 30 minutes! But the drama component worked just as well, and the two were weaved together in near perfect synergy. There are multiple memorable scenes from both sides of the coin (for example Tracy Letts in the car, Christian Bale after the race). I think everything works on this film, cinematography, editing, sound design, performances ( Matt Damon is great, but Bale steals the show). It’s hard to not give this 5★ even though that feels slightly too generous. But I can always fix that on a review, so for now, why not.

Life was simpler when you were a kid because you didn't really understand what you were doing. mid90s is a mood piece about growing up and the search for belonging. Jonah Hill isn't trying to tell us a classic coming-of-age story or show us Stevie, the protagonist, growing up during his adolescence. Instead, he presents us with a boy exploring new places, trying to fit in, since he's never felt at home. His life experiences become commonplace, just as most of the film's scenes show him skateboarding as an ordinary activity. However, that doesn't mean he hasn't been scarred along the way. Stevie is wasting his life, but it's presented as something ordinary: drugs, alcohol, and even a sexual relationship with an older person. All of this shows how, in his desire to fit in, he has forgotten who he is: a kid. My main problem is that Jonah Hill avoids conflict throughout the film. It's a mood piece for most of its runtime, and in the second half, a conflict is introduced to bring the story to a meaningful conclusion, but I never feel the impact the film is actually aiming for. On the other hand, I love how Jonah Hill recreates the 90s instead of viewing them from a modern perspective, but with an atmosphere that truly feels authentic to the era. (Rating before posting 3.0)

C'est bien, sans plus. Stevie a treize ans, vit avec une mère absente et un grand frère qui le tabasse, et trouve refuge auprès d'une bande de skateurs du magasin du quartier. Ils le surnomment Sunburn. Il découvre la première clope, le premier verre, le sentiment d'appartenance et il se met de plus en plus en danger pour exister à leurs yeux. Premier film de Jonah Hill, largement autobiographique. Ce qui frappe, c'est la forme : tourné en 16 millimètres, en format 4/3, avec une bande-son grunge et hip-hop qui recrée immédiatement l'époque. Lucas Hedges est glaçant en grand frère. L'idée la plus juste du film, c'est que la violence que subit Stevie ressort en violence qu'il s'inflige lui-même. Mes réserves : c'est très mince narrativement. 84 minutes d'une errance assumée, les personnages secondaires se confondent dans un flot de dialogues improvisés, et le film s'arrête brutalement sur quelque chose d'inachevé. Le film est aussi accusé de complaisance, et il est difficile d'ignorer que quelqu'un d'autre que Jonah Hill n'aurait jamais obtenu les droits des Pixies et de Nirvana pour un scénario aussi léger. Un premier film sincère et joli. Pas grand-chose derrière.

There's a vibe to Mid90s that I found incredibly comfortable. Jonah Hill really succeeds in recreating something that feels authentically 1990s rather than simply decorating a movie with nostalgic references. I was born in 1979, so in the middle of the 90s I was around 15–16, roughly the age of the kids in this movie. I wasn't part of the skateboarding subculture, I was into death and black metal, and those worlds didn't cross over all that often, although there were exceptions. My younger brother was much more into skateboarding, although slightly later, toward the end of the 90s and into the early 2000s. But even without sharing the specific subculture, Mid90s captures something I recognize as true about being a teenager during that period. There was nothing particularly extraordinary about 13- or 14-year-olds partying every weekend, drinking, smoking cigarettes or smoking weed. I'm certainly not saying it was healthy, but within teenage culture it often felt completely normal. In that sense, the movie reminded me quite a bit of Kids , except considerably more positive and hopeful. Bad things happen in Mid90s , and these kids certainly aren't making consistently sensible decisions, but the movie doesn't treat their lives as one long descent into disaster. Where Kids feels like a downward spiral, there's my 90s reference, Mid90s is mostly about kids hanging out, finding friends, doing stupid shit and having fun. There's danger and self-destructive behavior, but it doesn't consume everything. And perhaps that's why the nostalgia works so well. Hill doesn't just recreate the clothes, music and skateboards. He captures something about what being young actually felt like before you were old enough to look back and recognize how reckless some of it was. I really liked Mid90s . Not because my adolescence looked exactly like this, but because somehow it still felt like the 90s.

Even though most of the things that happen are pretty absurd for a 12 year old, it all still feels authentic. I also appreciated that it was under 90mins, well paced, well shot, solid all round.

We frequently superficially see troubles with Stevie’s relationships at home, some really intense fight scenes with his brother… and himself. But at the end of the day no developments are really explored, it’s just counter intuitive. I think some people misinterpret this kind of meandering plot to be artistic, and therefore have value, but in my opinion it just feels lazy. It feels as though I was ripped off from a brilliant story. “A lot of the time we feel that our lives the worst, but I think that if you looked in anybody else's closet, you wouldn't trade your shit for their shit .” - Ray

❝ a lot of times, we feel like our lives are the worst. but i think if you looked at anybody else’s closet, you wouldn’t trade your shit for their shit. ❞ dirigido por jonah hill em sua estreia como diretor, mid90s acompanha stevie , um garoto de 13 anos que vive em los angeles nos anos 90 e encontra em um grupo de skatistas mais velhos. stevie vê naqueles meninos aquilo que parece faltar em sua própria casa ⨾ pertencimento. definitivamente, não é um filme sobre skates. é sobre aquele momento da vida em que você ainda não sabe quem é, mas já sente que precisa ser alguém. é sobre crescer antes de estar preparado para crescer, sobre a necessidade quase desesperada de pertencer a algum lugar e sobre como, durante a adolescência, às vezes confundimos ser aceito com ser amado. em casa, stevie convive com um irmão que frequentemente o diminui e o agride, fazendo com que ele cresça acreditando que nunca é forte, corajoso ou “homem” o suficiente. a relação entre os dois é complicada, porque existe uma violência constante, mas também existe uma espécie de espelhamento, pois stevie parece observar o irmão justamente para descobrir como um homem deveria ser, enquanto o próprio ian parece estar reproduzindo violências que também recebeu. a mãe deles, por outro lado, é uma personagem interessante. ian comenta que ela mudou quando stevie nasceu, deixando para trás uma vida em que fumava, levava homens para casa e aparentemente vivia de uma maneira mais desregrada. ela tenta ser uma boa mãe, mas não parece saber exatamente como lidar com o filho quando percebe que ele está começando a se perder. e isso é muito real. às vezes pensamos nos pais como pessoas que deveriam saber exatamente o que fazer, mas eles também estão aprendendo a ser pais enquanto os filhos aprendem a ser filhos. existe uma impotência muito grande em assistir alguém que você ama se aproximar de coisas que podem machucá-lo sem saber exatamente como impedir. quando stevie encontra os meninos pela primeira vez, existe uma fascinação até meio infantil no olhar dele. e essa fascinação diz muito sobre a transição para a adolescência. stevie olha para aqueles garotos como se eles soubessem alguma coisa que ele ainda não sabe. eles fumam, bebem, andam de skate, falam palavrão, ficam com garotas, enfrentam perigos. para stevie , aquilo tudo parece representar a liberdade e a maturidade que ele acredita precisar alcançar. e não demora muito para que ele seja influenciado por eles. os garotos passam a ser praticamente sua nova família. e tudo o que stevie precisa fazer para se tornar parte daquele grupo, ele faz. se precisa beber, ele bebe. se precisa mentir, ele mente. se precisa ultrapassar algum limite, ele ultrapassa. não necessariamente porque quer fazer todas aquelas coisas, mas porque quer continuar sendo chamado para fazê-las. o grupo não é perfeito. eles são imaturos, preconceituosos em diversos momentos, cruéis, impulsivos e muitas vezes irresponsáveis. mas também são reais. existe humanidade naquela imperfeição. eles brigam, se provocam, se machucam, riem juntos e, principalmente, estão tentando descobrir quem são. ray e fourth grade foram, para mim, os personagens que mais gostei do grupo. ray funciona quase como o equilíbrio entre todos os outros. ele é querido pelos meninos, ajuda o stevie e parece ter uma consciência que os outros ainda não desenvolveram completamente. ele participa das loucuras deles, mas não parece completamente dominado por elas. existe uma sensibilidade nele que faz com que seja fácil entender por que steve se aproxima tanto dele. fourth grade , por outro lado, é muito mais introspectivo. e achei interessante como o roteiro utiliza justamente o silêncio dele para construir sua personalidade. ele não precisa falar o tempo inteiro para sabermos que existe alguma coisa acontecendo dentro dele. ele gosta de filmar e sonha em fazer um filme, o que é particularmente bonito porque, de certa forma, ele já está tentando transformar a própria realidade em imagem. ray comenta que o fourth grade passa por dificuldades financeiras, e mesmo assim, em algumas situações, os outros garotos tratam o sonho dele com certo desdém. é um detalhe pequeno, mas que diz muito. ele provavelmente se sente triste, talvez até humilhado, mas não transforma isso em discurso. ele simplesmente guarda. e isso combina perfeitamente com a personalidade que o filme constrói para ele. ruben é outro personagem importante justamente por representar uma masculinidade muito mais agressiva. ele parece precisar esconder constantemente qualquer sinal de fragilidade. em determinado momento, quando stevie agradece por alguma coisa, ele o repreende e associa o agradecimento a algo “de bicha”. é uma fala reveladora porque mostra como, para aqueles meninos, determinados comportamentos são associados ao feminino e, consequentemente, vistos como inferiores. o próprio ray revela que ruben é agredido pela mãe e passa grande parte do tempo fora de casa. e isso muda um pouco a forma como enxergamos sua agressividade. não para justificá-la, mas para tentar entendê-la. ruben parece reproduzir no mundo aquilo que aprendeu dentro de casa, se você demonstra fragilidade, alguém pode usar isso contra você. então ele constrói uma versão de si mesmo que precisa ser dura o tempo inteiro. inclusive, é muito interessante como o filme aborda a masculinidade sem transformar isso em uma grande explicação. ela está nos diálogos, nas brincadeiras, nos insultos, nas agressões, na necessidade de provar alguma coisa e até na maneira como os meninos lidam com seus próprios sentimentos. eles querem parecer invencíveis porque, para eles, vulnerabilidade parece ser sinônimo de fraqueza. e isso continua extremamente atual. é claro que mid90s é um retrato específico de uma época, mas não acho que seus conflitos tenham ficado nos anos 90. a necessidade adolescente de pertencer continua existindo. a pressão para parecer mais velho continua existindo. a masculinidade baseada em esconder sentimentos continua existindo. e hoje, talvez isso aconteça também através das redes sociais, onde existe uma pressão ainda maior para construir uma identidade antes mesmo de sabermos quem somos. stevie quer parecer mais velho para ser aceito pelos garotos. e hoje, muitos adolescentes fazem coisas semelhantes para serem aceitos por determinados grupos, comunidades ou círculos virtuais. a tecnologia mudou, mas a necessidade humana não mudou tanto assim, queremos ser vistos. a cena envolvendo a garota mais velha é, para mim, uma das mais desconfortáveis do filme justamente porque stevie é apenas uma criança. não existe glamour naquele momento. existe nervosismo, insegurança e uma criança tentando atravessar uma experiência para a qual claramente ainda não está preparada. e mesmo assim, depois disso, ele é tratado como um “ganhão” pelos outros meninos. isso é muito triste porque revela outra característica da adolescência, muitas vezes, os próprios adolescentes transformam situações desconfortáveis em troféus porque aprenderam que aquilo representa maturidade. a cena não precisa dizer que stevie está preparado ou não. o desconforto já está no rosto dele. e isso também me fez pensar em quantos meninos são simplesmente deixados para descobrir tudo sozinhos, sem orientação, e acabam aprendendo sobre masculinidade, sexo, relacionamentos e maturidade através dos próprios amigos, da internet ou de experiências para as quais ainda não possuem estrutura emocional. e é por isso que a infância de stevie parece ser acelerada durante o filme. no começo, ele ainda é claramente uma criança. mas, conforme se aproxima dos meninos, parece existir uma necessidade crescente de abandonar essa infância. ele começa a beber, fumar, falar e agir como os outros e experimentar coisas novas. existe uma urgência em crescer. e talvez a pergunta mais intrigante seja: por que ele sente que precisa crescer tão rápido? porque, dentro de casa, ele não se sente suficientemente forte. na rua, porém, existe a possibilidade de construir outra versão de si mesmo. a estética do filme contribui demais para isso. a fotografia granulada, o formato e a textura quase de uma gravação antiga fazem mid90s realmente parecer um filme encontrado em uma caixa de fitas antigas. existe uma sensação nostalgia muito presente, não é simplesmente mostrar como eram os anos 90. a imagem parece uma memória, algo que alguém poderia ter gravado naquela época e encontrado anos depois. é uma estética que combina muito com a história porque adolescência também funciona assim na memória. quando olhamos para determinadas fases da nossa vida, não lembramos de tudo perfeitamente. lembramos em pedaços, uma música, uma rua, uma roupa, uma pessoa, uma conversa, uma sensação. e a fotografia parece capturar exatamente isso. a direção de jonah hill é bem contida, mas essa naturalidade é uma das maiores qualidades do filme. em alguns momentos, o filme parece tipo um documentário. isso também se deve muito às atuações, principalmente à de sunny suljic como stevie . a atuação dele é extremamente natural. existe algo muito verdadeiro na maneira como ele olha para os outros personagens, especialmente quando está tentando entender como deve agir. ele não parece estar interpretando uma criança tentando ser adolescente, parece uma criança realmente tentando descobrir como ser adolescente. mas eu gostei das atuações de todo o elenco. os diálogos possuem uma espontaneidade que ajuda a criar a sensação de que estamos apenas observando aqueles meninos. a trilha sonora também contribui muito para essa sensação de época. gostei bastante de como ela complementa as imagens. as músicas ajudam a construir a identidade daquele universo e reforçam a sensação de estarmos realmente nos anos 90. eu gostei do final. depois de tudo o que aconteceu, stevie sofre um acidente e vai parar no hospital. e o que mais gostei nessa conclusão é justamente o fato de que os meninos continuam ali. para mim, isso simboliza que, apesar de todas as atitudes problemáticas, daquela imaturidade e das coisas ruins que aconteceram, existe uma amizade entre eles. eles se importam uns com os outros. talvez ainda não saibam demonstrar isso da maneira mais saudável, mas estão ali. é um filme sobre crescer, sobre masculinidade, violência, amizade, solidão, descobertas e sobre ser visto. e também é sobre perceber que não precisamos continuar sendo aquela versão de nós mesmos que criamos apenas para caber. e acho bonito que o filme não transforme nenhum personagem em certo ou errado absoluto. o irmão do stevie é agressivo, mas também carrega suas próprias feridas. ruben é chato, mas também vive uma realidade de violência. os meninos influenciam stevie negativamente, mas também oferecem a ele uma coisa que ele precisava, a companhia. a mãe falha em perceber algumas coisas, mas também parece estar tentando acertar. ou seja, todo mundo está meio perdido. e isso fala muito da adolescência.

Four stars, and Jonah Hill's directorial debut earns them by understanding one thing most coming-of-age movies fake: kids don't join a group because they like skating, they join because the group provides a functional family with clearer rules than the one at home. Shot on 16mm in 4:3, with an aspect ratio and grain that isn't a gimmick but a memory format, "mid90s" follows a small kid with a violent older brother who falls in with older skaters. And Hill's real insight is that the crew are not cool, they're 17-year-olds with their own terror, and Ray, the one with actual talent and a way out, is the only person in the film performing adulthood on purpose. The soundtrack is a flex (Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross scoring a movie whose needle drops include Wu-Tang and Morrissey), and the period detail is exact in the way only lived experience gets: the Street Fighter cabinet, the Discman, the specific hierarchy of who gets to talk at the shop. The hospital scene, and the home videos over the credits, land the thesis: everybody's carrying something, and skating is just the excuse to be outside together. Four stars. You literally take the hardest hits of anyone I've ever seen.

“mid90s a fourth-grade film.” I loved the cinematography and relationship between the characters. There’s also so much depth with every single one and they all acted like they were actually LIVING in the situation. They highlighted many key points of what a parent does to a child and how it affects them. Ex: Ruben’s mom beating on him and his sister —> a child having to resort to alcohol and drugs + self loathing and doing everything to seem cool in other peoples perspectives. Also the ongoing “trend” in that area is to basically smoke, drink and fuck bitches. They’re so well attuned to that, so they won’t even attempt to get out of the “hood”. Second thing is that Stevie’s mom seeing her reflection in Stevie’s friends and immediately trying to save him, but then realizing they ACTUALLY care about him and were practically staying overnight at the hospital for him. Overall it’s very well articulated and meaningful.

Yeah, you could say Mid90s is just another typical skate film. The atmosphere and soundtrack are weirdly beautiful when paired together, but really beneath the nostalgic feeling the film gives you through its visuals and lighting that captivate you with scenes that feel like memories that don’t even exist. But really even after all the cinematography that goes behind it all, deep down it really isn’t that beautiful. It’s true focus is really more about belonging and acceptance and how belonging can easily be mistaken as acceptance especially in your youth, this stems from loneliness and unfortunately most turn a blind eye to this. Not so much about skateboarding really. Settling to be around people just because you feel like you belong but really it’s just acceptance. Stevie really is just a kid trying to fit in like every other kid , trying to grow up too quickly, picking up adult like traits even the bad qualities, is it because it makes him feel older or is it really because it makes him feel wanted ? Like the quote, “A tree falls the way it leans”. Sometimes it’s better to stand as your own tree, held down by your own roots, growing upwards rather than letting every gust of wind decide the way you grow, ultimately deciding which way you lean. Don’t regret anything and take what you can from the people, learn from it. But don’t ever let them decide what you become. You can grow from what surrounds you without becoming a product of it, but only you have the power to decide that.

Mid90s foi, para mim, um daqueles filmes que conseguem transformar uma história aparentemente simples em algo muito mais sensível e significativo. Acompanhar Sunburn (aos menos intimos, Stevie) descobrindo a adolescência através do skate, da amizade e da necessidade de pertencer me pareceu genuíno justamente porque o filme não tenta romantizar completamente essa fase da vida. Existe diversão, liberdade e descoberta, mas também existe violência, insegurança, negligência e uma masculinidade que, muitas vezes, é construída através da necessidade de parecer mais forte do que realmente se é. Um dos aspectos que mais gostei foi o senso estético. A fotografia em 4:3, a textura granulada e a ambientação dos anos 1990 fazem o filme parecer uma memória antiga, quase como uma fita VHS encontrada por acaso. As roupas, os skates, as ruas e até a maneira como os personagens se comportam contribuem para essa sensação de autenticidade. É uma estética que não parece estar ali apenas para representar os anos 90, mas para fazer com que eu me sinta dentro deles. Também achei a crítica social muito bem construída porque ela não é apresentada de maneira excessivamente didática. O filme mostra, através dos próprios personagens, como crianças e adolescentes podem reproduzir comportamentos violentos, preconceituosos ou autodestrutivos simplesmente porque estão tentando descobrir como se encaixar no mundo. Stevie quer crescer depressa, mas, ao mesmo tempo, ainda existe nele uma ingenuidade infantil que torna algumas de suas escolhas especialmente dolorosas. E, talvez por isso, Mid90s tenha se tornado ainda mais especial para mim por ter sido assistido ao lado de alguém especial . Isso inevitavelmente passou a fazer parte da minha própria memória do filme. No fim, acho bonito quando uma obra consegue ultrapassar aquilo que existe dentro da tela e se misturar às nossas próprias experiências. Mid90s me deixou justamente essa sensação; a de ter assistido a uma história sobre crescer enquanto, de alguma forma, eu também estava criando uma pequena lembrança minha.

during the end credits jack black points at david bowie, lou reed, and the velvet underground in the middle of his after-school club's jam sesh and screams into the mic 'i do not know that guy!' . it's school of rock in miniature: easywatching because there's nothing new here; it is just a list of credits but for the whole film. the magical first instance when dewey discovers his students can play musical instruments sees the camera draw back from him specifically to frame all the children as a band as they play "smoke on the water"—the start of the school of rock as a group of equal members remains centred on him throughout, and on an intergenerational repurposing of the old culture. it's a narcissistic framing that is narratively contested by his insistence that all the kids have a say over their final song, but he is the one who persuades them, and when they come out again for their encore, the choice is made to focus on him before the camera turns up to the ceiling. that kind of authority is an abuse of power over children. joan cusack even repurposes 70s paedophile wooderson's 'all right, all right, all right!' catchphrase from dazed and confused to congratulate every last one of them. rocking out becomes intertextually associated with perverted forms of desire and age-as-authority. kids aren't the future, they're the past, and nobody knows who they are or what they're playing.

School of Rock is proof that if you shout loudly enough, people will call it a “classic.” Dewey Finn spends the whole film committing about 47 crimes before breakfast. He steals his roommate’s job, lies to an entire school, tricks the parents, ignores the curriculum, and somehow gets rewarded instead of getting escorted out by the police. Disney morals? Nope. Just pure chaos. Jack Black acts like he’s being paid by the decibel. Every five minutes he’s either screaming “ROCK!”, jumping on a desk, or pulling a face that looks like he just stubbed his toe. I was exhausted just watching him. The students are the only professionals in the building. They’re ridiculously talented, and somehow end up teaching themselves while Dewey’s masterclass consists of “play louder.” The story has more plot holes than Swiss cheese. Nobody checks his qualifications. Nobody questions why the “teacher” keeps disappearing with the class. Nobody thinks it’s weird that lessons have turned into rehearsals for a rock competition. Apparently common sense took the day off too. The Battle of the Bands is actually good—but that’s like saying the breadsticks were the best part of a terrible restaurant. Final rating: ⭐½ out of 5. Great music, brilliant kids, and one of the least qualified teachers in movie history. If this film taught me anything, it’s that confidence can apparently replace a teaching degree.
There are perks of charm that shown through with Jack Black, but I mostly found him insufferable. I think this would hit better if it was a nostalgia watch, but this was never one of my watches.

A thousand people at a weekday battle of the bands. Nobody hearing a drum kit outside of the room. Even as a kid the idea of how grounded the photography and style is completely clashed with the story in a way I couldn’t explain but meant I couldn’t get behind it. I’m good with it not making sense, but not if you’re asking for emotional investment. Do it like Scott Pilgrim and support the zaniness with a style. There’s no credibility to the setting but the style insists on capturing this “reality” feel that doesn’t work for me. Remake it animated and do it way weirder with a fully original set of songs in a secondary world and you’re in business.

Una commedia leggera che vive interamente del carisma e della simpatia travolgente di Jack Black. "School of Rock" Director: Richard Linklater Writer: Mike White Cinematography: Rogier Stoffers Editing: Sandra Adair Music: Craig Wedren Starring: Jack Black, Joan Cusack, Mike White, Sarah Silverman, Miranda Cosgrove, Joey Gaydos Jr. Runtime: 109 minutes Release: 2003 A comedy about rock music that understands why music matters "School of Rock" is one of those rare studio comedies that feels almost effortless even though nearly everything about it is carefully constructed. On paper, the premise is ridiculous: a broke, immature guitarist impersonates a substitute teacher at an elite prep school, discovers that his students can play instruments, and secretly turns the class into a rock band so he can enter a competition. In lesser hands, the concept could easily have become nothing more than a vehicle for Jack Black’s enormous personality. Instead, Richard Linklater and screenwriter Mike White turn it into a warm, funny, and surprisingly sincere film about creativity, confidence, education, collaboration, and the importance of discovering something that makes you want to participate in the world. What makes "School of Rock" endure is that it never treats rock music simply as decoration. The guitars, songs, records, and musical references are obviously part of the film’s personality, but music gradually becomes the language through which the children discover abilities and identities that their highly structured school environment has not encouraged. Dewey Finn initially sees the students as tools he can use to return to the stage, but the more time he spends with them, the more his selfish obsession begins to transform into genuine mentorship. He starts noticing their fears, insecurities, strengths, and personalities, and the film becomes as much about Dewey learning how to care about other people as it is about the children learning how to play rock. Direction: Richard Linklater makes chaos feel natural Richard Linklater is an unexpectedly perfect director for this material because his filmmaking has always been interested in character, conversation, time, and people gradually revealing themselves through interaction. Those instincts keep *School of Rock* grounded even when Jack Black is operating at maximum intensity. Linklater does not attempt to compete with Black’s energy through frantic filmmaking. Instead, he creates a stable environment around him and allows the collision between Dewey’s enormous personality and the rigid world of Horace Green to generate the comedy naturally. The classroom feels like a genuine space rather than a stage built around a comedian. The students react individually to Dewey, and Linklater gives them enough screen time to become recognizable people rather than a collection of child actors waiting for Jack Black to deliver another punchline. This becomes essential as the story progresses because the emotional climax depends on our understanding that the band belongs to all of them, not just to Dewey. Linklater’s restraint is especially important because the premise could easily have become exhausting. Dewey is loud, impulsive, and constantly performing, so the direction wisely refuses to make the entire film behave the same way. By keeping the camera relatively grounded and allowing performances to dominate, Linklater makes the chaos feel spontaneous rather than manufactured. The screenplay: selfishness gradually becomes mentorship Mike White’s screenplay is much smarter than its broad comedy premise initially suggests. Dewey is not introduced as an unconventional but secretly brilliant teacher. He is genuinely irresponsible. He lies to obtain the substitute-teaching position, neglects the curriculum, exploits the students for his own ambitions, and initially views the entire class primarily as a way of returning to the Battle of the Bands. That selfishness gives the character somewhere meaningful to develop. Dewey never becomes a conventionally mature adult, nor does the screenplay strip away the qualities that make him ridiculous. Instead, his transformation occurs through attention. He begins listening to the students, discovering what each of them needs, and realizing that helping them become confident matters more than simply using their talents to make himself look good. The screenplay handles this development through small interactions rather than moralizing speeches. Dewey notices that Lawrence worries he is not cool enough to belong in a rock band and immediately reassures him that his musical ability makes him valuable. He recognizes Tomika’s extraordinary voice beneath her insecurity and gives her a space where she can use it without being embarrassed. He understands Summer’s intense need for responsibility and turns that quality into a strength by making her band manager. Even the students who do not play instruments are given meaningful roles in costumes, lighting, security, and technical support. This is where Dewey accidentally becomes a genuinely effective teacher. He has no formal pedagogical knowledge, but he becomes attentive to who his students are rather than simply what they are expected to achieve. Jack Black: a performance built entirely around commitment Jack Black is the obvious center of "School of Rock", and it is almost impossible to imagine the film working with another actor. Dewey Finn could have been unbearable, but Black makes him lovable because he commits completely to every ridiculous impulse the character possesses. There is no ironic distance between Black and Dewey’s love of rock music. When Dewey hears a great riff, discusses a legendary guitarist, or tries to explain the emotional importance of a song, he behaves as though he is discussing something sacred. His physical performance is just as important as his comic timing. Dewey teaches with his entire body, jumping across the classroom, imitating guitar solos, conducting imaginary bands, singing riffs, dancing, pointing, and reacting to music with almost religious intensity. His enthusiasm becomes contagious because Black never suggests that Dewey’s passion is a joke, even when Dewey himself is ridiculous. There is also more vulnerability in the performance than the film is sometimes given credit for. Dewey has failed as a musician, been rejected by his own band, and has almost no stable adult identity outside his dream of becoming a rock star. His arrogance frequently functions as protection against the possibility that he may simply not be as successful as he imagined he would become. Working with the students gives him a new relationship with music. Instead of needing music exclusively as a vehicle for his own recognition, he begins learning how satisfying it can be to help someone else discover their voice. The children: the film’s real secret weapon The child ensemble is one of the main reasons "School of Rock"remains so enjoyable. The students are not written merely as precocious little adults or as interchangeable comedy props. Each has a recognizable personality, function, and insecurity, which allows the class gradually to become a genuine ensemble. Zack is a gifted guitarist whose creativity is restricted by his father’s expectations. Lawrence doubts that his personality fits the image of a rock musician. Tomika has an extraordinary singing voice but is frightened of being judged. Summer is ambitious, controlling, and extremely organized, qualities that could easily make her irritating but instead become invaluable once she is given responsibility. Miranda Cosgrove’s performance as Summer is particularly funny because she approaches the band with the seriousness of a corporate executive managing a major organization. One of the film’s loveliest decisions is that Dewey finds a role for almost everybody. The project is never limited to the children talented enough to stand at the front of the stage. Lighting, costumes, security, management, and technical work all become part of the band's identity. The message is therefore not simply that every child is secretly a musical genius. It is that a creative community becomes stronger when people discover where their abilities fit within something larger than themselves. Rock music is often associated with individual rebellion, but "School of Rock" ultimately turns that rebellion into collaboration. Education: the wrong teacher who understands something important "School of Rock" is not really an argument that formal education is bad, nor does it suggest that Dewey’s deception is acceptable simply because the children enjoy his classes. What the film does criticize is an educational environment that can become so focused on achievement, discipline, and measurable success that it leaves little space for experimentation. Horace Green is prestigious and academically demanding, but many of its students have internalized anxieties about perfection, parental approval, appearance, and failure. Dewey enters the school as perhaps the least qualified person imaginable, yet he introduces something the institution appears to lack: permission to experiment without immediately worrying about whether the result is correct. He allows the children to make noise, fail, try again, and discover talents that have nothing to do with grades. More importantly, he treats their creative interests seriously. He does not condescendingly praise them adults sometimes praise children for doing something cute. When Zack writes music, Dewey treats him like a songwriter. When Tomika sings, he treats her like a vocalist. When Summer manages the band, he treats her like a manager. That respect matters because children can often recognize the difference between an adult who is humoring them and an adult who genuinely believes what they are doing has value. Rock music as a philosophy The film understands rock as more than a musical genre. For Dewey, it represents freedom, authenticity, rebellion, collaboration, and the right to resist identities imposed by other people. His lectures on rock history are funny because he treats them with absurd seriousness, but underneath the comedy lies a sincere belief that art can provide a language for emotions people otherwise struggle to express. This becomes especially important for Zack. He lives under a father who already seems to have determined what kind of future his son should pursue. Writing and performing music gives Zack a means of expressing himself outside that structure. Tomika’s singing allows her to occupy space with confidence rather than apologizing for herself, while Lawrence discovers that musical talent can give him a sense of belonging even if he does not resemble his own idea of what a rock musician should be. The children are therefore not simply learning old songs because the filmmakers enjoy classic rock. They are learning that creativity can become a way of defining yourself rather than accepting every definition other people have already created for you. Cinematography: staying out of the way of performance Rogier Stoffers’ cinematography is deliberately unobtrusive, which is exactly the right choice for the film. The visual style does not attempt to compete with Jack Black’s performance or the energy of the music. Instead, the camera provides enough stability and spatial clarity for the performances to remain the focus. The classroom scenes are particularly effective because the arrangement of the children gradually changes as the band develops. Early in the film, Dewey dominates the room as an outsider imposing his personality on the students. As the children become more confident, the classroom begins to feel increasingly communal, with the ensemble occupying more of the frame as active participants rather than passive listeners. The concert material naturally becomes more dynamic, but even there the film prioritizes readable performance over excessive montage. We can see the children playing together, understand where they are positioned onstage, and experience the performance as something genuinely collective. That clarity helps sell the essential fantasy of the film: these children have actually become a band. Editing: comedy built through rhythm Sandra Adair’s editing is crucial because so much of "School of Rock" depends on rhythm. Jack Black produces an enormous amount of verbal and physical energy, and the editing knows when to remain with him and when the funniest choice is to cut to the children silently processing whatever ridiculous statement he has just made. Their reactions frequently become punchlines in themselves. The editing also handles the musical progression effectively. The band does not immediately sound polished. Rehearsal scenes gradually introduce individual components before allowing them to come together, which gives the final performance a genuine sense of progression. We have watched these children learn how to function as a group, so the concert feels like the culmination of work rather than a magical transformation produced by the screenplay. Adair also balances several tonal modes without making the film feel fragmented. Broad comedy, school satire, musical rehearsal, family conflict, and emotional vulnerability move easily into one another because the pacing never treats them as entirely separate kinds of movies. Joan Cusack: repression slowly cracking open Joan Cusack’s Principal Mullins is one of the film’s best supporting performances because she initially appears to represent everything Dewey rejects. She is formal, anxious, controlled, and deeply concerned with preserving Horace Green’s reputation. Her entire identity seems constructed around behaving exactly as she believes a prestigious school principal should behave. The film gradually reveals that this rigidity is also a performance. Mullins has suppressed parts of herself in order to maintain authority, and the moments when those parts begin slipping through are hilarious because Cusack plays them with incredible precision. Her reactions are never broad enough to destroy the character’s credibility, which contrasts her public and private personalities even funnier. She also reinforces one of the film’s broader ideas: children are not the only people trapped by expectations. Adults can become equally imprisoned by roles they believe they have to perform. Dewey’s chaotic presence disrupts not only the students but also an adult who has forgotten that she once possessed interests beyond professional responsibility. Comedy: why the film remains funny A major reason "School of Rock" has aged so well is that most of its comedy comes from character rather than topical references. Dewey is funny because of the intensity with which he experiences music and his complete inability to recognize normal professional boundaries. Summer is funny because she approaches a school band with the seriousness of an executive managing a multinational company. Mullins is funny because she is desperately trying to prevent her carefully controlled personality from collapsing. The humor also rarely depends on humiliating the children. Dewey may tease them, but when genuine insecurity appears, his attitude changes. The film understands the difference between joking with someone and turning their vulnerability into the joke. That warmth allows the comedy to become affectionate without losing its edge. The movie can recognize that practically everyone in it is ridiculous while still respecting them. Parents, expectations, and identity The parents become increasingly important because they represent another layer of expectations surrounding the children. Zack’s father is the clearest example, having already imagined a particular future for his son and regarding creative interests as distractions from that path. The film does not spend enough time with every parent to develop each family dynamic deeply, but collectively they represent an adult tendency to decide what success should look like before children have had enough life experience to understand what they actually care about. This gives the final concert additional meaning. The children are not only performing for an audience; they are revealing versions of themselves that developed outside direct parental supervision. Their parents suddenly have to confront abilities, interests, and confidence they did not necessarily know existed. The Battle of the Bands therefore becomes a form of self-definition. The Battle of the Bands: succeeding without needing to win One of the smartest choices in Mike White’s screenplay is the decision not to make conventional victory necessary. A lesser version of "School of Rock" would require the children to win the competition because the trophy would function as proof that Dewey’s methods were correct. That would actually weaken the film’s message. The children have already succeeded before the result is announced. They walk onto a stage, perform something they helped create, work together under enormous pressure, and experience the joy of having an audience respond to them. The official competition result therefore becomes secondary to the internal transformation that has already occurred. This reinforces the film’s broader argument about creativity. Art does not become meaningful only when an institution gives it first place. The value can exist in making something, sharing it, and discovering what the process changes inside you. Dewey’s transformation: from wanting attention to learning how to give it Dewey begins the film desperate for an audience. Almost every aspect of his personality is organized around wanting people to watch him play, recognize his talent, and confirm his identity as a serious musician. Even his decision to form the children’s band initially emerges from that same selfish desire. By the ending, he remains loud, theatrical, and unmistakably Dewey, but something important has changed. He has learned how to share the stage. His love of music is no longer exclusively about expressing himself; it has become something he can give to other people. That is the real character arc. Dewey does not mature by abandoning rock and becoming a conventional, responsible adult. He matures by discovering a more generous form of the passion he already possessed. Teaching changes him because it transforms enthusiasm into responsibility. For the first time, his musical knowledge and energy become useful to people other than himself. Linklater’s humanism The film fits surprisingly comfortably within Richard Linklater’s wider body of work because beneath the studio-comedy framework is his familiar fascination with people discovering themselves through conversation, community, and time spent together. Linklater rarely approaches characters with contempt, even when they behave foolishly. That generosity is crucial to "School of Rock". Dewey could easily have been treated simply as a loser, Mullins as nothing more than an uptight authority figure, and the children as recognizable school stereotypes. Instead, each is allowed enough humanity to become more complicated. Linklater’s direction suggests that people can change without needing to become completely different people. Dewey remains Dewey, Summer remains intensely ambitious, and Mullins remains a serious principal. Growth does not require erasing personality; it requires learning how to use that personality differently. Why the film still works The central idea of "School of Rock" has aged remarkably well because children still need opportunities to discover what they care about before adults decide what they should become. The specific rock references may belong largely to previous generations, but the emotional experience is timeless. Every child understands wanting to discover something they are good at. Every teenager understands the frustration of feeling that adults have already planned a future on their behalf. Every artist understands the excitement of realizing that something private can become communal when other people join in. That is the feeling the film captures so effectively. It is not ultimately about creating professional musicians. It is about discovering the thing that makes you excited enough to practice, collaborate, fail, improve, and show up again. Conclusion "School of Rock" remains one of the great feel-good comedies of the early 2000s because it never confuses optimism with emptiness. Beneath Jack Black’s enormous performance and the film’s infectious music is a thoughtful story about education, creativity, confidence, mentorship, and the importance of adults who notice what children might become rather than simply informing them what they should become. Richard Linklater directs with enough restraint to keep the film grounded while allowing Jack Black to operate at full intensity. Mike White’s screenplay gives Dewey a meaningful transformation without removing the immaturity and eccentricity that make him entertaining, while Sandra Adair’s editing balances comedy, music, and emotional development with remarkable ease. The child ensemble gives the film its heart because each student is allowed to become a participant in the story rather than merely an accessory to Dewey’s journey. Most importantly, the greatest thing Dewey gives the students is not musical ability, because many of them already possess talent before he enters the classroom. What he gives them is permission to take that talent seriously. He gives them permission to be loud, to fail, to experiment, to occupy space, and to discover versions of themselves that may not fit comfortably within the expectations surrounding them. The children return that gift by giving Dewey something he has spent much of his adult life searching for without understanding what he actually needed. They give his love of music a purpose beyond his own ego. He finally discovers that standing onstage does not become less meaningful when somebody else receives the applause, and that sharing his passion can be more satisfying than demanding recognition for it. That is why "School of Rock" remains so joyful. It understands that enthusiasm becomes truly meaningful when it becomes generosity, creativity becomes more powerful when it becomes community, and sometimes the teacher who appears completely wrong for the classroom can still teach something valuable because he is the first adult willing to take a child's passion seriously.

I’m not sure why I’ve never really liked this movie. I wanted to give it another rewatch since it had been a while, and I’ve been on a bit of a movie binge lately. I wanted to see if my opinion had changed at all. It hasn’t. I don’t particularly like Tony’s character. I understand that he isn’t supposed to be a good person, and I appreciate other pieces of media that center around morally bad or complex characters. I enjoyed Breaking Bad and American Psycho. With Tony, however, I feel like he’s simply a stupid person, which makes his psychotic nature more frustrating and, to me, much less nuanced. The one redeeming quality I can give him is that he didn’t want to kill the two kids. Other than that, I just think he’s a genuinely terrible and unintelligent person. The only reason he gained power in the first place was by screwing over the other gangs, and I never felt like he was truly the untouchable drug kingpin the movie seemed to portray him as. From the beginning, he had the cops after him and constantly had people coming after him. Yes, he made a lot of money, but it didn’t last very long. In the end, it felt short lived. His downfall always felt inevitable. Overall, I understand the cultural importance of this movie, and there are definitely a few scenes that I really enjoyed. But even after another rewatch, I still found myself thinking why did this movie have to be three hours long? Lol. I remember going to friends houses and you would see the iconic movie poster on the wall, or a frame of him at the end of the movie. Quoting it constantly. My only other exposure to the Scarface franchise besides what was said above was actually the video game for the Nintendo Wii. Why did I own this game at 12, I don't know but I did. I never beat it, it was an open world GTA clone which is funny because Vice City is obviously a clone or heavily inspired by this film. En fi, últimament estic molt trista i desconnectada i em costa apreciar l’art en general. Aviam com surt la següent.

Até onde uma ambição que pega fogo pode te levar, com um orgulho tão ignorante? Tony Montana veio de baixo, igual a gente… Quis enriquecer e ser o dono do mundo, igual a gente… Quis mudar o jogo e dar a volta por cima, também igual a gente… Até porque todos queremos riquezas, mansão, um belo carro, ter nossa família ao lado e aproveitar a vida. Tony com certeza trouxe esse mesmo fogo de ambição, ousadia e coragem! Coragem! Tudo o que ele tinha era sua palavra e sua coragem. Todo problema que enfrentou enquanto era um Zé foi inspirador. Ter atitude nas suas escolhas e não fugir, desejar incansavelmente a mulher que, para ele, era um troféu, ter a vida que sente merecer. Estávamos observando a volta por cima enquanto Tony cuidava de tirar os tubarões do mar, até restar somente ele. E ele conseguiu… Mas a arrogância precede a queda. Depois que conquistou tudo, o que restou? Uma visão de sua esposa drogada? Que passou de um troféu a um peso morto. Seu melhor amigo? Que morreu pelas próprias mãos por causa de seu ciúme doentio com sua irmã. Tudo o que sobrou foi tédio e a incapacidade de se manter sóbrio. (Brinde: kg de cocaína.) Tony foi corajoso, ambicioso e ousado. Não há melhor definição para ele do que a garra de alcançar o topo. Mas do que adianta toda aquela ambição se no fim, você acaba cego pelo orgulho e pelo egoísmo? No fim, ele realmente não precisava de ninguém. Mas também morreu sozinho pelos mesmos motivos. A queda da coroa, um leão enfraquecido pelo vazio após conquista. Sempre mire alto, confie em si e seja ambicioso. O mundo é dos ousados. The World Is Yours 🌎🏆

Eu assisto "Scarface" de Brian De Palma como a versão boa de "Psicopata Americano". Um típico filme de auge e queda, executado de uma perspectiva interessante. Pessoalmente, o que caracteriza muito o longa é o ato final, a "desgraça" de Tony Montana. Justamente o que observo como problema em relação à obra de Mary Harron previamente citada. Pontuo bastante a conexão entre os filmes pois os dois possuem diversas semelhanças no nicho de história que busca ser contada. Para avaliar, é necessário compreender qual ponto de vista foi tomado ao assistir o filme. Existe uma certa vilania acerca do protagonista, cuja é retradada de forma excelente, onde você deve se esforçar para não torcer pelo bem do mesmo. É exímia a construção da linha tênue entre a sua trajetória ser justa ou não. É daí que se tece o título de antí-herói . A palavra perfeita para definir o longa. Apenas lamento como é decepcionante observar algumas pessoas assistirem "Scarface" como se a ideia de "fazer o que é preciso pra chegar no topo" fosse algo natural e sadio... Enfim, um clássico!

***Revisit to see if my feelings on Scarface have changed as my movie tastes have matured and aged. I was very impressed with how well Carlito's Way was shot and how well each scene seemed to flow into the next. I've seen Scarface maybe three times, and while it's a perfectly fine movie, I had always thought it was overrated. This watch is too see if my more nuanced appreciation for cinematography and certain filmmaking styles will make me appreciate this film more. Relationship between Tony and Elvira seems off to me. Scarface is a fun ride, and I enjoy the ride, but I like I find more flaws in the journey. The editing is poor. The performances and connectivity between a lot of the actors feels off. Scarface is a good movie, with many memorable sequences, but it's less a sum of all parts movie and more individual stand-outs, like the cinematography. I love the feel of this Miami ride, and while shots aren't necessarily sewn together as I prefer, the shots themselves are vibrant, colorful, and full of style. I see why so many rappers and rogues love this movie so much. Scarface is a gangster who doesn't take shit from anyone, gets what he wants, and takes what he wants. This movie is more 'trash gangster' than 'Prestige gangster', which I feel I under appreciated as a genre. The movie hits a different tone 2/3 of the way through the movie when Tony reaches his apex. The film becomes more fun and announces itself with the 'Push It' montage. I don't love the script. I'm not the biggest Oliver Stone fan, and I don't know how much of the script De Palma changed, but certain plot lines just don't quite work for me. While he has his moments, of the elite Al Pacino performances, this is lower on my list. I prefer the cocaine mania of Ray Liotta in Goodfellas to the psychopath Al Pacino cocaine acting. He was absolutely awesome when snorting the comically large mounds of coke. The Gina plot isn't hammy enough to be enjoyed for pure trash, but it isn't well written enough to get any points from a prestige drama. Scarface is definitely elite trash crime, but I prefer Carlito's Way. I do have a much greater appreciation for Scarface for what it is as opposed to what it isn't. 84/100

“The very fact of appearance - the urge to appear - shows a claim for recognition and praise. All that appears wants to be seen and recognized and praised. The highest form of recognition is love: volo ut sis. - The wonder implies affirmation. - Hannah Arendt - My analysis (i.e. thesis) about this movie: I think Tony is a closeted homosexual. I know it’s far reaching, but I have some arguments, here we go. While the film explicitly presents Tony as hyper-heterosexual and aggressively driven by power, money and woman, perhaps this is a facade. Tony’s relentless and crude objectification of woman (including Elvira and Gina) functions as an armor rather than genuine desire. Sidenote: in the hyper-macho criminal world of 1980s Miami, showing any vulnerability from traditional masculinity would mean immediate death. His hyper-fixation on woman is performative! He actively suppresses or is hiding his true feelings. Manny is Tony’s closest confidant and roommate. Their relationship goes far beyond partnership, displaying a domestic intimacy. I felt a weird underlying romantic tension. Tony’s intense possessiveness over Manny, is kinda obvious and his violent reaction when he discovers Manny and Gina’s relationship, it is romantic jealousy and betrayal. And the ending scene with Gina. The intense repulsion and flinching Tony exhibits when forced into a sexualized dynamic with woman who is physically close to him is reinforcing the idea that his attraction to woman is a facade . I could give more examples, but I think you can come up with some examples by yourself. To conclude: great movie! I recognized a meme 🤗

Nose quién es el guionista. Pero dejarlo trabajar. En los momentos en los que le dejan expresarse y hace que Tony Montana hable es genial. A veces con un simple diálogo metafórico puedes explicar toda una historia, desde los inicios en cuba, hasta lo más alto de la pirámide capitalista. Con UN SIMPLE DIÁLOGO. Si consigues demostrar que puedes explicar todo el personaje de Tony solo con eso, deberian tener más peso las palabras y no tanto los pium pium. Si esto se hubiera dado podría considerarlo un 5. Actuación loquísima, TODOS (Michelle Pfeiffer no te conocía pero creo que es la mejor actuación femenina que he visto). Que bien ver gente actuar así de bien. Las escenas tampoco eran preciosas pero utiliza muchos recursos que me gustaron mucho. La música me ha flipado, me recuerda a Tarantino en algunas cosas. La comedia (bien metida siempre) me encanta. El ritmo de la peli es lo que me ha parecido lo mejor. Son 3 horas de peli, pero es que lo requiere. Gracias por no querer agotar las reservas de dopamina todo el rato. No hace falta poner escenas de acción y tiro y música todo el rato, de esta manera cuando escuches música sabes que el director te quiere transmitir algo, SI SEÑOR. APRENDE NOLAN. En fin, los gangsters y el camino del héroe no son mis cosas favoritas sinceramente, pero es que todo lo que he comentado es mi mierda. Peli recomendable y realmente considero que si no te gusta o es menos de un 3,5 no entiendes nada. La escena del restaurante es de lo MEJOR que he visto en el cine. Me emociona y todo. Mezcla crítica política + explicación de personaje + suspense + actuación LOCA, y sin música... Pelos de punta.

Given how despicable Tony Montana is, I wasn't expecting to enjoy this as much as I did; but I found myself captivated by Montana's escape from being caged by Cuba's communism, only to run into the tiger's mouth of American capitalism, dragging others with him to be eaten. The movie is excessive, violent, grotesque, dehumanizing because it's the culture these characters live in. Only wealth and status matter to Tony. He wants Elvira as a wife for status. He wants kids for legacy. He wants it all just to prove he can. It's ambition without end. I understand the criticism of Tony's character being empty, but I actually prefer this than trying to portray someone who's abhorrent as "interesting" or "sympathetic". Tony is a scumbag that just gets scummier. There's no pretense about it. He's not naive, nor an innocent in over his head. He asked for it. And he got what he asked for. It's suitably nihilistic. I also think the movie has an immaculate style. I sometimes find De Palma's direction visualy indulgent, but not here. The staging, cinematography, wardrobe, soundtrack, are all superb. Not to mention the performances, highlighted by Pacino. Amongst American gangster films, Scarface does stand apart. It's a great film about a man who wants greatness, but doesn't understand what it means to be great.

What made the first two Toy Story films work so well was the sense of deeper characterisation and internal conflict that formed an emotional backbone for the toys’ colourful adventures; Woody learning to accept Buzz in the first film or weighing the decision to become a museum piece in the second both served as the kind of substantial character arc that is conspicuously absent from the third, which here reduces him to a righteous Cassandra figure trying to rescue his friends from daycare well before its hidden darkness is revealed (a saviour complex that the fourth film correctly chooses to deconstruct in order to properly close the loop on him as a character). In trying to give the toys what was presumably going to be one last adventure, it sacrifices that particular sense of character for the sake of a perfunctory prison-break parody and a handful of precisely-calibrated emotional moments around which the entire film seems to have been reverse-engineered. The recent sequels had their flaws, but they still understood the need to give these toys some semblance of interiority that could be challenged by more than just the excitement and thrills posed by external obstacles - as a result, the inclusion of a Totoro doll seem less like one iconic studio tipping its cap to another than it does an ironic reminder of how far removed Pixar could get from Ghibli’s nuanced approach to animation.

11 years on from Toy Story 2, the trilogy was completed with an epic prison escape movie written to close out the franchise. Toy Story 3 is a film I’m very conflicted on, because in fleeting moments I catch the brilliance the high letterboxd score would suggest and the third act is (mostly) as good as they say. The ending is enough to make any grown man sniffle, it would have been a great place to leave the franchise if it didn’t ultimately continue. But I have serious gripes with the film I can’t ignore, that frankly leave it well short of the first two films in the Toy Story trilogy turned pentalogy Firstly a brief note on the creation process. Toy Story 3 began life in 2004, remaining at the tentative stage due to the complications of the Disney deal I touch on in my Toy Story 1 and 2 reviews. Eventually Disney bought out the company, and work was restarted on Toy Story 3 with a new script and an absurd $200 million budget. That is over twice the budget of Toy Story 2 which I remind you was scrapped and restarted entirely. In 2010 the movie finally released to much critical and commercial success, becoming the fourth highest grossing film of all time (now barely in the top 50, inflation is a funny thing) and featuring on multiple top 10 films of the 2010s lists The film mostly moves away from the A plot B plot structure of the first two films and instead has the gang almost entirely together. Woody has a short stint away from the Daycare, outside of that we stick with the entire cast of toys the whole way through. Getting some big problems out the way early, the cast here is not even half as good as they were in Toy Story 2. Mr Potato Head is a shell of his former self, Ham might as well be an extra, Slinky has been neutered to having no jokes at all, Jessie has much less bite than her debut appearance. I laughed maybe twice, three times the entire film. Meanwhile Toy Story 2 had me in stitches the whole way through. The biggest casualty is Buzz, who they so clearly have no fucking idea what to do with so they do a ‘Buzz is back to his default setting’ story AGAIN. In all three of the original Toy Story trilogy we have Buzz thinking he’s not a toy, that’s absolutely egregious. The second justifies it with it being a seperate Buzz and the comedy being on point, here he’s placed in an antagonist role and it’s ass. Speaking of ass and antagonists, Lotso fucking sucks. It’s just stinky Pete but again! It’s the exact same villain but worse in every conceivable way. One of Disney’s worst villains, a complete charisma vacuum who is half baked and poorly written The themes of Toy Story 3 are around growing up, moving on, accepting that things change and making peace with that. At least, that’s what the final act would suggest. But unlike the first two films which did a brilliant job to make the plot contribute to the greater themes being explored, Toy Story 3 forces it’s ideas into the first and last 15 minutes with absolutely nothing in-between. So for a good amount of the run time, it really is just ‘woody was right the whole time 😱’ which we’ve done already and a prison escape movie. Alas, it’s not even a very good prison escape movie with the escape sequence being undercooked and not on par with the first two films action sequences. Toy Story 1 and 2 are not only funnier but more dramatically intense, Toy Story 3 uses middling jokes as a crutch for a lack of interesting stakes because again the villain is pathetic and the personal stakes for anyone other than Woody feel minuscule Yes the last stretch is great. The imagery of the incinerator rules, although the aliens saving them with the giant claw borders on Dues Ex Machina in its absurdity and somewhat undercuts the whole melting alive thing. The scene where Andy plays with the toys with Bonnie is beautiful. Woody saying ‘so long, partner’ and realising he belongs with the other Toy’s and not at College is great. I just wish these moments felt more earned, I don’t think much of anything in the second act resonates with the resolution thematically or even tonally Toy Story 3 is a misfire in the franchise for mine. It doesn’t have anywhere close to the meticulous plotting or comedic timing of the first two films, and is for mine a step below in just about every way. This includes animation by the way, the Toys move far more cartoonish with looney toons physics which takes away a huge part of the charm of the original two films. The toys actually moved like toys, in the third instalment they don’t. It’s the attention to detail that really derails the end of the trilogy for mine, and is probably why I didn’t have a visceral reaction to a fourth or fifth or sixth that others have had. I’d even argue that while Toy Story 3 has a nice ending it doesn’t wrap up the entire franchise in this perfect bow that should never have been touched. It’s the end of Andy’s story but Woody and especially Buzz don’t get anything close to satisfying conclusions to their journeys. And yet in the Andy farewell movie we spend almost all of it away from Andy… again! Wouldn’t it have made way more sense to spend more time with Andy and actually explore that relationship beyond a sense of duty. Explore the emotional dilemma Woody faces, loyalty to his best friend or acceptance that his friend grows up in a way he won’t. And how Buzz relates to that, drawing back to the first film in which Woody reacts to potential replacement with resentment and jealousy. We can see how Woody’s character has evolved through his connection to Buzz and with age. As is, this isn’t even close to the perfect farewell film people insinuate it is
