Maybe I'm too cynical for my own good but I did not like this one. I was 14 when it came out and just old enough for the sentiment of one final romp with my toys to resonate that very much doesn't exist as a nearly 30 year old. Be that as it may, I still found it in my heart to appreciate the tight little movie the first one is and the second takes the themes of toys to an absolute extreme that speaks very broadly about mortality and abandonment. This movie only ever gets close in the opening, when after two movies of hijinks to keep being alive secret, the first plan is a literal desperate call to be seen. It's a futile plan everyone knew wouldn't work but what else are you supposed to do when eternity is staring you in the face? The movie falls off a cliff when they get to the daycare. The first two movies felt they did a lot to show that how a person handled a toy was an extension of who they were. Here I find the very staunch and unexplored binary of the young children "not playing right" compared to the older children dull, especially compared to the subtle details of the household that informed Sid as a character. It reminds me of something that bugged me in the Barbie movie where it's obviously selling you on how the toy is a vehicle for your imagination but still makes very clear there's a "right" way to play with it and the "right" way is always in corporate interest. Barbie is also in this movie so maybe it's a Mattel thing. There isn't much to the daycare outside of it's prison motif. Unlike The Prospector who's self loathing was birthed of never being played with and only valued as a collector's item, Lotso and his big scary baby are jokes. What if the evil prison warden was a cuddly teddy bear and his heavy was a big scary baby? These random toys gamble in shady puke green settings to establish they are evil and take joy out of running toys through the ringer but one exposed lie and quick 10 second speech about fascism from Barbie and I guess the gang did prison abolition? I actually said in my review of the first one that I didn't want to succumb to snarky literalism but it is clear that the first two movies are about "toys" in the broadest sense where they represent trust, innocence, and youth. This movie is about "toys" as literal objects. It's an exercise in melodramatic toy existentialism and gratuitous toy violence so that you feel bad for not loving plastic enough and maybe even buy some more plastic. This isn't to say that toys aren't meaningful, just to say that in the first two movies the toys are passive agents to a child's imagination. Woody himself is not special, his position as a kids favorite toy is what's special, and it's a spot you can lose at any given moment so you need to appreciate it while you can. The movie brings this idea home with the ending decently enough if you're a fan, I'm not totally heartless and it's not bad having Andy unable to give up Woody for a moment as a way to represent him uncertain about leaving that childhood behind. I just personally wish the movie was more about that tension with Andy and not masculine buff toys calling Ken gay or Latin Lover Lightyear in pre-school Alcatraz. The only thing keeping this together and me believing that Andy has an emotional connection with some squeaky toys from a pizza restaurant crane game is the fact that I've seen the first two movies.

Toy Story 3 is a movie that has all of the potential to be the single greatest movie for kids ever, but throws most of its chances away by following a few of generic formulas that the previous two installments already solidified. The main characters in this movie are absolutely spot on and perfectly characterized: Woody's whole philosophy of not abandoning his child and whole skepticism and all the parallels to Lotso's well constructed story arc and lore were perfectly shown throughout the whole runtime, especially in the scene where the bear abandons the toys in the garbage dump for absolutely no reason. The last heartwarming sequence of the film, with the toys moving on from Andy's care onto Bonnie's hands and all of dynamics changing, perfectly encapsulates the movie's core message and serves to a perfect finale for a beloved trilogy. Lotso is a great villain, Pixar's best, per say, but his companions (for most part) serve only as plot devices. Different from the group of protagonists that have actual personalities and feel like characters we may love (although some, like Mr. Potato Head, may be a bit flanderized here), their redemptions feel unearned and unrealized, except for the Big Baby and Ken. And Spanish Buzz sucked. However, to be fair, these are just nitpicks. For a kids movie, it is not expected that it takes a dark direction or that it follows great dark philosophies, serving as a lesson to kids that "sometimes, to love is to let go", and accept new cycles (just like Kung Fu Panda 4 tries to do and fails miserably). The whole cinematography, roller coaster of emotions, voice acting, animation, character designs and overall plot are absolutely excellent and stunning, especially in the movie's highest point, which is the dumpster scene. A really, really great lesson on how to make a movie rich for children and extremely entertaining adults, simultaneously. But not enough for me to consider it as a full masterpiece, especially as it falls into comercial traps to try and sell itself more often (Spanish Buzz).

“Authority should be derived from the consent of the governed, not from the threat of force.” - Barbie. Change is terrifying - to have to confront the idea of your comfort being threatened, something you’ve known and experienced being replaced with something new and frightening, it takes a lot to overcome it. The Toy Story series have been a lot of things - it’s been more than 30 years since the first one revolutionised animation and thy just released a new one, the fifth in a long line of critically and commercially acclaimed films, but none of them are as good as Toy Story 3; its not just about sentient plastic, but about love, growth, comfort, purpose, betrayal and the idea of moving on, and it’s constructed in a manner that is inexplicably beautiful because of its masterful script and direction. Out of the three films so far in the series (and from the ones that came after), Toy Story 3 is the most emotionally mature, mainly because of how well it deals with the aforementioned themes - in a manner that is not just easy for a child to understand, but also for an adult who grew up with these films to appreciate and love. What starts as a standard lost and found story that has become the standard operating procedure for these films quickly evolves into a full blown “heist-like” feature, supplemented with some of the most heart-rending sub plots you could find in a film that is supposed to be marketed towards children. The tonal consistency in the screenplay is astounding, because this film manages to be so many things without trying too hard to be - it’s sad, funny (cackling and giggling funny), intelligent and down-right moving. The film also draws strength from the fact that it holds one of the most outrageously well written villains I could imagine. Lotso is literally Dr Doom levels of machiavellian evil, and it’s shockingly good! This is a character who’s heart was torn apart and is so full of pain and resentment that he refuses to accept any kind of attempt at redemption, right until the very end - it’s all done so well that you fully understand why he is the way he is, but never sympathise or justify his actions because of how cruel he is. It’s fucking brilliant I tell you, way too brilliant for a children’s movie. At its core, Toy Story 3 is about change, and how some people are able to cope with it, and how some aren’t. There’s a reason this is called one of the greatest animated films of all time, and it’s a title that is truly warranted.

Toy Story 3 is a great conclusion to Toy Story series, you’ll see what I mean when I talk about the fourth film. Looking through the movie, the first thing is that this is mostly a prison break film, which is certainly a unique option but it’s done very well with the style change. The animation has gotten to a point where it is equivalent to real life, especially with all the grime the toys get and the incinerator with millions of moving trash pieces by physics. The characters are very good, with all the original cast returning, expect for Bo, who would have broke into a million pieces during most of this film. The new characters are just as good, we get Lotso, possibly the best of an original animated villain by Pixar besides Syndrome, then an specific Barbie and Ken, probably the best at teaching me about the Barbie line without watching all 37 animated movies by Mattel, Ken is voiced by Micheal Caine, so he’s a British Ken. Then for all of Bonnie’s toys, they all done well in the film, some interesting casting is Trixie being Mabel from Gravity Falls, and Mr. Pricklepants being voiced by the late-80s Bond, Dalton. I personally think the best part though is Andy throughout the film. I, myself, am growing up, and I can relate to Andy aging and giving his toys away to a new generation. The ending still does make me cry to this day, and that is telling on how impactful this movie is. If there is a series that should all get 5 stars together, I'll say this one may be a contender. I guess the only bad thing is that Disney bought the rights to the cymbal monkey toy and, even though they never use it ever besides this film, they will file a lawsuit against any film using the monkey toy like The Monkey. I guess this is what happens when Disney is a capitalist company owning a product line patent.

“Tell me I’ve lived a good life. Tell me I’m a good man” Someone else said Saving Private Ryan works for a metaphor as US involvement in wars in general, in the sense that there’s always a private Ryan to save, a cause to fight for, and the sacrifice made will always be greater than the life saved. In trying to convince the audience that this great sacrifice is the point of war or why it’s necessary, the film misses the fact that this is precisely why war is irredeemably pointless. The film wants to portray all our lead heroes as victims of brutality who want it to end, but also encourages them to be perpetrators of brutality. Upham is the best example of this. He starts the film as a staunch pacifist, someone who wants to bring an end to the brutality on both sides through strict adherence to the Geneva conventions. By the end of the film however, motivated by revenge, he gives into his rage and kills a surrendered German soldier, starting the cycle of violence and brutality once again. The film frames this loss of empathy as heroic. None of my issues with the film are in the directing/filmmaking of it. Spielberg is great and he’s really firing off all cylinders here. But none of that matters (in fact it might make it worse) if the script that directing is supporting creates a world where war is always justified as long as you have a private to save.

I just watched this movie for the first time in 30 years. And while the film is nothing short of an astounding technical achievement, it is as morally and philosophically bankrupt as a film like this could possibly be. ﻿ ﻿Setting aside the events that led up to D-Day and the US entry into a two-front war, this film makes two arguments that I find absolutely appalling: ﻿ ﻿1) That a pacifist subjected to the horrors of war can be thus justified in the committing of a cold-blooded murder. ﻿2) That all who come after owe it to those who gave their lives to be better people because of their sacrifice. ﻿ ﻿When the Captain says "Earn this" to Ryan, I thought that was a really lousy thing to do to another human being. The plot had already established that not only had Ryan had no say in the mission, he vehemently disagreed with it, and wanted nothing to do with it. So for the captain to say that is to put a burden on Ryan that he in no way deserved. ﻿ ﻿But that isn't even the point of that line. Spielberg is trying to tell all of us that we owe it to those who died to earn their sacrifice. And while one can certainly commend them for ending the tyranny of the Nazis, that doesn't mean we all owe it to them to live the lives that they did not get to. Their sacrifice was in the name of freedom. To me, this film seems to make the argument that the sacrifice was in the name of war. ﻿ ﻿Captain Miller could have died anywhere in Europe. He and his team could have died on Omaha Beach. But because they died on that bridge, that doesn't make Private Ryan indebted to them for a sacrifice he did not ask for. And to see a broken old man on that beach 50 years later asking his wife for validation is just piling on. ﻿ ﻿And Upham's murder of the German soldier he previously campaigned to release is somehow meant to show that the horrors of war can change even the least warlike of men. But the manner in which this happens is in purely cold blood, as justification for Upham watching him shoot the captain. Upham has a perfect position to fire his weapon in combat, and the movie could have done that. Instead, Upham takes the prisoners, and shoots the one in cold blood. ﻿ ﻿Nothing justifies this murder. We are meant to see Upham reshaped by war, but to what end? That murder is justified in some context? Upham's lack of remorse in his action contributes to the idea that Spielberg is saying the murder is justified, but I don't agree. ﻿ ﻿I left the movie feeling very unsettled. There's a lot of emotional manipulation here, and a lot of scenes that ring very hollow thirty years later. And while this may be a strong technical achievement, as a film - as a work of art - I find it lacking.

Okay, the first thought I had as the movie was getting started was, holy shit the sound design and choreography in this movie is absolutely phenomenal. The first action scene is extremely memorable but the highlight is the sound and atmosphere throughout the entire movie. That’s the real star of the movie, sorry Tom Hanks. That’s where my praise ends for this movie. It’s a war movie but what war movies always get wrong is that patriotism/nationalism has no place in a war movie. It cheapens the horrors of war when this movie tries to have its cake and eat it too. It wants to say, “isn’t this horrible how so many people are needlessly dying?” But simultaneously makes it seem like the American troops are the heroes. I get that WWII is sort of a layup in that America was fighting true atrocities, but war movies love to gloss over the innocents from the opposition to instead focus on the militants from the “good side”. We see people kill enemies that have surrendered and disregard for civilians from Tom Hank’s troop. I think the only good war movie can be an anti-war movie which is not this movie. It glorifies war but wants to act like it shows how atrocious war is at the same time which makes it fail overall. But goddamn I love Tom Hanks and would be lying if the movie wasn’t solidly made and acted which earns it a three star rating despite my major flaws and concerns with the movie. It’s genuinely well made and had me invested the whole time, I just can’t get behind war.

Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan is a structurally interesting war film, and features several exceptional moments throughout but also some highly conventional war tropes and a weak plot which make the message of the film a little difficult to take at face value. Firstly, the film features one of the most iconic war sequences in film history, featuring flawless kinetic handheld cinematography and epic uses of quick zoom ins and camera movements, perfectly encapsulating the horrors of war. However, after that groundbreaking intro, I feel the film really loses its momentum rapidly. It evolves from a revolutionary war epic to a highly conventional and unoriginal war story, relying overly on traditional sentimentality (especially at the finale) and predictable war tropes. While the film throughout still continues to use groundbreaking techniques, it feels like a significant diminish in originality, making it feel quite generic overall, However despite its unoriginal plot, it still remains an highly impressive technical feat in cinematic history.

I put this on during a flight from Europe thinking that I would watch the first half hour — a terrific and terrifically horrifying sequence of the Allied landing on Normandy — and then turn it off. But this time I was fascinated by the incredibly weird treatment of gender and watched it all the way through. The most striking scene in this respect is when the group of soldiers searching for Ryan are sitting in an abandoned church, lit only by candles, talking about their mothers. Borderline schmalzy and uncanny, this scene anticipates the *extremely* schmalzy closing scene, set decades in the future, when the now-aged Ryan tearfully asks his equally aged wife, “Am I a good man? Did I lead a good life?” Jeez guy please answer these questions for yourself. Women in this film exist only to be the passive foils of men, whether as bereaved mothers or supportive wives. The closest thing to an actual female character is a young French girl, maybe five years old, who is stranded in a bombed out building with her family. Her desperate father throws her down from above into the hands of one of the group of soldiers. After a fire fight, while the girl cowers among the soldiers, she is passed back to her father and the soldiers move on. The lesson here is that this world is an exclusively male one. Emotional complexity exists only among the men, whose relationships are at once fraternal, or father-son, or strangely erotic, with a tremendous sense of bodily intimacy. A very strange movie. Again, the terrible schmalzy ending is a huge misstep, much like the amazingly awkward ending of Schindler’s List. How you could make Jaws and then make those two is beyond me.

Saving Private Ryan should be relegated to the category of okay movie. After almost thirty years since my original viewing, it is hard to remember why this film was so lauded. I remember as a kid the theater being completely silent when it concluded, patrons with heads hung low, shuffling out in remembrance of what was lost and won. In retrospect it seems like it received such critical praise and accolades because the greatest generation was dying off and guilt did the rest of the work. Somehow Spielberg won Best Directing over Terrence Malick's The Thin Red Line, released the same year and a better film by every measure. I will give Saving Private Ryan Best Sound, Sound Editing, and Cinematography, but none of those awards require Spielberg. He directed a boring story that generates so much momentum in the first twenty minutes from the iconic D-Day landing that the energy alone carries you across the finish line. The rest of the film is a ragtag bunch of Rangers looking for Private Ryan, and just like Tom Hanks' squad asking why they are hunting for him, I too was wondering why this movie deserves praise for a boring fetch quest with no compelling answer as to why anyone cares about Ryan outside of his mother. The acting ranges from meh to okay. Part of the problem is Spielberg created tropes for characters. None of them felt real. The Rudy character as a scared soldier with a heart of gold, the rough around the edges guy from Brooklyn who means well once you get to know him. Maybe my age or internet-saturated storytelling has ruined my patience for this, but they mostly felt one-dimensional and wooden with zero character development across the entire runtime. My biggest gripe is the ending, which plays like a video game. Characters have plot armor that lets them run through bullets fired from fifty different Nazis, artillery strikes, and flak cannons without a scratch, unless the plot demands otherwise. About ten Americans with limited resources take on a battalion of Nazis with multiple tanks in their own WWII Battle of Thermopylae, fighting over a bridge that could be repaired in a week but is somehow of vital importance. The most egregious part is that each main American soldier kills approximately fifty Nazis apiece, as hoards of Germans seek out American bullets like moths to a flame. I was rolling my eyes. Bad writing, bad directing, and I am scratching my head as to why this was considered good even by 1998 standards. Saving Private Ryan is the cinematic equivalent of the books your English teacher forced you to read in high school. The same false arbiters of culture who decided Wuthering Heights and Slaughterhouse-Five must be preserved for future generations have decided this film is sacred. Saving Private Ryan is patriotism bordering on jingoism dressed up as prestige cinema.

Spielberg works his magic once again. The first 30 minutes or so of this film are masterfully shot, written, acted, and edited. It’s a genuinely unflinching, brutal, and deeply heartbreaking depiction of World War II that I have not seen anything like. The pain, the horror of it all, is ridiculously intense and it really puts things into perspective. The cinematography throughout is absolutely breathtaking, using natural landscapes, framing, and camera motion to perfectly capture the various emotions of the film. Tom Hanks delivers the standout performance here. I grow continually more impressed with his acting range and how he is able to portray such complex characters so well. Matt Damon is also great, as usual, and the supporting cast in general is very good as well. The storyline is extremely compelling (bring Matt Damon home 🤯) and results in an emotional, epic journey for a small squad of soldiers searching for one man. It truly feels like an epic journey in so many ways. I wouldn’t have minded if it was maybe just a half-hour shorter, as I found some of the really powerful moments not to be the loud, chaotic combat scenes, but the smaller-scale, intense interactions between soldiers just trying to keep surviving and getting through these traumatic experiences. There is a great amount of both, but my only real complaint with this movie is that it feels a bit long in parts. However, that’s a small nitpick in what is otherwise a ridiculously entertaining, important film that is masterfully made. There’s a reason that Spielberg is considered one of the best to ever do it. His range as a director is simply remarkable. He can create lighthearted, family friendly crowd pleasers like ET and then turn around and deliver a haunting, gorgeously shot war epic that captures the horrors of World War II.

This was such an easy 5 stars before some truly baffling creative decisions. The crude humor during moments of genuine mortal tension repeatedly pulled me out of the film. I understand what the characterization of Upham is doing and why he behaves the way he does, but frankly, I couldn’t care less. Everything about him repulsed me: the cowardice, the naïveté, his constant glorification of war, and especially the fact that he repeats what the film itself frames as a mistake by releasing more prisoners. And why have Steamboat come back? What exactly was the message there? Was it to suggest that you shouldn’t spare your enemies? That good deeds sometimes don’t go unpunished? Or that you should continue doing good despite that possibility? If it was the latter, I don’t think the film communicates it particularly well. And that’s what makes this so frustrating. This is still a fantastic movie. I had a genuinely great time watching it. Tom Hanks is stellar as ever, the plot is compelling, and the cinematography and action sequences are incredible. But man, I genuinely can’t remember the last time a film irritated me this much.

That opening battle might be one of the most insane things I’ve ever watched. Spielberg doesn’t make D-Day look exciting or heroic in the normal movie sense. People are drowning before they even reach the beach, bullets are ripping through soldiers, explosions make Miller temporarily lose his hearing, and medics are trying to save people who are already basically dead. The shaky camera, washed-out look, sound, and complete confusion make it feel like Spielberg is dropping you into the middle of Omaha Beach instead of letting you comfortably watch it. What surprised me is that the rest of the movie is much quieter. The mission to save Ryan sounds heroic until the soldiers start questioning why eight men should risk their lives for one person they don’t even know. Tom Hanks is perfect as Miller because he never feels like some unstoppable war hero. He’s exhausted, scared, his hand won’t stop shaking, and he’s just trying to keep his men together long enough to finish the mission. Wade’s death and Mellish getting slowly stabbed were especially hard to watch. I do think the movie loses a little momentum between the opening and final battle, but when that last battle starts Spielberg somehow manages to make everything feel chaotic while still letting me understand where everyone is and what they’re trying to do. “Earn this” is such a brutal thing for Ryan to have to carry for the rest of his life. After *Schindler’s List* and now this, Spielberg might be even better when he takes away all the spectacle and forces you to look directly at people.

I have empathy for everyone who has been to war. That being said, it must take an extraordinary amount of courage to go to war knowing that you may very well die and that survival itself can feel like a miracle. A forma como Spielberg retrata a guerra é tão realista e intimista que mostra que os soldados não são heróis invencíveis, mas humanos. A cena mais memorável, pra mim, é o momento em que, antes de acontecer o ataque mais violento do filme, os soldados restantes ouvem  e cantam "Tu est partout", da Édith Piaf, em um gramofone improvisado no meio das ruínas. Isso humaniza eles, de certa forma, e rompe com o silêncio opressivo antes do ataque. Eles meio que deixam de serem soldados e voltam a serem civis, com famílias, casas, sonhos. Além disso, a cena em que Upham fica travado na escada no dilema de subir ou não, por mais que possa dar ao público um ar de covardia vindo do tradutor, é extremamente realista. Diante de soldados corajosos e acostumados com o caos da guerra, Upham representava a inocência do grupo, tendo até defendido um soldado alemão antes. A paralisia ao entregar as munições enquanto um americano morria no andar de cima mostra que Spielberg desmitifica o heroísmo de todos os soldados da guerra, retratando também o medo. A reação de Upham representa, mesmo que estressando o público, a reação mais provável e humana de um civil jogado em um combate. Eu até lembrei, na hora, do Dae-Ho, em Squid Game, que tem uma reação idêntica à essa, ficando paralisado e em pânico ao ter que entregar as munições ao grupo durante a rebelião. Uma reação completamente humana. Por fim, a reação de Upham acaba o humilhando, quando os soldados alemães passam por ele e nem atacam, mostrando que eles não o vêem como uma ameaça. E o desfecho é que ele acaba cometendo um crime de guerra, matando o soldado alemçao que ele mesmo havia insistido pra ficar, como forma de vingança ao Capitão Miller. Spielberg mostra como a guerra corrompe, até mesmo a pessoa mais inocente do grupo. A guerra tira a humanidade dos soldados.

Saving Private Ryan é um daqueles filmes que conseguem fazer a guerra parecer algo físico. Não é só assistir aos personagens lutando; existe uma sensação constante de caos, medo e desorientação. A sequência inicial do desembarque na Normandia é provavelmente uma das representações mais impactantes de combate que já vi. Spielberg não tenta transformar aquilo em uma batalha "bonita". A câmera fica próxima dos soldados, o som é agressivo e tudo acontece de maneira extremamente caótica. Também gosto bastante de como o filme equilibra as grandes cenas de batalha com momentos mais silenciosos entre os personagens. A missão de encontrar Ryan funciona como uma estrutura para discutir o custo humano da guerra e o significado de sacrificar algumas vidas para salvar uma pessoa. Tom Hanks funciona muito bem como Miller porque ele não é apresentado como um super-herói. É um homem tentando cumprir uma missão enquanto carrega o peso de tudo que está acontecendo ao redor. “Earn this.” The famous final words of Tom Hanks’ Captain Miller as he dies on the bridge at the end of Saving Private Ryan. I don’t think we fully comprehend what we have when it comes to freedom in the United States. Captain Miller and his band of brothers embark on a mission to save just one soldier, and one by one, they sacrifice themselves to secure his freedom and his future. As Miller lies dying, his final words to Private Ryan are simple: “Earn this.” That phrase feels increasingly distant from the hearts and minds of Americans today. What are we supposed to earn? Most of us honestly don’t know. We have grown up surrounded by freedoms of every kind, so completely immersed in them that it can be difficult to imagine another reality—one in which those freedoms are absent, restricted, or taken away entirely. Freedom can never be treated as something guaranteed. It requires vigilance, but it also requires something more: responsibility toward one another. We inherit a country and a way of life purchased, time and time again, through the sacrifices of people we will never meet. I hope that, in brotherhood and sisterhood, we can continue striving to earn this—not because freedom should have to be earned as a condition of possessing it, but because sacrifice deserves remembrance, gratitude, and a willingness to leave something worthy behind for the generations that follow us. One of the greatest films ever made. In nearly every way, Saving Private Ryan is a masterpiece.

I would like to start off by saying that as someone who really loved Do the Right Thing I was very excited to watch this movie. I mean, who wouldn't after reading that premise right? The sheer concept of a black cop infiltrating the KKK immediately got my attention...yet this film almost completely falls apart on every level. The first and last 5 minutes are great. The last scene with Ron and Patrice especially actually had me lock tf in, that was a powerful way to wrap the story up in a way I never expected. Everything else is kinda ass. I just wanna say that the editing in this movie is unironically one of the worst I've seen. The shots have absolutely no continuity after cutting, it keeps cutting in the most awkward moments, the genuinely powerful speech at the beginning has some really goofy closeups of the audience for some reason, there's just endless examples of atrocious editing that made it impossible for me to have fun with the film. This movie should have been a comedy, but for some reason it's a terrible one even with a premise this silly. There's nothing snappy about the intentionally comedic lines, it's just kind of awkwardly lumbering in its own rhythm and it's not funny. The acting is fine but nothing memorable. Adam Driver gave a better performance in Megalopolis of all things than this movie. The social commentary here also is just surface level as hell and cheap. It's genuinely shocking coming from the man behind one of the most nuanced movies on race tensions, that the main thing explored here is white people are racist. Any room for nuance set up by the plot of the movie: Adam Driver wrestling with his Jew heritage, Patrice's, and her people in general, hatred of cops, Ron's weird insistence on believing in changing the system from inside never truly being explored nor challenged, the racist cop(s) in Ron's department, and so much more are just...dropped? They don't reach anywhere close to resolution nor is there any development with these themes, they're just mentioned briefly and discarded. Why does Ron need to be on the phone? Why can't Adam Driver just be on the phone and meeting them in person? The premise itself has holes, and throughout the entire movie I honestly don't know what our characters are doing in the KKK. Do they really learn anything of value? Do I, the audience, even learn anything from watching this movie? There's not even like a comical examination of KKK's weird activities and procedures like I thought they would, it's like there's barely any research done into the organisation you're making a movie about. The whole movie is just Adam Driver and Ron dicking around in the KKK and hearing white people spam hate speech. It's not entertaining, funny, nor educational. It's cheap . The fucking 5 minutes KKK cutscene in Django Unchained with Quentin Tarantino as a racist Klan member was like a thousand times more entertaining than this movie in a fraction of its screentime.

It's always a bit difficult to rate films based on true stories. It raises questions such as : should you aestheticize things that weren't ? Should a film's faithfulness to real events affect its rating ? Does it still need to be entertaining in the way it's directed ? In terms of pure feeling and a basic judgment, I can't help feeling that the film is wasted potential. It's only near the end that it comes close to the level of stress and tension that could have been present throughout the entire film, and it was only when real footage was shown for a few minutes that I felt genuinely hurt and outraged. Going back to the questions I raised at the beginning, I think the film tried too hard to stay entertaining and visually appealing, to the point of becoming almost comical by adding subtle humor to every scene and turning every character into a caricature. Or maybe white supremacists really were that ridiculous back then and I'm the one who's wrong ? But I think it's more likely a huge mistake on Spike Lee's part, combined with mid acting and mid direction. There's a serious lack of raw scenes showing the emotional struggles some of these characters may have gone through. The film almost gives the impression that social segregation wasn't all that violent, that racists were only a minority and that infiltrating a group of dangerous unstable sick individuals is just routine. And after a few quick searches, it becomes clear that the film is far from Ron Stallworth's real story. He first spent three years infiltrating black activists and radical black groups before infiltrating the KKK for nine months, not just one for a night and the other for a month. In conclusion, Spike Lee reduced reality to the story of a somewhat cool black cop infiltrating a group of somewhat stupid racists who do some not so nice things. But on the whole, it’s not a complete disaster with no substance or form. It’s just that looking at the film’s overall rating I get the impression that everyone has kind of agreed it’s a very good movie that represents the cause well. I suppose the intention was there, and the goal was still to highlight an important and underrepresented period of history, so let’s not be too harsh either.

the police, in rural colorado in the 70s, were working AGAINST the KKK? right. blatant copaganda and assimilation ideation. which makes sense given Spike Lee’s association with the NYPD, where they gave him over 200K for an ad campaign to promote relationships between the police and the black community. the characters seemed completely flat, what was Ron’s backstory? what were his motivations? why did Patrice get actively assaulted by a cop and then have no discussion about it? just a cut to an aestheticized montage. this was truly a disappointment on so many levels, not that we can expect radical media from large media corporations, but the premise seemed interesting while the film slowly descended into nonsense. especially the last scene at the bar with the cringe dialogue and arrest of the racist cop who had assaulted Patrice prior in the film, who was arrested on the grounds of saying racist shit? disgusting and tone deaf.

Assistir a Infiltrado na Klan em 2026, 8 anos após sua estreia nas salas de cinema, é olhar por um monóculo fotográfico de lente embaçada. Em menos de uma década, o zeitgest já se metamorfoseara de tal maneira que o filme de Spike Lee é, no frigir dos ovos, indesvencilhável do clima  da política ocidental de 2018 - seja para o bem ou para o mal. É facilmente perceptível ao se analisar a recepção do longa-metragem que, sobre as condições de seu primeiro lançamento, foi possível que a empreitada dos "irmãos Stallworth" reproduzida em tela potencializasse uma apoteótica comoção ideológica sobre sua audiência. O  notável valor motivacional das cenas da KKK e do Movimento Negro - as quais o idealizador justapõe mais de uma vez, consciente e ironicamente, pela montagem paralela tão querida por D. W. Graffith - são capazes de afetar ao espectador graças ao desconforto ou a empatia. Porém, não creio ser possível dizer o mesmo sobre o aparato textual e formal de sua obra. Indeciso entre representar sua aventura policial como um retrato cosmético capaz de desfrutar assumidamente do apelo psicológico de seu aspecto retro , com suas superfícies polidas e lustradas; uma homenagem direta às sensibilidades nutridas pelo cinema setentista, do split screen ao grão do filme; ou um comentário anacrônico, cru e comovente sobre a violência racial, Lee não finca-pé sobre nenhuma das oportunidades estéticas que tais possibilidades o permitem, cruzando tais iniciativas em um híbrido no mínimo mal aproveitado. Lapsos de genialidade na direção ou inventividade na montagem não conseguem ocultar uma obra fundamentada no maniqueísmo entre forças opostas - cartunizadas ao máximo na pura bondade ou maldade, arquetipizadas na estudante radicalizada de rostinho bonito e no klansman retardado bobão - que só conseguem funcionar como cosmos narrativo quando mediadas e superadas pelo ímpeto individual do good cop boa pinta. Ao mesmo tempo, questões que fujam da obviedade identitária (como a ambiguidade entre a branquitude e a etnia judaica pautada no personagem de Driver e toda a problemática do racismo como opressão sistemática e estrutural da nação branca estadunidense) são propriamente escanteadas em favor de um thriller policial que deixa a desejar, com excessão de uma ou outra sequência dinâmica na segunda metade da minutagem. Assim, Spike Lee busca filmar suas personagens diante da necessidade de atuação civil e corporativa sem, por outro lado, permitir-se explorar devidamente as ambiguidades técnicas e ideológicas de seu projeto artístico. BlacKkKlansman , sobretudo, é um filme pouco catártico e corajoso estetica e textualmente para o papel de cinema político que buscou exercer.

I found myself bothered by numerous “plot holes” and issues with the story during this, only to look it up and find out that some of the most ridiculous shit in this movie is actually real. Yes it is based on “some fo real shit” as stated in the opening of the movie, but some of these details I just couldn’t believe. Yes, Ron Stallworth actually made the mistake of using his own name when first contacting the KKK. Yes, he actually got a white detective to handle in person interactions while he spoke to members on the phone. Yes, not a single KKK member noticed that their voices were different. Yes, when David Duke came to Colorado Springs, Stallworth’s police chief actually chose to assign him (the only black man in the entire force) to Duke’s protection, and when he objected his chief actually told him that “no one else is available”. All of this seemed pretty convenient while I was watching and I was ready to hate, but it turns out all of these details are true lol. Segunda película que veo de Spike Lee, segunda decepción que me llevo. Sinceramente no tengo demasiado que reprocharle, no me parece una mala película, puedo apreciar perfectamente lo que hace, pero al igual que me pasó con Inside Man, terminé la película pensando que me gustó más lo que Spike Lee quería decir, que la película que hizo para decirlo. BlacKkKlansman está cargadísima de problemáticas sociales y raciales, o sea, ésta directamente gira en torno a una historia real sobre la secta racista más conocida de la historia. Y claramente banco el mensaje, la crítica y lo absurdo que resulta todo esto. El tema es que la película nunca me llevó un punto más allá. La premisa es cuanto menos entretenida de ver, y tiene situaciones que en el papel deberían ser tensísimas o incómodas, pero en ningún momento percibí que la película llegara a explotar realmente. Todo avanzaba y rara vez sentía que algo tuviera verdadero peso, incluso la historia termina siendo bastante predecible. Y aunque no tengo ningún problema con los finales felices, este me pareció demasiado hollywoodense para tratarse de una historia basada en hechos reales. De hecho, el cierre terminó de confirmarme esa sensación, ya que en vez de sentir que la película había llegado naturalmente a un punto de quiebre, sentí que Spike necesitaba detenerse para recordarme cuál era el mensaje que acababa de ver durante dos horas. Tal vez también tengan algo que ver las expectativas. Ya que ésta, junto a Malcolm X y Do the Right Thing son películas que llevaba muchísimo tiempo queriendo ver, y entre las críticas y todo lo que se escucha sobre ellas, terminé llegando con las expectativas por las nubes. Esperaba que esto me demostrara por qué Spike Lee ES Spike Lee, pero no pasó. Aún con todo esto, le tengo una fe increíble a las otras dos.

I can't really ignore that this is copaganda. We are meant to sympathize with the struggles of our main character when his girlfriend challenges him and is very upset when she finds out that he's a cop, because she just 'doesn't understand'. He actively combats her on her beliefs repeatedly, and I felt that the story was painting her as ignorant and not understanding of how much the police system of America exploits black suffering. It completely invalidates and sidelines the fact that the justice system in America, especially during that point in history, was extremely racist and often negatively black and impoverished communities. We are meant to see Ron's girlfriend, Patrice, as some radical who just can't see past her pig hating lenses and trust her well meaning cop boyfriend, who only wants the best for their people. She even seems to ease up at the end of the movie, which is fine since the man that assaulted her was going to be punished for his crime, but it seems unfaithful to her original character. One of the biggest critiques people have of America's justice system, racism aside, is that it doesn't rehabilitate — it punishes. This seems ideal when you consider that pedophiles and other offenders of violent crimes will suffer, but it doesn't account for the fact that people like thieves and loiterers are also in there suffering. Some people think it's adequate, but it doesn't actually do anything proactive to prevent crime and often causes more issues than solutions. This is often something socialists and pro black activists complain about, and during the Black Panther era, dismantling the prison system was very, very important to their politics. Although I definitely believe that degenerate deserved to suffer for what he did to Patrice, the Patrice we know at the beginning of the story wouldn't abandon her political beliefs for any one at any time, not even for her boyfriend. This means, that in some attempt at character growth, Patrice abandons her politics and trusts the police officers at the end of the story. Hm. It's almost like the writers wanted to paint the police as heroes and convince those watching that movements like the pro-Black movements need police officers to keep them safe. The movie is meant to make us feel like you can fix the system from the inside, and it humanized police officers and the system in a way that made them feel more like victims than perpetrators. Cops are not your friends. Other than that, the movie was pretty good. The actors did a phenomenal job, shed some light on the KKK and how these racists paint themselves as charismatic to fool the population and seem more reasonable than they truly are. It definitely had its good sides, and its funny moments. Just wish they toned it down on the police dick riding.

So well directed. But also so flawed. I’ll always be a fan of Spike Lee but he’s newer work really lacks the bite of his earlier work. Do the Right Thing and Malcolm X clear this. Some amazing sequences and humor but the thin line between fiction and reality and the cop-ness of it all really drags it down. The real life story is certainly compelling but the story decides to fictionalize some incredibly important aspects such as Flip’s identity, Ron’s personal philosophy, and Patrice. Patrice is the most frustrating part of all of this because she is an incredibly compelling character and her and Ron’s conversation about Blackxploitation films on the bridge is arguably one of the best scenes (shout out Shaft). If you’re going to tell a “true” story, don’t let the fictional stuff become more compelling than the real life story. This is clearly meant to be a response to modern politics and an analysis of the growth of political racism in the United States, which is incredibly compelling but it loses all credibility when the whole police department of an incredibly right wing town are all relatively supportive of the black guy (expect for the one guy but the writers clearly wanted a scapegoat). 30 for 30: 2018 BlacKKKlansman✊🏿👻 This Spike Lee joint tells the story of two cops, one white and one black, that launch an operation to go undercover within the KKK. What comes out is a haunting yet still very relevant look at an America built on a racism. While I don’t think anything can ever top Do the Right Thing, I’m always seated for whatever this director puts out. I think what made that film an all timer for me is it asks a lot of questions about what is the “Right Thing”, particularly when it comes to inequality. I think this movie kind of builds on that theme, but amplifies it to a much higher degree with greater consequences. A fitting thing for when this movie came out that is still the same today. Politics are much more polarizing today. But, I also think Lee is much more unapologetic to excuses for racism than even his early films. The last 5 minutes of this lays it out clear. There are still limits to changing the system from within and hate has been on the rise again. Movie MVP: Going to go with Spike here. The director adds such a cool groove to this film that makes it feel both like a film in the 1970s, when it takes place, and in the late 2010s. It is bleak subject matter for sure, especially when the director uses real world examples of racial injustice and racism. Also really liked how the director challenged different forms of hate and how it should be tackled. Adam Driver’s character is just one example of this. He may not be visibly a target of racism, yet he is Jewish and would be the target of the same hate groups. There’s an interesting question in here of “well, why aren’t you doing more?” when fighting injustice that affects everyone. I think Spike does a good job of showing there are the good things that can come from working together to tackle such subjects. Favourite quotes: “You know the way to sell hate? Affirmative action, immigration, crime, tax reform, he says no one wants to be called a bigot anymore because Archie Bunker made that too uncool. So, the idea is under all these issues…everyday Americans can accept it. Support it. Until eventually, one day he gets somebody in the White House that embodies it.” “Sheeeeeeee-it!”

Nick Cave's "O Children" is doing career-best work here, and I resent it deeply for being wasted on this scene. Two people slow dance in a tent for absolutely no narrative reason beyond "the other one left the room," and somehow the movie wants me to feel something warm about it. I do not. I feel the specific discomfort of watching Ron's worst suspicions about his own crush confirmed in real time, and he's not even there to object. The Ron-less stretch should just have been Hermione crying, Harry carefully avoiding the word "Ron" like it's a landmine, and a silence Harry doesn't know how to fill, because he doesn't know how to deal with emotional women. That's the scene. That's the whole scene. But naturally the script's solution is "put on music, problem solved." It feels like two actors got a note that said: "dance like you're together, so people will question if this should have been a thing." Beautiful needle drop, genuinely upsetting choreography of feelings, zero actual conversation to back any of it up. I'd rather rewatch the tent scenes where nothing happens than this one where something almost happens and shouldn't have.

𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗿𝘆 𝗣𝗼𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗹𝘆 𝗛𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀: 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝟭 takes the franchise into its darkest and most visually mature territory yet. The improving technology certainly helps the visual effects, but the film's beauty comes primarily from its filmmaking. Every camera movement feels motivated, every frame feels deliberately composed, and the visual storytelling is consistently strong. The performances are equally impressive, with the characters' fear, grief, and uncertainty coming through convincingly. The film's biggest weakness is its runtime. At nearly two and a half hours, some scenes feel unnecessarily prolonged, and the film could have benefited from tighter editing. While the slower pace allows the characters' emotional struggles to breathe, there are moments where it becomes more tedious than deliberate. The sound design and score, however, effectively elevate the atmosphere and tension throughout. Still, 𝗗𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗹𝘆 𝗛𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀: 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝟭 is a well-crafted and emotionally grounded entry that successfully sets the stage for the finale. Overall, I give this movie 2/5 stars. !!!SPOILERS BELOW!!! Things I liked/Didn’t like: I feel like the only reason this movie exists was to quickly get rid of Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine. There hadn’t been any mention of adamantium poisoning in any of the other X-Men movies, so it feels totally random that he begins to feel the effects now. Adding that and the random Wolverine clone felt like a half-baked way of nerfing him and getting rid of him. And while his acts at the end of the movie are heroic, I think dying in battle with the rest of the X-Men is a noble death that Wolverine deserved. Logan is a movie I really wanted to love more than I actually did. The biggest strength is the atmosphere. Hugh Jackman gives a really committed performance, and I liked seeing Logan in a much more vulnerable stage of his life rather than as the nearly unstoppable Wolverine we’ve seen before. I also liked the idea of Logan being forced to become a protector again when he’s clearly trying to leave that life behind. His relationship with Laura gives the story an emotional center. That being said, I found the movie pretty slow in places, and I didn’t connect with the story as much as I expected to. Some of the darker elements felt like they were there more for shock value than because they actually added something meaningful to the story. I can absolutely understand why people consider this one of the best X-Men movies, especially because of Hugh Jackman’s performance and the way it closes out Logan’s story. For me, though, it just didn’t hit as hard as I wanted it to. Good performances obviously but was cringe and just not that good of a marvel movie. respect it though!

Logan is obviously a very good film, but I don’t think I love it as much as a lot of people do. Hugh Jackman is brilliant, and seeing Wolverine old, broken and completely worn down gives the character more weight than most of the earlier X-Men films ever managed. I really like the relationship between Logan, Charles and Laura too. It feels much smaller and more personal than the usual superhero film, which definitely suits the story. The violence also finally feels like what Wolverine should actually be capable of. After years of fairly clean X-Men action, this version of him feels dangerous. But the film is very bleak, very slow in places, and I think that affects how much I actually enjoy watching it. I respect what it does with the character, and the ending definitely lands, but it is more of a film I appreciate than one I would constantly go back to.

You know what I miss? Comic book movies being actually inspired by their source material. Taking the ideas or themes at the heart of an iconic storyline and then making a conscious effort to rework and reimagine those influences for the screen. Logan is a far from being a faithful adaption of Old Man Logan, and that’s a good thing . That story gets to stay within the medium of comic books, so that this one can stand on its own merits. This movie takes the core premise of an aging Wolverine on a road trip, and spins that into a Western-inspired send off Hugh Jackman’s live action version of the character. The rest, the movie makes it’s own, folding in an emotive farewell to Professor X, as well as introducing X-23, not to set up future spin-offs (à la the MCU) but as a thematic component of the story being told. Logan is about endings; they’re messy, imperfect and sometimes all we can hope for is making the best of the limited time we have left, and trying to find some peace and comfort when we get there. It’s heartfelt and earnest, and it’s more concerned with doing it’s characters justice than pointlessly recreating panels or costumes from its source material for audiences to point and gawp at. I always know who you are, it’s just sometimes I don’t recognise you.

Maldita obra maestra. Definitivamente, es de las mejores películas de superhéroes de toda la historia. Su argumento es simplemente impecable, marcando unas dinámicas muy pesimistas y oscuras con esa premisa tan atrapante y con un conflicto que, mientras más se va cocinando, va siendo más interesante, que brilla por el arco del protagonista, por el contexto en donde se desenvuelve y por la madurez e impotencia con que ocurre todo. Los personajes son grandiosos; Charles está en una faceta lúgubre y que nunca se le había visto al personaje; X-23 es una muy buena adición y se gana la pantalla en muchos momentos, además de tener un origen muy oscuro, lo que la vuelve más enigmática; y Logan… nunca me deja de sorprender lo tan bien desarrollado que está este héroe y que, mientras más sale en productos, más se sigue exprimiendo, mostrando aquí una faceta única y compleja, pero, esencialmente, dándole una conclusión a este gran personaje memorable, muy emotiva y muy revoltosa, pero al final coherente con lo que ha sido el personaje desde un inicio. En cuanto a los antagonistas, creo que no tienen el mejor desarrollo, pero sus motivaciones son bastante sólidas y, al final, creo que demuestran que menos es más; lo que se muestra de ellos es suficiente para tener un motor de avance y para que sean desagradables. En general, creo que es una experiencia sublime y que te deja un sentimiento de impotencia que nunca se va y no hace más que crecer. Las batallas son muy buenas, sus escenas de acción son frenéticas y tremendas y, uff, es MUY violenta, llena de sangre y con instantes que, aparte de exprimir las habilidades o condiciones de sus personajes, te hacen voltear la mirada de la pantalla de lo grotesco o aparatoso que sucede. En cuanto a lo que le reprocharía, porque ciertamente no es una película perfecta, está que tiene algunos agujeros de guion, unos momentos muy convenientes o incongruentes, ambigüedades, diálogos muy explicativos y algunas decisiones creativas que pudieron haber sido aún mejores. Aun así, creo que, una vez más, es una de las mejores películas de superhéroes y, gracioso, creo que lo que más le ayuda es que no se siente como una película de superhéroes; rompe con el molde tradicional y con la misma estructura, terminando en algo que se siente muy diferente, más complejo y con matices más marcados. Además, y hablando de otras cosas, también hay que decir que su cast es simplemente maravilloso: Patrick cada que aparecía casi me hacía llorar, Dafne tiene momentos formidables e impactantes que, considerando que es su primera aparición, la vuelven memorable y salvaje (de buena forma), y Hugh, no puedo decir nada que no haya dicho, es impresionante, aquí hace su mejor interpretación de todas y, aunque sigue con el manto del personaje hasta la fecha, creo que es indudablemente una conclusión perfecta para el y… hace un trabajo espectacular. En conclusión, Wolverine es uno de mis personajes favoritos de la historia y creo que esta es una inmejorable película para cerrar su arco. No es una película perfecta, pero a mí me pareció impresionante en todo momento, catártica, compleja y dura por lo que aborda y… me hizo llorar muchísimo de impotencia. Me encantó, pero no es algo que podría ver todos los días; me hizo sufrir.

Let's get the obvious defense out of the way first, because you'll hear it from every critic who's ever taken a film theory 101 class: "Daniel Day-Lewis's performance is a towering achievement." Sure. It's also the film's biggest problem. A two-and-a-half-hour movie that survives entirely on the strength of one man's scenery-chewing is not a great film — it's a great audition tape wrapped in 158 minutes of your patience being tested. **The Pacing Is a Crime** Paul Thomas Anderson wants you to sit in silence. A lot. The opening fifteen minutes have no dialogue, which critics call "bold" and normal people call "a warning sign." This isn't tension-building — it's a director who fell in love with his own silences and forgot that atmosphere without momentum is just dead air with better cinematography. Entire scenes exist to communicate "time is passing" when a single title card would have done the job in half a second. You don't need to watch a man dig a hole for four minutes to understand that oil drilling is hard work. We get it. It's 1898. There's dirt. **Daniel Plainview Isn't a Character, He's a Costume** Plainview doesn't develop — he arrives fully formed as "bad" and spends the runtime getting worse in increasingly cartoonish ways, culminating in a finale so over-the-top it plays like parody of itself rather than tragedy. There's no arc here, just escalation. A character who starts as ruthless and ends as ruthless-but-louder isn't a study in the corrupting nature of capitalism — it's a flat line dressed up as a mountain range because the actor delivering it is loud enough to convince you something changed. "I drink your milkshake" isn't a chilling final gasp of a broken man; it's a meme that happened to occur inside a prestige film. **Eli Sunday Is a Cardboard Cutout** Paul Dano's Eli exists purely as a punching bag — literally, by the end — so that Plainview has something to dominate. He's not a real antagonist with competing logic; he's a strawman preacher built exclusively so the film can score cheap points against organized religion while congratulating itself for depth. Their rivalry has no texture, no give-and-take, just two men shouting past each other for two hours until one hits the other with a bowling pin. That's not a thematic payoff. That's a bar fight with a film degree. **The Score Is Doing the Emotional Labor the Script Won't** Jonny Greenwood's score gets credited with "unsettling dread," but strip it away and what you're left with is a script that mistakes vagueness for profundity. Scenes that feel important only feel that way because strings are screeching underneath them. Take away the music and half these "iconic" moments are just two men standing in a field not talking. **The Ending Doesn't Land — It Faceplants** "I'm finished" is supposed to be the exclamation point on a two-and-a-half-hour descent into moral rot. Instead, after 140 minutes of glacial restraint, the film suddenly sprints into full-blown melodrama, tonally severed from everything that came before it. It doesn't feel earned; it feels like Anderson ran out of ways to end the movie quietly and decided the loudest possible note would pass for "unforgettable." Loud isn't the same as earned. **Why Half a Star, Not Zero** Because the cinematography is genuinely good, and Day-Lewis, even in service of a thin character, is never boring to watch. That's it. That's the whole case for the other half star. Everything else — the pacing, the thematic shallowness dressed as depth, an antagonist with no interior life, a finale that abandons its own restraint — earns exactly what it gets: almost nothing.

Since the film decides to operate according to the logic of reality in its first half—the oil industry, competition between capital, land transactions, and religious power—it should faithfully follow the principle of “genre self-discipline,” rather than using unrestricted allegorical ellipses to pass off gaps in narrative logic as something profound. H.W. is sent away without receiving the psychological continuity that should follow from such an event, while Bandy’s land can only be treated as the object of a transaction involving Daniel’s dignity, or rather, a kind of checkpoint—the reversal of power and the impotence of capital. Is there some way, some sufficiently grounded and authoritative image or line of dialogue, that could make this absence vivid, rather than asking the audience at a crucial moment to silently accept an allegorical mode of thought? Once a film chooses to enter a particular realm of reality, it should respect the logic by which that realm operates. The film should therefore maintain, as far as possible, a consistent narrative logic within itself.

There Will Be Blood es la película más sobrevalorada del siglo XXI. Para empezar, sus personajes están terriblemente escritos; son caricaturas sin verdadera profundidad. Tomemos como contraejemplo a David Fisher de Six Feet Under: es un hombre gay, pero también un ferviente creyente y conservador. Ambas facetas coexisten, dotándolo de complejidad. El personaje de Eli, por el contrario, es solo un patético y descarado estafador. Carece de esa hondura espiritual o contradicción interna que te permite empatizar con él, por muy terrible que sea. Por otro lado, la caricatura máxima es Daniel Plainview, un personaje con menos matices que Scrooge McDuck, el cual solo es un bufón que desea dinero (nadie sabe para qué) y poco más. Si el director quería retratar a los tiburones de la incipiente industria petrolera norteamericana, olvidó que estos hombres formaron enormes dinastías; no eran viejos huraños que acumulaban dinero para morir solos. Plainview parece una mezcla entre Charles Foster Kane y Ebenezer Scrooge, pero despojado de su humanidad y complejidad, quedándose solo con su lado más patético. Para colmo, tanto Paul Dano como Daniel Day-Lewis sobreactúan, lo que rompe cualquier atisbo de empatía. Paul Thomas Anderson los usa como personajes tesis (Religión vs. Capitalismo), pero se olvida de darles vida. El apartado técnico tampoco se salva. La música es una auténtica abominación que no encaja en absoluto con el ambiente. Es el equivalente a meterle música tecno a The Searchers o Lawrence of Arabia. La fotografía es buena, pero nada del otro mundo. Ese mismo año, No Country for Old Men o The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford presentaron trabajos infinitamente superiores. Además, se notan situaciones muy forzadas donde el director intenta pasarse de listo, como la pretenciosa ausencia de diálogos en ciertas escenas. La historia es minúscula, el conflicto apenas memorable y el guion parece un borrador mal hecho. Esto queda al desnudo en su patético final: un duelo intelectualoide que ni siquiera llega a serlo, donde el personaje de Dano no tiene réplica y solo lloriquea para que Plainview suelte un discurso nihilista digno de Reddit. Lo que queda, al final, es un monumento a la mediocridad.

I watched this movie last year so my memory might be slightly foggy but I did not like There Will Be Blood and here's why. Theoretically, the movie is my shit, about a man's obsession slowly twisting him into something unrecognizable from the start of the movie. Wow, that's very interesting! Is it though? They somehow find a way to make this interesting, character journey into a 2hr and a half film that felt like 4 hrs. Now, perhaps its me not connecting to the western genre overall, but this movie really fucked me up. I couldn't connect with any of the characters due to the pacing, if there's a study on how not to do pacing it'll be this movie. Now, Mr. Plainview himself is a man that drills oil, and eventually starts a drilling business in a small town. There we meet Paul Dano's Eli, who's the antagonist of the movie. And Mr. Plainview is there for a few years and his business really got kicking but his son is now deaf due to an accident in one of the drills, its very common and that scene was great I'll give them that. But the conflict between Plainview and Eli just wasn't all that right to me, I know Eli is supposed to be this weird church man that always like swing the religion across Plainview's face, all of that I get. But the "legendary" milkshake scene is just weird, I don't understand it at all, do they even have milk shakes back then? I drink up all your milk shake? Wtf is that supposed to mean? Si algo me ha enseñado el arte es que no hay mejor forma de explorar la condición humana que con los matices, y por esto es que no puedo ser fan de esta película. Verán, esta película nos plantea a sus dos personajes principales como “dos caras de una misma moneda” y el final (que no me gustó) como Daniel destruyendo a su propio reflejo, cuando, según lo que muestra, no es el caso, haciendo que el punto de la película se sienta empujado por el director. ¿Por qué digo esto? Verán, La Biblia y la teología están redactadas de tal forma que cualquier duda ellos buscan una forma de procesarla, tipo: si algo sale mal, es una prueba; si dudas, te faltó fe; si te atacan, es el enemigo, etc., etc. Eli no tenía las herramientas emocionales ni intelectuales para cuestionar eso. Para él, actuar como un profeta y buscar sanar a la gente no era un fraude; ponerlo como la cara de una moneda de alguien mucho más intencionado y manipulador no es una comparación justa. En la película se nos menciona el tema del maltrato (jamás lo elaboraron, solo lo mencionaron) hacia Mary, la hermana de Eli, por parte de su padre cuando ella no quiere rezar, por lo cual uno asume que lo mismo le pasaba a Eli, lo cual incluso lo convierte en una víctima, diría yo; una víctima que se convierte en victimario, pero una víctima al final del día. ¿Entienden mi punto? Compararlo con un misántropo multimillonario y sin escrúpulos como Daniel y pretender que pensemos que es una pelea de iguales no funciona. Al querer forzar la tesis, no hay nada de neutralidad, ni una exploración más a fondo de la fe, no hay nada de matices aquí, y por ende tampoco esperanza, ni una solución, ni personas decentes, haciéndola, para mí, muuuuy pesada y aburrida. Y no estoy pidiendo que la película defienda la religión; si quería el director enfrentar a Daniel y Eli como dos fuerzas opuestas, habría sido mucho más interesante mostrar con mayor profundidad qué significa la fe para Eli y para la comunidad, en lugar de utilizar principalmente la religión como un conflicto. Y sobre H.W., desde el inicio nos mostraron que lo veía como una extensión de él mismo, por eso hasta le daba alcohol, bien hasta ahí, por eso entiendo que se sienta traicionado, ¿pero que le diga que nunca lo quiso? 🤦‍♂️ ¿ven mi problema? Esta película siempre busca que los personajes se vuelvan más oscuros, pero de una forma que parece que pasa porque así lo quiere el director y no porque sean contradicciones humanas. Por eso odié tanto el final, no solo porque la pelea me parezca mal coreografiada, ni porque me pareció ridícula en comparación de la seriedad del resto de la película, sino también porque dejó varias cosas inconclusas y un mensaje muy limitado. No la volvería a ver, me aburrí.

Una costante nei racconti di cinema di Paul Thomas Anderson è senza dubbio quella di applicare l’istantanea di un determinato tempo cronologico a ciò che fa vedere allo spettatore. L’America di un segmento storico preciso che rispecchia la sua storia in ogni sua forma, incarnandone i luoghi, i costumi, le abitudini e l’aspetto sociale che comprende il periodo. L’affresco culturale nel film del 2007 “Il petroliere” rappresenta l’immagine della caccia all’oro nero di fine Ottocento, che ha come protagonista indiscusso Daniel Plainview, interpretato dal tre volte premio Oscar Daniel Day-Lewis. Tra l’altro, questa performance lo porterà proprio alla vittoria della prestigiosa statuetta. Daniel Plainview e la fame di potere La narrazione di un cacciatore di petrolio spregiudicato, che erge un’impresa a conduzione familiare, composta soltanto da lui e il suo bambino come socio. In questa pellicola alcune figure cercano di spiccare con lineamenti differenti, ma tutti hanno un solo unico obiettivo velato nella testa: arricchirsi. Le oltre due ore e mezza del film spiegheranno che i mezzi per arrivare al traguardo, per alcuni, contano fino a un certo punto, ma spesso bisogna fare i conti con chi i conti li ha saputi fare e mettere in pratica, oppure ha saputo muoversi in anticipo e con maggiore astuzia. Così Daniel è disposto a tutto pur di trivellare terreni per ottenere petrolio: anche disfarsi di un figlio o rinfacciargli l’amara verità delle sue sfasate origini, e scoprire una messa in scena utile per il fine. Allo stesso modo, c’è chi usa la parola di Dio per i suoi scopi, per poi rinnegarla se necessario al momento opportuno, al limite fingersi un parente di qualcuno più vicino alla ricchezza per trarne beneficio. Ma il tempo finisce sempre per rivelare il trucco, svelando e premiando solo chi ha saputo giocare bene le sue carte e prendersi tutto. “Voglio guadagnare così tanto da stare lontano da tutti.” Isolamento, violenza e spirito del West Daniel farà terra bruciata intorno a lui, cercando di non farsi fregare da chi vorrebbe la sua torta senza il sudore della fronte, oppure da chi vorrebbe mangiarsi anche solo una fetta. Questa avida guerra personale contro chiunque tende ad isolare l’individuo, spronandolo a togliere di mezzo chi prova a fregarlo o mettersi di traverso, senza fare prigionieri. Perché in queste ultime battute western lo spirito del selvaggio West non sbiadisce alla nuova fame di ricchezza economica: tende a divampare nell’uomo disposto a scannarsi per i propri affari e tutto ciò che ha in tasca, senza dividerlo con nessuno. “Io guardo le persone e non ci trovo niente di attraente. Io vedo il peggio delle persone.” Tecnica e nichilismo La storia scorre attraverso tecnicismi da pellicola impeccabili, dall’ottima fotografia ad aspetti narrativi che immergono lo spettatore nel contesto, sbattuto in faccia già soltanto grazie alle espressioni del protagonista, che per larghi tratti iniziali non ha bisogno neanche di parlare. Passando per alcuni monologhi di cortesia davanti alla comunità, fino a discorsi serrati e psichedelici che buttano fuori il proprio essere, immagazzinato e nascosto insieme allo spietato egoismo che si cela dietro un classico volto di uomo d’affari. Il successo del nichilismo sta tutto nella cinicità famelica del protagonista, che smonta la filosofia di ogni suo antagonista, svestendolo fino all’ultima goccia di sangue e confermando il capitalismo come sola e unica vera dottrina del tempo.

Je ne pensais pas être capable de haïr le capitalisme encore plus. Pis là je me suis rappelé que le capitalisme est un jeu d'hommes orgueilleux et égocentriques. Pis, avant que je tombe dans l'analyse, wow. Daniel Day-Lewis a donné une des meilleures performances que j'ai jamais vues par un homme dans l'histoire hollywoodienne. On sentait une rage intense, une peur profonde, une grande confusion et une immense violence canalisée. C'est le genre de jeu d'acteur que les gens essayent d'associer à Robert de Niro. Je crois aussi que la limite de l'expression qu'il présente n'est pas due à son jeu d'acteur, mais au personnage. C'est un homme de violence et, en ce sens, Day-Lewis incarne le personnage avec une immense exactitude. Venant d'un historien, j'aime beaucoup l'écriture de ce film. On comprend que c'est une critique du capitalisme et du Rêve. Daniel incarne le "self-made man". L'homme qui s'est enivré d'une idée de grandeur en ignorant la petitesse de ses valeurs. Le choix de la période de prospection et du développement des pipelines dans le sud californien fin XIXe, début XXe, est incroyablement pertinente. C'est la période la plus importante dans la formation de l'imaginaire culturel américain. Certes, il s'ancre dans une tradition d'américanité digne de l'Almanach du Petit Richard, mais il s'incruste bien dans le fantasmagorique univers du début d'Hollywood. On est en train de créer les archétypes. On voit à l'écran les balbutiements du Cow-Boy et de l'Indien, la création du cinéma de foi, le lancement du cinéma historique et militaire. Bref, on est à la genèse de l'image. Et le film propose de briser cette image contemporaine. Elle présente un homme rapaillé qui s'est perdu dans un rêve d'or noir. Une figure qui est en discorde profonde avec le capitalisme de gentlemen rockerfelleriste, et le pionnier du Manifest Destiny. C'est une attaque directe à la fondation même de ce sur quoi se repose le rêve américain actuel. "I am the Third Revelation" Daniel hurle de manière injurieuse à Eli, un pasteur, alors qu'il lui garnotte des boules de bowling et lui fissure le crâne avec une quille. L'homme qui est si riche qu'il peut acheter la croyance. Un écho sanglant de Nietzsche sous la forme bien imagée que Dieu est mort dans le sang noir d'un nouveau système de croyance prépondérant à la finalité divine. On voit dieu comme un service, une utilité pour la conscience. La personne qui considère que le profit est l'outil de l'Église se fait laisser giser pour mort sur une allée de quille bien cirée. La morale chrétienne a formé une grande partie des normes criminelles du XXe siècle. C'est une réalité sociale, mais aussi individuelle. Lorsque l'on comprend le personnage troublé de Daniel Plainview, on comprend une violence capitale subséquente à la morale aveugle. Musique 4/5 Pas beaucoup de chansons origniales, mais des classiques quand même Setting 5/5 historiquement accurate Jeu d'acteur 5/5 exactement le personnage écrit

There Will Be Blood was a very interesting movie that, at first, I thought I was going to dislike. The beginning started off quite slow and was beginning to lose my attention, but the sudden graphic deaths throughout the film surprised me and immediately pulled me back in. I almost rated it three stars, but after seeing the ending, I finally understood what Eli Sunday and Daniel Plainview represented. The writing of their relationship, and the eventual reversal of their roles, was very well done. Earlier in the film, Eli saves and baptizes Daniel with water, calling it the “blood of Christ.” By the end, Daniel is surrounded by his own “blood of Christ” in the form of alcohol, which Eli also gives in to. The conclusion, with Daniel killing Eli after Eli had once “saved” him, was an ending I did not expect and made me appreciate the film much more.

I genuinely thought Eli was just gonna have a one sided beef with Daniel, turns out they’re both just as greedy for power and money, literally two sides of the same coin. And I guess capitalism won, Daniel ended up getting what he wanted but at what cost… he wasn’t very happy To be honest I had low expectations, not because of the production, performance or anything related to the film, but because of me. I thought I wouldn’t like it, but it was awesome, I truly enjoyed watching it. I’m always impressed by Daniel Day-Lewis, every time I watch a new movie of his, he’s always so different and unrecognizable, yes i’m aware he’s a three time Oscar winner for best actor and he’s just doing his job, but damn was he really good at it.. Paul Dano, well I don’t have much to say but I know that he’s always been a remarkable actor. The production for the film was incredible as well, the visuals are fantastic, although I have to say the score is genuinely the best part of the movie, it sounded eerie and almost scary, I particularly loved it. Anyway this is my second PTA movie, am I too quick to judge if I say he’s a brilliant writer and director? It’s debatable but i’m sure I know a lot of people would agree

قمة في الإبداع، وتدخلك وسط العالم الرأسمالي وحشي رائع. و لكن الشيء الذي لم يتوفق فيه الفيلم هو اختيار الممثل بول دانو الغير غير مناسب أبدًا، نظرًا لعدم قدرته على تجسيد تعابير وجه شخصيته، فعندما نتمعن في تعابير وجهه لا نعرف هل الشخصية فرحانة أو غاضبة، بل يحافظ على أسلوب وجه واحد لفترة طويلة من الزمن، عكس تمثيل دانييل داي لويس الذي تغلغل في شخصيته وعاش داخلها. اجد ايضا ان بعض الاختيارات الموسيقية كانت out of place و لا تناسب اللقطات التي وضعت فيها وللاسف هناك ضعف واضح في جودة كتابة الشخصيات الثانوية، فمن دون شخصية بول سانداي نجد أن كل شخصيات الفيلم موجودة فقط لإحياء وإكمال شخصية دانييل الجشعة لنا. و الآن نمر الى الوجبة الرئيسية وهو تحليلي الشخصي لشخصية دانييل : دانييل رجل براغماتي، جشع، ومولع بالسلطة ، يتعامل مع الناس وفقًا لما يمكنهم أن يقدموا له، ويستطيع تغيير أسلوبه حسب مصلحته، دون أن يسمح للمبادئ الأخلاقية و الدينية بأن تقف في طريق أهدافه. سر تعامله السيئ مع ولده، بعد أن أصبح أصم، هو أنه بدأ يراه كعبء أكثر من كونه شخصًا يمكن أن يساعده و ذلك عبر استغلال وجهه البريء للتفاوض، وهذا يتناسب مع شخصيته النرجسية المحبة للمال والسلطة التي بُنيت بشكل جيد طوال الفيلم. والأهم أن قسوته تجاه ولده لا تبدو نابعة من كراهية شخصية له، بقدر ما تبدو نابعة من الطريقة التي ينظر بها دانييل إلى الناس: قيمتهم مرتبطة بمدى فائدتهم له. ويظهر هذا بوضوح في حواره مع أخيه المزيف ، فطوال مدة الحوار يحاول إشعاره بالاستنقاص، وكأنه يقول له: "أنا المسيطر هنا، وأنت مجرد حشرة". لكنه يستعمل الأسلوب المعاكس عندما يحاور شخصًا يحتاج إليه من أجل مصلحته. أما انفجار شخصيته الحقيقي فيظهر في تخليه عن ولده، ثم في الطريقة التي يتعامل بها مع كل شخص يحاول الاقتراب من ثروته أو أخذ جزء منها. بالنسبة إلى دانييل، من يحاول الوقوف في طريقه يا إما ينتهي به الأمر مقتولًا أو في طريق مجهول على متن قطار. فدانييل لا يريد فقط أن يمتلك، بل يريد أن يكون هو صاحب اليد العليا في كل شيء ، ويرى نجاح الآخرين كأنه استنقاص من نجاحه هو. لذلك يصبح نجاح الإنسان الآخر بالنسبة إليه تهديدًا شخصيًا، وكأن العالم عبارة عن مسابقة لا يستطيع فيها أن يشعر بالرضا إلا إذا كان هو الفائز و المسيطر على كل شيء. و اخيرا النهاية كانت مخيبة للآمال ، من ناحية كتابة الأحداث، كأنها لعبة قط وفأر ، عندما يفر الفأر أخيرًا من القط، يقرر الفأر العودة مرة أخرى إلى القط في النهاية.
