Sporadic display of Spielberg-era Hollywood know-how in terms of physical production, lighting, music. Feels more directly connected to 80s kids adventure films (The Goonies, Labyrinth) than it does to anything that followed it. There are seeds here that I like. Still - a film can weather a flat-footed director or a tentative lead actor, but both together are pretty fatal. Radcliffe seems actively intimidated by the camera early on, and where Grint or Watson often over-emphasize their lines and facial expressions, he drops them with a slightly baffled, apologetic air. There's a kind of negative space where a character should be. Director Chris Columbus makes no allowances for the roughness of his lead trio - instead, he insists on a regime of unforgiving close-ups that magnify their limitations as performers, particularly when they're required to react with wonder, anger, or amusement. This vacuum at the heart of the project can't be compensated for by all the character-acting going on around the edges, although Hurt, Harris and Rickman all have indelible moments. Quidditch is a badly designed sport.

Harry Potter e la pietra filosofale è uno di quei film che sembrano molto più belli perché sono circondati da un’enorme fama, non perché lo siano davvero. Dietro l’estetica magica e l’atmosfera apparentemente incantata, ho trovato una storia sorprendentemente semplice, prevedibile e priva di quella profondità che ci si aspetterebbe da un’opera considerata così importante. Il problema principale è la sceneggiatura: tutto sembra costruito per introdurre un mondo fantastico, ma quasi nulla viene realmente approfondito. I personaggi vengono presentati in modo superficiale, le relazioni si sviluppano velocemente e molte situazioni sembrano accadere semplicemente perché la trama ne ha bisogno. Anche Harry, che dovrebbe essere il centro emotivo della storia, risulta spesso più passivo che realmente protagonista degli eventi. Il ritmo poi è un altro punto debole. Il film alterna momenti estremamente lenti ad altri in cui gli avvenimenti vengono risolti troppo facilmente, dando la sensazione che manchi un vero senso di tensione. Anche la tanto celebrata atmosfera magica, per quanto visivamente piacevole, non riesce a compensare una storia che personalmente ho trovato poco coinvolgente. Capisco perfettamente perché possa essere amato da chi è cresciuto con questo universo, ma togliendo la nostalgia e il peso culturale del franchise, rimane un film abbastanza infantile e prevedibile. Più che trasportarmi in un mondo fantastico, mi ha lasciato con la sensazione di assistere a una lunga introduzione a una storia che, forse, comincia davvero solo dopo. In definitiva, un film sopravvalutato: affascinante nell’idea, ma molto meno nella realizzazione. Mi aspettavo magia, meraviglia e una storia memorabile; ho trovato soprattutto un’avventura semplice, lenta e decisamente meno speciale di quanto la sua reputazione lasciasse intendere.

The ambiance carries this film. The swirling score accompanying the breathtaking panoramic views of old English castles and buildings well-worn by eccentric inhabitants in old garb creates a pristine portrait of a civilization unbeknownst to us; one that exists in its own little space in the world. It’s fitting that Diagon Alley looks  like it was built from the alleyways of London, a Freeform shape made of neglected cracks and corners forgotten by the world, because in a way that’s the essence of Harry himself. There’s so much beyond what our eyes can see. In the film, Harry is the ultimate example of a blank slate protagonist. A little boy who was never allowed the answers of his past, never allowed to bring his suppressed emotions to light, unearthing his empathy and bravery with every new discovery through this bombastic and unrelenting 2 1/2 hours. “She knows more about you than you.” “Who doesn’t” Could you image an 11 year old boy saying that? Harry is such an isolated, melancholy figure discovering the person he always could have been. That he, and everything, is more than meets the eye. A snobbish attitude can mask insecurity. Fame and prestige do not bring happiness. Good and evil aren’t as blunt as they appear. The nostalgia hits so hard that I often forget how clunky the film can feel. Scenes more from one to the next almost haphazardly. Bringing the exposition heavy book to the screen was never going to be easy, and what we have here is rather commendable. Each scene does serve a purpose, but I just wish our characters had more to say and do throughout. My favorite scenes are ones of somber contemplation. I’d by lying if I said the emotions didn’t hit, but the barebones mystery and whirlwind pacing can be difficult to latch onto.

Minha opinião sobre: Harry Potter e a Pedra Filosofal — Re-assistido em 2026 Fazia bastante tempo que eu não assistia a um filme de Harry Potter , então paramos recentemente para rever o primeiro filme da franquia. Minha esposa está bastante empolgada para assistir à nova série da HBO, que será lançada neste Natal, então entramos no clima e decidimos revisitar os filmes antigos. Harry Potter e a Pedra Filosofal continua sendo um ótimo filme de aventura infantil. É muito satisfatório rever o elenco desse primeiro filme. Cada criança parece ter sido escolhida a dedo para interpretar seus respectivos personagens, e isso logo se torna uma das grandes magias da obra. É impossível não sentir um certo carinho ao ver esses atores tão jovens dando vida a personagens que se tornariam tão marcantes nos anos seguintes. O roteiro é um pouco simples e as reviravoltas são relativamente fáceis de descobrir. Mas a magia desse filme não está necessariamente na complexidade de sua história, e sim na maneira como ele apresenta ao público o gigantesco universo bruxo criado por J.K. Rowling. E nisso o filme não falha. Tudo foi pensado de maneira muito cuidadosa para que nós, como espectadores, nos apaixonássemos por Hogwarts desde o primeiro momento em que conhecemos a escola. O mundo bruxo é um lugar extremamente curioso, cheio de regras próprias, criaturas, objetos mágicos e possibilidades que despertam a imaginação. É fantástico observar a criatividade por trás dessa obra, conectando raças, monstros, feitiços, salas, professores e alunos em perfeita sintonia com a grande escola de magia de Hogwarts. O filme consegue ser tão encantador que, em determinado momento, você se pega pensando: "Quando será que vou receber minha carta para estudar em Hogwarts?" Continua sendo um ótimo filme, mesmo com efeitos visuais que hoje podem parecer mais datados. Eles ainda cumprem muito bem sua função de construir aquele mundo e proporcionar a sensação de aventura que a história precisa. Um destaque especial para o torneio de Quadribol, que nos apresenta um dos esportes fictícios mais legais já criados para o cinema. É muito divertido acompanhar toda a dinâmica das partidas e perceber como aquele universo consegue transformar até mesmo um esporte em parte importante de sua identidade. Os atores mirins também entregam demais. A sintonia entre eles e o carisma de cada personagem fazem do filme um verdadeiro show de fofura — algo que combina perfeitamente com essa primeira aventura. Estou bastante empolgado para continuar revendo os filmes dessa franquia. Acho que em breve vou assistir novamente ao segundo... Ou será que devo esperar a série da HBO?

Honestly, it’s just a checklist of clichés. You know the type: the absent piece-of-shit father who abandoned his daughter for a woman he secretly loved, or a career he tried to build, or a job he needed for money, or an adventure he wanted — anything but her. Then the whole film is him trying to make amends. His life is a wreck, so we’re supposed to see him as helpless: booze, pills, bar fights, dead-end jobs, unpaid rent, screaming matches, and self-pity. Here, the only difference is that he left her for a man (he’s gay), and instead of booze, pills, and bar fights, his rock bottom is overeating and obesity. If they’d cast a Black actor, the cliché bingo card would be full. Whatever. Even The Wrestler by the same director is the same old cliché — he basically just repeated himself.

The ugliness of human vices, portrayed in such a convoluted mess of the various critiques of religion and the healthcare system, a miserable plot, and in my opinion, the most over-the-top and worst portrayal of teenage angst of a rebellious teenager (which is later copped out as a personification of evil.) This movie is very good at making one uncomfortable (in a good way), and I see the movie’s highs as it reflects upon the prevalence on the good conscience of humans as it relates to combatting one’s guilt or sin. This is especially true with Charlie’s behaviour towards Ellie. And Thomas’ character. As ugly as one’s wrongs may have been, is there enough good in one’s future actions to repay such moral debts? Apart from my praise on that aspect, I really think that the movie just fails to really be great on expanding the various points of discussion to which it outlines. Religion, healthcare, eating disorders are some of the main talking points, but if it serves to just be a backdrop to the aforementioned conscience of human beings, then it served very well. But I honestly felt like these themes are just very superficial and were only used for shock-value or to make the story more sad. The movie is disgusting, but its good and meets the mark for what its trying to go for.

critique, The Whale (2022, Darren Aronofsky) The Whale aura toujours une place particulière pour moi. C’est le premier film que j’ai vu avec la personne avec qui je suis encore aujourd’hui. À l’époque, je ne savais absolument pas ce que j’allais regarder. Je ne connaissais quasiment rien du film, je ne savais pas à quoi m’attendre, et pourtant j’avais adoré. Forcément, le revoir aujourd’hui est assez particulier. Parce que même si j’ai toujours beaucoup d’affection pour ce film, je l’ai trouvé beaucoup moins intéressant et surtout beaucoup moins touchant que lors de mon premier visionnage. Pourtant, son sujet continue énormément de me toucher. Je n’ai jamais vécu une situation aussi extrême que celle de Charlie, mais je comprends certaines choses dans ce qu’il traverse, notamment cette solitude, cette culpabilité et cette impression d’être complètement enfermé dans sa propre vie. Mais avec le recul, j’ai aussi beaucoup plus vu les défauts du film. J’ai notamment trouvé l’écriture beaucoup trop appuyée par moments. Certains dialogues donnent parfois l’impression que les personnages doivent absolument expliquer ce qu’ils ressentent, alors que les situations auraient parfois été beaucoup plus fortes si le film avait simplement laissé les émotions parler d’elles-mêmes. J’ai aussi eu du mal avec certains personnages. Je les trouve intéressants sur le papier, mais parfois trop écrits comme des moyens de faire avancer le drame. Certaines réactions m’ont paru excessives, et ça m’a empêché de croire complètement à certaines scènes. Et puis il y a le côté très mélodramatique du film. Lors de mon premier visionnage, ça m’avait énormément touché. Aujourd’hui, j’ai davantage ressenti la volonté du film de me faire pleurer. Et forcément, ça fonctionne beaucoup moins sur moi. En revanche, Brendan Fraser reste vraiment excellent. Sa performance est impressionnante, et il arrive à rendre Charlie profondément humain malgré tous ses défauts et toutes ses contradictions. J’aime aussi beaucoup le huis clos. Le fait de rester quasiment tout le temps dans cet appartement renforce cette impression d’enfermement. Charlie est prisonnier de son corps, mais aussi de ses choix, de son passé et de la vie qu’il a construite autour de lui. C’est probablement ce qui me touche encore le plus dans le film. Mais aujourd’hui, je ne peux plus dire que j’ai adoré The Whale. Je garde énormément d’affection pour lui, forcément, parce qu’il est lié à un souvenir qui compte énormément pour moi. Mais si je mets complètement ce souvenir de côté, je trouve simplement que c’est un film bien moins subtil et moins bouleversant que dans mes souvenirs. Je suis content de l’avoir revu. Même si, finalement, je crois que je préfère le souvenir que j’en avais.

Un homme souffrant d’obésité morbide, dont le corps semble lui rappeler à chaque instant que la prochaine seconde pourrait être la dernière. Pourtant, la nourriture, que son propre corps semble considérer comme un salut, n’est pas vraiment présentée comme une addiction. Elle apparaît davantage comme une forme de pénitence, intimement liée à sa relation précédente. Quels que soient les excès, ceux-ci finissent par avoir des conséquences, et le film n’hésite pas à les montrer. Mais au-delà de l’aspect physique, ce qui est particulièrement difficile à voir, c’est une personne qui semble progressivement s’autodétruire. Le film est traversé par des moments profondément difficiles, marqués par la souffrance, la culpabilité et un véritable dégoût de soi.

A Baleia foi um filme que me deixou desconfortável de uma maneira que eu acho que era exatamente a intenção. O Charlie é um homem que está vivendo os últimos momentos da própria vida e sabe disso. Ele está extremamente doente, isolado e preso dentro de uma rotina que parece ter diminuído até quase desaparecer. Mas o filme não começa tratando Charlie como uma pessoa monstruosa ou como alguém que merece aquilo. Ele mostra um homem cheio de arrependimentos. A relação dele com a filha Ellie é provavelmente a parte mais dolorosa. Ela é cruel com ele. Mas a crueldade dela não aparece simplesmente porque ela é uma adolescente "má". Existe uma história inteira de abandono, raiva e ressentimento por trás. Charlie sabe que falhou. E ele não tenta convencer Ellie de que não falhou. Ele simplesmente quer uma última oportunidade de fazer alguma coisa certa. A atuação do Brendan Fraser é realmente impressionante porque grande parte da interpretação está no rosto e na voz. Existe uma tristeza muito profunda nele. E a câmera também ajuda muito. O formato quase fechado faz o espectador sentir aquela sensação de confinamento. Tudo parece apertado. O apartamento. O corpo. A vida. As possibilidades. E talvez seja justamente isso que torne o filme tão difícil. Charlie não está tentando salvar a própria vida. Ele está tentando encontrar algum significado antes que ela termine. E quando o filme chega ao final, eu não sinto exatamente alívio. Sinto tristeza. Mas também sinto uma espécie de compaixão por alguém que passou tanto tempo acreditando que não merecia ser perdoado. É um filme sobre culpa, mas também sobre a necessidade humana de acreditar que ainda podemos ser vistos como pessoas depois de cometer erros. E acho que essa é a parte que mais fica comigo depois que os créditos sobem.

Film davvero fantastico che tocca argomenti complessi come disturbi alimentari, solitudine e l’abbandono di sé stessi dalla prospettiva di un  protagonista affetto da un problema come l’obesità di cui (personalmente) non ho visto molto parlare nel cinema; tutto ciò in meno di due ore e senza essere banale. Charlie (il protagonista) data la sua salute è confinato in casa e nel corso della sua ultima settimana di vita vediamo proprio come lui cerchi di riconnettersi con tutto quello che aveva abbandonato: come ad esempio sua figlia elly. Il personaggio secondo me più sottovalutato del film è il missionario (di cui non ricordo il nome), il suo personaggio secondo me sta a rappresentare l’ostinazione di Charlie e anche il suo ottimismo fastidioso quasi arrogante (come lo definisce Mary la ex moglie di Charlie). Il missionario dalla prima scena del film si è ostinato ad aiutare Charlie a qualunque costo ed è la stessa cosa che fa il protagonista nei suoi ultimi giorni con sua figlia, l’unica differenza è il fatto che il missionario lo fa cercando di dimenticare la sua vecchia vita mentre Charlie lo fa per cercare di recuperare la sua di vita passata e vediamo come alla fine del film la situazione si ribalta, dato che il missionario tornerà dai genitori e Charlie cercherà nei suoi ultimi respiri di abbandonare quella vita di tristezza e tornare nei suoi ricordi felici, come vediamo che ci riuscirà. Parlando del finale: secondo me è stato molto intelligente anche perché come lo fai finire un film del genere? Uno stacco a nero sarebbe stato fin troppo banale e quindi penso che questo finale surrealista sia stata la scelta migliore anche se penso che lui che ascende al cielo uccida un po la tensione.

Who's afraid of a protagonist who is abjectly fat and also morally deplorable? Seemingly many. The discourse is long-winding and diverse yet I think the utter disgust of The Whale, an adapted play of ugly emotional outpouring, the revival of a viscous past, and certainly nothing beautiful to look at visually, irks many in their yearning for a harmony in a story that rewards beauty and deplores the ugly. Charlie is a psychologically beguiling character who embodies a descend into gluttony and sloth, an active manifestation of a desire to withdraw following loss, which renders him a simultaneous victim and perpetrator of avoidance to those around him. His struggle with obesity is almost framed as a carnal punishment for his immediate act of gluttony, pursuing his forbidden sexuality and escaping with his lover; he is burdened with the consequences of his withdrawal, his wife brandishes him a deadbeat and his daughter wants nothing but his eternal damnation in grease-laced hellfire. The Whale is a manifestation of the deadly sins of the human condition to some degree, with Charlie representing a combination of sloth and gluttony (although I think to simply demarcate Charlie along his patterns of eating would be reductive, as I'll explain), while his daughter is wrathful, her deep-seated anger and intention for immediate action contrasting with Charlie's inertia. Charlie's obesity could've been replaced with another gluttonous issue, alcoholism, drugs and the same point could've been made, not to say that I disagree with the film's execution, in fact I laud them for tackling subject matter usually addressed humorously (haha, look upon the perils of this fat fuck and laugh!), for there's countless films about alcoholics. Charlie suffers from a binge eating disorder as a result of trauma, and as a result of his disposition, conflict-avoidant and seeking constant pleasure (the film is framed by Charlie masturbating, and there are constant scenes of his consumption of sugar, an infatuation with sweetness and ecstasy), he is unable to graduate from these harmful patterns, ultimately swallowing himself, and those around him up. Charlie is not only victimising on himself, wrapped in the twine of masochism, he performs these rites disgustingly just by existing, which I think explains the critical upset people have at this to some degree. His visual pain is horrible to witness, he is unable to be romanticised, for to be fat is to be abject, to be alienated from society's metanarrative over aesthetical beauty. The hegemonic power of beauty deserts our protagonist, leaving him unable to be sympathised with or related to, no pretty edits will be made of his suffering, only edits that lampoon his story as something hilarious and ironic. Such is the state of the modern consumer of the arts. Death can function as a wonderful writing device for the extraction, the confession of truth, in fact the confines of the setting slowly pluck the truth out of the characters. The news of Charlie's imminent death spread from Liz to Charlie, to Ellie and Thomas, and then eventually his ex-wife Mary; the epistemic revelation suddenly compels people to discover the truth before the horrid inevitable occurs, the story an eventual confession chamber for deep-seated reservations and emotions. Perhaps, the film is quite blatant in its expressions, lacking subtlety (there's an almost laughable lack of such in Ellie's dialogue, demarcating her intentions almost constantly, that she wants this or wants that). The film does not narrate with its environment or through non-verbal expressions so much as it does with loud, confessional-style dialogue and discussions of context surrounding the emotions we see splattered on the wooden floor. It has its benefits, yet at times I did feel that how the characters felt could've been handled more delicately, allowed to fester for much longer. The Whale prides itself on having nothing left unsaid, especially reflected in Charlie's motivations. Death performs a latent function as something that unites people, as Charlie notes almost humorously; all of his cherished ones unite, only at the advent of his demise, after years of stifled truths and assumptions. The ritual of death allows the ones that are left to unite for a cause, that of the lamentation and memorialisation of the deceased. The morbidity is the most beautiful aspect, and for that I cannot help but view The Whale with beauty in its morbidity and reflection of the grimy reality. The stone is overturned to reveal bile that has festered for what appears to be forever.

All the characters are coping with depression here in one way or another. Liz is enabling Charlie. Charlie with his emotional eating. Ellie in acting out, being cruel to feel cold and emotionless, Thomas struggling with God and essentially his own self, his morals. The Whale is desperation of individuals trapped inside their own emotional prisons. Every single person in that apartment is deeply flawed and at times actively difficult to like, yet the story makes their defense mechanisms feel entirely earned. Watching Charlie's gentle optimism clash against his slow self-destruction, or seeing Ellie's cruelty contextually understood as a shield for her abandonment. Hong Chau’s character represents the tragedy of codependency. Terrified of losing another person after her brother Alan's suicide, her caretaking morphs into enabling. She brings Charlie high-calorie food while simultaneously taking his blood pressure. Her love is undeniable, but her trauma makes her an accomplice to his destruction. Thomas attempts to frame Charlie's condition as a spiritual crisis rather than a human one. Running from his own personal failures, he uses evangelism as a distraction, attempting to "save" Charlie in order to validate his own shaky moral compass. Sadie Sink’s character handles depression through rage. Feeling abandoned by her father, she projects a cold, malicious exterior to ensure no one can hurt her again. Throughout the film, Charlie repeatedly listens to an essay analyzing Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick. The essay points out that Melville wrote about whales extensively just to distract the reader from his own sad story. Moby Dick is the motif to talk all about how we all distract ourselves from ourselves to not feel the pain. Charlie’s entire career as an online English teacher revolves around begging his students to "write something honest". He sees society constantly putting up "pasteboard masks” to hide ugly, uncomfortable feelings. The Moby-Dick essay represents the one piece of pure, unvarnished honesty Charlie holds onto. When he forces Ellie to read it to him in the climax, it becomes a moment of mutual liberation. By acknowledging the sadness and loneliness in the book, Ellie acknowledges her own, allowing Charlie to finally let go and float upward, stripped of the literal and metaphorical weight that anchored him. The final moment directly ties back to Ellie’s essay. She wrote that Melville’s book was about confronting sadness directly rather than hiding behind distractions. By confronting the truth of their relationship and reading the essay together, both Charlie and Ellie stop hiding. Charlie got what he wanted, doing one good thing about his life. He doesn’t die in despair but rather dies liberated and so he vanishes into the white.

Me pareció un gran inicio para la trilogía. Lo que más me gustó fue cómo desarrolla el origen de Batman y muestra la evolución de Bruce Wayne hasta convertirse en el héroe que todos conocemos. La historia está muy bien construida y logra que entiendas perfectamente las motivaciones del personaje. Christian Bale hace un buen trabajo como Batman, aunque personalmente creo que ha tenido actuaciones mejores en otras películas. También me gustó mucho la participación de Cillian Murphy, quien aporta bastante a la historia. Mi escena favorita fue la batalla final, donde Batman se enfrenta al mal para salvar Gotham. Aunque no es mi favorita de la trilogía, sí me dejó con expectativas muy altas para la siguiente entrega y es una película que volvería a ver después de un tiempo. Algo que hace especial a esta película es la forma en que Christopher Nolan utilizó cámaras IMAX para muchas de las escenas más importantes. Esto permitió mostrar Gotham, las persecuciones y las secuencias de acción con una escala impresionante que todavía hoy se siente espectacular. Además, Nolan intentó evitar el uso excesivo de CGI, prefiriendo efectos prácticos siempre que fuera posible. Gracias a esto, muchas escenas conservan una sensación de realismo que las hace envejecer mejor que otras películas de superhéroes de la misma época. Esa combinación entre IMAX, efectos prácticos y una dirección muy cuidada es una de las razones por las que la trilogía sigue siendo tan recordada.

Eight years after the last live-action Batman movie I watched, I finally came back to Batman Begins , and it felt like I was being treated like this stuff actually mattered. It felt like the character had grown up with me. The first half almost mirrors growing up, losing something dear to you, and learning to move forward through struggle. The second half gave me almost everything I wanted from a Batman movie since I was young: Batman existing in the real world, while still feeling larger than life. It does feel somewhat episodic, with the first half being incredibly grounded and the second becoming more detached and fantastical, but I can come back to this movie time and time again for many years to come.

Chris Nolan gets a lot of flak for his sound mixing and mastering. Generally, I think that criticism is overstated, but it is really bad here; this goes from whispered dialogue to sounding like you’re sitting in the front row at the Indy 500, then back to whispered dialogue at break-neck speeds. I got tired of quickly turning it up and quickly turning it back down before I decided this movie isn’t good enough to warrant such effort. I will say, though, that deliberately living a quasi-nomadic/homeless lifestyle in an under-developed country for no reason is a very billionaire thing to do. It feels like the first hour of this was life-changing for Jack Dorsey. It takes a lot for me to dislike a Batman movie. Most—this included—can range from watchable to pretty cool. I don’t dislike this one, but it certainly is nothing special. I’d take either Schumacher film over this in a heartbeat.

I absolutely loved Batman Begins, and for me, it’s the best movie in the trilogy. I know that for most people it’s The Dark Knight, and I completely understand why. But for me, Batman Begins is Nolan’s best Batman movie. Honestly, I even prefer it to The Dark Knight. The main reason is pretty simple: The Dark Knight is an incredible crime thriller with Batman and the Joker at the center of it, while Batman Begins is, above all, a movie about Batman. And I think that makes all the difference. What I love most about Begins is that it actually takes the time to show Bruce Wayne becoming Batman. He doesn’t just put on the suit and suddenly become a hero. Bruce first has to figure out what he wants Batman to represent, and why he even needs to become Batman in the first place. That’s also why I love the way the movie handles the bat itself. Bruce doesn’t choose the symbol just because it looks cool. He takes something that terrified him as a child and turns that fear into something he can control. He becomes the thing he was once afraid of. Because Batman is supposed to be frightening. He shouldn’t just be a superhero who came and beats up bad guys like TDKR . He has to be a presence, almost a legend. Something criminals think they see in the darkness. And Batman Begins understands that better than the other movies in the trilogy. Some of Batman’s first appearances are still some of my favorite moments in the movie. Nolan barely shows him at first. You see pieces of him, you hear him, you feel his presence before you really see him. He’s almost filmed like a creature hiding in the shadows. And that connects perfectly with Gotham. Gotham city feels dirty, corrupt, dangerous and almost suffocating. What I really like is that Nolan doesn’t make it feel like a giant comic-book set. He makes it feel like a real city, while still giving it that dark, almost gothic atmosphere that fits Batman perfectly. I also think Gotham reflects Bruce’s state of mind. The more he discovers about the city, the more he understands what he has to fight. And as Bruce gets closer to becoming Batman, the entire movie/photography seems to get darker with him. That’s also where I think the movie’s focus on Bruce really pays off. Ra’s al Ghul and scarecrow are important, but they never completely takes over the story. The movie is still about Bruce Wayne. It’s about his fear, his anger, his guilt, and ultimately his choice to turn all of that into something meaningful. Because Batman isn’t just the costume or the gadgets. It’s that permanent contradiction at the heart of the character: Bruce uses fear and violence to fight crime, while constantly refusing to become a murderer himself. And I think Batman Begins understands that contradiction better than the other movies. That’s ultimately why I prefer Batman Begins. The Dark Knight might be the more impressive movie overall, but Batman Begins feels more like a movie that actually understands why Batman is Batman. And for me, that matters more. Also the only real flaw I have with the movie is the fight choreography. Some of the action scenes are difficult to follow because of the way they’re shot and edited, and unfortunately, I think this becomes even more noticeable when you watch the entire trilogy specially TDKR. Looking at all three movies together, you start to realize that Nolan simply isn’t very good at choreographing hand-to-hand combat. The ideas behind the fights are often good, but the execution can feel messy and lacking in visual clarity.

Being totally honest, I don’t care much for Nolan’s Batman trilogy as a whole. I adore The Dark Knight , but it feels like an outlier. Batman Begins is decent, but it’s unsure of itself and I’ve never found its story or characters very engaging. And then there’s this, in my mind Nolan’s one and only truly bad movie. I skipped this one when I last rewatched these, back in 2023; it’s one I’ve never really been able to sit all the way through, nor revisit, but, after watching the new animated Knightfall film and binge-reading the comic run, now felt like the time for reassessment. Nothing’s changed. Nolan’s propulsive filmmaking keeps it far more engaging than it deserves to be, I’ll admit, and there are lots of things I do genuinely like in here — but the vast majority of this just does not work. It doesn’t work because, fundamentally, the film is utterly uninterested in its own material. It isn’t overstuffed, yet every single narrative thread feels so flimsy and undercooked, and it’s all thrown together in a way that feels incredibly clunky. Like, for example, the audience obviously needs to care about Marion Cotillard’s character in order for a lot of this to work, but it’s almost like Nolan knows we won’t care and doesn’t care to give it the focus that it needed to change that. It’s kind of baffling. Nolan having The League of Shadows as an overarching threat in this trilogy is really quite lame, but made worse by the fact the writing around it is so weak. Writing aside, though, there isn’t even good action in this one. Hans Zimmer‘s score papers over some cracks, but I can’t think of a single action sequence I had fun with. Batman’s barely even in this. What’s even worse is the actual fight choreography, and if you have more than a cursory glance at any of the background extras during big brawls, you’ll be in hysterics . On the flip side, I like Anne Hathaway’s Catwoman. Some of her best work, and perhaps the best use of her talents. I love everything Michael Caine’s Alfred and Morgan Freeman’s Lucius do. I’m always happy to see Burn Gorman, even in a bit part. And I liked that scene when Batman says “so that’s what that feels like” (which was borrowed from the Kingdom Come comics). What I wish I could say I loved is the interpretation of Bane, because I think Tom Hardy is giving a pretty perfect performance. I even like his voice, as odd as it is; this is the only on-screen Bane that captures his intimidating intelligence and also retains his ‘otherness’. The mask is great too, and I like how Bane isn’t a lone wolf and retains the menacing patience from the Knightfall run. But… it just isn’t Bane is it? He’s a League of Shadows goon with a thing for Talia al Ghul and a mask that gives him painkillers. It’s such a shame, and not because it’s inaccurate — because it’s uninteresting. Beyond that, there are just so many plot holes and distractions. Whenever I try engaging with this one on more than an absolute base level it’s so difficult to enjoy. How did Batman get back into Gotham? Why did Bane fly out to the desert prison simply to give a little speech and fly straight back again? In what world would they send *checks notes* every single police officer in the city into the sewers in a tactical operation? How are all the policemen okay when they come out of the sewers? And Matthew Modine’s character and Talia have two of the least convincing deaths in the history of film, Talia’s now infamous. And, urgh, his real name is ‘Robin’. I have a huge amount of love for his work, so I don’t mean this as an insult, but Nolan has never been a perfectionist. Nowhere is that more obvious to me than in this movie.

I was expecting to go into this movie open minded with the fact that you either like this one or you don't like this one, I am right down the middle. This movie has many things going for it and it is well made, but the story is filled with so many stupid moments that hamper my enjoyment of the film. To get the good stuff out of the way, this movie is well made in every aspect you expect from a director like Nolan with the shots, the composition, the lighting, everything. Almost every actor gives it their all in this movie with special mention going to Anne Hathaway as Selina, being my favorite performance in the movie. I like some of the action scenes, as they are the few times that you actually get Batman in it. The ending has many stupid moments, but I do like the ending Bruce gets in the end. But now to get into all the story problems in this movie. Bane straight up sucks in this. He doesn't really have the intimidation you expect from Bane, since his plan is so extra that he loses all his luster, also doesn't help that the voice is really bad and sounds cartoony as ever, what also doesn't help is that there is a twist villain in this movie and it is one of the biggest middle fingers to this movie as they expect you to be surprised, but instead you are left confused as ever as to why she is here in the first place, her motivation makes no sense and contradicts itself so hard that you get whiplash, also her death is the fakest shit I have ever seen in a movie in awhile. The pacing is so bad, as you spend so long before you get any Batman whatsoever and then you have to wait minutes to hours on end to get to a scene that actually advances the story or shows you something interesting. I think what kills this movie for me is how stupid some of the logic of the decisions and story beats are, like we are sending every cop down into the sewers, because plot, we need Batman to be locked up for 8 years cause plot, and all the other logistical shit that almost everyone has talked about already. I didn't want to despise this movie, but I can't bring myself to say that it is good, at best watchable, at worst, it is a movie that tries to fit 3 batman stories into one. I cant believe I am saying this, but this is literally Spider-Man 3 of the trilogy (I am sorry Spider-Man 3, you are at least funny).

Tudo é o fim do mundo, seja na guerra, num prédio sitiado por terroristas ou numa briga de casal. E os recentes filmes do Batman, por conta da envergadura, extrapolam ainda mais tal culto, aumentando o volume, as fagulhas e o sofrimento aparente. Sem desmerecer as qualidades do filme, temos sempre uma corrida contra o relógio para salvar dezenas, milhares ou milhões. Ou tão somente o filho de Jim Gordon – um dos motivos, na minha opinião, que fazem do segundo filme o melhor da série. O outro motivo, tão ou mais importante, é a presença do Coringa. Afinal, não existe Bane capaz de superar tal personagem. Dito tudo isso, “Batman - O Cavaleiro das Trevas Ressurge” é um final muito digno para a trilogia (sempre trilogias!). Amarra as pontas e nos entrega um Batman no limite da amargura. E que precisa penar e perder para aprender a se reerguer e até mesmo passar o bastão, por quê não? Para quebrar este herói, inclusive fisicamente, Bane é o vilão apropriado. E para mostrar que existe mais do que uma Rachel Dawes na vida, nada melhor do uma Mulher-Gato. Hardy e Hathaway estão muito bem. O primeiro, limitado a olhares, gestuais e mudanças de entonação, faz muito só com olhares, gestuais e mudanças de entonação. A segunda, limitada a nada, flui, literalmente, entre vários mundos, sem nunca deixar de flertar com Bruce e com Batman. Estabelecer esta conexão entre a vilã-não-tão-vilã e o herói era fundamental, e o filme faz isso a contento. Como sempre, a trama trabalha de forma coerente seus muitos coadjuvantes, valorizando mais uma vez Alfred, Gordon e Fox. E a importância de John Blake (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) não deve ser esquecida. Muitas vezes o filme é quase só dele. Nolan também sabe bem criar cenas de ação que não são só computação. Têm ritmo, dinâmica e uma tensão sempre bem engendrada. Às vezes a mão pesa e surgem alguns exageros, mas a gente releva pelo todo. Afinal, várias das hipérboles são também os pontos de conexão com os quadrinhos. Isso porque, por mais que digam que estas histórias do Batman são baseadas na realidade, elementos como o Poço, as explicações vilanescas ou o aprisionamento dos policiais nos subterrâneos são simplistas demais se não fosse esta uma história de super-herói. Sem falar que qualquer um conheça um mínimo de Batman sacou cedo demais o principal “twist” da trama. E mesmo quem não conhecia poderia pegar rapidinho, bastando apenas ouvir com cuidado alguns diálogos (por vezes comprometidos pela péssima legendagem). Vale dizer também que o filme conta com a pior cena de “morte-de-pessoa-à-beira-da-morte” de toda história do cinema. Uma péssima interpretação de alguém que não é usualmente ruim assim. Mesmo com defeitos, o filme é um digno fechamento da série, como eu já disse, sendo equivalente a “Batman Begins”. O que não é pouco, já que “Batman - O Cavaleiro das Trevas” situa-se num patamar muito acima e dificilmente seria batido...

-kinda Batman Tenet, in that the more you think about any one scene, the more your head hurts (but without the it’s-all-vibes-baby tenet magic to it) -there’s just a lot of stuff going on here. It’s probably not worth trying to pinpoint one issue when there are so many (Gotham PD’s just…hanging in the sewers for 3 months? Did the Dent Act abolish all crime? Couldn’t Bruce Wayne just…say he didn’t make those stock trades? Etc etc), but one fix I think would’ve gone a long way is just nixing the entire prison hole thing. If you had Bruce out of commission but still hiding in Gotham, you could keep the focus within the city, and we might get more room to explore the ramifications of Bane’s occupation (it’s hinted at, but if this really is a “no but really eat the rich” populist revolt, think there needs to be a few more scenes conveying this, otherwise it all feels a bit empty). It’s a Batman movie without a lot of Batman, which I think could be alleviated a bit if Bruce at least sees/experiences all of it firsthand. -in a weird way, this rewatch made Reeves’ Batman look a lot better by comparison, despite suffering from a similar level of glut. Reeves going full noir/graphic novel feels downright refreshing after Nolan seemed to almost get tired of his own grounded take on the character. -it’s interesting how this feels like Nolan’s last formally conventional movie. From this point on, all of his movies play with time and structure, nonlinear narratives and interwoven temporalities, etc. After really finding the juice in this area with Inception, it’s easy to wonder if he felt burdened (re: bored) by the straightforward nature of this one. -to that point: a lot’s been speculated about Nolan’s seemingly recent fascination with Great Men™️ who regret their big game changing innovation, and, you know, what that might say about him. Despite not always loving the “every movie’s about the director” framing (probably true, but can invite simplistic readings), Nolan’s fixations present biographical lenses too obvious to ignore. -The bummer reading of this for Nolan is probably the real-world tragedies completely out of his control that he nonetheless might feel guilt about by association, from Ledger’s death to the DKR shooting (to be clear: he shouldn’t feel any guilt about either, but could understand from a human perspective how it’d be hard not to). -BUT my less-bummer theory is that, if Nolan’s working through some kind of artistic regret, it might be the way his work—his creative fascinations and how successful early on they were—became misinterpreted by others as his version of cinematic dogma. -whatever you think of Nolan’s “take” on Batman+superhero movies in general, at the time it felt groundbreaking, particularly his grounding of a fantastical, mythical genre with a sense of real-world stakes, logical narrative causes+effects, etc. (evoking his later take on the Odyssey). But I’ve never gotten the sense that Nolan thinks this is the end-all-be-all approach to cinematic storytelling, merely this was his approach to finding interest within the material. -I was struck watching Nolan’s criterion closet video recently when he picked Lost Highway, an incredibly un-Nolan movie in many ways. He explains that he didn’t enjoy the movie on first watch, yet on rewatches and thinking through it, he came to love Lynch’s ability to visually show illogical dream logic onscreen. For a guy that loves logic-based puzzle stories grounded in high-stakes spectacle, I thought it was telling to pick something that’s nearly the opposite. -all this to say: I think Nolan’s an appreciator of all kinds of cinematic language and storytelling approaches, not merely his own. And the longer his career goes on, the more he seems intent on playing with form (think his critics would say rather rudimentarily, but still). So I wonder if his “big regret” (if he does have one), is people deciding his “realist” approach was “best”, and not one way among many to tell a compelling cinematic story. -TLDR: Hathaway rocks, Bane voice good, etc.

Bon, une fois de plus je ne suis pas trop d'accord avec la note de tout le monde. Perso, j'ai trouvé ce film plus abouti que le précédent, sans être non plus un très bon film. La saga se conclut d'une bonne manière pour moi. Bane est certes un méchant moins marquant que le Joker, mais ça marche très bien aussi, surtout avec le twist de fin, c'est vraiment intéressant comme idée. J'aime bien l'idée du côté « réaliste » des costumes des personnages ; j'ai souvent du mal à prendre au sérieux un personnage habillé comme un champion d'arène de Pokémon. Ici, le parti pris est de ne pas en faire trop et d'adopter une imagerie aussi réaliste et moderne que possible (sauf pour Batman qui fais autant amateur que dans les précédent film). Fini la Catwoman sexy en cuir, bonjour la Catwoman « équipée en voleuse », et pour moi le pari est 100 % gagnant, ça marche du feu de Dieu. Dans cette suite, le scénario est plus poussé que dans le précédent film et l'ambiance est mieux réussie. Le décor de la prison est magnifique aussi je trouve, mais Nolan pêche encore sur le montage qui arrive à la fois à être trop mou et trop rapide sur des moments qui mériteraient plus de tension. J'ai vraiment du mal avec ce côté-là de sa réalisation. Quelques petites incohérences par-ci par-là et (SPOIL ICI : Catwoman et l'idée du passage de flambeau avec Robin sont presque bâclées et auraient tellement pu être meilleures). Mais bref, j'ai préféré ce film à The Dark Knight. C'est une excellente suite et une bonne conclusion pour la saga, mais Nolan pêche encore et est le seul frein et véritable défaut du film au travers de sa narration et de son montage.

Nolan concludes his reimagining of the Batman myth with a sumptuous film that pays homage to the war movie genre, presenting a clash that is no longer merely one of ideals but between actual factions in a desperate battle to save not only Batman’s soul— who is now more weary and battered than ever and must rediscover the motivation to fight— but also to save the very essence of the motivation that drives him to act: his city. Gotham City takes center stage more than ever, at the mercy of Bane, a ruthless villain masterfully portrayed by Tom Hardy, accompanied by a supremely convincing Catwoman played by Anne Hathaway. Here, Nolan consciously chooses to remove the protagonist for long part during the second act in order to tear him down and rebuild him in one of the most powerful and emotional scenes in Nolan’s filmography. The direction is, as always, extremely elegant and delivers thrilling fight sequences. The film’s flaws all lie in Marion Cotillard’s character, who is given a somewhat clumsy plot twist that fails to provide a fitting payoff for Bane’s character—who, in fact, deserved something better. But Nolan makes up for it with a marvelous ending that elevates Batman to the status of a true legend and expresses boundless love for the character.

The Dark Knight Rises is a wonderful end to a masterfully crafted trilogy. This is the first Chris Nolan Batman film I ever saw. I went to the theater with my buddies to watch this with no context on the rest of the series, and to be honest I can’t really tell you how I felt about it at the time, but I probably thought it was cool. As the years have gone on, and I’ve watched this trilogy of movies many times, I’ve always really, really loved The Dark Knight Rises. And with this analytical rewatch, the reasons I like it are kind of hypocritical. If you compare the things that I don’t like about The Dark Knight, but like about The Dark Knight Rises, you’ll see a lot of inconsistencies. But for whatever reason The Dark Knight Rises really, really works for me. I’m not quite sure if Christopher Nolan didn’t really wanna make a third Batman film, because there are parts of this that feel a bit phoned in, and that is something I’ve never thought of Christopher Nolan before. The first 20 minutes of this film are really choppy and out of sorts. It’s clunky. Scenes don’t really go well into each other. It’s kind of a mess, and while this was going on I was like, man he kind of phoned it in. But once you get past that part, for the next two hours and 20 minutes you get an epic conclusion to the Dark Knight trilogy. I love that this film feels somewhat like a James Bond movie. The globe-trotting, the scale, the larger-than-life villain — it just has that vibe. I actually kind of love that Batman is hardly in this film. He’s almost more of this mythical creature than a superhero. It creates this really interesting mythos and it allows for multiple times for him to come back to action, and it’s epic every time. Man, when that music swells and the Dark Knight is out — chills every single time. Tom Hardy’s performance as Bane is menacing just as much as it is kind of silly, and it totally works for me. I love the characterization of Bane. His voice is so over the top and his little one-liners are so silly, but I think it adds to the mental state of Bane. He’s just a crazy British guy who was trained by the League of Shadows and lived in a hole for his whole life. It’s awesome. Anne Hathaway — good Lord Almighty, what a Catwoman. She not only looks the part but she is so good at bullshitting people. She changes her attitude on a dime. It shows how much range she has as an actor and it’s something that’s been kind of brushed over, but she’s the best actor in this film easily. I can go on and on about the entire cast to be honest. Michael Caine, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Morgan Freeman, Gary Oldman — all are just perfectly cast, and seeing their stories come to an end is such a delight. This film had me really in awe through most of it. The scale of how many people they have in the streets of Gotham fighting, or the Batwing flying around — it all just looks so great and it’s so not half-assed. So to circle it around from the beginning of this review, the beginning of this movie is just a little janky, but this film is not half-assed. And I will say still to this day, after re-watching this whole entire trilogy, I still enjoy The Dark Knight Rises more than The Dark Knight. Thanks for listening.

Absolutely painful Guardians of the Galaxy is a diffuse, unrestrained mess that constantly feels like it is tripping over itself. There are good ideas here, some legitimate emotional material, and a handful of performances and moments that work, but almost none of it is given enough discipline or breathing room to develop real weight. The movie is constantly moving, constantly talking, constantly introducing something new, and constantly trying to be funny. That energy is clearly part of the appeal, but for me it becomes exhausting. The worldbuilding arrives as a flood of names, factions, planets, relationships, and cosmic mythology before much of it has any dramatic meaning. The characters are introduced just as aggressively, but most of them remain surprisingly thin because the movie is always rushing toward the next joke, plot beat, or bit of exposition. That same restlessness hurts the emotional side of the movie. There are real arcs here in theory. Peter is supposed to move from emotional detachment toward connection and sacrifice, Gamora is escaping the control of Thanos and Ronan, Drax is masking grief with rage, Rocket carries the trauma of being experimented on, and Groot ultimately gives himself up for the group. None of those are bad ideas, but most of them feel more stated than fully dramatized. Peter is the clearest example. His arc has a beginning and an end on paper, and the callback to his mother gives it structure, but I never really felt him change all that much. The movie does not establish his emotional detachment strongly enough for his eventual heroism to feel transformative. Gamora has even less to work with because she is already planning to betray Ronan before we really know who she is. Drax is funny, but his grief is largely swallowed by the comedy surrounding him. Rocket and Groot have an emotional bond, but the movie asks for a payoff from a friendship it has mostly treated as comedic side character banter. The humor is probably the biggest reason none of this landed for me. It is not simply that I found most of it unfunny, the problem is that the movie seems almost allergic to sincerity. Whenever something begins to feel tense, emotional, or serious, there is often something to deflate it. It gives the entire movie the feeling of an elbow to the ribs. There are moments where the story finally allows itself to be sincere, and those moments are usually among the strongest in the film, which only makes the constant undercutting more frustrating. That is what ultimately makes the movie feel so sloppy to me. It has potentially interesting mythology, a found family story, trauma, revenge, abuse, sacrifice, and identity all inside it, but very little feels satisfyingly integrated. Ronan is barely more than a generic villain, Nebula isn’t much of a character, the Kree/Xandar conflict mostly exists as exposition, the Infinity Stone material should feel enormous, but even that gets folded into the same hyperactive, ironic tone. There are still things I like. Chris Pratt is charismatic, Dave Bautista gets most of the laughs that worked for me, the movie moves well, some of the imagery is imaginative, and there are a few sincere emotional beats that land when the movie actually allows them to. But those moments feel buried inside a movie whose entire sensibility I found exhausting. Rather than feeling like a refreshing expansion of the MCU, Guardians of the Galaxy feels like a loud, scattered tonal diversion that helped normalize many of the tendencies I would eventually come to dislike most about the franchise. There is enough life, craft, and isolated value here to keep it out of the absolute basement. But I hated watching it.

Guardians of the Galaxy funciona principalmente pela personalidade que James Gunn consegue dar a personagens que, isoladamente, poderiam ser pouco interessantes. Peter Quill, Gamora, Rocket, Groot e Drax começam como figuras incompatíveis e passam boa parte do filme discutindo, competindo e tentando sobreviver uns aos outros. É justamente nessa convivência que o filme encontra seus melhores momentos. A trilha escolhida por Quill também dá uma identidade própria ao universo cósmico e cria um contraste divertido com toda aquela grandiosidade espacial. O problema é que a história ao redor do grupo é muito mais convencional. Ronan é um antagonista pouco interessante, a Joia do Infinito funciona como mais um objeto capaz de destruir mundos e o terceiro ato retorna ao espetáculo previsível do gênero. O humor também nem sempre funciona para mim. Ainda assim, existe uma química genuína entre os protagonistas que sustenta boa parte da experiência. Guardians of the Galaxy me interessa pouco como aventura cósmica, mas funciona bem melhor como história sobre cinco pessoas improváveis aprendendo a permanecer juntas.

Quand le film laisse exister ça, il fonctionne vraiment. Rocket devient plus qu’un gag, Groot plus qu’une mascotte, et même Quill arrête deux minutes de jouer au mec cool. Mais James Gunn sabote souvent ses propres émotions une seconde trop tôt, comme s’il avait peur qu’une scène sincère reste sincère jusqu’au bout. Le film parle de gens qui se cachent derrière des blagues, puis passe lui-même deux heures à faire exactement la même chose.

I understand that it’s a satirical film making fun of stereotypes within the horror genre.  However, I didn’t think there was much plot, nor theatrics - the whole thing could have been wrapped up in 45 mins.  Elements of it were funny in a dark comedic way but realistically isn’t a brilliant movie when compared to all the other epic horror films out there. So, after years of resolutely talking shit, I decided to give Scream another try. Wes Craven's fourth most interesting meta horror film is almost universally beloved but, personally, I don't really see what the fuss is about. Still carrying the stink of Vampire in Brooklyn, Craven beats Joss Whedon to the punch for the obnoxious elder millennial teen banter (I can say it, I was the target audience) but the entire exercise feels, well, about as hokey and forced as Eddie Murphy trying to be a funny vampire. The self-awareness might have been impressive if Craven hadn't landed the one-two punch of Shocker and New Nightmare just a few years earlier. Shocker does all the same self-referential humor that Scream does but shows up with not only a real mean streak but also a complete lack of restraint. New Nightmare tackles the deconstruction of a genre Craven helped solidify with more  intelligence and genuine terror than Scream even hints at. It all feels like we've seen it before but Craven has decided to dumb it down for the folks in the back. Scream isn't helped by a wildly uneven cast. Drew Barrymore's opening scene is the highpoint of the film and sets a bar that nothing else in Scream even brushes against. Rose McGowan probably comes closest but an underwritten role does her no favors. Though Neve Campbell is perfectly sufficient as a final girl, she suffers from being given too little to upend in a movie thats supposed to be about upending expectations. Unfortunately, the good news ends there. David Arquette, who I have a genuine soft spot for, wanders in and out of frame uselessly as he's circled by Courtney Cox, whose intentions are vague. The always execrable Matthew Lillard and a Johnny Depp lookalike named "Skeet" fail to either smolder or clown effectively, with Skeet in particular seeming to be completely incapable of maintaining the mystery. I can't call Scream a bad film, its competent enough, but theres a bloodlessness and slick presentation that is a far way off from the guy who made you need a shower after Last House on the Left. It is, well and truly, just ok. It made him a bunch of money, though, and Wes deserved that. Level of concern your friends will have when you recommend this movie: low.

Trying to write my thoughts down on Scream as someone who's only seen a handful of iconic horror films feels like a losing game. It's so baked in irony and endless references to other films, most of which I was completely unfamiliar with, to the point where it got increasingly frustrating over time. I felt like I was thinking too hard about i for most of its runtime instead of appreciating it, which tends to be a bad sign when it comes to comedy. To give credit where it's due, the opening scene is absolutely insane and one of the few times I really understood why everyone loves this thing...it has everything you need for an effective horror cold open. Unfortunately, it's also one of the few times I felt like the film actually scared me. Admittedly, the whole film feels like a big joke I'm not in on, which is why it doesn't really work as a comedy. Meta movies like this are why I always pegged myself as not a horror guy; even when it's embraced as thoroughly as it is here, the tropes present still grind my gears a good bit. On the bright side, the deaths tend to be gnarly and the characters are likable enough every now and then that they can evoke a few laughs from my cold, charred heart. Two films in and it's a bit hard to tell what I think of Wes Craven so far. Red Eye wasn't a masterpiece by any means, but it was an entertaining and light thriller aware of its limitations with some great performances from Rachel McAdams, Cillian Murphy and Brian Cox. Many of the same stylistic traits in that film are here, but I couldn't bring myself to care about the outcome (and consequently who lives or dies) on the same level. I can see why Neve Campbell and Matthew Lillard went on to become iconic actors, even if I wasn't wowed by them here. It's a bit disappointing for me to not fall in love with the first horror movie I watch from such an iconic horror director, but I think I need to familiarize myself with more slashers and Craven's initial run of films to appreciate this one more. Need more self-aware horror like the original Funny Games (which was also way funnier!) and less like this.

Scream is one of those landmark moments in movies where there's pre-Scream slashers and there's post-Scream slashers. The way it laid bare the common horror tropes is something we take for granted these days; the whole "How to Survive a Horror Movie" started right here. It was incredibly clever and fresh for its time, but that subversive nature has been over-done so much throughout the years that watching it now feels downright bland. This movie's biggest sin is the annoying thing movies do where it points out that something is cliché or stupid but then also does it; as if pointing it out makes it better. That's kinda this whole franchise's conceit; being a slasher while commenting on itself. I do have to point out that seeing Scary Movie a lot has made a lot of moments here incredibly laughable and I can't help but think about the goofy parody parts instead of the serious ones. Dewey for instance is so inept, he might as well be the Doofy character from SM. I suppose this could be seen as an indictment of disturbed, privileged, horror movie-obsessed young white men, but that same obsession can also be seen as a saving grace so the message is a little muddy there. An element I do enjoy is that this makes the effort to show that Ghostface is definitely human and that victims who fight back do cause harm. I also liked the double-meta bit of Randy telling Jamie Lee Curtis on the TV to turn around while the killer is behind him; him saying "Behind you, Jamie" is Randy also talking to his actor self Jamie Kennedy, clever stuff. Overall important for horror history, but these days it kinda falls into the same horror heap it was trying to satire.

não consegui ver o mesmo filme brilhante que muitos falavam. Sei que a essência do filme é ser único e quebrar padrões, unindo humor com terror e essa parte até que o filme faz bem, mas tendo um olhar minimamente mais crítico, o filme deixa muito a desejar. O começo provavelmente é a melhor parte, com uma tensão engraçada, introdução dos personagens etc. Depois disso, pra mim o filme se perde um pouco, cenas completamente irrealistas, burras, desnecessaria e alem da falta de justificativa pro Stu fazer parte de tudo isso. O filme é divertido, tem referências legais e até vale a pena ver, mas não senti toda a grandeza mencionada. Talvez, seja tratado assim por ser um grande nome e um dos princípios do slasher ou da boa união do humor com terror, mas analisando o filme em si, sem levar em conta sua história, senti que realmente faltou algo.

scream permanece como um filme fundamental, mas sua consagração também criou uma espécie de blindagem crítica que transforma qualquer ressalva em heresia: basta mencionar que o roteiro é mais inteligente do que propriamente profundo, que os diálogos frequentemente confundem autoconsciência com esperteza ou que a revelação de billy loomis e stu macher é menos perturbadora do que o mito em torno dela para que a obra seja imediatamente defendida como uma perfeição intocável. wes craven e kevin williamson revitalizaram o slasher ao fazer seus personagens conhecerem as regras do gênero e ao transformar o repertório do público em instrumento de suspense, mas essa inovação não deve ser confundida com uma reinvenção absoluta do horror: scream é, sobretudo, uma síntese extremamente eficiente de ideias anteriores, uma obra que desmonta os clichês enquanto ainda depende deles para existir. sua inteligência está na forma, no ritmo, na mise-en-scène e na habilidade de fazer a expectativa do espectador trabalhar contra si mesma, não necessariamente na profundidade de suas conclusões. a abertura com casey becker continua sendo uma aula de construção de tensão, porque craven entende que o terror não nasce apenas da violência, mas da transformação gradual de uma conversa banal em um jogo de humilhação, controle e morte; depois disso, porém, o filme nem sempre sustenta a mesma precisão, alternando momentos de genuína ameaça com diálogos que soam excessivamente artificiais, como se os personagens estivessem mais interessados em demonstrar conhecimento sobre filmes de terror do que em existir dentro daquele mundo. sidney prescott é uma protagonista importante e muito bem defendida por neve campbell, mas sua trajetória ainda parte de um modelo recorrente do slasher: a jovem marcada pelo trauma materno, perseguida por uma violência que invade sua sexualidade, sua casa e sua relação amorosa. o que torna sidney mais complexa é justamente a descoberta de que o perigo não vem de um monstro distante, mas do namorado, do amigo e do ambiente masculino que parecia familiar; billy e stu não são os melhores assassinos da franquia, e suas motivações, quando finalmente expostas, parecem apressadas, superficiais e dramaticamente menores do que a tensão construída ao longo do filme. a ideia de que billy matou maureen prescott por ressentimento e que stu simplesmente o acompanha por uma combinação de instabilidade e submissão é funcional, mas não possui a dimensão psicológica que muitos fãs projetam sobre a dupla; a revelação é mais memorável pela encenação e pelo impacto histórico do que pela riqueza do texto. ainda assim, há algo profundamente perturbador na escolha de colocar a violência nas mãos de dois garotos comuns, e não de uma figura sobrenatural ou de um assassino fisicamente invencível: ghostface é icônico porque não é uma identidade estável, mas uma máscara que permite ao homem comum transformar misoginia, sadismo e desejo de controle em espetáculo. sob o humor, a metalinguagem e as referências aos clássicos, scream também revela como a cultura cinematográfica masculina frequentemente converte a violência contra mulheres em entretenimento, debate e trivia, enquanto as próprias vítimas precisam aprender as regras de um jogo criado para matá-las. o filme percebe essa contradição, mas nem sempre a enfrenta com a mesma contundência com que a apresenta; muitas vezes, sua crítica ao gênero é absorvida pelo prazer de reproduzir o que pretende questionar. visualmente, entretanto, a obra permanece extraordinariamente segura: a fotografia noturna, os interiores domésticos, a paleta fria e a arquitetura isolada de woodsboro criam um espaço onde a adolescência parece simultaneamente cotidiana e teatral, como se cada corredor pudesse se transformar em cenário de uma performance homicida. a trilha, a montagem e a direção de craven sustentam um equilíbrio raro entre humor, tensão e violência, embora o filme esteja longe de ser tão assustador quanto sua reputação sugere; ele intriga mais do que apavora, diverte mais do que assombra e permanece na memória mais pela sua personalidade do que pela capacidade de provocar medo genuíno. como grande fã da franquia, reconheço sua importância, amo ghostface e compreendo por que scream se tornou uma referência incontornável do horror, mas justamente por amá-lo não vejo necessidade de tratá-lo como uma obra perfeita: sua relevância histórica é maior do que sua consistência dramática, sua influência é mais revolucionária do que seu argumento e seu legado acabou sendo fortalecido por sequências que ampliaram, corrigiram e até superaram aspectos de sua fórmula original. scream continua sendo um filme excelente, carismático e decisivo para o slasher moderno, mas envelheceu menos como vinho do que como um retrato muito bem preservado de seu próprio momento, brilhante na autoconsciência, irregular na dramaturgia e muito mais desafiador do que assustador.

Τα πήγαινε τόσο καλά… μα στο το τέλος μου τα χάλασε! Το Scream είναι μια ταινία γεμάτη ατμόσφαιρα, που σε βυθίζει από την αρχή στο high school horror / whodunit στοιχείο της. Η σκηνοθεσία είναι υπέροχη, η μουσική εξαιρετική και, ειδικά για την εποχή της, η ταινία είναι γεμάτη σεναριακές πρωτοπορίες και meta ιδέες που την κάνουν πραγματικά ξεχωριστή. Όσο διατηρεί το μυστήριο γύρω από το ποιος το έκανε, λειτουργεί σχεδόν τέλεια. Για τα 2/3 της, είναι πραγματικά εξαιρετική. Το πρόβλημα έρχεται στην τελευταία πράξη, η οποία θεωρώ ότι ξεφεύγει αρκετά σε κλιμάκωση σε σχέση με όσα έχει χτίσει μέχρι εκείνο το σημείο. Χωρίς να μπω σε spoilers, θα προτιμούσα ένα πιο συγκρατημένο και λιγότερο εκτεταμένο φινάλε. In my opinion, Scream, released in 1996 and directed by Wes Craven, is a very interesting horror movie that combines suspense, violence, mystery, and some moments of humor. The movie tells the story of Sidney Prescott, a young woman who is being chased by a mysterious killer who wears a mask and calls his victims before attacking them. What I liked most about the movie is the way it creates tension. From the beginning, the viewer has the feeling that any character could become the next victim. The phone calls from the killer make the story even more suspenseful because he talks to his victims and plays with them before attacking. I also liked the way Scream uses the horror genre. It is not just a movie with scary and violent scenes. It also makes references to other horror movies and plays with some of the common rules of the genre. This makes the story different from other slasher movies and makes the viewer try to discover who the killer is. Another positive point is the characters, especially Sidney. Throughout the movie, she becomes stronger and more confident while facing difficult situations. The actors also help make the scenes feel more realistic and create a strong sense of fear and suspense. The killer's mask is another memorable part of the movie because it looks simple but is also very frightening. Even though I really enjoyed the movie, some parts can be predictable for people who are already familiar with horror movies. However, this does not completely take away from the suspense because the movie keeps the mystery about who is behind the mask until the end. Overall, I think Scream is a very interesting horror and suspense movie. I liked the way it combines the slasher style with mystery and humor. For me, it is a movie that keeps the viewer interested from beginning to end and shows why Scream became an important movie in the horror genre.

It was so obvious and also not so obvious. I loved both Stu and Billy’s acting (same for the other actors), but damn, Matthew Lillard and Skeet Ulrich put up with an amazing performance here. I have so much to tell about that movie but I’ll be short. This is the kind of movies I could rewatch again and again and would never get bored of. I think that’d be called a comfort movie, although Scream isn’t exactly the type of movie that makes you want to smile or laugh. But Scream , after rewatching it, is like predicting everything that will happen. We know who the killers are, we know who are going to die or not and yet, we don’t care. There are no surprises, but this feels comfortable. In a way, that is what makes horror movies comforting (in my opinion). I rate it as a 5* now because somewhere in my heart, Scream deserves it in every way.

Oftentimes I make this distinction in reviewing media that it’s either good (aka serious and complicated) or fun (aka easy on the brain and quickly dopamine-inducing). Most action movies I lump in the second box, and I don’t often complain about them not being good enough, because I get the purpose they serve for audiences. I also understand for a movie around 2 hours to land effectively, making it very entertaining is a sort of shortcut to sell people on it when the narrative isn’t up to par. It would be pretentious and wrong of me to claim being above dumb fun movies when my watched catalogue overwhelmingly consists of them, but the downside of these is that I leave the movie theater with not much of anything to say beyond “it was fun”. Therefore, it’s interesting to me when I have so much praise for an action movie that I can express in a meaningful way. Bullet Train is probably among the few movies in this genre that you will see on this list, and it’s through impressively clever and efficient writing that it squeezes so many things to love in such a short time. The movie from start to finish almost bombards you with plot elements, moving parts to the story ranging from throwaway dialogue lines to big actions like character deaths that have rippling effects on the rest of the story. Much like its location, it doesn’t slow down for a single second, making for an absolutely thrilling watching experience that fits in a staggering number of “OH SHIT I REMEMBER THAT FROM EARLIER IN THE MOVIE”. With no exaggeration EVERYTHING in this movie has a logical cause and effect and because it manages to stick the landing beautifully while tying all its loose ends together, it never feels overwhelming, even on first watch. It’s chock-full of small details that enrich every subsequent rewatch, and in this way it cements itself in the space of streaming services by making the re-experiencing of the story so close to the cinema viewing experience. At the same time, the movie is a beautiful example of avoiding tonal disonnance, a problem I have frequently with comedy action stories. Bullet train is a comedy first, drama second, but the serious moments work really well because of the character work around them. I have to point out how impressive it is to introduce so many characters in the span of a 2 hour movie, some of whom die in less than 15 minutes, that all evoke the sense they have more to their story than what’s presented. In the Wolf’s and Hornet’s first appearances, the movie disguises effective, concise exposition under the comedy of a rapid-fire flashback introduction that you would see in a much worse movie. This ability to work both fronts at the same time in comedy and storytelling with every character interaction is what allows them the freedom of multitudes, where tragic moments like Lemon’s death are given the necessary space to not feel jarring against the other light-hearted parts. The characters are, obviously, ridiculous to a point, exaggerated in fun ways, but not to the degree that they become one-trait caricatures (yes, including the oni-mask russian crime lord named the White Death). In the sharp contrast of these characters, where Ladybug, Prince and the Father feel like they could be from 3 different genres of movies, lie the most hillarious moments of the film that work in tandem with the foreshadowed elements to continously drive the plot forward, all the way to a bombastic ending with a villain death so amazingly anti-climactic you can’t help but want more. And yet, it’s over in the above mentioned runtime, and it’s impossible for it to overstay its welcome or ever get boring. I love Bullet Train a lot, and it’s a staple in my rotation of movies/shows I could rewatch for comfort dozens of times before I get bored. It has a very tight, well-written script that elevates it from a dumb fun action movie to a secret third thing: intelligent fun action movie. Please let this movie be one that gets milked to death with 10 more slightly worse sequels, I will be seated for all of them.

Chekhov's gun the movie. I have a weird relationship with this film. It’s one of those films I find to be very very mid, but I always remember it for some reason. And I want to like it more than I actually do. Like this film has all the stuff I like. A director and actors I like. A premise I like. A setting I like. It has bad people, doing bad things, in a bad world. Assassins, murderers, and criminals all confined in a small place, trying to get the same things. But this movie falls flat for me in a lot of areas. I find the action besides the ending to be very OK at best and bad at worst. I find the comedy only works with lemon and tangerine and no one else. The product placements are egregious. The editing does not trust the audience to remember stuff that was actually established within the dialogue. They got a Puerto Rican dude to play a Mexican to be barely in the movie. And one of my biggest complaints is Brad Pitt is absolutely dog shit in this movie. He’s unfunny. Completely unconvincing in the role. Like an asshole I read the book after watching the movie for the first time. And besides the fact, this is a sequel to another book so I had to read two books. Ladybug in the book is an unlucky fuck up, but he is competent at doing his job and not spouting unfunny therapy quotes. Aaron Taylor-Johnson is the standout of this movie if he does get to play James Bond it’s because of this film. He’s believable in the action scenes. He’s funny. And he’s just bad ass. Brian Henry as lemon is funny and steals the movie and all the scenes he is in. And finally Joey King is great as Prince in this movie. In the book the character is like a 12 year-old boy and I think the sex change honestly makes the character better. I don’t really care that the movie decided to be far more international than the very Japanese cast of the book. What it does make like the world building really unbelievable like in the book I believe that like all these seemingly pretty small scale assassins and criminals would be on this bullet train. Also, I kinda like how the book version weaves some of the characters from the first book in it. I also feel like it’s just a More self-assured story where the movie is very much trying to be more smarter than it is. I think the ending in the movie works for what it’s trying to do it’s big, It’s bombastic and it’s violent but I feel like the books is far more satisfying in a weird way. The books ending is definitely a bit underwhelming, but I think that’s a problem for all of his books because that happened in the first one as well. And also the celebrity cameos in this movie are also quite bad. I feel like giving roles to famous actors and musicians it’s fine, but why is Channing Tatum here to just make gay jokes. Why is Ryan Reynolds even get a cameo at the end? It feels like this movie had far too big of a budget and they needed to use it somehow. And honestly, yeah that is probably the problem. They made a pretty small stake story about a bunch of assassins on a train, and into a far too loud and bombastic Hollywood film. I kind of wish I would like to see a small Indy team try to do this story. For the pure fact that this movie has so many memes that still pop up every once in a while, it’s clear this movie did something right. Would I recommend it? Sure you could waste your time watching far worse movies. And I do enjoy parts of it, but I wish I enjoyed it more.

This is a fun film which suffers from biting off way more than it can chew. I did enjoy it a lot and felt some elements were really well done, while others fell very short. The best thing for me was the comedic acting. All the one liners and funny moments completely landed for me and I found myself actively laughing throughout. I thought the standout permanent was Aaron Taylor Johnson who was just absolutely hilarious. His back and forths as Tangerine with Lemon were outstanding and it really reminded me of Pulp Fiction in the best way. Brian Tyree Henry was great in his acting but the British accent was so so bad. I don’t know if it was kind of on purpose to be funnier but either way for me it was taking me out of the film and didn’t work at all. The action sequences also looked really good with some cool innovative moments where fight scenes felt punchier and more intense than usual. Brad Pitt was also great in this and played his part to perfection having enough to hold the movie together. The actual plot and the way the story all intertwines is what really lets the film down. There is just so much going on and nothing really substantial to mould it all together. There is also an issue with the serious moments where the films tone just doesn’t match. To me it should have just been a straight up action comedy and leave any of the deeper plot alone. I also found the direction a bit too slick and it made the movie come across as almost looking like an AI generated picture. The CGI and effects also didn’t look great. As an overall movie there is enough here to enjoy but I also wouldn’t go as far as to say I’m in a rush to see it again.
