Darth Vader gives Area Manager, right? (there's a longer version of this review, with more about my luckless adolescent career in the British civil service, but you'll have to go over to Substack to read that.) In my youth I worked for a while in the UK civil service. I wasn't the most hard-working or conscientious civil servant in that particular branch office of Her Majesty's Land Registry. In fact, during one episode of striking negligence and work-avoidance, there was an encounter with an Area Manager that, to this day, sends a shiver down my spine. What brought this to mind in watching the first and second movies in the original Star Wars sequence was Darth Vader’s striking Area Manager vibe. In The Empire Strikes Back he’s supposed to be the Empire’s most terrifying entity, a fearsome knight, damaged beyond pity (and somehow endowed with extra Force not available to others), a warrior but also evidently a man smart enough to slink away from the Death Star before the rebels blew it up. Vader’s spaceship in this episode is imaginatively called the Executor. The Death Star is gone but the Empire is back on the front foot. We wonder, was the destruction of its super-weapon actually an existential crisis for the Empire or did the rebels really just blow up a pointless, bloated boondoggle, somebody’s vanity project? Was the Imperial leadership secretly happy that this stupid, monolithic, over-budget piece of shit was atomised by the hippy retards from the rebellion? It’s his flagship but Vader's not actually the boss. He walks the decks with that awkward ‘I don’t actually work here but I could cause you pain’ authority. He drops in and throws his weight around. Near the beginning of this film he literally kills the ship’s commander - an Admiral with the perfectly Star Wars name Kendal Ozzel - for some tactical snafu (of course, the lore tells us that Ozzel is an over-promoted Imperial civil servant who deserved it anyway so that makes sense). On the ship Vader can do what he wants. He cruises around looking purposeful but obviously not 100% across the layout here. He’s allowed to use the service lift if he wants to but you can tell he doesn’t really know how to, so someone has to show him. The coffee machine in the staff lounge is beyond him and, although the toilets are in the same place on every deck, he can never find the VIP bathroom. In more recent Star Wars expressions - guerrilla war drama Andor, for instance - the Empire’s bureaucracy is fleshed out a bit. We learn more about its essentially colonial-extractive economics, we get some detail about policing (George Orwell the colonial police officer would have recognised these methods). At this point, though, two movies into the original sequence, Lucas’s Empire is still incomplete: a non-specific polity vaguely modelled on - what? Leopold’s Belgian Empire? Britain in India? Stalin’s Soviet Union? We know it’s brutal, arbitrary and acquisitive but we don’t get an org chart or a five-year plan. Vader’s status is essentially that of colonial enforcer. He’s not in charge (that’s the Emperor obvs) and he may not even be on the management committee. Strategy’s not his thing and he’s certainly not a figurehead. He’s important but he’s not a world-historical figure, despite his status in a state that spans a galaxy. Space Hegel would not have swooned and called Vader ‘the world-spirit in a tie fighter’. What Hegel thought he saw in Napoleon; his will to change everything, to overturn the old order and replace it with pure rationality, is not present here. And this obviously makes Vader, well, uninteresting. The history of the galaxy does not pass through him, he will not be remembered as anything other than a brute. To the Emperor’s Stalin he is not Trotsky but Beria. I’m no expert but I assume this explains the whole Sith situation - setting up a parallel regime in the shadowy, immaterial realm of The Force. It’s an effort to give Vader a more consequential role - beyond workplace bullying and brutalising the natives. Movies don’t need world-historical villains, of course. One-dimensional brutes are fine. But when a film aspires to importance, when we feel its creators are telling us something about the world - about power, dominion, government, family, society and so on - we need to believe that our villains have historical stature, even when they are not real. Kurtz, Lime, Corleone: all convince us that they sit at a critical juncture or that they will alter the direction of the larger storyline. It’s harder with science fiction, because there’s no historical context against which to set this villain and their villainy. But it’s not impossible. Bradbury, Herbert, Le Guin; Tarkovsky, Scott, Kubrick, all give us future villains who aspire to alter their timelines, leave a trace, beyond cruelty and domination. Operators who do more than enforce the plan. You’re going to have to forgive me for being prissy about this big, trashy, treasured entertainment brand but this is ultimately the weakness of The Empire Strikes Back and of the whole Star Wars franchise: this dumb, unmotivated conflict. This Empire: a vast, galaxy-wide enterprise, presumably built across centuries and at unimaginable cost - to those building it and to those who came up against it - apparently cares only about domination. And its necessary antagonist - its antithesis - the rebels, only care about opposing it. Neither apparently owns a positive vision for their world or for their people.

Wow, this might be the most overrated movie of all time. Beyond the visual spectacle and that classic score, there is almost nothing good here. In my previous review, I talked about the first Star Wars from 1977 and said that it was kinda good but had its problems. In this movie, those same problems return, but multiplied to the point where they fill the entire film. Things just keep happening and happening without any good construction or writing behind them. The relationships between the characters, my God, only get worse in terms of superficiality. It is painfully cringe-worthy to watch the forced romance between Han Solo and Princess Leia. The movie seems to imply that she, as a woman character, necessarily has to have a romance with one of the protagonists in order to be relevant in the film, because the plot keeps forcing this every time she appear, even when it doesn't make any sense. As I already pointed out in my previous review, her character is poorly written, and in this movie it only gets worse. The only character I genuinely liked in the first movie was Han Solo, and even they managed to ruin him here. Not even Harrison Ford could save it. The screenplay is so bad that it actually hurts. The dialogue sounds like it was written by a child. In fact, this entire movie feels like it came straight out of a story created by a child with an extremely vivid imagination. At one point, I just kept watching to see if it would remain this bad until the end, but I had absolutely no interest in what was happening, because this movie never managed to spark any in me. Finishing it was a struggle. The feeling I get is that all the visual spectacle and action scenes every five minutes are here to hide the superficiality and poor writing of the film. It keeps people engaged with explosions, gunfights, and spaceship chases. And judging by what people say about this movie, it seems to have worked. I genuinely don’t understand what people see as being so great here. I said I thought the first one already had problems, but I never imagined the second could be this bad, especially considering the acclaim it receives, which is even greater than the first film’s. And another thing: the performances are terrible. The material given to the actors isn’t good, and they didn’t have much to work with, since the writing of the characters is one of the worst aspects of this movie. But for God’s sake, the actor playing Luke Skywalker and the actress playing Princess Leia are absolutely dreadful. That probably explains why neither of them managed to land many significant roles outside the Star Wars saga. They aren’t the only terrible performances here, but I highlight them because they are playing the primary characters. In the end, the only memorable moments are the final sequence and the famous scene where Darth Vader reveals that he is Luke Skywalker’s father. Other than that, it is a pretty forgettable and overrated movie. Maybe this was the starting point for the culture of superficial blockbusters we see today, like superhero movies, for example. Films that use and abuse visual spectacle to hide their poor writing. I can say that Star Wars walked so Marvel could run. I was going to watch the entire original trilogy for the first time, but after this, I’m giving up. If this is supposed to be the best movie in the whole Star Wars franchise, I don’t even wanna know what the worst one is.

There’s always something so interesting and admittedly greedy when a writer/director see their movie do so well, they feel the need to make a sequel to capitalize on the success. Lucas himself was even half in and half out on it considering he gave the directing responsibilities to someone else. I think what made Star Wars work especially well is that they went into Empire seemingly planning on making a third as well. So this one allowed characters to breathe and explore other relationships. Luke spends all of maybe 5 minutes or so of screen time with everyone. He’s off getting lost, he’s healing, he’s being a pilot, then he’s with Yoda for a third of the film, then it’s the final battle. Hell they even split up R2 and 3P0 in this movie. They definitely went in with a few things in mind they wanted to get done. Get Luke started on being a Jedi, build up Han and Leia’s relationship (that part they could’ve done better imo), and make sure Vader is as intimidating and power housing as possible. And for the most part I think they did that very well. As for the twist, it’s so legendary. I’m pretty sure even before watching, I knew he was his dad. To be able to experience that for the first time would be legendary to see. I do like this movie a lot. I will say I do think I still like A New Hope just a little more. Mostly for it being a completed story and for seeing our group in action together. I love Yoda, I love Lando, our new characters add so much to the story and the franchise as a whole. Luke vs Vader is phenomenal from an emotionally aspect, yea not much else to add honestly.

The Empire Strikes Back ★★★★★ The Empire Strikes Back is one of the most perfect middle chapters in a trilogy ever created, and one of the best films ever made. As a kid, this absolutely blew me away. This was the Star Wars movie I would rent the most from the video store growing up, and returning to it now, it is easy to understand why it had such a hold on me. The story picks up with the Rebel Alliance hiding out on the frozen planet Hoth while the Empire searches for them. After the Rebels are attacked, Luke Skywalker begins a journey of Jedi training under the mysterious Yoda, while Han Solo, Princess Leia and Chewbacca attempt to escape Imperial forces. Their paths eventually lead them to Cloud City, where Darth Vader is waiting. The film expands the Star Wars universe considerably while giving its characters much more depth and putting them through some genuinely difficult situations. What makes Empire so remarkable is how much darker and more mature it feels than the original without losing the adventure and wonder that made Star Wars special. The Battle of Hoth remains one of the greatest action sequences in science-fiction, the introduction of Yoda is unforgettable, and the Millennium Falcon’s escape from the Empire is pure cinematic fun. Then there is the relationship between Han and Leia, which gives the movie an emotional center that balances all the spectacle. The film was directed by Irvin Kershner rather than George Lucas, who remained heavily involved as the creator and producer. Leigh Brackett and Lawrence Kasdan worked on the screenplay alongside Lucas. Lucas chose not to direct because he was simultaneously building Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, and the production ultimately became considerably more expensive and complicated than originally anticipated. The Hoth sequences were particularly brutal to make. The production traveled to Finse, Norway, where the crew dealt with temperatures approaching -30°C, heavy snowstorms and high winds. Some of the footage was shot only a few feet from the hotel because the weather made traveling farther nearly impossible. Fortunately, none of that misery shows on screen. It looks like another galaxy instead of a film crew wondering whether their fingers still work. The film opened on May 21, 1980, beginning its 70mm run in just 41 theaters across 16 cities before expanding. It had an $18 million production budget and earned $209,398,025 domestically during its original release. Later releases brought its domestic total to $292,753,960, while its worldwide total across releases reached $550,016,086. The original release also had an unusual box-office rollout by modern standards. It opened in a relatively small number of theaters, then expanded dramatically, reaching 1,278 theaters during its run. By the time it went wide, it was absolutely dominating the box office. Perhaps the greatest compliment that can be paid to The Empire Strikes Back is that it doesn’t feel like a movie designed simply to get audiences from the first film to the third. It stands completely on its own. The characters evolve, the universe gets larger, the stakes become more personal, and the filmmaking remains spectacular more than four decades later. Final Verdict The Empire Strikes Back is pretty much the gold standard for how to make the middle chapter of a trilogy. It expanded everything that worked about the original Star Wars, made the characters richer, delivered some unforgettable action and somehow managed to make the galaxy feel considerably bigger. For a movie that is essentially the middle piece of a larger story, it feels remarkably complete. Some sequels improve on their predecessors. This one helped define what a great sequel could be.

Empire Strikes Back didn’t just make the galaxy bigger, it made it deeper. It takes the adventure from A New Hope and gives it so much weight. Suddenly the galaxy now feels colder, darker, larger, and more complex.

“No like, I am your father” 2 hours of true cinematic greatness. This will forever be my favourite Star Wars film and there’s a reason it’s more often or not viewed as the best film. It’s just so great. The way this film presents the enemy is so incredible the “imperial march” soundtrack will always haunt me as I used to be terrified of Darth Vader as a kid and for good reason ! He is truly the figure head of this movie alongside Luke Skywalker. Every frame either of them are in just feels so important so poignant. They are involved in 3 all time scenes 3 of the best scenes not only in Star Wars history but in cinematic history aswell. The scene in degobah when he comes out from round the corner and we think we finally have this duel this duel of fates that we’ve been waiting for. It’s so scary to see Darth Vader in action like that, the way the camera moves and goes in and out of slow motion is genius. The first real fight on bespin is perhaps the best fight in the entire series, so quiet and restrained, Vader using his experience and his knowledge and Luke in contrast using confidence and sheer power at times to keep himself a float. It’s an unbelievable fight that lasts almost 10 minutes and 3 different sets! And of course who could forgot “no I am your father” one of the most influential moments in history one of the biggest plot twists in cinematic history and an absolute masterpiece in directing and story telling. The lead up to this is absolutely insane and I can imagine watching this in cinemas in the 80s not having a clue what’s about to come, I remember being shocked when I first watched it so watching it in the cinemas must have been a experience of a lifetime. The reaction from Luke the speech after from Vader it’s truly one of the best moments in the history of cinema, goosebumps every-time. Away from that we have so much more good in this film, Han and Leia were a great choice and whenever and whoever decided to have them 2 together should get a reward because there meant for each other. The back in forth they have throughout the whole first act makes the eventual pay off so worth it. Yoda is introduced as this scrawny almost annoying little green man but eventually his influence on the film becomes apparent, the whole degobah sequence is great. The introduction of the emperor is one of my favourite things as they present him in a way where we see Lord Vader bowing down and following orders from him. Standing over him speaking about the force and conveying that this is anakins son makes him seem and sound so powerful more powerful that anyone else, so harrowing in the way he speaks signifying to the audience that no matter how powerful Vader is he is the man in charge… absolutely mythical filmmaking. The sets, the cinematography, the soundtrack, the world building it’s all there in this film and to think it came out in 1980 is just absurd. It’s one of the greatest films of all time and will continue to stand the test of time for a very very long time. What a name aswell “the empire strikes back” fucking sick !

I know a lot of people absolutely love A Quiet Place. I wanted to. I really did. Especially because I genuinely like the actors involved. But for me, this film was mostly just boring. The central concept is interesting. A world where making noise can get you killed should create enormous tension. Every movement matters. Every sound matters. Even basic everyday actions suddenly become dangerous. On paper, that is a fantastic horror premise. In practice, I spent a lot of the film waiting for something to happen. And not in the good, tension building way. Just waiting. The movie relies heavily on silence and restraint, but for me that restraint never transformed into enough suspense to justify how little actually happens. That is especially frustrating because I can see why the concept works for other people. The silence creates vulnerability. The limited communication creates tension. The threat is constantly present. I understand all of that. It just never grabbed me emotionally. There were also far too many questions left unanswered for my taste. I do not need a horror film to explain every detail of its world, but I do need enough information to feel like the rules and the setting are more than just a convenient framework for suspense. Here, too much remained vague. That made the world feel less fascinating rather than more mysterious. The performances are good. The concept is good. The execution simply does not work for me. And that is probably the most disappointing kind of film. Not one where I cannot understand the appeal. One where I understand it perfectly and still feel absolutely nothing. A clever horror concept with strong actors that somehow left me more bored than tense, with too little happening and too much left unexplained.

A lógica interna do universo desmorona à menor análise, seja pela decisão ABSURDA da família de engravidar em um mundo onde o choro de um bebê é uma sentença de morte, ou pela conveniência de uma cachoeira barulhenta anular os monstros de forma tão óbvia. No final, o filme sacrifica o terror genuíno em prol de um melodrama sentimentalista e de personagens que tomam atitudes incompreensíveis apenas para fazer o roteiro avançar…

Amazing atmosphere. Great premise. Completely overshadowed by a glaring lack of basic common sense. First of all, who the hell decides to get pregnant in a world where a single baby's cry is an instant death sentence for the entire family? Second, we are expected to believe the entire global military power, hundreds of naval fleets, and top-tier research labs couldn't figure out that a basic high-frequency sound messes with the monsters? You don't need a railgun; you apparently just need a loud speaker playing feedback. Third, who walks through a hyper-dangerous acoustic wasteland and puts their kids, especially the youngest, most unpredictable one, all the way at the back of the line where nobody can see him? Dumb writers, amazing concept. 2 stars for execution.

I love the concept here. The fact that you literally can’t make a single sound without potentially dying is super intense. There were several moments where even I, as an audience member, was shushing the noises they were making. That being said, there was a stupid decision made just for the sake of having a second half of this movie. For whatever reason, after Beau died, Lee and Evelyn thought it would be a great idea to bring another baby into this quiet world. You know, a baby that cries all the time and has no control over the noises they make. So somehow Lee and Evelyn have another baby, and 9 months later they have to come up with this huge elaborate plan to make loud noises during the birth so Evelyn and the baby don’t die. It was a really stupid decision on their part, especially because this whole situation ends up getting Lee killed. Now Evelyn has three kids all by herself, one of whom is deaf and another who is a newborn. I also hated the look of the aliens. We’re in 2018 and they somehow look worse than the troll from the original Harry Potter movies. I did really like Lee’s sacrifice, though. He realizes he has to save his kids, who are separated from him in the truck. He quickly signs to Regan that he loves her and has always loved her because she thinks he hates her for Beau’s death. Then Lee screams at the top of his lungs so the aliens go after him instead of the kids. That was easily one of my favorite parts of the movie. I also think this set up a sequel well because now they know what the aliens’ weakness is. It’s a solid movie and I really liked the concept, but those complaints bring the score down for me. 58.16%

A Quiet Place has such a strong premise and there are definitely moments where the tension works really well, but I don’t think I connected with it as much as I expected to. John Krasinski and Emily Blunt are both really, really good throughout. Their performances do a lot of the heavy lifting because so much of the film relies on looks, body language and small reactions rather than dialogue. The family dynamic feels believable, and there’s enough emotion underneath everything to make the quieter moments work. I just struggled with how little actual dialogue there is. I understand that’s obviously the entire concept of the film, but there were definitely points where I found myself skipping forward 10 seconds here and there because the silence started to drag for me. It wasn’t necessarily boring, because there is always tension underneath it, but it did make parts of the film feel slower than they probably were. The sign language was also a problem for me because the version I watched didn’t actually give me subtitles for most of it, so there were quite a few conversations where I was basically just guessing what was being said. That obviously isn’t really the film’s fault, but it definitely affected my experience watching it. There are some really effective sequences though. The sound design is clever, the creatures are intimidating, and I liked how vulnerable the family always feels because one tiny mistake can basically get them killed. Krasinski sacrificing himself towards the end also genuinely got to me. I didn’t expect that moment to make me as sad as it did, but it works because the relationship between him and his kids has been built up so quietly throughout the film. I can completely understand why people love this, and I do think it’s a good film. I just don’t think the silent format fully worked for me personally. There were moments where I was really engaged, but there were also moments where I was just waiting for something to happen. Good premise, strong performances, great tension in places, but not one I connected with as much as I hoped.

Dystopia as a genre acts as a medium to warn the audience of a potential future. It comes as a warning as to what might happen if we don't change. Apocalypse is the ashes of dystopia and (in at least my mind) piggybacks off of similar concepts. In order for apocalypse to work it has to have rhyme, reason and a message. There must be cause and reason to our suffering. In AQP there is no cause. And there is so reason. All I gained from the ending was the empty feeling that I should've just doomscrolled tumblr instead and we are never once made aware of the causes of this apocalypse. While supernatural and monsterish apocalypse can exist they typically only work when tied to preexisting beliefs or a sublime divinity (like the 7 trumpets or mayan calender of 2012) so when a random out-of-the-blue unexplained creature shows up I simply do not care. What works in the apocalypse of movies like the 28 series is the undeniable humanity and plausibility of how it happened and what follows it. The first of the series haunts me because of the actions of humanity which I can frankly see people enacting but that terror of possibility is not present in this film. When I look at other apocalypse films I see warning and I see dread for the future. When I look at this I see a pathetic wet dream and a longing to be good. And I'll throw it a bone. It isn't good. It's perfect. Perfectly fucking mediocre.

Well keknya emang Wes Anderson bukan buat gw ya. Kek film anak anak, jir. Apalagi setelah nonton The Grand Budapest Hotel. Itu juga satu satunya film dia yang pernah gw tonton sebelumnya, terus gw penasaran sama Fantastic Mr. Fox ini. Tapi pas selesai nonton, reaksinya malah kek "dah gitu doang?” Sama kek pas nonton Budapest, gw akuin visualnya cakep banget, stylenya khas parah, tapi ceritanya tuh ga terlalu ngena ke gw. Entah emang gw yang ga cocok sama gaya si Wes atau gimana dah. Ini film basically tentang Mr. Fox, seekor rubah yang udah janji sama istrinya buat berhenti nyolong, tapi akhirnya balik lagi jadi pencuri karena gabisa nahan sifatnya sendiri. Dia nyolong dari tiga petani kaya dan bikin seluruh hewan di sekitar mereka kena masalah karena para petani itu ngejar mereka. Akhirnya, mereka harus kabur dan bertahan hidup di bawah tanah. Ceritanya simple banget, literally kayak dongeng anak anak yang dibikin jadi film stop motion superduper niat. Tapi keknya maknanya lebih dalam dari sekadar rubah yang nyolong makanan sih. Mr. Fox tuh kayak gambaran manusia yg susah lepas dari sifat dan ambisinya sendiri. Dia udah punya keluarga, kehidupan yang aman, bahkan udah janji buat berhenti, tapi tetap aja nyari sensasi dan pengakuan karena emang itu bagian dari dirinya. Di sisi lain, film ini juga ngomongin soal menerima diri sendiri dan beradaptasi setelah keputusan kita punya konsekuensi. Jadi yaa gw ngerti maksudnya sekarang, cuma tetap aja pas ending gw masih kayak, Lah udah gitu doangg?🗿 jujur buat ngehate nih film rasanya kek ilegal bat jir soalnya semua orang sukaa🗿🗿🗿

Alors... je dois reconnaître que d'un point de vue technique il est très très très chouette. Il y a beaucoup d'idées très fun et dynamiques dans l'animation, et on retrouve le style Wes Anderson qui marche généralement bien pour la mise en scène de l'univers. Maintenant mon gros souci c'est que je suis incapable de voir cette histoire autrement que par le prisme de l'adaptation. Je connais beaucoup trop par cœur et je suis beaucoup trop attaché à l'histoire originale pour l'oublier durant le visionnage. Et je n'ai pas vraiment, pour ne pas dire pas du tout, apprécié ce qui a été fait de l'histoire. Les personnages ont complètement changé (genre vraiment Maître Renard c'est un connard), leurs dynamiques sont à l'opposé de ce qu'elles étaient dans le livre, et je n'ai éprouvé aucune sympathie ou réelle émotion pour des personnages affreusement clichés et revus à l'extrême. Déçu par les dialogue aussi, d'une lourdeur que je ne comprends pas. Big up au doublage français nonobstant qui rassemble avec succès des pointures du métier (Emmanuel Garijo je t'aime) avec pour seule fausse note la prestation plutôt merdique d'Isabelle Huppert, et ce refus de traduction de "Mr Fox" là j'avoue je m'interroge. Mais même si on a vaguement plusieurs scènes qui sont les mêmes, la grande majorité du récit original a été complètement oubliée pour le rallonger artificiellement avec une intrigue originale qui trahit fondamentalement le point de vue sur le monde que Roald Dahl partageait grâce à son roman. Le coup de la recherche de ce réalisme dans la relation entre les animaux et les fermiers c'est n'avoir rien compris à la dimension de conte du récit de Roald Dahl, et donc n'avoir pas compris grand chose au roman. Si seulement on y gagnait à travers cette autre vision qu'est censé être l'adaptation, mais je trouve qu'aucun changement ne se justifie dans sa propre diégèse, et qu'aucun changement n'améliore le récit d'une quelconque façon. L'écriture est paresseuse, et c'est limite si j'arrivais à croire aux évolutions de personnages. Et la fin du film est à des années lumières de l'intensité du dénouement du livre, et de l'absurde dans lequel on est censé laisser les antagonistes (qui est censé être d'un effet critique impactant et dévastateur). Là c'est traité comme une vanne et on enchaîne sur pas grand-chose d'intéressant pour clore ce film de manière satisfaisante. Non pour moi c'est un échec, et d'ailleurs Anderson a beaucoup mieux réussi son pari récemment avec Henry Sugar en embrassant complètement la storytelling de Roald Dahl et en refaisant passer le narrateur au premier plan, lui qui est quelqu'un d'extrêmement important chez l'auteur. D'ailleurs il est censé l'être aussi dans "Fantastique Maître Renard". Bref, ce film a sans doute beaucoup de mérite objectif, et probablement plus que ce que je suis malheureusement capable d'en percevoir.

😎 xuao: Toda indicação/comentário que recebemos sobre o filme eram positivos e contemplavam sua genialidade, dito isso, acho que vimos o filme errado. 🤓 xuvana: É absolutamente fascinante a capacidade contemporânea de confundir esmero estético com relevância artística. Pudemos observar a subversão da fina ironia e fleumático humor britânico de Roald Dahl, transmutando assim sua sutil excentricidade em um carrossel de caricaturas americanizadas onde até mesmo o título — antes tributo a uma astúcia heroica paterna — desmorona em um eco irônico de pura vaidade e crise de meia-idade. Quanto ao humor e ao enredo... bom, seria preciso possuir ambos para comentá-los com rigor. O longa caminha resoluto na corda bamba entre não ser cáustico o bastante para divertir nem profundo o suficiente para instigar. Passamos mais da metade da projeção aguardando ansiosamente pelo famigerado clique✨ aquele súbito epiphany epifânico que justificaria os aplausos unânimes da turba entusiasta, enquanto tentávamos decifrar se o tédio que nos consumia era mérito genuíno do roteiro ou apenas o resultado dessa afetação blasé meticulosamente encenada para gritar ao mundo a sua própria e artificial singularidade.

فيلم حلو وخفيف وأجواءه كلش مميزة، وحبيت الألوان وطريقة التصوير والتفاصيل الصغيرة اللي بيه و الشخصيات لطيفة وكل شخصية إلها طابعها الخاص، والموسيقى هم جانت مناسبة للأجواء بشكل حلو. حسيت الفيلم عنده ستايل مختلف ومميز، ويخلي المشاهدة ممتعة حتى لو كانت قصته بسيطة. بس بصراحة فكرة الفيلم نفسها ما حبيتها كلش، وما حسيتها من الأفكار اللي تشدني أو تخليني أندمج وياها، وبعض الأحداث حسيتها غريبة شوي. مع هذا، طريقة تقديم الفكرة والجو العام للفيلم كانوا حلوين، وما ندمت على مشاهدته أبدًا. التقييم: ⭐️⭐️⭐️/5 A sweet and lighthearted film with a very distinctive atmosphere. I loved the colors, the cinematography, and the small details. The characters are charming, each with their own unique personality, and the music perfectly complemented the mood. I felt the film had a different and unique style, making it enjoyable even with its simple plot. However, I honestly didn't particularly like the film's premise; it didn't appeal to me or draw me in, and some of the events felt a bit strange. Despite this, the way the idea was presented and the overall atmosphere of the film were good, and I didn't regret watching it at all. Rating:5/⭐⭐⭐

Wes Anderson non è un regista facile o immediato e questo film ne è la piena manifestazione. Quello che può sembrare, all'apparenza, un semplice e divertente film d'animazione nasconde sotto la sua superficie chissà quanti significati nascosti. Visivamente, siamo davanti ad uno degli apici di questo cineasta, che fa della stop motion il sue mezzo perfetto. Il character design è strepitoso ed i colori utilizzati portano ad un'atmosfera accogliente e calorosa. Alcune sequenze sono strepitose, cito il combattimento tra Mr Fox e il retto o il bombardamento con le pigne. Come già detto, non bisogna certo soffermarsi alla sola superficie. Fantastic Mr. Fox merita di essere visto e rivisto e di essere analizzato in ogni dettaglio. Emblematica la scena con il lupo sul finale, che sprigiona tutta l'emotività che questa folle pellicola può emanare. Come con tutti i film di Anderson, ho bisogno di una seconda visione, ma ciò che ho visto mi ha già convinto molto!

The ending was sweet. I think it was an interesting story they were trying to tell. & you know A24 is gonna do it in a non straight forward way. I didn’t think it was bad, a little trippy though with the mix of shots of reality mixed thoughts sometimes crazy ones. On Charlie’s side I think they were trying to show some type of obsession & what that does after a prolonged time with no proper outlet. With Emma, I think they were trying to show the limits of human thoughts before executing on it. In a more straightforward way the movie literally talks about how many people we know or interact in society that have planned something heinous but didn’t go through with it. Like a school shooting. I think it’s interesting because most people would keep those dark thoughts to themselves no matter what. You know like the saying “even batman wouldn’t get this info outta me”. So the fact the Emma shares this evil intention of a school shooting with the group, and you see how the characters divulge after it is truly interesting. Especially because in real life I think people would be too guarded to even share information as sensitive as that.

The Drama, personally, wasn’t really for me. I feel like the whole conflict starts because of the man, who makes way too big of a deal out of a situation that could have been handled differently. Despite that, I found the way they carried out the story and how the conflict kept escalating really interesting. I don’t agree with the characters’ decisions, but I did enjoy seeing how far things went and how the movie developed the whole situation.

I understand that gun violence is not the point nor the discussion presented in the movie, but wow what a shallow and half-baked thematic exploration about morality and the capacity for change without tapping into any of its potential conversations it could have had about women, the psyche, and mass scale violence like this. I saw someone call this an “almost European take on gun violence discourse” (again, knowing that the point of this movie has nothing to do with gun violence) and I couldn’t agree more. Just a really flat, shallow arc. Zendaya’s character is portrayed as very sweet, demure, and shy, and so once the rising plot action was presented I expected something innovative and profound. Once I knew where the plot was going, I was SO BORED and genuinely said “oh that’s it. Someone read this script and decided to fund it.” Out loud. It gets two stars because I loveeee the visual storytelling and how this is shot. I think Zendaya and RP have such good on screen chemistry and want to see them together again. Idk babes… this could have gone anywhere and went nowhere. It was just so FLAT.

Maybe (definitely) I am too demanding when it comes to cinema and maybe (for sure) I am too strict with my ratings, but the plot was just not it. I was not too shocked by the plotwist because I already knew the film's premise so that surely changed my perspective of it, as well as the surprise-effect. Despite of these complaints, I love every single movie that makes me reflect about what I just watched, even if it might be a stupid and useless consideration. The way the story develops is absolutely absurd in my opinion, but still I caught it as an irrational metaphor for all the trust and stability issues that concern marriage. I am a bit disappointed by the fact that they probably added Charlie's cheating as a quicker and easier resolution in order to put him in a bad light and to help the audience being more empathetic with Emma. It worked indeed, even though the actions can't be compared, at least solely based on their objective nature. By highlighting the couple's mistakes (and exaggerating them till their limits) the story shows that no one is perfect, wether it be the most scenical or daily actions. Regarding Rachel's character, I've read so much hate towards her. Of course we cannot forget that she ruined someone's wedding, but anyway it seemed like Charlie and Emma's relationship was already on thin ice, so I wouldn't address all the responsibility on her. She might be an incoherent woman and a vendicative friend. At least she was right about one thing though: they're perfect for each other... because they're both equally mad, I would add. The ending saved the film. Totally expected and plain. However, exactly what I wanted to see.

The movie is about second chances. We all make mistakes. To be human is to err. What matters is not being perfect, but realizing our wrongdoings as soon as possible, taking accountability, and changing so we don’t repeat them. That’s what feels realistic. And that’s powerful. That’s also how civilization improves — by giving people second chances. Even the idea behind punishment in society is, ideally, to give a person time to understand their wrongdoing, its consequences, and eventually get rehabilitated. But reality is often very different. Drama explores this grey area. How important are second chances? How should we treat people who make mistakes? Should we define a person by their worst mistake? Is that really how we build a better world? Or should we make more of an effort to understand the context first?

“What’s the worst thing you’ve ever done?” That question is the catalyst for the titular drama in Kristoffer Borgli’s fourth feature film. I’ve only seen Sick of Myself before this, and Borgli certainly has a unique style and a certain type of feel connecting these films. That is overthinkers and the anxiety of how we are seen in the modern world. Borgli uses rapid editing, extreme close-ups, an unrelenting score, and my personal favorite in both these films, the worst-case scenarios our protagonists envision in their minds. This time around, though, I think Borgli is coming from a much warmer place, yet this film still has the unnervingly awkward humor that he’s really mastered. This film is about how the almost picture-book romance between Emma and Charlie we see in the opening sequence of the film is completely recontextualized once Emma reveals the worst thing she’s ever done. However, I would say what the film is really doing is showing what the worst thing Charlie has done is and his whole process leading up to it, which he was unable to answer when first asked. He completely fails to give Emma the proper empathy in this situation and lets his biggest questions fester in his head until it completely breaks him, leading him to fantasize about Emma’s past and make up false narratives about why instead of listening to her and seeing the person she has grown into. He even goes as far as deleting his entire speech about all the things he loves about her and cheating on her. Yet we do empathize with him while he is making every horrible decision possible in this film because, yes, learning what we do about Emma does fundamentally change how he sees her and how we, the audience, do. Emma is not given the grace that the other players of their game are. While both Rachel and Mike’s stories resulted in real harm, the societal taboo of Emma’s plan makes everyone immediately turn on her. I think the first question they should have asked Emma is why she didn’t go through with it. Instead, she is ostracized by Rachel, who shows her lack of growth from her adolescence, and Alana Haim does a great job portraying this mean-girl, holier-than-thou energy that I’m sure Emma had to deal with before. Also, you gotta feel bad for Mike cause he genuinely seems like a chill dude. Back to Emma, though, because as she and Charlie discuss it, we can understand the why, even if there never really is a why in these scenarios. Emma was young, lonely, insecure, new in a town with no friends, and bullied, and as she says, the aesthetic is what captured her, which I think is a common case for a lot of people in her shoes. Now, when the actual shooting happens in her town, Emma is confronted with the reality of the situation, and we see she’s not a psychopath but just alone, and she uses the tragedy to make friends. She starts protesting, and like she says to Charlie, it wasn’t her being a poser but waking up from her bad dream and escaping her fantasy, which does lead her to be the person Charlie writes about in the beginning. I think Charlie also comes to that conclusion in the end as he tries to deliver his speech at the wedding but completely collapses under all the stress he caused himself, which results in an incredibly cringeworthy but hilarious scene as he tries to communicate all those things about Emma, but instead he pukes out all his thoughts, ruining their wedding night and getting his ass kicked. In the end, though, we get this beautiful scene of Charlie going to the diner where Emma asked to go on their wedding night alone when he initially blew off the idea. This is where we see the difference between Emma and Charlie and why they are perfect for each other, as Emma also walks into the diner, orders her cheeseburger, and sits down with Charlie. And she does what Charlie couldn’t: start over and give Charlie a second chance, which is what I think the film is really trying to say. When you truly love someone, it means giving them a chance to improve with support to be better, which is what Charlie doesn’t do for their wedding DJ, which sets off this whole mess, and then they are stuck with this horrible DJ in the end. Also, the acting from Zendaya and Pattinson is phenomenal. I love what they are doing with their faces in this, reacting to everything. They also both give us such insight and empathy for these characters. Also, their chemistry is great in this, especially that opening sequence. Also, shoutout to Hailey Benton Gates for being a baddie in this. But yeah, The Drama is a hilariously cringeworthy but empathetic look into love and the baggage we all carry and hide from others.

The drama mi ha spiazzato perché mi aspettavo una cosa e invece me ne sono trovata un'altra molto più gradita. Cosa c'è di più pesante di scoprire qualcosa della persona che stai per sposare che ti lascia spiazzato e ti fa completamente cambiare prospettiva verso di lei? Nulla credo, e questo film ti fa sentire lungo tutta la durata proprio i sentimenti di confusione che provano dentro i due protagonisti (interpretati da due perfetti Robert Pattinson e Zendaya). L'intuizione brillante del regista non sta tanto nel segreto in sé — la confessione di Emma di aver pianificato una strage scolastica in gioventù, atto poi mai compiuto ed espiato attraverso un successivo attivismo contro le armi — quanto negli effetti psicologici che questa rivelazione scatena. Il passato non serve a giustificare il presente, ma diventa il detonatore di una crisi d'identità relazionale. Charlie si ritrova improvvisamente a convivere con una sconosciuta, ed è qui che il film scava un solco profondo nello spettatore: chi è davvero la persona che abbiamo accanto?In questo scenario, il film rifiuta saggiamente di dividere il mondo in buoni e cattivi. Non c'è un colpevole univoco. questa storia è una radiografia dell'ipocrisia umana: mostra con quanta spaventosa rapidità siamo disposti a revocare l'amore e la stima verso qualcuno, dimenticando anni di vita condivisa a causa di un singolo frammento del passato. The Drama diventa così una riflessione universale sul concetto di fiducia e sul peso del "non detto". Ci costringe a chiederci se siamo davvero capaci di ascoltare e accettare il cambiamento dell'altro, o se pretendiamo una purezza utopica. La verità che il film ci sbatte in faccia è tanto complessa quanto reale: ognuno di noi custodisce zone d'ombra e segreti inconfessabili. Amare qualcuno non significa pretendere la trasparenza assoluta fin dal primo giorno, ma avere il coraggio di accogliere anche i difetti dell'altro, accettando che la conoscenza di chi ci sta accanto è un processo continuo, imperfetto e che a volte provoca dolore. Leggo alcune critiche sul fatto che il film introduca il tema delle armi per lasciarlo un po' li ma a mio parere, per quanto sia un problema di attualità in America, non è ciò su cui il regista stesso si vuole soffermare. A mio parere la volontà era più quella di dare una lettura cinica della nostra società e ci riesce anche soltanto con un personaggio secondario, Rachel, forse uno dei più odiosi che abbia mai visto negli ultimi anni e che rappresenta proprio l'ipocrisia in persona. Tu che hai quasi rischiato di ammazzare un bimbo ti ritieni superiore di una che ha pianificato una strage a 14 anni solo perché ritieni che il tuo gesto non essendo pianificato è stato meno grave del suo e non vuoi nemmeno ascoltare le motivazioni dell'altro. Ho notato poi alcune critiche focalizzate sul tema delle armi da fuoco in America lamentandone una lettura parziale. A mio parere però le armi sono solo un pretesto narrativo per allestire proprio una cinica radiografia della nostra società. La volontà credo fosse proproo far emergere una distorsione sistemica che è incarnata da uno dei personaggi più odiosi viste in un film negli ultimi anni, Rachel. Lei incarna proprio l'ipocrisia elevata a norma sociale perché la sua assenza di empatia e la sfacciata presunzione di superiorità morale creano un cortocircuito etico destabilizzante: ho davvero il diritto di condannare una mia amica per un atto pianificato a 14 anni quando io stessa ho rischiato di causare un morto pur involontariamente? Davvero sono migliore dell'altro? È quindi grazie a questi che il regista ci mostra l'inflessibilità di una società che preferisce vantarsi delle proprie virtù senza capire la reale complessità insita nel processo di crescita dell'essere umano. la potenza del regista si vede anche in quelle scene che sembrano inizialmente ridicole ma riflettendo sono tra le più dramamtiche per le persone che stanno vivendo un momento simile e che a mio parere sono piro black humor. Un film che poteva essere un banale amici amici e poi ti inculano la bici ma che riesce sia a un'interpretazione ottima degli attori che da una serie di immagini e idee di regia a veicolare un messaggio potenzialmente banale in modo molto più crudo.

Acabo de ver esta gran película y me tenía súper ansioso. Tiene unas escenas tan bien construidas que me hicieron sentir la incomodidad de los personajes y lograron que me sintiera parte del juicio moral que se estaba llevando a cabo y justo fue de las cosas que más disfruté de la película: que nunca llegué a sentirme cómodo juzgando a ninguno de los personajes porque cada vez que me quedaba claro lo que pensaba de ellos, me daba otra razón para cuestionarme. El personaje de Rachel es exquisito y muy odioso, pero hace muy bien su papel de representar ese juicio social del que todos terminamos formando parte. La película logró llevarme por un viaje donde me la pasaba preguntándome si realmente es válido el juicio social que se le está haciendo a Emma, si la actitud de Charlie es la correcta y si realmente los personajes se merecen lo que está sucediendo. Me costó llegar a este pensamiento pero después de ponerme a analizar lo que veía entendí que  justo la película hace algo más interesante que andar jugando al abogado del diablo: Primero juzgas a Emma. Después empiezas a cuestionar a Charlie. Después cuestionas a los demás. Y justo al final me di cuenta que estaba juzgando desde una posición bastante cómoda. Y ahí está una de las cosas que más disfruté, me hizo preguntarme: ¿Cuál de todas nuestras versiones somos realmente? Emma fue una adolescente capaz de planear algo terrible. Emma adulta parece ser otra persona. Charlie llega a considerarse moralmente diferente de Emma pero termina haciendo algo que contradice la imagen que tiene de sí mismo. THE DRAMA no parece afirmar que descubramos una versión “real” de nosotros mismos. Más bien parece preguntarse si somos capaces de aceptar que una persona puede contener versiones de sí misma que se contradicen. En la película esto se vuelve muy evidente durante la boda, cuando todos terminan perdiendo la cordura y esas versiones que habían construido de sí mismos empiezan a romperse. The Drama jugó con mi cabeza todo el tiempo. Cuando crees que ya sabes quién tiene la razón, te pone otra cosa enfrente y te hace volver a cuestionarlo. Y bueno tanto Zendaya como Robert Pattinson 10/10 👏🏽 que bien se ven en pantalla lo hicieron increíble pt*m como te amo Zendaya.

I firmly believe what Rachel did is way worse than what Emma did, and that is the absolute truth.   Obviously, we can't ignore the marketing, which gave the movie a massive boost because it got everyone so much more invested. The most magical thing about this film is the core dilemma it presents: what's worse, something you merely thought about doing or something you actually did? Can people genuinely change after a long period of time? Does love really conquer all? How well do you actually know the person sitting right next to you? But above all else: to what extent do you even have the right to judge?   Asking these questions, alongside the movie's absurdist tone and the various events triggered by Emma's big confession, makes the film a thousand percent intriguing. On top of that, you have this insane level of acting from the entire cast: it feels like real life drama unfold. Those arguments, Charlie's sheer fear, and Emma being so misunderstood make for a incredible watch. Emma is easily my favorite character in the film and I love her. We've already established that I adore morally questionable movies, and this one delivered on every single level. Best of all, though, is the film's ultimate message: you can always get a fresh start.

Every adult in this film operates with the same scripted obliviousness - a village full of people who cannot hear a child asking a simple question, not because the film has something to say about how the world ignores children, but because the plot requires him to keep running. The frustration isn't the productive kind that builds toward meaning; it's the mechanical kind where you can see the hand of the script redirecting every conversation away from resolution, and by the halfway mark the contrivance has drained whatever warmth the premise held. Kiarostami would go on to make Taste of Cherry, a film that earns its circling - this one just circles.

Maybe I woke up on the wrong side of the bed this morning, I’ve been struggling as of late and this particular morning was especially heavy in some respects, but I was much less into this movie than I expected to be. In fact… It kinda did the opposite of give me hope? It’s rad that other people at Film School took Where Is The Friend’s House? as an exercise in compassion and humanity’s good, but uh… Woof. Every single adult in this made me so angry. They were so cruel and uncaring that it was hard for me to think that any of the kids who were so kind hearted here would ever grow up in a society where they could hold on to that goodness. It’s certainly impactful in its exploration of kids being much more compassionate than adults, but you pair what I took as a rather negative view of what the world does to people over time with the incredibly rhythmic (dare I say repetitive) structure and I couldn’t help but be left frustrated by this film. Maybe this is more so because I am so frustrated by the way life itself is going, however? There was some humor that I’ll admit vibed with me and the main character’s sweetness is undeniably wholesome at times, but the bleak portrayal of the adults and world around our protagonist constantly kept me in a state of discomfort. I was feeling a whole lot of dread for my own future as someone who has been desperately fighting to cling on to the hope I had as a kid. Where Is The Friend’s House? is an interesting movie that I think is well made on the whole but it just didn’t quite jive for me personally. In a weird way I guess I think it’s good, but still don’t really like it? I dunno. I feel guilty for not loving it but I did still end up having a great time chatting with folks at Film School about it after our screening. The night’s conversations definitely made me reflect on the movie in ways that made it much more compelling to me in retrospect. The drive to Portland was still very much worth it for that camaraderie too. It feels really good to be a part of a community and that was one of the things I was really worried about missing out on in life when I woke up this morning. So, at the end of the night my spirits were lifted a bit after all thanks to being among a room of friends who love my favorite art form as much as me and continually open my eyes to new ways of understanding film. Boy is this life hard though… Maybe I’ll have to revisit Where Is The Friend’s House? when mine is in a more stable place. Or at least a more hopeful one? Life can be a lot of things, but I’m not sure if stable will ever be one of them.

Kiarostami captures the suffocating frustration of being a kid in a world run by adults who talk over you, ignore your urgency, and enforce arbitrary rules. Watching Ahmed navigate the winding dirt paths of Koker feels absurdly suspenseful for a movie with zero high stakes on paper. It gets a bit repetitive in the middle, and the extreme minimalism demands real patience, but the quiet triumph of the final shot is pure magic.

Where Is the Friend’s House? is a film with some genuinely wonderful qualities, but personally, I just couldn’t fully connect with it. What bothered me most was the way the adults are portrayed. Ahmad desperately walks around the village trying to return his friend Mohammad Reza Nematzadeh’s notebook, yet one adult after another fails to properly listen to what he is saying. I understand that the film is trying to explore the idea that “adults don’t understand children,” but it often feels like the characters are deliberately written to make the audience side with Ahmad and become frustrated with the adults. There are several scenes where a child is desperately trying to explain his situation, only for the adult to keep talking about something completely unrelated. At times, it felt a little too obvious that the film was trying to make me go, “Oh my god, just LISTEN to the kid.” Of course, the adults aren’t all portrayed as simply bad people. Even the teacher has his reasons: Mohammad Reza Nematzadeh has repeatedly ignored the same rule, and toward the end he even tells the other students that people should be allowed a few mistakes. That makes it difficult to reduce the adults to a simple good-versus-evil dynamic. Still, the film’s structure clearly seems designed to push the audience emotionally toward Ahmad. In that respect, I think François Truffaut’s The 400 Blows, which deals with the same basic idea of “adults don’t understand children,” handles it much better. The adults there have their own reasons and circumstances, while the protagonist himself is far from blameless. Yet we still sympathize with him because nobody really understands him, leaving us with much more complicated feelings. That said, there are definitely things I loved about Where Is the Friend’s House? The music that plays when Ahmad decides to return the notebook and sets off on his journey is absolutely beautiful. It makes this simple errand feel like a genuinely huge adventure from a child’s perspective. I also loved the way the flower is used throughout the film. The flower Ahmad receives from the craftsman, and especially the flower placed inside the notebook at the end, is a beautiful touch. It quietly symbolizes what Ahmad did for his friend and gives the ending a lovely sense of aftertaste. I’m very drawn to Kiarostami’s cinematic sensibility and the beauty of his filmmaking, and I certainly don’t think this is a bad movie. I just found the way it portrays the relationship between children and adults somewhat too deliberate and manipulative for my taste. I still prefer Taste of Cherry, which I watched previously, especially for its ambiguity and the distance it maintains between its characters. This is only the first film of the trilogy, and I still haven’t seen the other two, so I definitely don’t want to judge the entire Koker trilogy based on this one movie. I’m 100% watching all three though. Can’t leave it at just one lol.

Прогулка с дедом и все последние сцены были оч красивы, ток из-за них мб и тянет фильм хотя бы на 4ку. My second Kiarostami, and a good one.  He seems to have a knack for capturing humanity.  I loved Ahmad’s conscientious commitment to his friend.  He knows he caused him trouble, and once he realizes it, he spends hours trying to make it right.  When the obvious solution fails, he simply finds another one. Doesn’t exactly paint parents or adults in a flattering light.  Maybe it’s exaggerated, but I definitely remember adults seeming dismissive to the point of exasperation as a kid.  I probably had the benefit of being able to speak up without much consequence.  The adults here seem especially strict, and uninterested in actually hearing him. The film has a beautiful understanding of a well-meaning child’s perspective.  Ahmad’s mission is enormously important to him, and Kiarostami makes it just as important to us.

Filmin ilk dəqiqələrində öz sinifim yadıma düşdü. Tanış səhnələr, uşaqların danışığı, aralarındakı münasibətlər… Bəzi sözlər də tanış idi. Uşaqların üzərindəki o gərginlik məni çox narahat etdi. Böyüklərin dünyasında adi görünən şeylərin uşaqlar üçün necə böyük bir məsuliyyətə çevrildiyini hiss edirsən. Bir tərəfdən də dostu ağlayarkən ona diqqətlə baxan o balaca oğlan var. Üzündən onun dostuna görə pis olduğu açıq-aydın görünür. Sonra çölə çıxanda dostunun yenə qayğısına qalır: yıxılanda onu ayağa qaldırır, balaca əlləri ilə şalvarındakı tozları təmizləyir, “ağrıyır?” deyə soruşur. Çox sadə hərəkətdir, amma o qədər dəyərlidir ki. Kaş bütün uşaqlar bunu bacarsa. Hətta uşaqlar yox, böyüklər də. Mən isə uşaqlıqdan yıxıldığım zaman özüm ayağa qalxmağı öyrənmişəm. Çünki başqalarının məni yıxıldığım üçün tənqid edəcəyini, zəif görəcəyini düşünmüşəm. Məni qaldıran bir dostum olmayıb. Bəlkə də buna görə filmdəki o balaca uşağın digər uşağa göstərdiyi qayğı mənə bu qədər toxundu. Sonra evdə ana ilə uşağın münasibəti göstərilir və yenə özümü gördüm. Uşaq dərsini etməlidir, amma anası onu dəfələrlə körpəyə baxmağa çağırır. Əlbəttə, uşağın anasına kömək etməsi pis bir şey deyil. Əksinə, kiçik şeylərdə kömək etmək normal və gözəldir. Amma burada məni narahat edən onun hər dəfə çağırılması idi. Uşağın öz məsuliyyəti, dərsi, narahatlığı sanki görünməz olur. Daha sonra uşağın dostunun dəftərini götürəndə üzündə yaranan narahatlıq… Anasına izah etməyə çalışması… Və nə qədər desə də, anasının onu dinləməməsi, anlamaması, inanmaması məni çox incitdi. Oğlan deyir ki, dostunun dəftərini ona qaytarmalıdır. Yorğun ana isə bunu onun dostları ilə gedib oynamaq üçün uydurduğu bir bəhanə kimi qəbul edir. Oğlan dəfələrlə həqiqəti deməyə çalışır, amma ona inanan yoxdur. Bu səhnələrdə uşağın nə qədər çarəsiz qaldığını hiss edirsən. Kədərlidir... Uşaqlığımda mənə inanılmadığı anlar gözümün önündən keçdi. Nə qədər düzünü desəm də, qarşımdakı insan artıq mənim haqqımda öz qərarını vermişdisə, sözlərimin heç bir əhəmiyyəti qalmırdı. Ona görə filmdəki uşağın israrla özünü izah etməyə çalışması çox tanış gəldi. Oğlanın babasının fikirləri məni narahat etdi. Onun dedikləri ilə razılaşmadım. Filmdə məni ən çox əsəbiləşdirən şeylərdən biri də bu idi: uşağın ətrafında bu qədər böyük insan var, amma demək olar ki, heç biri həqiqətən ona kömək etmir. Bəziləri kobud davranır, bəziləri laqeyd qalır, bəziləri isə uşağın dediklərini öz bildikləri kimi "anlayırlar." Qarşınızda balaca bir uşaq var. Necə bu qədər soyuq və hissiz yanaşa bilərsiniz? Böyüklər çox vaxt uşaqları eşitmirlər. Eşitsələr belə, onları düzgün anlamaq üçün kifayət qədər düşünmürlər. Bəlkə də filmin ən kədərli tərəflərindən biri budur. Sonra qapı ustası olan yaşlı kişi çıxır qarşıma. Və məncə, filmin ən gözəl hissəsi də məhz orada başlayır. O kişi balaca oğlana kömək edir. Sonra düzəltdiyi qapılardan, gördüyü işlərdən danışmağa başlayır. Danışıq tərzi, yavaşlığı, səsi… Sanki bütün film boyu eşitmədiyimiz başqa bir böyüyün səsini ilk dəfə orada eşidirik. O, uşağı tələsdirmir. Ona yuxarıdan baxmır. Sadəcə danışır. Və bəzi sözləri uşaq hələ tam dərk etməsə də, biz anlayırıq ki, yaşlı kişi əslində təkcə qapılardan danışmır. İnsanların zamanla özlərini, keçmişlərini, yaxşı olan hər şeyi unutmasından danışır. Öz köklərindən uzaqlaşmalarından. Elə bil insan böyüdükcə özündə olan bəzi yaxşı şeyləri bir-bir söküb atır və sonra nəyi itirdiyini də xatırlamır. Mən də şəhərləri heç vaxt sevməmişəm. İnsan aid olduğu yerdə qalmalıdır, deyirəm. Amma qəribədir, mən heç vaxt tam olaraq hara aid olduğumu bilməmişəm. Qoca kişinin yavaş yeriməsi, səs tonu, danışığı və o sakit qayğıkeşliyi isə mənə babamı xatırlatdı. Onunla söhbətlərimizi, birlikdə gəzməyimizi, mənə maraqlı şeylər danışmasını xatırladım. Gözlərim doldu. O qoca kişi filmdə ən sevdiyim insana çevrildi. Bəlkə də ona görə ki, bütün film boyu uşağın qarşısına çıxan böyüklər arasında onu həqiqətən görən az adamlardan biri idi. O, uşağın nə qədər balaca olduğunu yox, nə deməyə çalışdığını görürdü. Və sonda onun daşıdığı bütün kədər ilə evinə qayıtması məni çox sarsıtdı. Etdiyi işlərin, düzəltdiyi qapıların, bütün o zəhmətin bir gün yoxa çıxdığını görməyin yaratdığı xəyal qırıqlığı… Yaşlılığın amansız tərəfi… Ayaqqabılarını çıxarıb evinə girdiyi səhnədə isə artıq özümü saxlaya bilmədim. O evdə nə qədər tək olduğunu düşündüm. Həmin an təkcə qocanı yox, babamı xatırladım və hönkürtü ilə ağladım. Bu film mənim üçün dostunun evini tapmağa çalışan bir uşağın hekayəsindən daha çoxu oldu. Uşaqların nə qədər asanlıqla gözdən qaçırıldığını, böyüklərin onları necə tez susdurduğunu, bir uşağın “mən düzünü deyirəm” deməsinin belə bəzən heç kim üçün kifayət etmədiyini göstərdi. Amma bir tərəfdən də çox sadə bir şeyi xatırlatdı: bəzən bir uşağın ehtiyacı böyük bir şey deyil. Yıxılanda onu qaldıran biri, paltarındakı tozu təmizləyən balaca əllər, “ağrıyır?” deyə soruşan bir səs, ya da sadəcə ona inanan bir insan. Bəlkə də böyüdükcə ən çox itirdiyimiz şeylərdən biri elə budur: bir-birimizi həqiqətən görmək.

A true hero's journey. A story that appears to be about a boy simply returning his friend's school notebook reveals itself as heartwarming experience about doing the right thing in the face of adversity. I have seen a lot of conversations where people emphasize that this story is about childhood innocence, or that it's about being a good friend. I agree with those things, but what I don't see talked about enough is how this works as an analog for maintaining one's morals despite persecution. Yes, it is wonderful to see a young boy who is so willing to help his friend, but he is also doing so while facing relatively massive difficulties. While asking his mother if he could return his friend's notebook he accidentally took, she repeatedly ignores him. When she does finally listen to him, she doesn't believe him. Then she tasks him with taking care of his baby brother, or bringing her the wash basin as she's doing laundry. This boy isn't even able to sit and do his own homework uninterrupted, let alone get time to help his friend. It's only when he receives another chore to bring home some bread is he able to slip out, surely well aware of the punishment he will receive when he returns, to attempt to find his friend and return his notebook. We know this is just a strict parent, but this and other experiences with adults as the film goes along gives us a strong theme of staying true to your morals and operating under authoritarianism. Nearly every adult the boy interacts with is makes his journey more difficult. The mother is unreasonable, the iron door salesman is dishonest, and the grandfather is borders on sadistic in regard to his philosophy on discipline. Even with the massive consequences at stake (at least in the eyes of an 8 year old boy), he tirelessly pursues every lead he can to find his friend. He's not only good friend because he wants to return the book, he's good because of wanting to do the right thing even when he is at odds with authority and faces punishment. What the film does best is actualizing the stakes of life as a child. Even watching this as an adult, the film makes this boy's day of trouble feel like a world ending event. I've seen many who recommended this as a film for children, and while I agree, I think it would have a more profound impact on adults. A child may takeaway that you should always try to do the right thing and help your friends, but an adult watching this and learning to empathize with the "small" struggles of children would honestly make them better parents and kinder people as a whole. It's a lovely and morally sound film.

Grandfather's Friend: What I mean to say is, suppose the kid did nothing wrong. What would you do? What then? Grandfather: I'd find an excuse and give him a beating every other week. So he wouldn't forget. As my debut watch of an Abbas Kiarostami film, my expectations were extremely high for the first installment of the Koker trilogy, but boy was I blown away. Let's start to quickly say that the quote I selected to represent the film is for me not the most memorable, or may not portray the majority of what the film is based around, but it is for me the most pivotal moment of the film, giving the audience the truth as to the brutality of fear. Fear constantly lingers in the life of Ahmed's life, watching his classmate Mohamed getting berated for forgetting his notebook, leading to a threat from the class teacher of being expelled if the defiance continued. For obvious reason of the major threat being issued for a minor problem, Mohamed begins to cry, and when the teacher tells Mohamed to look back up to him, the camera cuts to Ahmed, who also listens to him out of reluctance, who's eyes look from the ground to the teacher's eyes. There should be authority in a class-room, there should be the difference between right or wrong clearly understood for all the students to learn, but to abuse the power given and cast the children you teach under an apprehensive spell feels wrong, making this film feel like a critique of Iran's education system, even though this probably isn't why everyone likes this film. Kiarostami is quick to show the mundane of Ahmed's life, the chores, the homework, and the reluctance from his mother to listen to him. He shows how Ahmed, despite his age, has some form of intelligence he carries, and persistently repeats the same dialogue in an attempt to convince his mother to travel from Koker to Poshteh through a zig-zagging path on a hill. Kiarostami shows the dehumanising neglect that affects Ahmed's life within and outside the school facility, and the other children, to work for their parents and constantly provide in need and support when asked for, which is a struggle for the teacher to instruct them to balance, with this being a constant theme that's bought up throughout. Yet, this shows the stereotypical dynamic of the mother's role in society, with her dirty, white clothing matching the washing that surrounds her, which shows at times she is without a purpose or a voice, someone to blend with the surroundings and do their job annually, without going further, making change or taking a different step, due to fear or potentially the way the patriarchal society sets up the woman's role. The inability to be capable of an identity can perhaps be interpreted as reflecting the political and social pressures of post-revolutionary Iran. Although I would not claim that Kiarostami is directly allegorising the Iranian regime, the restrictions placed upon Ahmed's freedom, both in and out the classroom made me wonder how authority can suppress individuality, creating an overwhelming culture surrounding Iran consistent of fear. This can all be interpreted from the first fifteen minutes, with long-duration, static shots used to show the mundane dullness of Ahmed's personal life, and the errands he runs, with the atmosphere of the white walls representing how the people can't escape the control enforced on them, and feels indoctrinated and forced to accept the radical changes surrounding them. The quote I highlighted was the first and only one I found on IMDB, but it resonated with me as to the meaning of this film as a critique of Iran's political state, but when I watched it, and the grand-father explaining how he was beat or given a penny weekly, regardless on his good behaviour, it shows the punishment descending beyond their own eyes. That in an inability to realise the transition that beatings without a motive is just cruel, and adds further fear on the children, shows that the grandfather may not fully accept what happened in his childhood, that the beatings he took didn't make him as a person, it would make some rebel. I guess Kiarostami may use this reflective conversation that abrupts the tight-pace the film uses when progressing through Ahmed's odyssey as a form of escapism to tell the audience metaphorically the message of the film, that the cycle of abuse does not shape how a person grows up for the better, and there needs to be a change that can enhance stability, perhaps further going against the Iranian regime with this. (This is all speculation, it's what I interpret after a first watch, but of course I could be wrong with all this.) A really cool use of cinematography and blocking is further used half-way when Ahmed reaches a child that has the same last name as Mohamed, but isn't him, and Kiarostami hides this through using him carrying a heavy box on his shoulders to cover his identity, in a genius way to add mystery and suspense. From the point-of-view shot, although the audience is certain that it won't be Mohamed, there is still speculation and possibility as to the identity of Mohamed. This further is a metaphor to the role of the teacher, that the mask they put on to try and help the children learn may not be who they really are, two different sides of the person, and that although in the beginning sequence the teacher may try to have order and rules within his classroom, the way he goes about the good intentions is wrong, so disappoints us like the reveal of the boy's identity, and makes a child cry. There are some really nice shots in this, of Ahmed running through the woods, of Ahmed walking up the hill to get to Poshteh, and the direction that Kiarostami takes you on in the journey is really genius, I love Kiarostami already from this. To be honest, the pacing did drag slightly, but now I write this review, it didn't at all, for I was confused as to the old man that takes Ahmed to a house, and what his purpose was, but it makes complete sense. The caring nature sparks a difference in Ahmed's life, who offers to help him and attempt to be kind, but by this time Ahmed is not entertained, rebelling and asking him to walk faster despite a clear lack of mobility due to age presumably, which Ahmed is oblivious to. Abkar (the old man) represents to us what Kiarostami would fantasise a perfect Iran would be portrayed as, with peace and innocence, yet the fragility is shown clearly through the wholes in his socks in his poverty-stricken house, where the red marks on his heel of his feet represent two things. One: there has to be a change in the direction of Iran for the common people, for the better good, and the direction that Iran may go down will be repetitive and a failure in some way or shape. Two: Despite the kindness that can be offered to Iran, there is no hope, and to the people when kindness is projected, they can't tell what it truly is due to the dehumanising nature of growing up in a household without rest from arduous chores. There is so much to pick out from a Kiarostami film, I love this with every word more I write of this, and I have also been reading a book on Iranian Cinema to gain more insight after adoring A Separation. A really highly-rated film for me, technically poignant, where a blend of an audience may believe it is an innocent film, or some may highlight the absurdity of all this trouble to give a notebook to complete homework, or the underlying damage that can cause kindness where everyone is blind to how the world works, that Iran expect the world to immediately be affectionate to them. Of course, I have a general understanding of Iran and a good understanding on the means of what makes a film brilliant, probably the longest review I done as it is so metaphoric and there is so much you can nit-pick on the basis of it being a film of a kid finding his friends house to return a notebook. The constant repetition of dialogue, the rooster's cries, the baby's screams, the same static extreme long-shots on Ahmed's journey to Poshteh, really makes this film feel like an experience, a feat accomplished by the wonderful Mr Kiarostami to heighten tension and suspense through constant, deliberate and annoying repetition of the basic means of sound. Damn. What a film. Is actually incredible what film can mean, and after only two A-level film lessons deep after GCSE, I feel I can write for days, as Kiarostami can seeminglessly make small stories feel with enormous, poignant weight.

Hay algo increíblemente hermoso en la sencillez de esta película. Lo que para un adulto es un drama menor, llevarse el cuaderno de un compañero por error, para el pequeño Ahmed se convierte en un caos. Lo más hermoso de la película es, sin duda, la pureza con la que está retratada la infancia. En un mundo de adultos que no escuchan, que están demasiado ocupados o atrapados en sus propias estructuras, la determinación de Ahmed brilla durante toda la película. Su determinación no nace del deber, sino de una empatía pura y un corazón gigante, el miedo genuino de que su amigo sea expulsado de la escuela por su culpa lo empuja a recorrer pueblos enteros, subir colinas y enfrentarse a lo desconocido.

Somos criados desde a infância, ao menos a maioria aqui no Brasil, a obedecer aos mais velhos sem questiona-los mesmo que eles estejam errados. E quando crescemos, nos tornamos esses mesmos adultos nas quais a gente não gostava.

Abbas Kiorastami's "Where is the Friend's house?" (1987) is a simple yet profound and meaningful film which has its own warmth and gives its viewers a tight hug. I've watched Abbas's masterpiece Close-Up and this is his second film, I've watched. There is something natural, pure and original about Iranian cinema and his films that watching them heals a part of you. The main idea of it is quite simple and plain, its of a boy Babek Ahmed Al-Pour who happens to mistakenly take Ali Reza Nematzadeh's (a friend) book. They were assigned a homework and incompletion of which could've resulted in a severe punishment. There is something unique, pure and special in the company of wise old-men who are upon the brink of their lives. I personally enjoy talking and discussing life with them for all the wisdom they carry with themselves. Similar, was seen in the film, when that old-man showed Ahmadpour, the way to his friend's house and the way back home. Theres this pure intimacy where they are so keen in just telling about themselves and what they've accomplished. I guess its to tell and resonate with us that they were once just like us. The boy Ahmadpour resembled Messi or its just me 😭 I think its extremely pivotal to listen to the children around us who want to be heard. Parents, teachers, elder siblings and others tend to neglect what the children are trying to say especially in Asian society. This further leads to child being emotionally unavailable and faces quite difficulty in expressing emotions. The ending scene with the flower in notebook has all my heart.
