"Mom, I accidentally took Mohammad Reza's book. I need to give it back." - Ahmed Ahmadpour And with something as simple as that, Ahmed, a boy from Koker, takes us on a journey to a distant neighbouring village called Postheh to return his friend's book before he gets expelled from class tomorrow morning for not completing his homework. The premise is simple, yet Abbas Kiarostami transformed it into a cinematic masterpiece. This is his most narratively conventional, but he still manages to fill each frame with the same humanism he displays throughout his oeuvre. Sometimes cinema doesn't need some gigantic tragedy to make us feel something. Sometimes all it needs is a boy trying to return his friend's notebook. And maybe that's why I have such a huge soft spot for this film. It feels strangely close to home, as I grew up in a similar mentality where children should be seen, not heard. Adults speak, and children do nothing but obey. Questions become disrespect, while disagreement becomes disobedience. And what makes the film even more interesting is how that behaviour becomes cyclical. Adults can reproduce the same dismissiveness and harsh discipline they themselves grew up with, passing it from one generation to another until nobody even remembers why children are supposed to obey in the first place. Here, Ahmed isn't fighting some grand villain. He's fighting a world of adults who simply won't fucking listen. That's what makes his tiny mission feel enormous. Again and again, we see expectations imposed on children by disciplinarians whose own behaviour can be contradictory. And through Ahmed's eyes, Kiarostami makes us understand how enormous these seemingly ordinary interactions can feel when you're young. Visually, Kiarostami once again applies his signature zig-zag road motif to symbolise his character's journey and life choices. Something as ordinary as a path across a hill can turn into an entire visual language. Ahmed doesn't simply travel from one village to another. He chooses to take that road. Not once, but twice. He could obey. He could forget about Mohammad Reza. He could decide that his friend's punishment isn't his responsibility. Instead, he keeps going. And that's what makes this tiny act so beautiful: he chooses empathy even when the adult world makes empathy inconvenient. There's so much more buried underneath that simplicity, too. Even questions of individual freedom and obligation toward others. Which eventually leaves me with a much larger question: how tf am I supposed to pursue my own freedom while preventing my neighbour from pursuing his? Suddenly, returning a notebook doesn't feel so small anymore. That's the magic of this film. Kiarostami takes an ordinary childhood problem and quietly expands it until you're thinking about society itself. What a marvellous film. I know I'll return to this one—not merely as cinema, but as a reminder of how we listen to children, how families communicate, and how something as small as taking another person's problem seriously can become an act of love. Maybe that's what I'll remember most. In a world where the adults repeatedly fail to listen to Ahmed, he never stops listening to his heart:)

Children's mind operate with the monotropism of autistic people. They cannot process anything until desired task is complete, entirely void of worry for the stress they put on their caregivers. Their empathy toward one another is like knowing it firsthand, a sort of phantom pain. That stubborn focus reminds me of when I was forbidden countless times never to play football in the house because i might break something. But how could I stop when I hadn't yet found the satisfaction of hitting a volley like that legendary Zidane volley against Leverkusen? The opportunity came when it was just me and my sister left in the house, turning the patio leading into the dining room into the ultimate pitch. I told her to cross the ball for me to catch on the volley and score through the living room. We did it about eleven or twelve times before she got fed up with doing the exact same thing without better results. On her very last attempt, I caught the ball clean, and it flew straight through the window. Yes, what I did was stupid, but i got the exact satisfaction i had been yearning for. I knew I was going to sleep with a swollen body from my grandfather's leather belt, so I dressed heavy like a medieval knight to cushion the blows. Interestingly enough, my sister never ratted me out, and I was never scolded for breaking the window, which felt very odd, because my grandfather would beat me for the pettiest things like breaking his cigarettes. Was the experiment worth it? Yell Yeah!!

El impulso animal y el verdadero arrepentimiento. Esta no la vean, muy mala. Me dejé guiar por el puntaje, pero revisé después de verla en IMDb y Rotten Tomatoes y era de 7. Como que solo es buena por el contexto cultural de Irán, entonces debe ser buenísima para los que se sienten identificados con las guerrillas de allá o algo así. Es algo parecido a Dedicado a las familias de los falsos positivos, pero allá en Irán. Se llama Un simple accidente. Es como romantizar para monetizar con la tragedia de otros y, de paso, alimentar más rencor. El negocio. Lo único que atrapaba era saber si el secuestrado sí era culpable o no. A la final sí, pero lo dejaron vivir. Hasta que lo hicieron arrepentirse a grito herido y entre el crujir de dientes, como si para los otros hubiera cierto placer en verlo sufrir. Pero ahí es donde la película puede verse desde un lado más profundo: como un juego mental que pone a prueba el pensamiento humano frente al impulso animal innato. Le dieron el descanso y asumieron ellos una carga más pesada kármica. El arrepentimiento real sería el cambio. Sin embargo, los humanos caemos fácilmente en la apariencia: creemos en los gritos y las lágrimas, cuando el verdadero arrepentimiento debería manifestarse en una transformación de la conducta. El verdadero conflicto no está solamente en determinar quién es culpable o inocente, sino en observar qué hacemos nosotros con el impulso de vengarnos cuando creemos tener la razón. Ahí es donde se pone a prueba la consciencia: si actuamos mecánicamente desde el dolor y el rencor, o si somos capaces de trascender el impulso animal y romper el ciclo.

Well, I’ve finally watched the last film among the ones shortlisted for Best International Feature at the 2025 Oscars and the winner of the Cannes Film Festival . Honestly, I don’t even have much to say about it. It barely feels like a film at all. If we take Sirât , for example, at least you can tell that the people behind it actually put real effort into making something worthwhile, that they prepared for the shoot and cared about the craft. Here, though, we get something closer to The Voice of Hind Rajab , where the movie feels like it was made on the fly simply out of a desire to condemn the system. Yes, there are some good moments, and the ending is easily the strongest part of the film. But the rest of it is almost two hours of pointless running around that becomes so painfully boring that you eventually stop caring enough to follow what’s happening. 1.5 out of 5 .

EIN EINFACHER UNFALL Kritik Review (2026): Ein einfacher Unfall möchte ein spannungsgeladenes Drama mit Thriller-Elementen sein und nutzt eine scheinbar alltägliche Situation als Ausgangspunkt für eine Geschichte über Schuld, Zufall und die Folgen menschlicher Entscheidungen. Die Grundidee besitzt durchaus Potenzial, doch die Umsetzung bleibt über weite Strecken überraschend kraftlos und entwickelt weder die emotionale Tiefe noch die Spannung, die das Konzept eigentlich verspricht. Die größte Stärke des Films ist seine Ausgangsidee. Die Vorstellung, dass ein kleiner Moment das Leben mehrerer Menschen grundlegend verändern kann, bietet interessante Möglichkeiten für ein intensives Charakterdrama. Einige ruhige Szenen zeigen kurzzeitig, welches Potenzial in der Geschichte steckt, besonders wenn der Film sich auf die persönlichen Konflikte seiner Figuren konzentriert. Auch die schauspielerischen Leistungen sind teilweise gelungen. Die Hauptdarsteller bemühen sich sichtbar, ihren Figuren emotionale Glaubwürdigkeit zu verleihen, und einzelne Momente wirken durchaus authentisch. Besonders die Darstellung von Schuldgefühlen und innerer Verunsicherung gehört zu den besseren Aspekten des Films. Visuell bleibt Ein einfacher Unfall jedoch eher unspektakulär. Die Kameraarbeit ist funktional und unterstützt die ernste Stimmung, entwickelt aber kaum eine eigene Handschrift. Auch die Atmosphäre bleibt trotz der dramatischen Thematik überraschend distanziert. Das größte Problem ist das Drehbuch. Die Geschichte besitzt zwar eine interessante Prämisse, nutzt diese aber nicht konsequent aus. Viele Konflikte werden nur oberflächlich behandelt, während wichtige emotionale Entwicklungen zu schnell abgehandelt werden. Statt die komplexen moralischen Fragen wirklich zu untersuchen, bleibt der Film häufig bei einfachen Antworten. Auch die Figurenzeichnung enttäuscht. Mehrere Charaktere wirken eher wie Werkzeuge für die Handlung als wie vollständig entwickelte Menschen mit eigenen Motivationen. Dadurch fällt es schwer, eine echte Verbindung zu ihnen aufzubauen oder ihre Entscheidungen nachzuvollziehen. Das Erzähltempo ist ebenfalls unausgewogen. Der Film nimmt sich viel Zeit für ruhige Momente, schafft es aber selten, daraus wirkliche Spannung oder emotionale Wirkung entstehen zu lassen. Besonders im Mittelteil entstehen Längen, da die Geschichte kaum neue Impulse setzt. Auch der Thriller-Aspekt bleibt hinter den Erwartungen zurück. Obwohl der Film mit Geheimnissen und Konflikten arbeitet, entsteht nur selten echte Spannung. Viele Entwicklungen sind früh absehbar, wodurch die Handlung schnell an Wirkung verliert. Das Finale versucht, die zentralen Themen zusammenzuführen und einen starken Abschluss zu bieten. Die Auflösung wirkt jedoch eher vorhersehbar und hinterlässt kaum einen nachhaltigen Eindruck. Fazit: Ein einfacher Unfall besitzt eine interessante Grundidee und einige solide schauspielerische Momente, scheitert jedoch an einem schwachen Drehbuch, flachen Figuren und fehlender emotionaler Intensität. Aus einer spannenden Ausgangslage entsteht ein überraschend unspektakulärer Film, der sein Potenzial nicht ausschöpft.

Jafar Panahi revient sur un terrain qu’il connaît bien : celui d’une société iranienne marquée par la peur, la répression et les blessures du passé. Le point de départ, pourtant prometteur, débouche sur un film qui peine à maintenir la tension annoncée. La mise en scène, volontairement dépouillée, privilégie les longues scènes de discussion et une approche presque documentaire, mais finit par donner au récit une certaine lourdeur. Le scénario part d’un dilemme moral intéressant — peut-on se faire justice soi-même lorsqu’on croit retrouver son tortionnaire ? — avant de multiplier les hésitations et les détours. Les comédiens sont peu convaincants, notamment dans les moments de confrontation, et leurs personnages restent parfois trop schématiques. La caméra, sobre et efficace, accompagne le propos sans véritable éclat visuel, tandis que le rythme irrégulier met à rude épreuve l’attention. Panahi mêle humour noir, politique et réflexion sur la vengeance, mais le message prend progressivement le pas sur l’émotion et le suspense. Ambitieux dans ses intentions, « Un Simple Accident » reste donc une expérience assez froide et démonstrative. À réserver aux spectateurs sensibles au cinéma politique et aux récits très contemplatifs. À ranger à côté de « Le Client » d’Asghar Farhadi (2016), pour son mélange de traumatisme, vengeance et dilemme moral dans l’Iran contemporain.

İçindeki öfkeyi sanatla dışa vurmuş ona yapılanın aksine filminde dahi şiddeti savunmamış. İzlerken karakterlerde gördüğüm şu his kalbimi burktu: Geçmişte çok fazla acı çekmişler, çok fazla şiddet görmüşler belki de bir raddeden sonra buna alışmışlar fakat ellerine aynısını yapma özgürlüğü geçse dahi bunu yapamıyorlar. Aldıkları intikam dahi o kadar insani bir yerden geliyor ki. Öfkeleri bile o kadar yumuşak, o kadar ikircikli. Canavarlaşamıyorlar deneseler de. İnsan kalabilmenin hikayesi. Il a souffert de la comparaison, je le trouve beaucoup moins malin que la pièce, dans laquelle on prend le parti pris d’organiser le procès du docteur Miranda, afin de savoir si oui ou non c’est bien lui. Et ça c’est prenant, alors qu’ici on se concentre sur tout un tas de personnages secondaires dont on a que faire. بنا به نقدِ استاندارد، محدودیتِ اخلاقِ جهان‌شمولِ «امر مطلقِ» کانتی (فرمانِ بی‌قید‌و‌شرط به انجام وظیفه) در عدم‌تعیّنِ صوری آن است: قانونِ اخلاقی به من نمی‌گوید وظیفه‌ام چیست، صرفاً می‌گوید باید وظیفه‌ام را انجام دهم. بدین‌ترتیب، فضا را برای اراده‌گراییِ تهی باز می‌گذارد (هرچه من تصمیم بگیرم وظیفه‌ام باشد، وظیفه‌ام همان است). اما این ویژگی، به‌هیچ‌وجه محدودیت نیست؛ بلکه ما را به هستۀ خودآیینی اخلاقی کانتی می‌رساند: نمی‌توان هنجارهای مشخصی که باید در موقعیتی خاص خود از آن‌ها پیروی کنم را از خودِ قانون اخلاقی استنتاج کرد — و این دقیقاً بدان معناست که سوژه، خود باید مسئولیتِ ترجمۀ فرمان انتزاعی قانون اخلاقی به مجموعه‌ای از تعهدات انضمامی را بر عهده بگیرد. پذیرش کامل این پارادوکس، ما را وامی‌دارد که هرگونه ارجاع به وظیفه به‌عنوان بهانه را مردود بدانیم: «هرقدر سنگین، هرقدر دشوار؛ چه می‌توان کرد؟ این وظیفه‌ام است». این برداشت که اخلاق کانتیِ مبتنی بر وظیفۀ بی‌قید‌و‌شرط چنین رویکردی را توجیه می‌کند، رایج است — بی‌جهت نیست که آدولف آیشمن، به‌منظور توجیه نقش خود در طرح‌ریزی و اجرای هولوکاست، به اخلاق کانتی ارجاع داد: او صرفاً وظیفه‌اش را انجام می‌داد و از دستورات پیشوا اطاعت می‌کرد؛ اما هدفِ کانت از تأکید بر خودآیینی و مسئولیت کامل اخلاقی سوژه، دقیقاً جلوگیری از چنین حیلتی است که در آن، تقصیر را به گردن «دیگریِ بزرگ» می‌اندازند. شعارِ استانداردِ ریاضت اخلاقی این است: «هیچ بهانه‌ای برای انجام‌ندادنِ وظیفه پذیرفتنی نیست!» اگرچه اصل مشهور کانت — Du kannst, denn du sollst!  («تو می‌توانی، چون باید!») — روایتی تازه از این شعار به‌نظر می‌رسد، اما به‌طور ضمنی، آن را با وارونگیِ به‌مراتب هراس‌آورتری تکمیل می‌کند: «هیچ بهانه‌ای برای انجام‌دادنِ وظیفه پذیرفتنی نیست!» دقیقاً همین ارجاع به وظیفه به‌عنوان بهانه‌ای برای انجام وظیفه است که باید ریاکارانه قلمداد شده و رد شود. آن ضرب‌المثلِ معلمِ سادیستی را به یاد آورید که شاگردانش را به طرز بی‌رحمانه‌ای تحت فشار قرار می‌دهد و شکنجه می‌کند؛ بهانه‌ای که برای خود (و دیگران) می‌آورد این است: «من خودم از اعمال چنین فشاری بر این بچه‌های بیچاره رنج می‌برم، اما چه می‌شود کرد — وظیفه‌ام است!» این، دقیقاً همان چیزی است که اخلاق کانتی یک‌سره منع می‌کند: در این اخلاق، من نه تنها در قبال انجام وظیفه‌ام، بلکه در قبال تعیینِ این‌که وظیفه‌ام چیست نیز کاملاً مسئولم. نتیجتاً، وقتی آنتون آلیخانوف (فرماندار منطقهٔ برون‌بومیِ کالینینگرادِ روسیه) محق بود گفت که کانت — که تمام عمرش را در منطقهٔ کالینینگراد (کونیگسبرگِ آلمان) سپری کرد — با جنگ اوکراین «ارتباط مستقیم» دارد، برحق بود. بنا بر استدلال آلیخانوف، فلسفهٔ آلمان — که «بی‌خدایی و فقدان ارزش‌های والایش» با کانت آغاز شد — «وضعیت فرهنگی-اجتماعی» را پدید آورد که، من‌باب مثال، به جنگ جهانی اول منتهی شد. از مقاله‌ی «ایران: از هیدگر تا کانتِ» ژیژک.

Man, this was an incredibly tough one for me to rate and review. First off, I gotta say that I really loved the basic premise. The beginning of the movie was very engaging and I was immediately intrigued by the central problems, but then the script became incredibly stagnant. I absolutely mean it when I say that this felt like a total snoozefest for me in the middle. While I appreciated some of the shots, the central plot hitting a full stop for the entire middle of the movie truly ruined the experience for me.  The lack of any musical composition also made it feel like an interminable high school play, and the attempts at comedy never once worked for me. You also barely get any character development, so there wasn't much for me to latch onto. I'm really not sure why this movie is so highly regarded. Some native speakers apparently complained about the lack of naturalism in the writing and that the Farsi felt off the entire time, but I'd have no way to know as a filthy monoglot American who only speaks English fluently and otherwise spends time on Duolingo. I just know that I got really bored of listening to inane arguments in the middle of this movie. Honestly, I would've rated this even lower if it weren't for the last 30 minutes that swooped in to save it. The moral dilemmas finally get interesting toward the end and delve into new territory. The audience also finally gets to chew on some real meat in the script towards the back-end. I really wish, for me, that it hadn't taken so long to get there and that the journey was either more impactful or more intriguing. I'd really have a hard time recommending this to anyone, as "Incendies" and any of Park Chan-wook's Vengeance trilogy ("Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance", "Oldboy", and "Lady Vengeance") take these ideas so much further. I feel like this could've either been a really good short film, like say 40 minutes, or it could've explored some depths it never got to. Obviously, I'm anti-regime and honestly any religious theocracy, and I'm also anti-American colonialism and imperialism (and honestly the Christians are trying to turn America into a theocracy anyway, which is ironic), and anti-Israeli genocide in Gaza, so this movie really just makes me sad for the people who are caught up in the middle of all of these systems and beliefs. The toll it's all taking on humanity just keeps rising and rising and rising.

Jafar Panahi examines different attitudes towards oppression against the background of a shifting moral landscape. A group of victims of state sponsored torture searches for the truth - or is it release, self justification, the courage they lost? One by one they find an excuse not to go any further. No one seems to acknowledge that killing an innocent man might be bad (they do occasionally discuss ethics of "becoming like their oppressors" though, which is not the same). Naturally, there is no legal, "nice" recourse in this case, other than perhaps tricking, exhausting or persuading the purported executioner into confessing, which is what eventually happens. All the while, money changes hands in form of bribes, tips and nonnegotiable gifts in currency, credit and kind, indicating that the world around the victims has found a new gravity well. The focus is mainly on the oppressed, leaving the one oppressor to play all the roles, from flat out denial to zealous defiance and sobbing contrition in rapid succession. His squeaky artificial limb provides both the spark for the narrative as well as a reminder that torturers often recruit from among the tortured. Otherwise, the narrative dynamics remains heavily lopsided. Overall a solid entry, if theatrical and somewhat unfocused, with long speeches directed at the audience and a predictably neat ending. Glimpses of the quotidian and of a shared hope for the future.

VIFF Review #22 IT WAS JUST AN ACCIDENT/ یک تصادف ساده  - Iran/France Iranian New Wave master Jafar Panahi scored a massive critical triumph when his latest satirical drama, IT WAS JUST AN ACCIDENT, took home the Palme d’Or at Cannes earlier this year. Naturally, my expectations ran high for his political dissection of regime trauma and retribution. Yet, soon after its gripping premise is established, it becomes clear that the underlying suspense is weighed down by an increasingly broad farce. The ensemble, mostly survivors of a notorious intelligence officer, plays out their conflicts and quarrels for laughs, perhaps as a means of softening the severity of the film’s premise. For me, this approach made it difficult to connect with the characters or their emotional journeys. The narrative begins to feel repetitive and even tedious, despite the occasional tender moment that manages to humanize the story. By the time the film reaches its final, undeniably powerful shot, I found myself admiring the idea more than the execution.

Interesting to see a conventional film from Panahi after No Bears as an introduction. It Was Just An Accident is fine but I really dunno about the Palme D’Or and all the hype. It’s a variation on a concept that’s been done many times before and the only real unique element is the director’s personal history and present circumstances. It’s well made but entirely banal in execution for this sort of thriller. Park Chan-Wook was a lot more Hitchcockian and formalist with No Other Choice, but that gave him the space to play with the tempo and drive the suspense according to his will. In contrast, Panahi locks himself into a simple path that marches towards a predetermined goal without anything like the Jimmy Stewart character in Rope to complicate and unravel the scheme. There are interesting moral questions posed in pursuit of revenge but none of them are new, novel, or approached in a unique way. At the end of the day, the film is about the journey to the decision not to retaliate in kind and its consequences, which has been a particularly live topic since Come And See rose to prominence in popular film discussion. It’s always worthwhile to bring questions of what constitutes justice to art and film. Again, Antigone was more or less written by Sophocles to sway the public on controversial legislation about how funerals were to be conducted and he elevated it far beyond the utterly banal stakes of his motivation. As such, It Was Just An Accident lacks the emotional texture and ambivalence towards being an Iranian in Iran that fuelled No Bears. We don’t get anything like Panahi’s terror at having accidentally crossed the border because irregardless of his struggles with the regime, home is home.

It was just an accident  starts with a long static  shot of a family (not a completely warm one) in a moving car. We get a sense that an accident is going to happen just as the movie title suggests and it happens- the car hits a dog. But the interesting thing is that it was not the accident the movie is focusing on. That accident ties the driver to another person who, as the movie unfolds slowly, comes across as a workers' rights activist who was put in jail and lost almost everything in life. The movie becomes tense as he suspects the driver is the corrupt officer who wrongly put him in jail. He kidnaps him and plans to kill him but is in a moral dilemma since he can't confidently identify him. So he searches for other inmates of jail to help him. His indecision over whether to kill him or not is the central thing that drives the movie forward. Initially we think he is a man blinded by revenge. But his human side slowly comes to the surface. Every inmate he meets and who joins him are of different views. One wants to kill him no matter what, another one knows that killing him changes nothing but still carries a rage, one is ignorant. These people can be understood as the projection of the main character's inner psychological conflicts. The use of static long shots with tight framing and boxed aspect ratio generates a sense of feeling stuck in the dilemma. The movie is grounded in realism with natural lighting, neutral colour tones and ambient sound design which is exactly why the climax's shift to dramatic lighting lands hard. There is a single isolated element of sound at the ending that creates a sense of anxiety that no amount of dialogues can't. It makes the movie a haunting experience

Continuing my unplanned dive into Palme d'Or winning mysteries with my first film produced in Iran and my first film from Jafar Panahi. 2025's It Was Just an Accident had been siting on my watchlist since it made the rounds last year as a Best Foreign Picture nominee, and I'm surprised it took me this long to finally get to it. The genres themselves are all right in my wheelhouse, but the way Panahi explores the common themes of revenge and trauma found in the crime genre is refreshing and poignant to addressing the political struggle in Iran. Panahi himself is known for being at odds with the Iranian regime and has been imprisoned multiple times due to his art, and that rebellious anger lends itself to the blending of fictional narrative and real political struggle that gives this film power. Based on the reviews and the first 30 minutes, I was expecting a blend of morbid black comedy and social commentary similar to Bong Joon-Ho, but to my surprise the narrative quickly gave way to a complex Rashomon-style reckoning with the country's past through the eyes of four different prisoners deciding what to do with the man who tortured them. Is taking pleasure in revenge a necessary step for revolution or does it slowly corrupt your own morals, taking just as much pleasure in the pain of others as the oppressor? The most impressive part of Panahi's tackling of the subject is it refuses to give easy answers. It commits to being didactic without ever feeling heavy-handed, in part due to how natural the performances by the main cast feel. Vahid Mobasseri's performance was every bit conflicting and challenging as it needed to be as the centerpiece, Mariam Afshari has possibly the most powerful arc in the whole thing, and watching Ebrahim Azizi wrestle with his demons at the end was endlessly cathartic. It has all the contained energy of a chamber film, but never loses sight of its purpose or drags in its pacing. Brilliant themes and storytelling aside, Panahi and cinematographer Amin Jafari have a knack for framing long takes that suit the flow of the film perfectly. The dialogue being so rapid fire and layered in the final 20 minutes almost distracts from how it's effectively one long take executed to perfection. It's filmmaking stripped down to its bare essentials by necessity, and executed so well that the minimalism works in the film's favor. It's been said before, but that final minute might be one of my favorite scenes of the decade so far. Chills. My interest in Iranian cinema as well as going through more Palme d'Or winners has been solidified here. Watch it if you haven't.

This is a movie full of quiet moments where you can see the internal turmoil that the characters are going through as they reckon with how their past traumas inform their present predicament, but then there are a few moments of explosive emotion that will absolutely knock you on your ass. Jafar Panahi examines how living in an authoritarian regime infects all who live under it from those complicit in it maintaining power, those punished for daring to question its rules, and everyone in between. There are moments when you're watching this movie where you can maybe see the seams from how he shot it in secret, but most of the time there's no evidence that this was different from any other film production. You can see why Iran is keen to prevent his films from being seen, but good on him for getting work like this done.

IL SUONO DI UN TRAUMA BENDATO Con Un semplice incidente (Yak taṣādof-e sāde), Jafar Panahi firma una delle opere più potenti, eticamente stratificate e spietate del cinema contemporaneo. Ciò che si apre come un banale imprevisto automobilistico notturno si trasforma rapidamente in un thriller psicologico da camera di devastante forza emotiva. Al centro del film c'è Vahid, un meccanico che crede di riconoscere nel suo cliente l'ufficiale dei servizi segreti che un tempo lo ha torturato. Ma il vero colpo di genio di Panahi sta nella costruzione del dubbio: privi della vista durante la prigionia, la memoria delle vittime si aggrappa unicamente al campo sensoriale. Una voce raschiata, un odore, il suono sordo di una gamba strisciata sul pavimento. Il sound design diventa così un personaggio a sé stante, un ponte angosciante tra il trauma passato e un presente incerto. Nel coinvolgere altri ex detenuti per confermare l'identità dell'uomo, il film solleva un dilemma morale lacerante: qual è il limite tra giustizia e vendetta quando la certezze vacillano? Panahi orchestra il tutto con una maestria rara, muovendosi al confine tra tensione claustrofobica e una sottile, grottesca ironia sulla fragilità delle convinzioni umane.

In the worst moments of my life, you were there, you supported me. I will never forget that. I don’t want to upset you with my problems. It Was Just an Accident says so much through such a deceptively simple story. One seemingly contained event gradually opens into a chasm of chaos, and I found that surprisingly reflective of life itself—how easily we can fall down our own rabbit holes, struggling with circumstances that are sometimes beyond our control and sometimes made even messier by our own choices. I really felt the characters’ pain as they grappled with morality, anger, and the question of what the “right” thing to do even looks like when you’ve been deeply hurt. The film made me think about how fragile our sense of morality can become once suffering becomes personal: justice can begin to resemble revenge, certainty can give way to doubt, and even the people who believe they are doing the right thing can lose themselves somewhere along the way. Maybe that is one of the crueler truths of being human—we want clear answers to our pain, but life rarely gives us clean villains, clean choices, or clean endings. Watching that chaos slowly unravel was one of the most compelling parts of the film for me. Underneath everything is a deeply human question about what we choose to do with the wounds we carry, and whether holding onto them protects us or simply allows the past to continue shaping who we become. Considering everything it took for this film to be made, I found it even more impressive just how much it manages to say with so little.

It was such a strong beginning to lead to, basically nothing. The film has some charm. I like the normal life story of a regular man working in a labor intensive job to try and have a happy life with his wife and kid. He goes through hardship as year after year time slips by, losing more time with the people he loves. This is all great stuff and has me very invested, until it doesn’t. The film feels like it loses direction. Some things that bothered Robert early in the film have no meaning later on. At least there was a conflict that gave the film some plot. After the big fire that leaves him in grief, he does almost nothing the rest of the film. There is a good scene or two though, especially the crying scenes that Joel Edgerton nails, but it doesn’t move his character along almost at all. It’s just deep conversation after deep conversation until we get to the final 20 minutes of the film (which is completely rushed/unearned and the worst part of the whole story). I never minded the slow pace of the film because I was expecting it to go somewhere, but it didn’t. Two big positives: The cinematography is so interesting. Whether the focus of the shot is down the middle or in the corner of the screen, it’s always intriguing. 1000% makes the film better. The acting is very moving at times. Joel Edgerton and William Macy both have emotional performances that enhance their characters greatly.

Vale la pena, di tanto in tanto, diminuire il battito, accorgersi di ciò che c’è intorno a noi e unirci a tutto. Un po’ come succede a Robert Grainier nel finale del film Train Dreams. In un periodo storico nel quale si tende a velocizzare l’arte e diminuire i tempi di fruibilità per mancanza di attenzione, bisogna saper tornare alle origini e riconciliarsi. Saper ascoltare davvero il mondo e le emozioni che ci travolgono, belle o brutte che esse siano, è in qualche modo necessario. È una parte di messaggio implicita che può essere estrapolata dalla pellicola del 2025 di Clint Bentley. Se vi aspettate concentrati di modernità, allora non è qualcosa adatto a voi, ma riesce a esprimere ugualmente concetti attuali pur essendo contestualizzati nel passato. Ci sono sensazioni e delicatezze che non contemplano i ritmi attuali e hanno bisogno di essere espresse nella loro forma autentica. Dilatare, per assaporare a pieno un’esperienza diversa, che magari non vi verrà in mente di riguardare, ma in qualche modo lascia il segno. Ciò che colpisce fortemente è la componente fotografica, un lavoro che rende molto bene l’idea del regista. Ma gli elementi che impressionano maggiormente sono i suoni, i rumori di qualunque cosa. Che sia la caduta di un albero secolare tagliato, oppure l’esplosione di un carico di dinamite, ogni dettaglio rappresenta la sottolineatura del regista all’ascolto. Come se davvero fossero queste le vere sensazioni di vita. A farcelo notare, in alcuni frangenti, è lo stesso protagonista. Quando chiede, nei momenti di intimità, alla sua compagna Claire Thompson di pronunciare il suo nome, perché è solo quando è lei a pronunciarlo che gli piace così tanto. E poi c’è il tema forte del dramma e degli anni che passano. I tormenti con cui dover convivere, la tragedia della perdita delle persone amate, come per Robert in quell’incidente fatale, sono persecuzioni dell’anima. Così come lo specchio del periodo storico e le piaghe del razzismo e delle differenze etniche che lo sfiorano. Sono tutti macigni che il personaggio principale si porta addosso più dei suoi vestiti. Tra incubi notturni e le chiacchiere di vecchi boscaioli incontrati nelle stagioni lavorative. La clessidra della vita continua a scorrere inesorabile, spesso senza rendere conto di attimi che ormai sono passati. La chiusura finale è quasi un tentativo di spronare a vivere emozioni forti, di percepire in profondità per non restare soltanto sul pelo dell’acqua. Momenti intensi che riescono a mostrarti la realtà e forse, finalmente, far capire il senso di tutto.

A beautiful movie as far as cinematography is concerned, but that is, unfortunately, about all that can be said for it. Much of the movie is unnecessarily narrated in a way that insults the intelligence of attentive viewers. The story completely falls flat, particularly the main character’s unaccountable arc of crushing guilt, which he experiences for many reasons but no good ones (e.g. for a crime that he did not commit, but rather actively tried to prevent, and maybe also for cutting down trees). His guilt is also just there as a floating plot point that ultimately doesn’t affect any of his actions. The woke racial and environmental messaging was somehow extremely heavy-handed and impossibly convoluted at the same time; I wouldn’t know what to take away from the movie even if I agreed with its creators. The characters were generally uninteresting, and the ending was somehow bad enough to be disappointing even considering how bad the rest of the story was. At the end of the day, Train Dreams is a beautiful movie in terms of visuals, but would be better as a screen-saver than a movie.

This movie was very disappointing. It had beautiful visuals and a good soundtrack, but everything else fell flat. It gave the impression of a director much less intelligent than Terrance Malik trying to mimic his style. The narrator is extremely overly didactic, almost like he’s speaking so audience members scrolling on their phones can still understand what’s happening. Though it spans decades, and the change in the times is meant to be a central theme, it really doesn’t do a great job of communicating those changes visually. There is some woke stuff in general such as a reference to mass deportations in the first three minutes and a goofy anti-logging environmental message. Most baffling is the main character’s recurring guilt dream. Early on in the movie, he witnesses a (hamfistedly portrayed) racially motivated murder of a Chinese railway worker. Throughout the movie he has dreams of that man, and seems to feel guilt about the incident. However, he did not participate in the murder, nor did he even stand idly by. He acted in the indisputably objectively correct manner and attempted to stop the murder even to the point of attempting to physically stop the men preparing to commit it. His guilt over something he witnessed but actively tried to stop is ridiculous.

manifest destiny ass movie about the big strong rugged white men who "built america." this movie in a lot of ways feels spiritually similar to american war flicks in how it shifts the agency and responsibility of the violence away from the people committing it. these arent those evil colonialsts they are just regular old guys trying to make a living for their family!! can you really blame them for the destruction they caused, i mean they didnt know any better they though there were trees to last for 1000s of years!! it plays into one of the central ideas of manifest destiny and American expansion which is that colonialsts are owed something for all the labour they put into colonizing and "civilizing" the land. i really dont know what this movie has to say about people of colour. Robert is the "perfect" american protagonist because he is somehow entirely naive to the racism of the society he grew up in. this is not to say that everyone in the 20th century was racist but that they would atleast be aware of it, right!? like robert hun you know why that chinese man was thrown of the bridge... are you trying to tell me he never worked with people who held racist opinions and was able to put two and two together?? in that scene, other than the three loggers carrying him away, all the other men remain quiet and passive, as if the violence was a sort of taboo and not just an accepted systemic practice.. also i dont fully understand why they just throw him off the bridge, its weirdly inexplicable and irrational to the point where it felt meaningless. like was it a hate crime, a punishment?! idk but whatever it is it didn't feel like it reflected the true nature of the systemic oppression towards east asian people in the rail industry. i find that so fascinating cause the way in which asian workers were treated like disposable assets made to do the dirty and dangerous work in service of something bigger mirrors how the loggers are treated!! the inclusion of the black character and him being the only point where the movie acknowledges racism felt crazy out of touch. in a similar vain to asian rail workers, black americans have the exact nuanced relationship with manifest destiny that this movie wants to explore!! i think the scene was meant to establish kinship between black people and the loggers, both peoples who gave up blood sweat and tears to build america while being erased by those who profited off their labour. but like there is a MONUMENTAL GAP between the historical context of black labour and that of the loggers. sure robert having to work a dangerous job and only being able to see his family periodically sucks for him but like that is no where near akin to slavery and cultural genocide. also the scene makes racism seem like part of the "old world" the movie is transitioning out of. hes getting revenge for something that happened in the past and all these white guys are actual super chill with black people dw!! and what would a manifest destiny movie be without an indigenous character who has an inexplicable connection with our white protagonist!! movie about grief and the toll of destroying nature and they dont use him to explore any of that.. this movie feels to inconsequential and boring to be that outraged by it. its a fairly harmless movie that makes sense for our current political context. i honestly wouldve rated it higher if there was more trains in the movie called train dreams.

Questo è quello che succede quando si cerca di imitare Terrence Malick e invece si finisce a fare un esercizio di stile, bello da vedere e freddo da morire. Train Dreams, ispirato all'omonimo romanzo, racconta la monotona vita di Robert Grainier (Joel Edgerton), un falegname che ama sua figlia e sua moglie più di qualsiasi altra cosa. Purtroppo, il lavoro lo tiene impegnato per molto tempo, rendendo pochi i momenti che può trascorrere con la sua famiglia, fino a quando un giorno non si ritroverà a fare i conti con un evento che gli cambierà la vita. Quando dico che vuole cercare di imitare un gigante del cinema come Malick, intendo che, così come lui, il regista Clint Bentley ha cercato di realizzare un'opera dove la fotografia vale da sola il biglietto e un film molto riflessivo che vive di sottrazione. In quest'ultimo elemento, però, ci troviamo davanti a un fallimento totale. Il film effettivamente cerca di trasformare una vita semplice e banale in una sorta di dramma riflessivo, cercando di dare almeno un senso di riflessione ed epicità dove apparentemente c'è il vuoto. C'è la routine. Purtroppo, il film non riesce in questo intento. Sono veramente pochi i momenti che colpiscono o riescono a suscitare un minimo di emozione o riflessione; per il resto, ci si trova davanti al piattume più totale. Le uniche note positive del film sono la fotografia, curata da Adolpho Veloso, che è splendida, e l'interpretazione di Joel Edgerton che, seppur, ripeto, non mi abbia causato nessuna emozione a livello facciale ed espressivo, non mi sento di bocciare. In conclusione, Train Dreams è un film che guarda ai giganti del passato cercando di imitarli, ma l'unica cosa che è riuscito a restituirmi è una sensazione di freddezza, perfino in un'opera che mostra l'esatto contrario.

Voto: 6.1/10 Interpretato da un solido Joel Edgerton, Train Dreams si muove tra i vasti e silenti spazi dell'America dei primi del Novecento, tentando di costruire un affresco elegiaco sulla vita di un taglialegna tra marginalità e progresso industriale. La confezione formale possiede indubbi meriti visivi, affidandosi a una fotografia di grande impatto che cattura la severità della natura selvaggia e a una recitazione misurata, capace di conferire una certa dignità materica ai momenti di solitudine del protagonista. Tuttavia, l'impianto complessivo finisce per adagiarsi su una lentezza eccessiva che spesso confonde la contemplazione con la stasi, penalizzato da una sceneggiatura frammentaria che fatica a dare coesione emotiva e drammaturgica agli snodi esistenziali raccontati, lasciando affiorare un senso di ripetitività e di progressivo distacco nello spettatore. L'opera ambisce a riflettere sul conflitto originario tra l'espansione della modernità capitalista e la dissoluzione delle comunità rurali, incarnando nel percorso del protagonista la condizione dell'individuo schiacciato dalle grandi trasformazioni storiche e tecnologiche. La figura del lavoratore isolato vorrebbe farsi archetipo della solitudine umana di fronte all'avanzare inesorabile di un'industrializzazione divoratrice, simboleggiata dall'arrivo delle ferrovie e del disboscamento intensivo. Eppure, il discorso ideologico e concettuale rimane spesso in superficie, imbrigliato in una retorica bucolica un po' scontata che guarda alla natura con un lirismo privo della forza corrosiva o della reale profondità critica necessarie a graffiare veramente lo spettatore. In conclusione, pur sorretto da una dignità artigianale innegabile e da un rigore formale apprezzabile, il film si arena in una narrazione a tratti evanescente e inconcludente, incapace di lasciare un segno duraturo e risolvendosi in un esercizio di stile nostalgico che rischia di scivolare troppo rapidamente nell'indifferenza.

cinematography is nice in a less iconographic way and moreso in a —as someone else put it— “instagram-edit-oriented-approach” with consistently saturated and contrasting nature shots of trees against sunsets, blue skies, red fires, etc. it certainly looks really good and exudes a genuinely calming energy, especially early on into the film. a nice, quiet picture of the life of a man who is caught in the midst of the rapidly changing 20th century, still grappling with loss and meaning in life. really anchors you into his life as it feels it churns to a stop while things grind on around him. i really do respect the message, but i find how the narrator takes such a large and active role in delivering it a little annoying. (1) he has a nasally, modern voice that stands out more against the earthy, serious energy of much of the rest of the movie and (2) he articulates almost every morale and meaning at pivotal scenes, never comfortable enough to let the image and acting speak for itself. telling me explicitly how grainier is feeling at all moments and narrating every wise-cliche-on-how-to-navigate-life was kind of annoying. finding out this was adapted from a book really made sense since it seems like the movie really didn’t want to let go of the mystical prose, so they layered it all over this movie. for a film that looks quite good, and is working with prose that has a unique brevity even i love, it just gets to feeling less poetical and more frictionless, mechanical, and cold. a friend who stopped by described it as a ‘documentary’, and though it may have been a look into grainier’s life on purpose, i certainly hope the movie didn’t intend to feel as as sanitized and impersonal as that. also the experience watching this was a little bit diluted so maybe if i revisit i can award the 4 ⭐️

A very moving film that explores grief, loss, the passing of time, and the complex layers of an ordinary life. One that moves through big and small, loud and quiet transformations, and the struggle to find peace in a world that moves too fast. I loved the use of the train as a symbol of progress and destruction: of moving forward while inevitably leaving so much behind. It is also a story about unfairness, loss, and sorrow, and about memories slowly fading as time moves on, but trying to hold strongly to them no matter what. I also loved how the film gives importance to an ordinary life and to the people who often go unnoticed by history. The people whose lives and work helped build the world we inherited, even as they were themselves affected by the injustices of their time. Fantastic cinematography and great performances. Joel Edgerton did a fantastic job portraying Robert Grainier; he did an impeccable job capturing grief and loss. I really love when people can act with their eyes. I wish they had released this in theaters because it was absolutely worth it. I also kind of wish this film had been talked about more during awards season.

Segunda vez assistindo a Sonhos de Trem, e fui ainda mais impactado do que na primeira. Acho que, por já entender que se trata de um filme mais contemplativo e de ritmo lento, consegui ter mais paciência e me entregar melhor à proposta da obra. Um dos maiores destaques é, sem dúvida, a fotografia assinada pelo brasileiro Adolpho Veloso. O uso predominante de luz natural para retratar as florestas e as ferrovias do início do século XX é impressionante, criando imagens de uma beleza e um realismo excepcionais. A atuação minimalista de Joel Edgerton também merece destaque. Com poucos diálogos e muita sutileza, ele entrega uma performance extremamente contida e expressiva, que considero uma das melhores de sua carreira.

Red Dead Melancholy. A quiet film about life. "The world's an old place. Probably nothing it hasn't seen by now." There is perhaps no better way to depict the ruthless passage of time than to capture the mundaneity of everyday life. Train Dreams does precisely that, presenting us with the life story of one Robert Grainier - a logger residing in America's Pacific Northwest. On the one hand, Robert's life could be dismissed as quite unremarkable, but that's where Train Dreams comes in - alluding to the fleeting joys, lingering heartaches, and bittersweet memories that make up life. It's a film that likes to emphasise how small we all are, and how trivial and fleeing life is within the grander scheme - but that that triviality is no good or bad thing... it just is. Life just is. Robert's 20th century life bears witness to phenomenal change across the decades. His profession is transformed by industrial revolution into a corporate powerhouse that fells the forests faster than they can regrow. His youth is born of inspiration from the Old West in all it's simplicity and racism, whilst his elder years see the rise of megacities and the outer space orbit of the Earth. Before it even delves any deeper, Train Dreams is brilliant at showing how the world outpaces us all. The entire film consists of the varying meetings and partings we experience through life, stressing how so few of them are within our control. We don't always get to meet people on our terms, and we don't always get the goodbyes that we would like. And whilst Robert's life is full of the unique hardships that come from living off the land, his emotional journey is far more universal. He endures insurmountable grief, he feels like an imposter as both age and the world advance on him, and he goes through all manner of different connections in life that shape his own existence in ways both big and small. Train Dreams remarks that the smallest insect is as vital as the mighty river, but also that everything within the world looks very small when you look at the vastness of it all. The sentiment goes that life has no real innate meaning or purpose, but that that can be okay if we make our peace with it somehow. Beautifully shot, Train Dreams allows the scenery to lift just as heavily as the acting and the writing do. None of it is slight, and yet it always feels like we're at arms length. Robert lives, laughs and loves as much as the next man, but he embodies that age old paradox of feeling like someone we completely relate to whilst also feeling like we really don't know him at all. Joel Edgerton does a superb job portraying Robert - a somewhat introverted man but equally personable and vulnerable, whilst convincing us that he fits in to this challenging post-West scene. An assortment of other faces you'll be trying to identify crop up throughout, each leaving an impression on Robert, but equally on us - as the anecdotal encounters Robert enjoys throughout his life are genuinely engaging. You know when you get that fleeting, bittersweet connection to someone you're going to only know for the shortest of times? This film depicts that sensation brilliantly. The random colleague you work with more than once, the passenger on the train you strike up a conversation with, the man at the local store who's only ever said five words to you and yet you feel you know him. Train Dreams revels in those sorts of encounters - the ones you remember years later. So much of this film is about memory, and the finite lifespan of it. We're shown in several ways how memories are as mortal as the people who possess them, and their fading is a cause for grief as much as the passing of any actual person. Train Dreams lingers in memories, the whole film narrated retrospectively, even. Whilst much of the film dwells in depressing spaces and haunting thoughts, it aims for a lighter conclusion that differs from the source material (which opts for a somewhat more downbeat climax) - this divergence works fine, but might well be the only weak link in a film that otherwise strives to not insult the emotional intelligence of the viewer. Make no mistake, the film is still something of an acquired taste given it moves about as fast as the ancient glaciers it references, but it's mostly a film rooted in feeling, and isn't afraid to prioritise a lingering scene defined by dialogue over a scene where things are physically happening all of the time. Train Dreams is engaging, contemplative, and evocative but never slight. It paints a simple image, through which the most elaborate emotions can be experienced, and the futility of life can be reckoned with - in all it's lack of meaning. -- 89% -- Train Dreams ranked in 2025

I’m probably the only person who didn’t cry during this movie, mostly because I was busy taking a nap. I fell asleep halfway through and honestly, my brain just checked out. I get that this is a massive hit for people who want a "good cry," but for me, it felt more like an endurance test in emotional manipulation. Maybe it’s because I actually have a healthy relationship with my family? The whole premise of treating a grandmother like a strategic asset or a bank account feels so alien and cynical that I couldn't find a way into the story. If you don't have that specific baggage of a fractured, transactional family life, the "tension" here just feels like people being unnecessarily difficult. It’s hard to stay awake for a reconciliation that shouldn't be this hard in the first place. Technically, the movie is paying a heavy "sadness tax." Every time those slow piano chords kick in, it’s like the director is tapping you on the shoulder saying, “Okay, start crying now. This is the sad part.” I value restraint and emotional honesty where the stakes feel earned. This felt like the opposite. It doesn't earn its emotions; it demands them through pacing that is slow enough to be a sedative. The acting is solid, and I can see why people like it, but it’s just not for me. I’d much rather watch experts being competent at their jobs or a story that subverts tropes instead of leaning into them this hard. If you need to clear your sinuses with a tactical tear-jerker, go for it. But if you prefer a movie that respects your intelligence without spoon-feeding you the "feels," you might end up catching some Z’s like I did. The Verdict: A well-made sedative. Great if you need a cry, even better if you need a nap.

Únicamente busca causar tristeza en el espectador para generar un falso sentimiento de empatia y conciencia en él, pero evidentemente si el espectador no se da cuenta es una falsa consciencia. Soy alguien sensible, la película me hizo llorar y me sentí manipulado por ello; por suerte una reflexión posterior acerca de que algo no se sentía bien... al menos esta película me enseñó algo que nunca olvidare: qué una película sea capaz de hacerte llorar no la hace buena. La pornografía genera los estados emocionales qué busca y eso no lo hace una buena obra cinematografíca; obvio la pornografía emocional también genera el sentimiento que busca.

Accept what cannot be changed. Discovering that there is money to made in looking after elderly folks who will write you into their will, a college dropout starts spending time with his cancer-ridden grandmother in this sentimental drama from Thailand. The idea of taking care of senior citizens with cunning ulterior motives is intriguing, but the film is more focus on the grandmother/grandson bond. The movie has a considerable fanbase and there is certainly something sweet in how gradually comes to appreciate his grandmother for more than just her money. All such character growth is telegraphed so far in advance though that it is hard to sit through over two hours of fluff just to see him reach an obvious conclusion about what matters in life. The film is also beset from one of the most cloying and maudlin music scores in recent memory. While the character growth in the film is predictable, the movie admittedly goes in some unexpected directions in its second half, but with a few too many false endings before the actual conclusion arrives, it is hard to say that the film ends on a strong note. It is also a bit irksome how the grandmother's cancer diagnosis is used as a plot device with the film uninterested in exploring how the condition impacts her; it is not even until the second half of the film that we discover what type of cancer it is. With solid performances all round, particularly from Usha Seamkhum as the dying woman who always suspects what others are not prepared to tell her, the appeal of the movie is easy to see, but Bad Genius is far better option for those wanting to check Thailand off their Letterboxd World Map.

love can be extraction. we love for reciprocation, perform care to solicit reward — monetary, social, and psychological. but to suggest that we love purely out of selfishness is to ignore the ache of grief, the jubilance of laughter, and the harmony of imperfect togetherness. perhaps we love so much that we ache to be loved back unselfishly, we don’t want to be taken care of if it is predicated on reciprocity, protection, and loyalty. in wanting this we misconstrue the care of those who love us most — those who selfishly extract love from us as we do love from them. everyone is implicated in the economy of affection. love involves exchange which may you leave you feeling indebted, expectant, or fraudulent. if love exists in the material world, burdened by material interests, can it ever transcend material incentives? if love is entangled with obligation and inheritance, can it ever be legitimate in the absence of reward? perhaps imperfectly reciprocal love is not saliently deceitful.

Como toda boa garotinha criada por vó, qualquer história sobre velhice e vovós fofas me faz chorar. Então minhas expectativas estavam muito altas pra esse filme. A premissa é interessante: um rapaz, folgado, interesseiro e mal educado, decide cuidar da sua avó doente por puro interesse, na esperança de que ela lhe deixe alguns bens quando morrer. Mais um filme sobre o arco de redenção do protagonista detestável, pensei. Plot batidíssimo, mas emocionante, pensei. O filme é triste, claro. Uma velhinha adorável enfrentando um câncer terminal e a solidão, com familiares detestáveis a seu redor. Acontece que o filme não faz mais que o mínimo ao emocionar. Ele se escora no sentimentalismo do espectador, que certamente vai lembrar de sua própria avó e sentir saudades ou, se viva for, se apegar ao pavor de perdê-la. Pra se certificar do choro da audiência, é adicionada uma trilha sonora de piano emocionante ao fundo. Além do choro, sobra muito pouco: a atuação da vovó, que sem dúvidas é o ponto alto do filme, e algumas reflexões que provavelmente você já teve na vida se você tem mais de 13 anos e já entendeu como a vida funciona. A tão prometida redenção do personagem é intempestiva, abrupta e forçada. Não convence, já que o protagonista passa 80% do filme esperando pela herança ou de birra por não tê-la recebido. No final, usa o dinheiro que a própria avó guardou ao longo dos anos, pra pagar um jazigo bonito e realizar o sonho da velhinha. Convenhamos, isso é o mínimo que um neto minimamente decente faria nessas circunstâncias. Como alguns já falaram na sessão de comentários aqui: não é porque um filme é triste que ele é bom. Esse aqui simplesmente é raso e apelativo.

I kept waiting for this to really get under my skin, but it never quite found a way in. It has plenty to say about family, guilt, and the strange urgency with which we suddenly make time for the people we love when that time is already running out. Some moments genuinely spoke to me, especially the observation that old people only seem to smell because we no longer spend enough time close to them. It’s such a small, unassuming line, yet it carries an uncomfortable truth that’s hard to shake. The story is at its strongest when it explores caregiving and inheritance. The daughters submissively shoulder the burden of looking after ageing parents, putting their own lives on hold without expecting recognition, while the sons remain the natural heirs when it comes time to divide what is left behind. It was heartbreaking seeing the grandmother, despite having lived through that same unfairness, unconsciously reinforce it herself. No one questions it because, in so many cultures, these roles are passed down just as unquestioningly as the inheritance itself. That understanding of family is what makes the final act slightly frustrating. I believed every awkward silence, every petty argument, every buried resentment, and every small act of love that somehow survived beneath it all. But I never believed the grandson’s transformation. I kept waiting for a moment that would fundamentally change the way I saw him, something that would make everything leading up to the ending fall into place. Instead, we’re simply expected to accept that he’s changed without ever really witnessing that change. By the time the credits rolled, I found myself appreciating what the story was trying to do more than what it ultimately achieved.

Une très belle découverte ! "How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies" est un film thaïlandais qui raconte l’histoire de M, un jeune homme un peu paumé qui apprend que sa grand-mère est en phase terminale d'un cancer ... Lorsqu’il voit qu’une de ses cousines a hérité après s’être occupée de son grand-père, il décide à son tour de se rapprocher de sa grand-mère avec une idée assez simple en tête : devenir son héritier. Évidemment, derrière ce point de départ archi glauque se construit progressivement quelque chose de beaucoup plus humain. Le film dégage une profonde tendresse. On s’attache forcément à cette mamie drôle, énergique, qui taille tout le monde et qui a une sacrée personnalité. Et forcément, la voir décliner petit à petit alors que la relation avec son petit-fils évolue rend l’ensemble de plus en plus touchant. J’ai beaucoup aimé la manière dont cette relation se construit, sans chercher constamment à provoquer l’émotion. Ce sont surtout les petits moments du quotidien, les habitudes, les discussions parfois anodines et le temps passé ensemble qui finissent par donner énormément de valeur à leur histoire. Et derrière cette relation, le film parle très joliment de la famille, du temps qui passe, de ce qu’on donne aux autres et de ce qu’on finit par laisser derrière nous. Il y a quelque chose d’assez universel là-dedans : parfois, on ne réalise vraiment la valeur du temps passé avec quelqu’un que lorsqu’on commence à comprendre qu’il est compté. La fin est très émouvante et vient parfaitement conclure l'oeuvre : Très sympa !

Cómo hacerse millonario antes de que muera la abuela es una película que, bajo una premisa aparentemente sencilla, consigue hablar de algo mucho más universal: la familia, el tiempo y todo aquello que damos por hecho hasta que podemos perderlo.Lo que más me gusta es que no necesita grandes giros para emocionar. La relación entre M y su abuela se va construyendo con pequeños momentos, silencios y situaciones cotidianas que terminan teniendo muchísimo peso. El final, cuando M entiende que el verdadero valor nunca estuvo en la herencia, sino en el tiempo que pasó con ella, funciona precisamente porque la película llevaba todo el rato preparando ese momento.Puede ser algo manipuladora emocionalmente en ciertos puntos, pero me parece difícil reprochárselo cuando consigue que sus personajes se sientan tan cercanos.Una película sencilla, muy humana y de esas que te dejan pensando en tu propia familia.

This movie has inspired me to rewatch up, it reminds me of it. ‘When am I going to be first’ This movie was beautifulll. CINEMA Death doesn’t give you time. You don’t get time to right all your wrongs, to ask all the questions you want, to find out the intentions behind every good or bad deed, even to say your goodbyes. Death makes you think about all these things, and the list of things to do before you can’t anymore just grows and grows. It’s incredibly cruel, but the pressure of prioritising certain things makes you realise who you are and gives you deeper insight into others. Idk if the movie was tryna say that, but It made me see the beauty in what’s meant to be a somber time. M’s development during the movie was heartwarming, but the most impactful part of the movie for me were the grandmas tears after M shouted the quote I used in the beginning. The need to be first, or to own, or succeed doesn’t mean anything when you’re nearing your end, when you’ve been forced to actually chose what’s important, yet we chase it our whole lives. You’ll never be satisfied. Grandma realised this, realised she had done the same, and could do nothing but cry. She came to realise what was important, and realised it was tearing the people around her apart. The anti capitalism vibes are strong here. "Perspectivas acerca do envelhecimento" total. Amo como as nuances são construídas nesse filme, como a dor tá lá mas é sutil, muitas vezes mostrada pelo ressentimento que a avó sente em relação aos outros familiares, pela solidão. Isso também acontece com o amor, ele existe por cada um dos filhos e dos netos, mas parece que com o tempo, ele vai sendo sucateado pela falta de manutenção, o que falta é carinho e intimidade, mas o amor existe, na romã que ela planta e cuida pro neto desde que ele era criança, na conta do banco que ela fez pra ele e alimenta até o dia da morte, mesmo que ele não tenha nem noção disso (😭). Acho que a relacao de todo mundo ali é muito centrada no dinheiro e no que a avó vai deixar quando morrer, mas achei interessante essas pequenas coisas que ela fazia ainda em vida e ninguém percebia. Isso sem contar o cuidado pelo filho mais novo. Gosto muito como o M se aproxima por dinheiro e vai recusando isso ao longo de todo filme, primeiro porque ele almejava mais (quando o filho mais velho oferece uma retribuição pelo tempo q o Neto cuidou da avó), mas depois porque ele realmente cria um carinho pela avó e ele vai vendo todo mundo pelos olhos dela (quando o filho mais novo oferece o que sobrou do dinheiro da venda da casa como agradecimento, mas ele recusa pq sabe que o filho vai precisar daquele dinheiro porque nao pode contar com mais ninguém). Até a parte que ele se irrita quando descobre que ela "não deixou nada pra ele", parece que ele se irrita muito mais por nao ser o favorito (as outras coisas são consequência) do que não ter herdado nada. Enfim, filme muito lindo.

Gostei pra caralho desse aqui. Acho interessante como o Volume 2 é um pouco diferente do Volume 1, mas ainda consegue manter a mesma essência. Enquanto o primeiro é mais focado nas lutas e na violência, esse aqui já dá mais espaço para o desenvolvimento dos personagens, principalmente da Noiva e do Bill. Gostei de como exploraram melhor o passado dos personagens, explicando um pouco mais de como era a relação da Noiva com o Bill e também mostrando um pouco do treinamento que a Noiva teve com o Pai Mei. A parte final do filme me surpreendeu bastante. Acho que é porque eu tava com uma expectativa muito alta de que ia ser uma luta bem longa entre os dois, mas, por mais surpresa que eu tenha ficado, achei interessante eles terem focado em algo mais pessoal. Com os dois conversando e relembrando o passado antes de ela aplicar a técnica dos cinco pontos pra matar ele. Mesmo sendo uma cena simples e rápida, foi marcante. E o final dela com a filhinha dela é bonitinho. Enfim, eu amei os dois filmes. O primeiro me ganhou pelas cenas de luta e pela estética, e o segundo, pela história e pelo desenvolvimento dos personagens.

It really stands in the way of this film being enjoyable at all. While the themes extend insightful ideation on identity, hetero-patriarchy, sex-desire capitalism, stalking, and para-sociality the dramatic overtone of SA and their brutal drawn out depiction makes it hard to consider these themes. La verdad, malísima, no me gustó para nada. Siento que perdí mi tiempo; no entiendo cómo tiene 4.2 estrellas, no puedo verlo ni entenderlo. Es una película que trata sobre Vietnam... y mirá que podés hacer un peliculón, pero hicieron una película malísima. Primero, porque siento que fue una parodia total hacia la guerra: se da a entender que los estadounidenses no son buenos para sus guerras propias, solamente para su propio negocio, jajaja. Además, muestran como que la guerra era una película, grababan cómo se morían. Es tan absurdo que me creo que hayan hecho eso, en la vida real. Y entiendo que es asi la pelicula trata sobre la parodia pero igual. Después sentí que es mala cinematográficamente, ya que nunca sentí pena, ni ningún otro tipo de sentimiento hacia la misma. Desde el principio dije 'qué carajo estoy viendo', diciendo chingadeces, y luego es como que se separa en dos la película y no tiene nada que ver una parte con otra. Totalmente malísima.
